title: Methodology and Research Disclosure
description: How this book was researched, what has been verified, what has not, and how readers can read the status of a chapter.
text: Methodology and Research Disclosure This page states how the book was made. It is written so that a reader can tell the difference between what has been checked, what has been asserted, and what remains open. What the book is The book is a narrative history built around primary sources. Each chapter prints documents from movements, states, witnesses and critics, and sets them beside the scholarly arguments about what they mean. It does not offer a single verdict on socialism or capitalism. Its governing standard requires that the same evidentiary rules be applied to socialist governments, capitalist governments, movements, opponents and witnesses alike. The book is not neutral in the sense of avoiding judgements. Where evidence establishes responsibility, it says so. Where evidence is thin, it says that too. Objectivity here means accurate evidence, consistent standards, transparent reasoning and conclusions proportionate to what the sources support. How it was researched The manuscript was assembled with substantial AI assistance. Research agents located sources, extracted claims, checked URLs, compared translations and drafted text. Human editorial responsibility rests with the project author. There is no named team of historians, no university affiliation and no external academic peer review. Readers should not assume that a chapter has been read by a qualified specialist in its field. A 20 reviewer internal pass and a separate audit process produced reports on every chapter. The audit extracted 7,189 material claims from 99 documents, of which 3,220 were classed as high stakes. It produced 343 verification reports and 58 adversarial falsification reports. These are internal, AI assisted checks. They are useful for finding inconsistencies, broken sources and unsupported claims. They do not establish historical authority. What has actually been verified URLs were checked by opening them and judging the content, not by trusting HTTP status. The URL audit covered 1,223 links; 1,110 were judged sound. Claims were checked against the cited pages where those pages could be opened. A match shows that a cited page contains the names, dates or numbers in a claim. It does not show that the claim is true, that the source is reliable, or that the interpretation is sound. 26 corrections were logged. Only six log entries cite an independent re verification report, and one of those was marked for rework. The remainder rest on coordinator sign off. 326 findings from the audit are recorded as still present in the manuscript. A subset of 17 high confidence falsified, refuted or misattributed claims has now been corrected; the others await adjudication. A bibliography reconciliation found more than 1,300 chapter URLs that do not appear in the consolidated bibliography. This is a reconciliation task, not proof that those sources are unreliable. No external academic reviewer has checked any chapter. No correction in the project is described as independently verified by a qualified historian. Editorial history An early compiling document in the project's research files was written explicitly from within the Marxist Leninist tradition and excluded anti communist and intelligence material. That source rule was retired on 22 November 2026 and replaced by the current standard, which requires engagement with academic historiography and forbids suppressing credible evidence because it complicates a political interpretation. Changing a policy does not rewrite the manuscript written under it. Twenty five chapters carry a last updated date of 22 November 2026 and should be read as the most likely to retain assumptions from the earlier approach. The other chapters were produced by the broadening programme after the decision. A systematic re audit of the earlier chapters for inherited assumptions remains outstanding. Levels of certainty The book distinguishes the following levels of confidence. These describe evidence, not political agreement. | Classifica

title: Editorial & Source Policy
description: How the book uses primary sources, journalism and historical scholarship, and how it handles attribution and uncertainty.
text: This book explains socialism and communism through documentary evidence. It draws on the writings of political thinkers, the records of parties and states, the testimony of people who lived through events, contemporary reporting, and the work of historians who have studied the evidence. Primary sources Primary sources are central. They include political writings, manifestos, speeches, letters, party congress records, government documents, constitutions, court proceedings, newspapers and periodicals, memoirs, oral histories and photographs. Each is read as evidence, not as an automatically reliable account. An official record may conceal a failure. A newspaper may reflect the interests of its owner. A memoir written decades later may reshape the past. The book asks who produced a source, when, for whom and for what purpose before using it. Range of evidence The book is not limited to sources produced by movements or governments. Contemporary journalism, police and court records, intelligence material and academic research may all help establish what happened. Where such sources are used, their origins and limits are stated. Historians are engaged where their work helps explain the evidence, and disagreements between them are described with the methods and evidence behind each position. Attribution and uncertainty Claims are attributed to the source that makes them. A government's description of its own policy is presented as what the government said, not as proof that the policy worked. A party's account of a dispute is presented as that party's account. Where evidence is contested, the book states what is known, what is uncertain and what historians disagree about. It does not suppress credible evidence because it complicates a political interpretation, and it does not manufacture balance between well supported findings and unsupported claims. Ordinary people Where evidence permits, the book includes the experiences of workers, peasants, soldiers, women, prisoners, families and critics. Testimony is introduced with the witness's identity, their relationship to the event, when the account was recorded and what it can establish. The book does not invent dialogue, private thoughts, sensory detail or scenes. Quotations and citations The policy requires that quotations reproduce their sources accurately, that omissions are marked, translations identified, and invented quotations, page numbers and archive references excluded. It requires each significant claim to be linked to a supporting source and each chapter to end with a bibliography. These are requirements, not a certification that every chapter currently meets them; known gaps are described in the methodology page. ← Contents · Next: Primary Text Bibliography

title: The Theoretical Backbone
description: Definitions, historical materialism, the dictatorship of the proletariat, socialist political economy, currents, glossary and reading list.
text: These ideas were written by particular people in particular circumstances, and they changed as those circumstances changed. A mode of production is the historically specific way a society organizes the making and distributing of goods, including both the tools and skills available and the social relations through which people work. Socialism and communism, in the tradition discussed here, are names for stages in a historical process rather than fixed moral ideals. In the later Marxist Leninist usage, socialism names the lower phase, with public ownership and distribution according to work, while communism names the higher phase, with abundance and distribution according to needs. That process was argued, not observed in advance. The texts record what writers claimed, how parties and governments restated those claims, and where scholars have disagreed about them. Four things need to be kept apart. The first is the theory: arguments about history, value and class made by Marx, Engels and their successors. The second is intention: what revolutionaries said they wanted to build. The third is the programmatic language of states that called themselves socialist, set out in constitutions, party rules and textbooks. The fourth is what actually happened in those states, including the lives of the people who lived under them. A constitution can declare that an economy works in a certain way without establishing that it does. The discussion that follows is mainly about the first three. Evidence about the fourth comes from historical research and is treated elsewhere in this book. Where a document is a program or an official self description, it is identified as such. What did "socialism" and "communism" mean? In the Communist Manifesto "communism" names a movement and a standpoint, not a blueprint. Marx and Engels wrote that communist conclusions "are in no way based on ideas or principles that have been invented, or discovered, by this or that would be universal reformer. They merely express, in general terms, actual relations springing from an existing class struggle" (Marx and Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party , chapter II). Engels later identified the "basic thought running through the Manifesto": that the economic production and social structure of each epoch form the foundation of its political and intellectual history, and that the proletariat "cannot attain its emancipation from the sway of the exploiting and ruling class, the bourgeoisie, without, at the same time, and once and for all, emancipating society at large from all exploitation, oppression, class distinction, and class struggles" (Engels, preface to the 1883 German edition of the Manifesto ). The more precise usage that became standard in Marxism Leninism treats socialism and communism as the lower and higher phases of a single communist mode of production. The Soviet Academy of Sciences' Political Economy textbook stated it directly: "Communist society passes through two phases of development: the lower phase known as Socialism, and the higher phase known as Communism. In the first stage, communist society cannot as yet be free from the traditions and traces of capitalism, from whose womb it has emerged" ( Political Economy , chapter 40). This was the voice of an official textbook written decades after Marx, not his own wording. Marx's 1875 Critique of the Gotha Programme is the source on which that later terminology drew. He described the first phase as "a communist society, not as it has developed on its own foundations, but, on the contrary, just as it emerges from capitalist society; which is thus in every respect, economically, morally, and intellectually, still stamped with the birthmarks of the old society from whose womb it emerges" (Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme , Part I). title: Robert Owen: The Factory, the Village and the Labour Exchange
description: On New Year's Day in 1816 Robert Owen stood before the people of New Lanark and opened a school.
text: On New Year's Day in 1816 Robert Owen stood before the people of New Lanark and opened a school. The mill village in the Clyde valley was his to manage, and the address he gave that morning was printed and preserved, with a manuscript copy later entering the royal collection. "We have met to day for the purpose of opening this Institution; and it is my intention to explain to you the objects for which it has been founded," he said (Robert Owen, address at New Lanark, 1 January 1816, as reprinted in the 1927 Everyman edition). The Institution for the Formation of Character, as he called it, would take children almost as soon as they could walk. He fixed ten as the age for entering the mill, "before which age, none of them will be permitted to enter the works" (same address). No reply from the audience survives. What remains is the employer's voice, setting out a claim about how people become who they are. A doctrine put to the test Three years earlier Owen had published the first of his essays under a title that promised a new way of seeing society. "Any general character, from the best to the worst, from the most ignorant to the most enlightened, may be given to any community, even to the world at large, by the application of proper means," he wrote (Robert Owen, A New View of Society , First Essay, written 1812, published 1813). The sentence is a claim about cause: character is made by surroundings, and surroundings can be remade. Owen dedicated the essay to William Wilberforce and addressed later essays to the superintendents of manufactories; workers were not his first readers. He said the doctrine had been tried for twenty years, including among two or three thousand people at New Lanark, and gave figures for his returns. Those figures were his own, and the essays state a programme rather than what workers experienced. The surroundings he wanted to change were those of the factory. In a tract of 1817 dedicated to the British Legislature he described what he said he had seen: "In the manufacturing districts it is common for parents to send their children of both sexes at seven or eight years of age, in winter as well as summer, at six o'clock in the morning, sometimes of course in the dark" (Robert Owen, Observations on the Effect of the Manufacturing System , 1817). He asked for a twelve hour day, no work under ten, six hour days for children under twelve, and basic literacy. A twelve hour day was a reform then, not a rejection of factory work. Why were children still starting at nine? Reading the amended bill in committee in 1818, Owen wrote to the Prime Minister, the Earl of Liverpool: "It permits children to be employed at nine years of age for twelve hours and a half per day" (Robert Owen, letter to the Earl of Liverpool, 1818, as reprinted in 1927). He named the cotton spinners, several of them members of Parliament, who resisted the bill. Nearly forty years later, writing his autobiography in his eighty sixth year, he recalled a Poor Law Committee that debated for two days behind closed doors before deciding not to hear him: "this committee debated for two whole days, with closed doors, whether or not I should be examined by them" (Robert Owen, The Life of Robert Owen , 1857, recalling 1817). The 1819 Factory Act fell short of what he wanted, and his memory of the committee cannot be checked against its minutes. The school and the county Owen's eldest son ran the New Lanark schools and described them in 1824. Robert Dale Owen counted about 600 pupils, classes of twenty to forty and infant classes of two to five. He described dancing and singing masters, no artificial rewards or punishments, and the silent monitor, a coloured block that recorded conduct without a rebuke. "The children are governed, not by severity, but by kindness; and excited, not by distinctions, but by creating in them a wish to learn what they are to be taught," he wrote (Robert Dale Owen, An Outline of the System of Education at New Lanark , 1824

title: Fourier, the Passions and the Phalanstery Experiments
description: In 1822 Charles Fourier set down the size of the community he wanted built.
text: In 1822 Charles Fourier set down the size of the community he wanted built. "An association of 1500 or 1600 people requires a site comprising at least one square league of land," he wrote in Théorie de l'unité universelle (Charles Fourier, "The Establishment of a Trial Phalanx," first published 1822, translated by Jonathan Beecher and Richard Bienvenu (1972)). He wanted water, hills, a forest, proximity to a city but enough distance to exclude intruders, and seven eighths of the members to be cultivators and manufacturers. Capital would take the form of transferable shares, with profits divided among capital, labour and talent. The first phalanx should stand in a warm climate. A phalanx was his name for the association, a phalanstery for its building. The numbers fixed the scale that every later attempt had to meet or explain away. Making work lovable Fourier was a commercial clerk in Besançon who published his first book in 1808 and spent his life elaborating a system of social organisation. Work, he argued, had not always been repulsive; it had been made so. "Morality teaches us to love work: let it know, then, how to render work lovable," he wrote (Charles Fourier, "Attractive Labour," translated by Julia Franklin (1901)). A rightly arranged association would pay partners by dividends, divide payment among capital, labour and talent, vary sessions about eight times a day, set friends to work with rivalries in clean workshops, divide labour minutely, allow free choice of occupation and guarantee a minimum. This is a design problem, not a description of anything achieved. The design rested on a theory of the passions, Fourier's word for the faculties people are born with, including those moralists call vices. Fourier wrote: "My theory confines itself to utilizing the passions now condemned, just as Nature has given them to us and without in any way changing them." (Charles Fourier, "Of the Role of the Passions," translated by Julia Franklin (1901)). The theological premise belongs to the argument: the passions are given by God and should be used, not repressed. In a group of about 1,600, contrasting series would form around different tasks and people would move between them. Series and groups were his terms for those teams. The number was a constant in the system, not a size tested by experiment. His criticism of commerce was sharper than his predictions. Engels, who read Fourier's unpublished manuscripts in La Phalange in 1845, selected a passage on trade and mocked "the conversion of the sea into lemonade, the couronnes boréale and australe, the anti lion, and the conjunction of the planets" (Frederick Engels, introducing Fourier's On Trade , 1845). That list is Engels's summary of Fourier's forecasts, not a word for word quotation. Engels thought the criticism of society better than the German philosophy he opposed, and omitted Fourier's positive system. The praise and the mockery belong to a young communist defining his own position. An experiment that never was Condé sur Vesgre fell far short of Fourier's scale. His own explanation protected the theory. "If social experiments have miscarried, it is because some fatality has impelled all speculators to work with bodies of poor people whom they subjected to a monastic industrial discipline," he wrote in a posthumous manuscript (Charles Fourier, "The Phalanstery," from the Manuscrits de Fourier (1851), translated by Julia Franklin (1901)). A trial phalanx, he said, had to contain a graduated range of fortunes. Louis Reybaud, a journalist writing for an elite review, told the sequence differently in 1837. Baudet Dulary and the Devay brothers pooled their estates, clearing began, funds ran short and the work stopped. Reybaud was not there and wrote to invite ridicule, but preserved the order of events. His verdict was "Il y avait eu avortement, mais il n'y avait pas eu essai." In English, there had been a miscarriage but no experiment (Louis Reybaud, "Socialistes modernes. II

title: The Conspiracy of Equals: Babeuf and the French Left of the 1790s
description: On 25 June 1793 Jacques Roux stood before the National Convention in Paris and asked what the revolution's declaration of rights was worth to a person without bread.
text: On 25 June 1793 Jacques Roux stood before the National Convention in Paris and asked what the revolution's declaration of rights was worth to a person without bread. A constitutional priest and an officer of the Paris municipality, he spoke for two sections and the Cordeliers Club and said: "Freedom is nothing but a vain phantom when one class of men can starve another with impunity." (Jacques Roux, address to the National Convention, 25 June 1793, translated by Mitchell Abidor). He demanded the death penalty for hoarders and monopolists, the requisition of necessities and a constitutional ban on speculation, and he cited women's low wages as evidence. He asked: "And can the property of knaves be more sacred than the life of a man?" (same address, 25 June 1793). Roux spoke in his own name. "Enragés" is a label attached afterwards to a current of angry speakers, not a party he led. His question survived him: legal equality could leave the means of life in the hands of a few. The common happiness In the Arsenal section a society's rules of July 1793 admitted women and men on equal terms, met four times a week, rotated officers and charged ten sous a month so the poor were not excluded. That is one section's rules, not every club in the city. It shows the world of meeting rooms and subscriptions in which the 1790s left worked. A police observer examining Roux after Marat's assassination treated his look at Marat during a quarrel as evidence of revenge, noting two witnesses' surprise. Roux denied the threat and was released once Charlotte Corday was arrested. The report shows how readily a facial expression became evidence of intent. Babeuf had reached a position of his own earlier. In a private letter of 8 July 1787 the young researcher of feudal land titles in Picardy, not yet calling himself Gracchus, found an equal division of goods better than equal rights of inheritance. He was reading Rousseau rather than repeating Jacobin slogans. In 1794, commissioned by the Convention to attack Jean Baptiste Carrier, he itemised depositions about the drownings at Nantes and called for Carrier's execution, insisting that such crimes must never go unpunished. His approval of the acquittal of Carrier's co defendants sits awkwardly beside his later defence of insurrection. Released after the rising of 13 Vendémiaire in October 1795, Babeuf announced a paper. Its prospectus gave the maxim: "The goal of society is the common happiness." (Gracchus Babeuf, prospectus for Le Tribun du Peuple , 1795, translated by Mitchell Abidor). He promised irregular issues and argued that a people's paper must tell the people everything, not keep secrets from them. A prospectus is a promise to subscribers, not evidence of what the paper achieved. The Republic of Equals By April 1796 the programme was on Paris walls. The Analysis of the Doctrine of Babeuf , a placard sanctioned by the movement's leaders though not written by Babeuf, set out equal natural right, work as an obligation, labour and pleasures in common, and the constitution of 1793. Its declaration was blunt: "In a real society there should be neither rich nor poor." ( Analysis of the Doctrine of Babeuf (placard), April 1796, translated by Mitchell Abidor). Another article added: "The rich who don't renounce their excess in favor of the indigent are the enemies of the people." (same placard, Article 8, 1796). Babeuf denied authorship in court but accepted the doctrine. The prosecution made the placard central to its charge of planned pillage. Sylvain Maréchal, a poet and militant atheist in the secret leadership, wrote the Manifesto of the Equals that year. It moved past the declarations of 1791 and 1795 and past the agrarian law, meaning a redistribution of land. Its demand was explicit: "We lean towards something more sublime and more just: the common good or the community of property! No more individual property in land: the land belongs to no one." title: The People's Charter: Chartism and Working-Class Politics in Britain, 1838–1848
description: On 14 June 1839 a large roll of paper was carried into the House of Commons.
text: On 14 June 1839 a large roll of paper was carried into the House of Commons. Thomas Attwood, the MP for Birmingham, had helped draft the petition and now presented it; members laughed at the roll. A sympathetic ally rather than a man of the movement, he spent his speech on the defensive: "I never, in the whole course of my life, recommended any means, or inculcated any doctrine except peace, law, order, loyalty, and union" (Thomas Attwood MP, House of Commons, 14 June 1839). He said it carried 1,280,000 signatures from 214 towns and villages and some 500 public meetings. The Speaker then ruled that a member presenting a petition could not speak at length. That roll was the most visible part of Chartism, the first mass working class political movement in Britain. The petition pointed to a document published a year earlier. The People's Charter of May 1838 was not a rallying cry but a complete draft of an Act of Parliament, thirty six pages long, with thirteen sections, rules for registration, a mechanism for secret voting, annual parliaments and £500 a year for members. Its authors were the London Working Men's Association committee, with William Lovett and Francis Place taking the leading hand. The six points were a programme that could be printed as a bill and read clause by clause: a vote for every man, a secret ballot, no property qualification for MPs, equal electoral districts, annual parliaments and payment of members. "Universal suffrage" then meant every adult man; women were outside it. A draft Act of Parliament The Charter's preface explained the authors' distrust of earlier reformers: "We have seen one zealous Reformer after another desert us as his party was triumphant, or his interests served." (London Working Men's Association, address prefixed to The People's Charter , 8 May 1838, third edition September 1838) That calculation also decided who was left out. They did not claim women were unfit to vote; they feared that including women's suffrage would rouse prejudice and "retard the measure" for men. On this point a movement built on the claim that working people performed the duties of citizens gave way to the calculations of a parliamentary campaign. The Female Political Union of Newcastle rejected the doctrine that politics belonged to men: "We have been told that the province of women is her home, and that the field of politics should be left to men; this we deny." (Female Political Union of Newcastle, Northern Star , 2 February 1839) They linked overwork and under education to political exclusion and built organisations with rules and funds. The Charter's exclusion of women therefore did not mark their absence from the movement. It marked a limit in what its male authors would ask Parliament for. Freemen and missionaries The first national petition put the claim in the movement's own language: distress followed from political exclusion, "the few have governed for the interest of the few." Its most quoted line claimed citizenship rather than charity: "We perform the duties of freemen; we must have the privileges of freemen." (National Petition, 1839, reprinted in William Lovett, Life and Struggles , 1876) The text closed with a formal prayer to the Commons. It omitted equal electoral districts, a point Lovett and others disputed with Attwood. The first Chartist Convention met in London on 4 February 1839 to decide what should happen if Parliament refused. Its fifty three delegates, by Lovett's count, included John Frost and Feargus O'Connor. They argued over moral force and physical force, meaning persuasion and lawful pressure on one side, the threat of armed resistance on the other. Missionaries went out with strict instructions "to refrain from all violent and unconstitutional language, and not to infringe the law in any manner by word or deed" (instructions to Convention missionaries, 1839, recorded by William Lovett in 1876). title: The Workmen's Republic: France, 1848
description: On 26 June 1848, the day after the heaviest fighting in Paris, the photographer Charles François Thibault made an image of the barricades in the rue Saint-Maur.
text: On 26 June 1848, the day after the heaviest fighting in Paris, the photographer Charles François Thibault made an image of the barricades in the rue Saint Maur. Early photographic exposures could not capture movement, so the picture shows the street in daylight after the attack: a substantial barrier thrown up in a working class district. It cannot show who built it or what happened there. It fixes a fact the written accounts can blur: for four days the eastern districts had fought the army and the National Guard, and the barricades were physical structures in ordinary streets (Thibault, barricades of the rue Saint Maur, 26 June 1848; countertype at Musée Carnavalet, original at Musée d'Orsay). Four months earlier the city had brought down a king and proclaimed a republic. What connected February to June was a demand that fitted into three words: the right to work, meaning the claim that a government must provide employment for those who could not find it. In February workers forced the new government to recognise it. In June they fought over its collapse. The sequence is well recorded because its witnesses disagreed sharply. A conservative deputy, a British diplomat and a revolutionary journalist all described the June fighting as a conflict between classes, then drew opposite conclusions. February Barricades went up in Paris on 22 and 23 February, the king abdicated, and a provisional government was declared at the Hôtel de Ville. Marx, writing two years later, records how workers imposed themselves on it. The worker Raspail gave the Hôtel de Ville a two hour ultimatum over the proclamation of the republic, and a worker named Marche pressed the claim for work. On 25 February the government decreed the right to work and promised social institutions; on 28 February it created a Commission for Workers with Louis Blanc as president and Albert, a worker, as vice president. The commission was housed in the Luxembourg Palace, from which it took its name. The Luxembourg and the workshops The Luxembourg Commission began taking evidence on 1 March. Its own published proceedings record 150 to 200 worker delegates sitting in the chamber once occupied by the peers of France. The two demands they pressed hardest were set down in the minutes: "Réduction du nombre des heures de travail ; Abolition du marchandage" (Luxembourg Commission proceedings, 2 March 1848), a reduction in working hours and an end to marchandage , the practice of letting middlemen subcontract pieces of work to poorly paid artisans. Employers and workers were heard separately, and the commission secured a one hour reduction in the working day. The record is a managed self presentation, giving workers' demands as the chair recorded them. Marx judged that the commission had no budget and no executive authority; its authority was real only where the government conceded it. The right to work took a different institutional form in the national workshops, administered from the rival Hôtel de Ville rather than the Luxembourg. Enrolment grew quickly, and the work offered was relief work, chiefly earthworks, at low pay. Marx called them "English workhouses in the open — that is what these national ateliers were." (Karl Marx, The Class Struggles in France , Part I, written 1850). Émile Thomas, appointed to direct the workshops, defended them in a 1848 book reprinting the decrees and official papers. He describes his removal from Paris by ministerial order in May, which Lord Normanby, the British minister, independently recorded. Thomas was answering criticism and hostile to Blanc; Normanby's government had not formally recognised the republic. Their agreement is the more useful for being unwilling. June On 22 June workshop workers marched, chanting that they would not be sent away, and Tocqueville records delegates warning the Executive Commission that they would take up arms if the workshops were closed. title: Property Is Theft: Proudhon, Mutualism and the Cooperative Moment
description: In May 1846 Karl Marx, then in Brussels, wrote to a printer in Paris asking him to handle France in a regular correspondence between German, French and English socialists: 'So far as...
text: In May 1846 Karl Marx, then in Brussels, wrote to a printer in Paris asking him to handle France in a regular correspondence between German, French and English socialists: "So far as France is concerned, we all of us believe that we could find no better correspondent than yourself." (Karl Marx to Pierre Joseph Proudhon, 5 May 1846, MECW translation) Within eighteen months that correspondent had published a book length public verdict against him. When the printer died in 1865, Marx wrote of him with respect. The quarrel can be followed in the letters and books themselves rather than in the labels later attached to it. The printer was Pierre Joseph Proudhon, born in 1809, the son of a cooper in Besançon and largely self taught. His book What is Property? An Inquiry into the Principle of Right and of Government appeared in 1840, when he was thirty one. He argued that neither labour nor occupation nor law could create property, and rejected majority sovereignty and the government of man by man. Mutualism, meaning a scheme in which workers organised their own credit and exchange, grew from that anti political premise. He was also the first to call himself an anarchist, meaning an opponent of government rather than of order. A printer's challenge The book's famous passage was a deliberate provocation. "Why, then, to this other question: What is property! may I not likewise answer, It is robbery, without the certainty of being misunderstood; the second proposition being no other than a transformation of the first?" (Pierre Joseph Proudhon, What is Property? , ch. I, 1840, translation by Benjamin R. Tucker) The phrase was not his: Brissot had used it before the French Revolution. His target was narrower than the slogan: property that let one person live from another's labour. He repeatedly disclaimed any wish to build a system. In 1842 he stood before a jury in Besançon, charged with attacking property, inciting class hatred and insulting the government, and used the trial as a platform: "I have only written one thing in my life, gentlemen jurors, and I will tell you that thing right away, so there is no question: Property is robbery." (Proudhon, court defence, Besançon assizes, 3 February 1842) He set out a wages and deduction account of exploitation, using a shoemaker's five franc pair, and told the jury that to abolish that robbery it was necessary to universalise it. They acquitted him after an hour. The trial report is an edited extract by someone else and the defence was self serving, but the event made him a public figure. Marx approached this man in 1846 with an offer that included paying postage. Proudhon's reply of 17 May set conditions that also diagnosed their difference: he would not lead a new orthodoxy and rejected political revolution as a means of reform. "I would therefore prefer to burn Property by a slow fire, rather than give it new strength by making a St Bartholomew's night of the proprietors ..." (Proudhon to Karl Marx, 17 May 1846), he wrote, proposing an economic combination that would turn the theory of property against property. Written to a prospective collaborator in conciliatory language, it remains the clearest first hand statement of why they could not work together. The break Proudhon published System of Economical Contradictions, or The Philosophy of Poverty in 1846 and 1847. Its method treated value as a contradictory social relation, with use value and exchange value moving in opposite directions, and proposed a law of proportionality of values in which justice meant that proportionality. This lay behind the later exchange bank proposals. Marx answered in 1847 with The Poverty of Philosophy , whose foreword was a public verdict on a former collaborator: "M. Proudhon has the misfortune of being peculiarly misunderstood in Europe. In France, he has the right to be a bad economist, because he is reputed to be a good German philosopher." (Karl Marx, foreword to The Poverty of Philosophy , Brussels, 15

title: The Commune Lived: Paris, March–May 1871
description: On the morning of 18 March 1871 a crowd gathered on Montmartre to take back the cannons that the government had tried to remove.
text: On the morning of 18 March 1871 a crowd gathered on Montmartre to take back the cannons that the government had tried to remove (Prosper Olivier Lissagaray, Histoire de la Commune de 1871 ). That government had withdrawn to Versailles after the national defeat and the winter siege of Paris. Louise Michel, a schoolteacher and combatant who was there, recalled that the National Guard, the citizen militia, fraternised with the troops instead of fighting them, and that two generals, Clément Thomas and Lecomte, were killed. She wrote that account fifteen years later, so it is a recollection rather than a transcript. What survives is a set of records made by people who had to explain the Commune, a local governing council, after it was crushed: its own decrees, a court record, memoirs written in exile and an inquiry held a generation later. Together they show a municipal administration, a military defence and a policy of reprisal, and participants disagreed about all three. The decree of 5 April A placard of 25 March summoned the electorate to choose a Commune, and the vote gave the rising an institutional form. Michel remembered women building and holding a barricade at the Place Blanche in the fighting of May: "Les femmes, aux jours de Mai, élevèrent et défendirent la barricade de la place Blanche. Elles tinrent jusqu'à la mort." ( Mémoires de Louise Michel , written 1886). The document that fixes policy most sharply is the decree of 2 prairial an 79, or 5 April 1871, printed in the Commune's own Journal officiel . Article 4 declared that detainees held under the decree were "the hostages of the people of Paris". Article 5 supplied the consequence: "Toute exécution d'un prisonnier de guerre ou d'un partisan du gouvernement régulier de la Commune de Paris sera, sur le champ, suivie de l'exécution d'un nombre triple d'otages retenus en vertu de l'article 4, et qui seront désignés par le sort." (Article 5 of the hostage decree, 5 April 1871). A decree records an intention, not its application. Gaston Da Costa, then twenty and a chief of staff who helped move prisoners from Mazas to La Roquette in requisitioned vans, told the 1897 inquiry that the decree had not been carried out as it was written. The killings at La Roquette and in the rue Haxo followed a different and improvised path. A second document concerns a bargain that was never made. Benjamin Flotte, a longtime associate of Auguste Blanqui, argued in an 1885 pamphlet that some seventy four hostages, among them the Archbishop of Paris, could have been exchanged for Blanqui, and he held Adolphe Thiers responsible for refusing. Flotte wrote as an advocate, in openly polemical language. His pamphlet establishes that the exchange was proposed and how he judged its refusal; it does not establish Thiers's motive. Voices from twenty six years later In 1897 La Revue blanche asked participants and contemporaries to explain the rising. The answers disagree. Ernest Daudet, who had lived in Paris during the Commune, called it "Je considère l'insurrection de 1871 comme un crime abominable, — un crime de lèse patrie — encore que je ne tienne pas pour également criminels tous ceux qui y prirent part." (Ernest Daudet, inquiry, 15 March 1897). Henri Rochefort, who backed the Commune against Versailles but opposed carrying out the hostage decree, said he had come close to being shot by a council of war. Ranc, a Commune member, described his own attempt at conciliation, and Melliet named the Commune's fault as not knowing and not daring. Da Costa explained how the word hostage had been heard: "Le peuple, la masse, ne comprenait pas bien le sens du mot otage et traduisait naïvement : curé, agent." (Gaston Da Costa, inquiry, 1 April 1897). The editors themselves conceded that hostile replies were scarce. These are statements by people with reputations to protect, not a balanced sample of opinion. The social composition of the council rests on firmer evidence. Jacques Rougerie's figures, quoted by

title: The First International: An Organisation in Documents, 1864–1876
description: On 28 September 1864 a public meeting at St Martin's Hall in London, called after an address on the Polish insurrection to Paris workers, founded the International Working Men's Association.
text: On 28 September 1864 a public meeting at St Martin's Hall in London, called after an address on the Polish insurrection to Paris workers, founded the International Working Men's Association. Its purpose was to link workers' organisations in different countries in one permanent body. Wilhelm Eichhoff, a German socialist whose first history of the Association was written with Marx's help, described the moment: "The meeting gave birth to the International Working Men’s Association." (Eichhoff, The International Workingmen's Association , 1868). This was internationalism before it meant a state system or a Comintern. In practice it was a correspondence network, a subscription of a penny a member, a statistical inquiry into working conditions, strike solidarity and a running argument about whether workers should take political power at all. The organisation kept records of unusual detail: an address and rules drafted by Marx, a Minute Book of weekly meetings, congress resolutions with named vote counts, and a quarrel conducted in circulars that both sides intended as evidence. The address and the rules The founding documents were written in a sub committee that contained rival programmes. Marx told Engels on 4 November 1864 that Odger and Cremer had organised the meeting, Le Lubez had invited him, and he had supplied Eccarius, a German worker, as a speaker. Major Wolff put forward Mazzinian statutes, named for the Italian nationalist Giuseppe Mazzini, and the Owenite Weston, a follower of Robert Owen's cooperative socialism, offered his own programme. Marx displaced both with a text of his own. "It was very difficult to frame the thing so that our view should appear in a form that would make it acceptable to the present outlook of the workers’ movement." (Marx to Engels, 4 November 1864). The General Council, the body elected to conduct business between congresses, adopted the address and rules on 1 November. Its Minute Book is terse but not silent: "The amendment being carried, the word “profitmongers” was struck out and the Address was unanimously agreed to." (General Council minutes, 1 November 1864). The address drew on British parliamentary and official statistics to argue that growing trade had not reduced working class misery, and ended with the claim that working class emancipation had to be won by workers themselves: "To conquer political power has, therefore, become the great duty of the working classes." (Marx, Inaugural Address , October 1864). The rules gave the Association an annual congress and an elected General Council with power to add to its own number, act as an agency between sections and publish reports. Their shortest maxim was "no rights without duties, no duties without rights" ( General Rules , October 1864). A programme is not a neutral description, and the text circulated in languages that altered it. Marx later noted that the 1864 Paris translation had dropped both the phrase "as a means" and the words about the abolition of all class rule, which changed what the preamble said about political movements. Arguments about Proudhonism were live in the German speaking sections as well. When the editors of Der Social Demokrat asked Marx to judge the recently dead Proudhon, he objected: "You yourself have now to accept responsibility for having imposed upon me the role of a judge of the dead so soon after this man’s death." (Marx to J. B. Schweitzer, 24 January 1865). He praised the style of What is Property? while dismissing Proudhon's later economics as the outlook of the petty bourgeoisie, the small property owning middle layer. The weekly work and the Commune The Minute Book records the ordinary business of building an organisation: a thousand copies of the address and rules ordered, the Bee Hive adopted as its organ, personal guarantees taken out by Council members for a rented room, and an address to Abraham Lincoln on his re election in 1864 pasted into the volume as a newspaper cutting. title: Before the Factory: Commerce, Land and the Origins of Capitalism
description: What the sources already in this book show about merchant wealth, the separation of producers from the land, and the making of a class that sells its labour, and what they leave out.
text: This book documents socialist movements and governments far more fully than the economic world they answered. Capitalism enters most chapters through its critics or through the institutions built against it. This chapter asks how capital and a class compelled to sell its working capacity came into being, using only evidence already gathered here. Commercial capitalism means trade for profit by merchants who buy and sell rather than produce. Wage labour means work sold by people who do not own the tools, land or factories with which they could work for themselves. Primitive accumulation is Marx's name for the historical process that created capital's preconditions by separating producers from the means of production. The sources contain Marx's account in detail and little independent evidence with which to test it. Marx was not writing into an empty field. Adam Smith's An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations , in Edwin Cannan's 1904 edition, is a non socialist account of how commerce and the division of labour increased productive power, and it criticised merchants who pursued state monopolies (Smith, Cannan edition). Its presence matters here: the socialist critique of capitalism was written against a political economy that could itself attack mercantile privilege. Neither text is a neutral description of industrial life, and neither supplies the tenant records or wage series that would test their claims. Marx placed the question inside a theory of modes of production, a mode being the historically specific way a society organizes the making and distributing of goods. In 1859 he listed "the Asiatic, ancient, feudal and modern bourgeois modes of production" as "epochs marking progress in the economic development of society" (1859 Preface). The same preface stated the premise later called historical materialism: "It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness" (1859 Preface). That is a claim about how to explain institutions. He warned that "no social order is ever destroyed before all the productive forces for which it is sufficient have been developed," a qualification often dropped (1859 Preface). Merchant wealth in the surviving record The closest this book comes to a documented case of commercial capitalism is not European. Rodney's research on the Upper Guinea Coast used Portuguese merchant records in England and Portugal and appeared in 1970 as A History of the Upper Guinea Coast, 1545 to 1800 (MIA Encyclopedia, "Rodney, Walter"). His better known book of 1972 moved from Africa's contribution to European capitalist development to the European roots of African underdevelopment up to 1885 and the colonial and neo colonial systems that perpetuated it (Rodney, preface and contents). Drayton traced the book's roots to the Caribbean, to Cheddi Jagan's account of how British Guiana's plantation and mining economy created wealth abroad and poverty at home, and to Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (Drayton, 2022). These are described research routes, not the ledgers themselves. Wallerstein observed in 1986 that the book had no footnotes, was not based on archival research and was openly didactic (Wallerstein review, 1986). Araujo later tested one of its supporting claims, that enslaved people were bought with goods of little value (Araujo, 2022). The exchange is a genuine dispute and a reminder that a sweeping account of merchant wealth can be argued over at the level of a single purchase. Marx's account and its mechanism Marx framed the origin of capital as an apparent circle: accumulation requires surplus value, the excess over wages that a worker produces for the owner of capital, surplus value requires capitalist production, and capitalist production requires capital already to exist. What is needed, he wrote, is "a primitive accumulation, an accumulation not the result of the capitalistic mode of production, but its

title: The Factory and the Working Day: Conditions, Discipline and Two Critiques of Capital
description: Engels's Manchester, the campaign over hours and child labour, and the difference between surplus value and alienation as claims about industrial work.
text: Friedrich Engels walked the industrial districts of Manchester in the 1840s and wrote down what he saw. The river below the town was not scenery but a consequence of how production was organised: "At the bottom flows, or rather stagnates, the Irk, a narrow, coal black, foul smelling stream, full of debris and refuse, which it deposits on the shallower right bank." Source: Friedrich Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England , written 1844 to 1845, English edition 1887 Engels was a young businessman living in the city, and his book mixes observation with official reports. It is a witness's polemic, not a measurement. Two claims about industrial work must be kept apart. Surplus value is Marx's term for the extra value that wage workers create beyond what they are paid, a claim about how production and payment are organised. Alienation is the condition in which the product and the process of a person's work confront them as forces that control them, a claim about the human relation to work. Both arise from the same body of writing, but they were made twenty years apart and are not the same proposition. What the witness and the reformer describe Engels's book was written between September 1844 and March 1845 and published in Leipzig in 1845 (MIA editorial headnote). The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes it as based on close observation of production techniques and living conditions and still widely regarded as his masterpiece (SEP, "Friedrich Engels"). He described the towns, housing, Irish immigrant labourers, mines and agricultural workers. He was not a worker and wrote with a political purpose. His pages are one observer's evidence, not a transcript of workers' words or a survey. Robert Owen, a mill owner at New Lanark, gave a more precise account of the working day because he was arguing for a law. In 1817 he said that "in the manufacturing districts it is common for parents to send their children of both sexes at seven or eight years of age, in winter as well as summer, at six o'clock in the morning" (Owen, Observations on the Effect of the Manufacturing System , 1817). He asked for a twelve hour day, no work under ten, six hour days for children under twelve and basic literacy. Reading the amended bill in 1818, he wrote to the prime minister: "It permits children to be employed at nine years of age for twelve hours and a half per day," naming cotton spinners, several of them MPs, who resisted (Owen to the Earl of Liverpool, 1818). The 1819 Factory Act fell short of what he wanted. In his autobiography he recalled a committee debating behind closed doors before deciding not to hear him (Owen, autobiography), a memory that cannot be checked against the minutes. Owen's school shows another side of discipline. His son Robert Dale described classes of twenty to forty and a "silent monitor," a coloured block that recorded conduct without a rebuke. "The children are governed, not by severity, but by kindness," he wrote in 1824 (Robert Dale Owen, An Outline of the System of Education at New Lanark ). He called the experiment partial and recorded that most children entered the factory at ten. The school could not undo what the mill and the household did outside its walls. Hours as a field of struggle In Lawrence, Massachusetts, the strike of 1912 began with a cut in hours from 56 to 54 a week without matching pay. The federal investigation reported that "during the first few days of the strike approximately 14,000 employees withdrew from their work, later accessions increased the number on strike to approximately 23,000." It recorded 296 strike related arrests producing 355 court cases and a settlement giving roughly 30,000 workers increases of between 5 and 20 per cent (Charles P. Neill, official report, 1912). Justus Ebert's IWW account describes a strike committee organised through nationality groups (Ebert). Both agree it was not formally an IWW body, though its chairmen were members. title: Slavery, Race and Capital: From the Atlantic Trade to the Wage of Whiteness
description: What the book's sources establish about enslaved labour, racial hierarchy and the different forms of coercion that capitalism inherited and transformed.
text: In his testimony to the House Committee on Un American Activities on 12 June 1956, Paul Robeson answered a question about Stalin by turning it back on the committee: "You are responsible, and your forebears, for sixty million to one hundred million black people dying in the slave ships and on the plantations." The number was his own rhetorical summation, not a count. The Trans Atlantic Slave Trade Database, known here through the National Endowment for the Humanities' project description, estimates that about 12.5 million captives were embarked in Africa and about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage. The figures measure different things (Robeson, HUAC testimony, 1956; NEH project description). Both statements belong in an account of how slavery figured in political argument. Chattel slavery means a system in which human beings are owned as property; wage labour means work sold by a formally free person who does not own the means of production; colonial forced labour means work compelled by an occupying administration through taxation, contract or punishment. Trade, plantations and the wealth they made Rodney's scholarly formation was in this history. His research on the Upper Guinea Coast used Portuguese merchant records in England and Portugal and appeared in 1970 (MIA Encyclopedia, "Rodney, Walter"). How Europe Underdeveloped Africa of 1972 set the slave trade inside a longer account of how Africa's wealth contributed to European capitalist development and how European power reshaped Africa in return (Rodney, preface and contents). Drayton found the book's roots in the Caribbean and in Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery , a line of argument tying plantation and mining wealth abroad to poverty in the producing countries (Drayton, 2022). Araujo tested one of Rodney's supporting claims, that enslaved people were bought with goods of little value, against later research (Araujo, 2022). These are disputes over evidence. Marx placed the traffic inside the origin of capital rather than treating it as a prelude. He wrote that in actual history "conquest, enslavement, robbery, murder, briefly force, play the great part" ( Capital , volume I, chapter 26), and described primitive accumulation as applying where it was not "immediate transformation of slaves and serfs into wage labourers, and therefore a mere change of form" ( Capital , volume I, chapter 32). The Communist Manifesto opened with "freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf" as opposed figures in earlier class struggles ( Manifesto , chapter I). The claim that capitalism inherited older forms of domination and recast them is therefore in the classical texts. What the sources here do not provide is a documented chain from a slave ship to a particular factory. Du Bois and the colour line as a labour question Du Bois made the connection between slavery, labour and capitalism the centre of his work without always using Marxist language. The Souls of Black Folk of 1903 answered the question "What have we done for this country?" by reversing the burden of proof. The nation, he wrote, received from Black Americans "a gift of story and song," "the gift of sweat and brawn," and "the gift of the Spirit," and he asked "Your country? How came it yours? Before the Pilgrims landed we were here" ( The Souls of Black Folk ). The same book named double consciousness and declared that "the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color line." In 1915 he argued that "it was the competition for the labor of yellow, brown, and black folk" that caused the war, and compared the German invasion of Belgium with the Belgian record in the Congo (MIA hosted review quoting the essay). Those words reach us through a review that selects and frames them. The argument sharpened in Black Reconstruction in America of 1935. Its chapter "The General Strike" held that enslaved people, by withdrawing their labour and fleeing to Union lines, made emancipation their own act rat

title: Empire and Underdevelopment: Colonialism as an Economic and Political System
description: Rodney, Cabral, Fanon, the Bengal famine, the Congo and the forms of imperial control that survived decolonisation.
text: By the fourth Pan African Congress in New York in 1927, Du Bois was printing resolutions that demanded land, self rule in Africa and the withdrawal of American troops from Haiti. One stated: "The attitude of all the imperial powers who own Africa is fundamentally wrong. They are seeking profit, not men; they want trade and industry more than civilization and spiritual uplift" (resolutions reproduced by Du Bois, October 1927). It was an organiser's claim, not a neutral finding, but it joins the economic and political. Imperialism here means a system in which states and firms extend power beyond their borders to secure markets, raw materials and investment outlets; colonialism means direct political rule over another people; neo colonialism means control through trade, finance and aligned local interests rather than formal rule. Underdevelopment here is a condition produced by the relation between societies, not merely a stage not yet reached. The argument about causes Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism , written in 1916, defined the epoch as "the monopoly stage of capitalism," monopoly meaning a branch of production dominated by a few large firms. He stressed that monopoly "does not eliminate" free competition "but exist[s] above it and alongside it," producing "acute, intense antagonisms, frictions and conflicts" ( Imperialism , chapter VII). It moved through concentration of production, banks, finance capital, the export of capital and the division of the world (chapter I). It was written to explain the collapse of the Second International in 1914. The economic critique of empire was not confined to Marxists. J. A. Hobson's Imperialism: A Study of 1902 examined how mercantile interests in the home country could manipulate state power to secure benefits in the colony (Hobson). Placing Hobson beside Lenin matters: it prevents the chapter from treating Marxism as the only source of the argument that imperial expansion served particular economic interests. Hobson's explanation and Lenin's are not identical, and neither is a neutral account of colonial rule. Lenin's draft theses of June 1920 called for a temporary alliance with bourgeois democracy in colonial countries while keeping communist organisations independent (Lenin, 5 June 1920). M. N. Roy's supplementary theses of July 1920 put the economic claim sharply: "The super profits made in the colonies form one of the main sources of the resources of contemporary capitalism" (Roy, 25 July 1920). Roy wanted communists to build workers' and peasants' organisations rather than follow the national middle class. The two texts record a disagreement and reach English through translations of differing provenance. Rodney refused a single cause account. In 1970 he held that partition was shaped by three factors beyond capitalist expansion: African social formations, racism within the capitalist superstructure, and African opposition (Rodney, The Imperialist Partition of Africa ). In 1971 he endorsed the claim that wealth drained towards the developed capitalist nations and that political independence did not halt economic exploitation (Rodney, 1971). Cabral defined imperialism as piracy moved from the sea to dry land, reorganised to exploit colonised peoples' resources. He distinguished direct rule from indirect rule through local agents, which he called neo colonialism, and held that the essence was the seizure of a people's right to develop its productive forces (Cabral, 1966). These writers share a framework but differ in emphasis; their claims are related, not interchangeable. Different rulers and different controls The Treaty of Nanking of 29 August 1842 shows the commercial terms behind military victory. It opened five ports to British residence and trade, ceded Hong Kong "to be possessed in perpetuity", abolished the licensed Cohong monopoly, and required China to pay a total of twenty one million dollars: six for the opium surrendered at Canton, three for debts

title: Repression and Organising: The Long Campaign for Labour Rights
description: Blacklisting, lockouts, police power and deportation on one side; charters, strikes, unions and achieved reforms on the other.
text: On the first of May 1926, in the pit village of Pendleton, a miner's wife told a reporter from the Manchester Evening News what a stoppage meant in her kitchen: "it is the women who have to find and put the dumplings in the stew." The sentence came from a newspaper that supported the government and survived because a local history society copied it out decades later (reproduced by the North West Labour History Society). What followed was the only general strike Britain has ever known. A general strike is a coordinated stoppage across many industries, so that one trade cannot be isolated. It ran from 3 to 12 May 1926 and drew roughly three million workers out in support of miners locked out, meaning employers closed pits and withheld pay until the men accepted terms. A blacklist denies work to named people, a strikebreaker replaces strikers, and a shop steward is elected by colleagues. This chapter follows both the machinery used against organisers and the reforms organisers won. The instruments of suppression Chartism met the law at the Westgate Hotel in Newport in the early hours of 4 November 1839. John Frost led a march from the mining valleys; the windows were smashed, the Riot Act was read, and soldiers fired. Henry Mullock, recalling the scene in 1897, remembered the crowd's movement rather than its politics: "We watched until they turned the corner of the Westgate and began smashing the windows" ( South Wales Argus , 1897). More than three thousand court documents survive from the treason trials. Who fired first is unclear, and witnesses testified after the event under a prosecution seeking convictions. Frost and two others were transported for life. Parliament was unmoved by the petitioning: in May 1842 MPs refused to hear petitioners at the bar and defeated the motion on the second Chartist petition by 49 votes to 287 (Hansard, 3 May 1842). In 1848 O'Connor claimed more than five million signatures; Commons clerks counted 1,975,496 (Chartist Ancestors). At Everett, Washington, on 5 November 1916, men landed from the steamer Verona and a dock confrontation left five Wobblies confirmed dead and two deputies killed by friendly fire. The first shot is unknown, and the IWW, local, AFL and socialist papers each framed the event differently (Walker C. Smith, The Everett Massacre ; University of Washington guide). Palmer set out his case in The Forum in 1920: "Upon these two basic certainties, first that the 'Reds' were criminal aliens and secondly that the American Government must prevent crime, it was decided that there could be no nice distinctions drawn." He cited "upward of 60,000" alleged agitators on confidential authority (Palmer, February 1920). Berkman and Goldman, deported in December 1919, wrote from Ellis Island of the "Red Ark" leaving families destitute (Berkman and Goldman, 1919). In a petition of 3 May 1927 Bartolomeo Vanzetti connected his case to the raids: "we were really tried not for murder, but for being Radicals, draft evaders, and pacifists" (Vanzetti petition). The evidence remains disputed; the petition is a defence argument, not a finding. The state intervened administratively as well as through police. The government took over the Morning Post and published the British Gazette under Winston Churchill. Its first issue said that "nearly all the newspapers have been silenced by violent concerted action." The TUC closed the whole press, including its own Daily Herald , then issued the British Worker after police raided the Herald's offices (Modern Records Centre). Ellen Wilkinson complained that a publicly subscribed service gave only one side ( Radio Times , 28 May 1926). Local Communist premises were raided and people imprisoned for producing bulletins. After the General Council ended the strike without guarantees, miners stayed out for seven months and victimisation followed. title: What Capitalism Achieved, and What It Cost
description: Productivity, machinery, consumption and reform, set beside the labour and environmental record, with an explicit account of what the sources cannot measure.
text: Lenin's first major work, The Development of Capitalism in Russia of 1899, made a judgment often missing from accounts written by socialists. Capitalism's "mission," he wrote, reduced itself to two propositions: "increase in the productive forces of social labour, and the socialisation of that labour." He paired it with "the full recognition of the negative and dark sides of capitalism" (Lenin, chapter VIII, section VI). That pairing is the right starting point. A history that records capitalist achievements without their costs becomes an advertisement. Productive forces here means the labour, tools, techniques and knowledge available for production; socialisation means that production comes to depend on many people working together rather than isolated households. The case for what was built The classical texts concede the scale of the change. Marx's 1859 preface laid down that "no social order is ever destroyed before all the productive forces for which it is sufficient have been developed" (1859 Preface). In Capital he described accumulation as a process in which "the more the capitalist has accumulated, the more is he able to accumulate" ( Capital , volume I, chapter 24). The Communist Manifesto argued that productive forces eventually become "too powerful for these conditions" of bourgeois property, so that in crises "a great part not only of the existing products, but also of the previously created productive forces, are periodically destroyed" ( Manifesto , chapter I). Engels gave the periodicity: "since 1825, when the first general crisis broke out, the whole industrial and commercial world are thrown out of joint about once every 10 years" ( Socialism: Utopian and Scientific , Part III). These writers did not deny the productive achievement. They argued that its form was unstable. The accomplishment they identified was socialised production. Engels wrote that "the means of production, and production itself, had become in essence socialized" but had been subjected "to a form of appropriation which presupposes the private production of individuals," a contradiction he called "the germ of the whole of the social antagonisms of today" ( Socialism: Utopian and Scientific , Part III). In Anti Dühring he allowed that state ownership "is not the solution of the conflict, but concealed within it are the technical conditions that form the elements of that solution" ( Anti Dühring ). Marx described work as an exchange of matter between people and nature common to every society ( Capital , volume I, chapter 7), while Engels warned in an essay of 1876 that "for each such victory nature takes its revenge on us" (Engels, "The Part Played by Labour"). Some of this can be seen at a smaller scale. Robert Owen showed that a mill could be run without the worst abuses and a school built inside a factory village. In 1816 he opened a school at New Lanark, fixing ten as the age for entering the mill; his son counted about 600 pupils (Owen address, 1816; Robert Dale Owen, 1824). G. D. H. Cole judged that Owen showed "low wages and long hours were not necessary to industrial success," while arguing that he was a bad leader of men (Cole introduction, 1927). In 1844 weavers and artisans opened a shop in Toad Lane, Rochdale, with a first stock of flour, butter, sugar and oatmeal, gathering twopence at a time (Rochdale Pioneers Museum, archived). A consumer cooperative is a shop owned by those who use it, with surplus returned in proportion to spending. John Kershaw, a founder who had begun in a mill at seven, remembered the trigger: "Distress was far and widespread. People were badly fed and badly clothed" (Kershaw, 1893). Rising consumption, where it came, was often organised by those denied it. Large infrastructure tells a similar story about who builds. Nkrumah described the Volta River scheme as a dam for hydroelectric power, the smelting of Ghana's bauxite and the electrification of other industries. The main dam was funded by Ghana, Britain

title: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
description: Lives, works and theory: historical materialism, surplus value, the state, and the two phases of communist society.
text: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote at a time when industrial capitalism was transforming Europe and political revolution seemed, for a period, possible. Marx was born in 1818 and died in London on 14 March 1883. Engels was born in 1820 and died in 1895. Between them they produced a body of work that later socialists, communists and historians have returned to for arguments about class, capital, the state and the possibility of a different social order. Their central claim was that ideas, law and political institutions have to be explained through the ways people produce the things they need. Historical materialism is the name later given to that approach: the view that the organization of production shapes social institutions and prevailing ideas, while people in turn act on the conditions they inherit. Surplus value is their term for the extra value that wage workers create beyond what they are paid. Alienation describes the condition in which the product of a person's work confronts them as something foreign that controls them. By the state they meant the institutions, such as government, courts, police and army, that exercise organized power over a territory. By crisis they meant a recurring breakdown in which goods and productive capacity are destroyed or left idle. By the transition to communism they meant a political period in which the working class was expected to take power and begin to reshape property and production. These arguments survive in published books, articles, letters and editorial prefaces. Every one of those documents has a date, an author and a purpose, and each must be read as evidence rather than as a verdict on itself. Engels's account of how he and Marx divided their work, written more than three decades after their first collaboration and after Marx's death, is a participant's retrospective statement, not an independent audit. Editors at the Marxists Internet Archive have supplied headnotes and indexes that are useful guides but are not primary texts. Modern scholars do not all agree about how the two men related to one another, or about how much of the theory belongs to each. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that the question of their intellectual relationship remains "sharply contested," and that the standard critical editions of their work are always issued as the collected works of Marx and Engels together rather than separately. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Friedrich Engels". Marx's road to political economy Marx studied law but, as he later recalled, pursued it "as a subject subordinated to philosophy and history" (Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy , 1859). The practical turn came in 1842 and 1843, when he edited the Rheinische Zeitung . In the 1859 preface he described what pushed him toward economic questions: "the deliberations of the Rhenish Landtag on forest thefts and the division of landed property," the controversy over "the condition of the Moselle peasantry," and "the debates on free trade and protective tariffs caused me in the first instance to turn my attention to economic questions." In the same years he met "an echo of French socialism and communism, slightly tinged by philosophy." He said he objected to it because he lacked knowledge, and admitted that lack openly (Marx, 1859 Preface). These were concrete grievances, not abstract puzzles: poor people gathering wood from landed estates, peasants in the Moselle valley facing poverty, and arguments over whether free trade would help or harm them. His first sustained reply was a critique of Hegel's philosophy of law. Hegel had argued that the state and legal institutions are the rational outcome of a developing spirit. Marx inverted that claim, arguing that legal and political forms arise from actual social conditions. title: Vladimir Lenin, Joseph Stalin and the Soviet Experience
description: Imperialism, the vanguard party, 1917, the NEP, socialism in one country, industrialisation and collectivisation.
text: In the first weeks of April 1930, an officer of the Ukrainian state security service compiled a confidential report on what workers were saying in the factories of Dnipropetrovsk, Kryvyi Rih and Kharkiv. Stalin had published "Dizzy with Success" a month earlier, blaming local officials for the excesses of collectivisation and telling peasants they could leave the collective farms. In the rolling mill of the Petrovsky plant, a worker named Bizhko welcomed the article because middle peasants had been swept up in the campaign against kulaks, the better off peasants. In the open hearth workshop, a labourer named Gasinsky said he had been starving with his family and hoped the markets would reopen. At the Kaganovich mine, a winch operator named Moroz was blunter: "All our newspapers lie about the gains of collectivization. In practice, everything is falling apart." The report was written for the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Ukraine and was never intended for publication. That is precisely its value. It records what people said when they did not expect their words to be read outside a police file. Source: REESOURCES, "Response from workers of the USSR to Stalin's article 'Dizzy with Success,' 1930", Central State Archives of Public Organizations of Ukraine, 1/20/3192/66 74. Those remarks were the reception of a set of arguments about capitalism, the party and the state that had been built over more than a generation. The men who made those arguments did not write for factory workers in 1930, but the consequences of their writings reached those workers directly. This account follows the texts in the order in which they were written, and sets beside them the evidence of people who lived through the results. Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, known as Lenin, was born in 1870 into a family of the raznochintsy, educated commoners who stood outside the old hereditary estates, in Simbirsk. His early revolutionary formation took place in Marxist circles during the 1880s and 1890s. He was arrested in 1895 and exiled to Siberia from 1897 to 1900, where he wrote his first major economic work. From 1900 he lived abroad, editing Iskra with Plekhanov, Axelrod and others. He became the leader of the Bolshevik faction after the split with the Mensheviks at the Second Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1903, and led the party through the 1905 revolution, the years of emigration, the First World War and the revolution of 1917. From October 1917 he served as head of the first Soviet government, Chairman of the Council of People's Commissars, until his death in January 1924. A year by year record of his activity appears in the MIA's Life and Work of V. I. Lenin . Joseph Vissarionovich Stalin, born Djugashvili, was born in 1879 in Gori, Georgia, and was formed in the Caucasian Social Democratic movement. He worked in the Baku oilfields strike wave of 1903 to 1904, was repeatedly arrested and exiled, and was a Bolshevik from the split. He joined the first Bolshevik Central Committee and worked on Pravda in 1912 and 1913. The MIA's 1947 Stalin biography records that "The Pravda of 1912... was the laying of the cornerstone of the victory of Bolshevism in 1917" and that Lenin "set the highest value" on Marxism and the National Question (Chapter IV). During 1917 he directed Pravda and the party's work in Petrograd. He served as People's Commissar for Nationalities from 1917 to 1922, joined the Politburo in 1919, and became General Secretary of the Central Committee in April 1922. That post became the base from which he built the party apparatus that underpinned his leadership. He led the USSR through industrialisation, collectivisation, the war against Germany, and the postwar consolidation until his death on 5 March 1953. Lenin's first major intervention was The Development of Capitalism in Russia , written between 1896 and 1899 and published in March 1899.
