title: Stalin: The Complete History and Writings
description: The full biography of Stalin and a systematic enumeration of every work in the MIA Stalin archive.
text: On 2 March 1930 Stalin published an article telling party activists that collective farms "must not be established by force". Seven years later the Soviet secret police issued Operational Order 00447, which sorted suspected enemies into two categories and gave each region a quota: the first category to be shot, the second to be sent to a labour camp for eight to ten years (Dizzy with Success; NKVD Order 00447, 30 July 1937). The distance between those two documents is the problem at the centre of this life. Stalin wrote the theoretical texts that defined Leninism for communist parties across the world, and he presided over a state that used coercion on a mass scale. Neither fact cancels the other. His career ran from a Georgian seminary to the Kremlin, and the record he left includes both arguments about how socialism should be built and the consequences of building it under a one party dictatorship. A Georgian seminary and the Bolshevik underground The official biographical chronicle attached to the first volume of Stalin's collected works records that Joseph Vissarionovich Djugashvili was born in Gori, Georgia, in 1879, entered the elementary clerical school there in September 1888, and began at the Tiflis Theological Seminary on 2 September 1894 (Biographical Chronicle). The seminary was one of the few routes by which a boy from a poor Georgian family could get an education under tsarism. It also produced revolutionaries: between 1896 and 1898 the chronicle has him running Marxist study circles, reading Marx's Capital and The Communist Manifesto , and becoming acquainted with Lenin's early writings. In January 1898 he organised a workers' circle in the Tiflis railway workshops. In August he joined Messameh Dassy, a Georgian Social Democratic group, where he formed with V. Z. Ketskhoveli and A. G. Tsulukidze what the chronicle calls "the core of the revolutionary Marxist minority". He was expelled from the seminary on 29 May 1899 for propagating Marxism and went to work at the Tiflis Physical Observatory (Ibid.). The years that followed turned propaganda into organisation. In 1901 he went underground, launched the illegal Georgian Marxist paper Brdzola ( The Struggle ) and joined the Tiflis committee of the R.S.D.L.P., the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. That party split at its Second Congress in 1903 into Mensheviks, who wanted a broad workers' party, and Bolsheviks, who wanted a small disciplined party of professional revolutionaries; the Tiflis committee followed the Leninist or Bolshevik current. In Batum he set up an underground press and led strikes at the Mantashev and Rothschild works. On 9 March 1902 he led a demonstration of more than six thousand workers. Troops fired, killing fifteen and wounding fifty four, and that night he wrote a manifesto about the shootings. Arrest followed in April 1902, then imprisonment in Kutais and deportation to Novaya Uda in Siberia, where he arrived in November 1903 (Biographical Chronicle). He escaped in January 1904, reached Tiflis, wrote the programmatic Credo on party disagreements, and moved to Baku, where he dissolved the Menshevik committee and formed a Bolshevik one. In December 1904 he led a general strike of Baku workers. At the Bolshevik conference at Tammerfors in December 1905 he met Lenin for the first time. His first substantial theoretical work, the series Anarchism or Socialism? of 1906 and 1907, set out a defence of Marxist dialectics and materialism against anarchism and introduced the philosophical vocabulary he used again thirty years later (Volume 1 contents). The years of tsarist reaction after 1905 were spent in Baku, in repeated arrests and in exile at Solvychegodsk. By 1912 he was in St Petersburg editing Pravda and writing for the workers' curia in the Duma elections. title: Mao Zedong, the Chinese Revolution and Maoist Theory
description: New Democracy, the mass line, people's war, the PRC after 1949, continuing revolution and the 1981 Resolution.
text: Mao Zedong led the Communist Party of China (CPC) through a revolution that ended in 1949 and then governed the People's Republic until his death in 1976. His career spans the fall of the Qing dynasty, the wars against Japan and the Nationalists, the building of a socialist state, and two of the twentieth century's largest human catastrophes. Maoism, the body of ideas associated with his name, was developed in the Chinese countryside and later adapted by movements on other continents. Any account of these years has to say where its evidence comes from. The official narrative is dominated by a document adopted on 27 June 1981, when Deng Xiaoping and his allies were settling the question of how the Party should judge its own past. The Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party Since the Founding of the People's Republic of China was drafted under Deng and Hu Yaobang, with Hu Qiaomu leading the drafting group. Its communique described the task as "the historic mission of setting to rights things which have been thrown into disorder in the guiding ideology of the Party" (Communique of the Sixth Plenary Session). The Resolution gives dates, figures and verdicts, and it remains the authoritative Party account. It is also a retrospective judgement produced for a political purpose. Deng told the drafters that "affirmation of the historical role of Comrade Mao Zedong and explanation of the necessity to uphold and develop Mao Zedong Thought" was "the most essential point" (Deng's remarks on successive drafts, 1980 81). This chapter uses the Resolution as evidence of what the Party decided to remember, and sets its claims beside the work of historians who have used census data, local archives, contemporary reporting and interviews. Where a claim is contested, the sources behind it are named and the method behind them is explained. The making of a revolutionary, 1893 to 1919 Mao was born in 1893 in Shaoshan, Hunan Province. The world he entered was one in which, in the Party's later words, "the Revolution of 1911 led by Dr. Sun Yat sen, the great revolutionary forerunner, overthrew the Qing Dynasty, thus bringing to an end over 2,000 years of feudal monarchical rule," but where "the semi colonial and semi feudal nature of Chinese society remained unchanged" (1981 Resolution, §2). Semi colonial here means formally independent but subject to foreign economic and political control. Semi feudal means that landlord ownership and tenant farming persisted alongside ports, railways and modern industry. Mao gave the same arc in his 1949 essay On the People's Democratic Dictatorship . He listed the Opium War of 1840, the search for answers abroad by "Hung Hsiu chuan, Kang Yu wei, Yen Fu and Sun Yat sen," the failure of the 1911 revolution, and the turn caused by the Russian October Revolution of 1917. In his words, "The salvoes of the October Revolution brought us Marxism Leninism" (Mao, 30 June 1949). Marxism Leninism here means the body of theory derived from Karl Marx and Vladimir Lenin as interpreted by the Communist International, the Moscow directed organisation that guided communist parties abroad. The decisive generational event was the May Fourth Movement of 1919, a student and worker protest against the Versailles settlement that gave German concessions in China to Japan. Mao's own periodisation treats it as the boundary between the old and new types of bourgeois democratic revolution. A bourgeois democratic revolution is one aimed at ending feudal rule and establishing a market society; Mao called the pre 1919 version "old" because it was led by the bourgeoisie, the property owning commercial class, and "new" because, after 1919, "the political leader of China's bourgeois democratic revolution was no longer the bourgeoisie but the proletariat" ( On New Democracy , §V). Proletariat means the industrial working class. In the same essay Mao calls "the new revolutionary process of the past twenty years (counting from the May

title: The DPRK, Vietnam and Cuba
description: Parties, ideologies, constitutions and socialist construction in North Korea, Vietnam and Cuba, including the 2026 congresses.
text: The constitutions of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, the Socialist Republic of Vietnam and the Republic of Cuba all place a single party at the centre of political life. All three describe the main means of production, meaning the factories, land, machinery and banks used to produce goods, as publicly owned. All three present socialism as the goal of the state. The language they use to justify that arrangement differs, and so does the history each tells about how it got there (DPRK 2019 constitution; Vietnam 2013 constitution; Cuba 2019 constitution). These documents are evidence of what each government wanted its citizens and the world to believe. They are not a measurement of what happened. A constitution says that a party leads; it does not show how a party leads. An official history says that a revolution was won by the people; it does not tell us how people experienced it. This chapter sets the self descriptions of the three states beside the work of historians and the testimony of ordinary people, and marks the points where the two agree, differ or cannot be reconciled. North Korea: the party's account of its origins Official DPRK sources present Kim Il Sung (1912 to 1994) as the founder of the Juche idea and the leader of the Korean revolution. In a treatise published in 1982, his son Kim Jong Il wrote that Kim Il Sung first advanced the principles of Juche at a meeting of leading youth activists at Kalun in June 1930. The treatise says this answered a practical need, because "a revolution should be carried out not by anyone's approval or instruction but by one's own conviction and on one's own responsibility" (Kim Jong Il, On the Juche Idea , 1982). In 1982 Kim Il Sung described Juche as "a man centred world outlook and a revolutionary theory for realizing the independence of the masses of the people" (Kim Il Sung, Answers to Questions Raised by the Director of the RSS News Agency of Nepal , 22 June 1982). Juche, in plain terms, is the claim that each country's revolution must be made by its own people, in a way that suits their own conditions, rather than by following instructions from abroad or copying another country's model. The Workers' Party of Korea (WPK) was founded on 10 October 1945. A party exhibition published for its seventy fifth anniversary calls this "a solemn declaration to herald the birth of a new type leadership political organization" and describes the party as "the revolutionary party of the Juche type" and "an integral whole" with the masses (Naenara, WPK anniversary exhibition). The same exhibition lists the stages the party assigns itself: founding the party and building a new country; leading the Fatherland Liberation War, which is the DPRK name for the Korean War of 1950 to 1953; establishing socialism and carrying out the Chollima campaign for rapid industrial production; building socialist industry and a self reliant defence capacity; carrying out ideological, technological and cultural change; and modelling the whole society on Juche. The order of events in the official account is broadly supported by other records. Korea was liberated from Japanese rule in August 1945, the WPK was founded in October, and the DPRK was established in September 1948 with a constitution adopted on 8 September (1948 constitutional text, reproduced by the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea). Land reform, the nationalisation of major industry and the organisation of agricultural cooperatives followed. The party's own history celebrates this as the "establishment of socialist system and the movement of Grand Chollima March" (Naenara, WPK exhibition). The historian Suzy Kim has shown what such a transformation looked like at village level. Using documents seized by American forces during the Korean War and now held in the United States National Archives, together with oral histories, she reconstructs land reform, elections, literacy schools and mass organisations in the years 1945 to 1950. title: Xi Jinping and Modern China
description: Upbringing, rise, writings and the "new era": Xi Jinping Thought, poverty alleviation, the Belt and Road and Chinese modernization.
text: On 24 October 2017 the National Congress of the Communist Party of China (CPC) amended the Party Constitution to include Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The amendment placed a sitting leader's name alongside Marxism Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Theory of Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development in the party's formal guide for action. It also gave a name to what the party calls the new era, an official division of history into periods that now shapes party and state documents. This chapter explains how the official accounts present Xi's life and rise, what the thought and its associated slogans mean in those accounts, and how independent historians and reporters have interpreted the same period. The documentary base is uneven. Official biographies, congress reports, constitutional texts and white papers survive in abundance, and they are quoted here as evidence of what the party and state said. They are not by themselves evidence that the policies worked. Where scholars have reached different conclusions, or where independent reporting and United Nations documents contradict official statements, that is stated in the text. Family and youth in the official biography The basic facts come from a biographical notice issued by Xinhua at the time of Xi's third election as president. It states: "Xi Jinping, male, Han ethnicity, was born in June 1953 and is from Fuping, Shaanxi province. He began his first job in January 1969 and joined the Communist Party of China (CPC) in January 1974. Xi graduated from the School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Tsinghua University where he completed an in service graduate program in Marxist theory and ideological and political education. He holds a Doctor of Law degree" (Brief introduction of Xi Jinping, 10 March 2023). The same notice lists his four offices: General Secretary of the CPC Central Committee, Chairman of the CPC Central Military Commission, President of the People's Republic of China, and Chairman of the PRC Central Military Commission. Official profiles describe the family as the place where his political formation began, a household in which Party service was treated as ordinary. They call his father, Xi Zhongxun, "a revered CPC leader", and quote Xi saying that his father had "devoted himself wholeheartedly to the Chinese people" and that he had pledged to follow in his footsteps (Xi Jinping leads China on new journey, 25 October 2022). A 2025 feature says both parents "participated in the revolution at a young age and were very dedicated to their work" and recalls that Xi Zhongxun took on childcare duties, including bathing the children and doing their laundry, when his wife Qi Xin worked far from home (Xi Story: Women breaking free from household chores, 11 October 2025). These are recollections published by state media decades after the events. They tell us how the official biography wants the family to be remembered. Xi's first job began in January 1969, when he was not yet sixteen. The 2022 profile describes the scene: "At 15, as an 'educated youth,' Xi left Beijing for a village called Liangjiahe in an arid part of Northwest China's Shaanxi province, carrying with him a small sewing bag embroidered with Chinese characters 'mom's heart' by his mother Qi Xin" (Xi Jinping leads China on new journey). An educated youth was a city student sent to the countryside to work and learn from peasants during the Cultural Revolution, the political campaign that convulsed China from 1966 to 1976. The 2017 profile gives the dates: "He stayed in Liangjiahe, a small village in Northwest China's Shaanxi province, from 1969 to 1975" (Profile: Xi Jinping and his era, 17 November 2017). The official account stresses physical work and hardship. It says he slept in cave dwellings, suffered flea bites, herded sheep, carried manure and hauled coal, and that he recalled wanting "to make it possible for the villag

title: Global Survey of the Socialist Camp
description: The Comintern, the Eastern Bloc, Yugoslavia, Albania, national liberation movements, and a table of socialist states past and present.
text: The communist movement that emerged from the First World War was never a single settled bloc. Its history can be read in the resolutions of its congresses and in the disputes that repeatedly divided it, from the founding of the Communist International in 1919 to the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. Three threads run through the record. The first is the attempt to build an international organisation capable of directing revolutionary strategy. The second is the argument about what socialism meant and how it could be reached. The third is the encounter between that argument and actually existing states, including the liberation movements that drew on the movement's documents while adapting them to local conditions. The Communist International The Communist International, also called the Comintern or Third International, was constituted in Moscow at its First Congress on 2 to 6 March 1919. Three events formed its background: the October Revolution of 1917, the revolutionary wave that swept Central Europe in 1918 and 1919, and the collapse of the Second International over the war credits of 1914. Its founding manifesto was signed by Christian Rakovsky, V. I. Lenin, G. E. Zinoviev, L. D. Trotsky and Fritz Platten. The manifesto defined the new body's task as "to sum up the practical revolutionary experience of the working class, to cleanse the movement of its admixtures of opportunism and social patriotism, and to unite the forces of all the true revolutionary proletarian parties in order to further and hasten the complete victory of the communist revolution" (Manifesto of the First Congress of the Comintern, March 1919). The same document set out the internationalist premise that the national state had "become too narrow for the development of the productive forces", that the proletariat must "transform the whole world into one cooperative commonwealth", and that soviets, or workers' councils, were the form of proletarian state power (loc. cit.). The Second Congress of July to August 1920 is usually treated as the effective founding congress because it settled the organisational and colonial questions. Its Conditions of Admission to the Communist International, known as the Twenty One Conditions, required that "every party that wishes to belong to the Communist International must bear the name Communist Party of this or that country (Section of the Communist International)". Member parties had to expel "notorious opportunists" and support the Soviet republics through "legal or illegal propaganda" among troops sent against them (Minutes of the Second Congress, Seventh Session, 30 July 1920). Lenin's Preliminary Draft Theses on National and Colonial Questions and the Congress of the Peoples of the East held at Baku in September 1920 established the proposition that the colonial and national question was a component part of the world proletarian revolution. Both the Chinese Communist Party and the Chinese Red Army later appealed to that thesis in their polemics (Comintern archive, Second Congress and Baku Congress). The later world congresses recorded the shifting line of the International. The Third Congress of 22 June to 12 July 1921 adopted a "new course" of united front tactics and partial retreat under the conditions of the New Economic Policy (report on the Third Congress). The Fourth Congress of November to December 1922 developed the idea of a united front "from below and from above" and addressed the German question and the fight against fascism (resolutions of the Fourth Congress). The Fifth Congress of June to July 1924 pushed the "Bolshevization" of member parties and the campaign against Trotskyism (Theses and Resolutions, Fifth Congress). The Sixth Congress of July to September 1928 adopted the programme associated with the "Third Period" and the colonial theses, and sharpened the polemic against "social fascism" (programme of the Sixth Congress; colonial theses). title: Constitution of the People's Republic of China
description: Official full-text link, constitutional history, the complete Preamble and key articles reproduced verbatim from english.www.gov.cn.
text: A constitution is the fundamental law of a state. It sets out the institutions that hold power, the limits on that power and the rights the state claims to protect. China's Constitution has been rewritten four times since the People's Republic was founded in 1949 and amended five times since the current text was adopted in 1982. Each version belongs to a distinct political moment. The 1954 text accompanied the transition to socialism, the 1975 text was written during the Cultural Revolution, the 1978 text belongs to the uncertain interval after Mao's death, and the 1982 text was part of the reform era's institutional settlement. The amendments, especially that of 2018, record later shifts in the balance between Party and state. Where the official text comes from The official English text is published on the State Council's portal. Two official hosts carry different amended versions, one reflecting the 2004 amendments and the other the 2018 amendments: the full text at english.www.gov.cn and a second amended text on the same portal. The promulgating body is the National People's Congress (NPC), the national legislature that the Constitution calls the highest organ of state power. The text is republished by the State Council's official English portal with attribution to npc.gov.cn (official text). The document currently in force was adopted in 1982 and amended in 1988, 1993, 1999, 2004 and 2018. Four constitutions and the politics behind them Before there was a constitution, the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, an advisory body that represented the Communist Party and allied groups, adopted the Common Programme of 1949. It served as a provisional constitution while the new state was being organised. The NPC's own overview states that the Constitution "was adopted at the First Session of the First NPC in 1954 and comprehensively revised by the NPC in 1982. The current Constitution is the one promulgated and put into effect after this revision." That sentence compresses four constitutions into two dates. The first Constitution was adopted on 20 September 1954 by the First Session of the First NPC. It had 106 articles and was drafted in the period when the leadership was moving from the mixed economy of New Democracy toward socialist transformation. Its Preamble says that "from the founding of the People's Republic of China to the attainment of a socialist society is a period of transition" and that the state's task was "step by step, to bring about the socialist industrialization of the country and, step by step, to accomplish the socialist transformation of agriculture, handicrafts and capitalist industry and commerce" (1954 Constitution, Preamble). Mao Zedong chaired the drafting committee and a small drafting group worked in Hangzhou; Soviet constitutional experience, including the 1936 Soviet constitution, was an important reference. Official accounts report that about 150 million people took part in the subsequent discussion, though the discussion was organised by the Party and government (official account of the 1954 Constitution; Byron Weng on the 1982 draft). Jerome Cohen's study of China's changing constitution treats the 1954 document as the first serious attempt to give the new regime a working legal framework, and asks whether such documents are merely propaganda or carry legal weight (Cohen, "China's Changing Constitution," The China Quarterly 76, December 1978, 794 841, DOI 10.1017/S0305741000049584). The second Constitution was adopted on 17 January 1975 by the First Session of the Fourth NPC, while the Cultural Revolution was still under way. It had only 30 articles. Its Preamble says that socialist society covers a long historical period in which classes and class struggle persist, and that "These contradictions can be resolved only by depending on the theory of continued revolution under the dictatorship of the proletariat and on practice under its guidance" (1975 Constitution, Preamble). title: Nine January: The 1905 Revolution and the First Soviets
description: On 9 January 1905, by the Russian calendar, a crowd walked through St Petersburg carrying icons and a petition to the Winter Palace.
text: On 9 January 1905, by the Russian calendar, a crowd walked through St Petersburg carrying icons and a petition to the Winter Palace. The same day was 22 January in the countries that used the Western calendar; Russia used the Julian calendar, thirteen days behind. The petition had been drafted by a priest, Georgy Gapon, with workers in his association, and it asked for an eight hour day, a minimum wage of one rouble for unskilled workers and women, and an end to overtime. It also asked for an amnesty, civil freedoms and a Constituent Assembly, an elected national legislature. The language was deliberately suppliant, addressing the tsar as a father, but it ended with a warning: "For us there are but two roads, one leading to liberty and happiness, the other to the tomb." (St Petersburg workingmen's petition, 9/22 January 1905). The text we possess is the one printed in Gapon's 1906 memoir, not the signed sheet, and the petition was never delivered to the tsar. A second translation, credited to Daniel Field, gives a sharper political formula that is absent from the first: "and to that end order that elections to the Constituent Assembly be conducted under universal, secret and equal suffrage" (petition, Field translation). The difference between the two versions is itself evidence that the document circulated in more than one form. Nine January Gapon led the march and later described reaching the Tarakanovskii Canal. "We were not more than thirty yards from the soldiers, being separated from them only by the bridge over the Tarakanovskii Canal, which here marks the border of the city, when suddenly, without any warning and without a moment's delay, was heard the dry crack of many rifle shots." (Gapon, eyewitness account written later in 1905). He remembered a boy carrying a church lantern: "A little boy of ten years, who was carrying a church lantern, fell pierced by a bullet, but still held the lantern tightly and tried to rise again, when another shot struck him down." (Gapon, same account). Gapon had reason to present himself as a leader swept along by events rather than a man who had walked a crowd into troop lines, and his statement that no warning was audible bears directly on the dispute over whether the marchers were warned. Alexandra Kollontai, then a young Social Democrat, was in the street with the demonstrators. "Bloody Sunday, 1905, found me in the street. I was going with the demonstrators to the Winter Palace, and the picture of the massacre of unarmed, working folk is for ever imprinted on my memory." (Kollontai, autobiography written 1924). She recalled trusting, expectant faces and the dead and wounded, and said the killings destroyed belief that the tsar could deliver justice. Her passage was written nineteen years later for a Soviet encyclopedia project, and its cadences may reflect later revolutionary convention. Robert S. McCormick, the United States ambassador, telegraphed Washington on 23 January that "No evidence of evil intent on the part of the workingmen was manifested nor was there any evidence of hostile intent by the crowds beyond jeering at the officers and soldiers." (McCormick telegram, 23 January 1905). An eyewitness told him an order to fire had been given in the Alexander Park, where he put the killed and wounded at about sixty. His telegram also repeated the false claim that the petition had been written by a German socialist, an error relayed from a large employer. Such a mistake shows how badly elites understood what they were facing. Counting the dead The shootings did not begin a strike; they met one already under way. An unnamed worker wrote on 8 January that "The workers swear that they will come out into the square on Sunday 'with their wives and children'." (Letter quoted in Lenin, Revolutionary Days , chapter 7, published 18/31 January 1905). Lenin, in exile in Geneva and not an eyewitness, printed that letter alongside reports of closed newspapers, mass meetings and police withdraw

title: February 1917: Bread, Soldiers and the Fall of the Tsar
description: On the morning of 23 February 1917, by the calendar Russia still used, women walked out of the textile mills of Petrograd and into the streets over the price and scarcity of bread.
text: On the morning of 23 February 1917, by the calendar Russia still used, women walked out of the textile mills of Petrograd and into the streets over the price and scarcity of bread. Russia's old style Julian calendar ran thirteen days behind the new style Gregorian calendar used in Europe, so that date is 8 March in Western reckoning. The distinction matters, because witnesses and historians switch between the two, sometimes in a single paragraph. Leon Trotsky, writing in 1930 from documents rather than from presence in the city, put the women at the centre of the opening: "A great role is played by women workers in the relationship between workers and soldiers." He had his own argument, that the revolution began from below while the parties lagged behind, and his pages are not neutral. But the women's strike is where the contemporary record starts. Trotsky gives about ninety thousand on strike on 23 February and, by the government's own figures, two hundred and forty thousand by 25 February ( The History of the Russian Revolution , ch. 7). The Petrograd Soviet, an elected council of workers' and soldiers' deputies that formed in the course of the week, later compressed the grievance into one line: "In place of bread, the Tsar's Ministers gave them lead." (Soviet of Workers' Deputies proclamation, 12 March 1917; translated by Frank Golder, 1927. Source) In place of bread The crowds made the streets unusable. Meriel Buchanan, daughter of the British ambassador, reached Petrograd station on 12 March and found the ordinary life of the city stopped: "There are no cabs," I was told gently. "They have all gone out on strike." (Meriel Buchanan, recalling her arrival at Petrograd station, 12 March 1917; written 1918. Source) From the embassy she watched armoured lorries full of soldiers, the burning of the Law Courts, the storming of the Military Arsenal, and the surrender of the Fortress and the Admiralty. Others stood closer to the firing. Stinton Jones, a British businessman with an office on the Nevsky Prospect who says he spent twenty of every twenty four hours in the streets between 10 and 14 March, recorded police volleys, a machine gun, and Cossacks who refused to charge. His explanations are coloured by a conspiracy theory about police agents provoking the crowd; his observations are another matter. "To call those Five Days a bloodless revolution is absurd; but to call it the revolution of restraint would not be very wide of the mark." (Stinton Jones, Russia in Revolution , 1917, p. x. Source) Police fired from rooftops, and the order to fire came from the city commander, Khabalov. How many died on 11 March is not settled by the surviving accounts. What is settled is that the crowd kept coming. They would not shoot The decisive fact of the week was that the garrison would not fire on the people. Sir George Buchanan, the ambassador, set out the sequence in a memoir published in 1923 and based partly on his contemporary dispatches. The Pavlovsky Regiment mutinied when ordered to fire, and the Preobrazhensky and Volynsky regiments followed. "The answer to that question was given on Monday morning, when the soldiers of one of the Guard regiments — the Preobrazhenski — on being ordered to fire, turned and shot their officers." (Sir George Buchanan, My Mission to Russia , vol. II, 1923, p. 61. Source) His daughter saw the same thing from a different window: "the soldiers of the Preobrajinsky regiment turned out and shot their officers; while on the other side the Military Arsenal was stormed" (Meriel Buchanan, 12 March 1917. Source). By midday on 12 March, Sir George Buchanan reckoned that some twenty five thousand troops had joined the people. N. N. Sukhanov, a Menshevik journalist sitting in the Duma, watched the armed units arrive and noted the absence of the men who should have commanded them: "There were no officers visible at all with the patrols and detachments." (N. N. Sukhanov, 27 February 1917; translated from Russian by J

title: The October Revolution of 1917
description: At ten in the evening of 7 November 1917, by the calendar used in Western Europe, a shot was fired inside the Winter Palace.
text: At ten in the evening of 7 November 1917, by the calendar used in Western Europe, a shot was fired inside the Winter Palace. S. L. Maslov, the Minister of Supplies in the Provisional Government, was in the building and wrote down what he heard within days: "At 10:00 PM a shot was fired in the palace, followed by cries and shots from the cadets." (S. L. Maslov, "The Taking of the Winter Palace," Delo Naroda , 11 November 1917. Source) In Russia the same date was 25 October old style, the calendar running thirteen days behind. The government whose minister sat in the palace had been formed in February, after the tsar's abdication, and had never commanded a reliable armed force. The Bolsheviks, the party led by Lenin, held a majority in the Petrograd Soviet by the autumn. What happened that night was an armed seizure carried out through the Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee, and the men and women who described it disagreed about almost everything except the government's isolation. The decision Lenin pressed for insurrection from hiding in the Vyborg district. In a letter of 12 to 14 September 1917, later published in 1921, he set out the strategic case before any date was fixed: "The present task must be an armed uprising in Petrograd and Moscow (with its region), the seizing of power and the overthrow of the government." (V. I. Lenin, "The Bolsheviks Must Assume Power," 12–14 September 1917. Source) This was an argument addressed to party colleagues, not a record of what they decided. Its claim that a majority of the people stood with the Bolsheviks was an assertion, and the elections to the Constituent Assembly later that year returned a plurality for the Socialist Revolutionaries. On 10 October old style, 23 October new style, the Central Committee carried a resolution moved by Lenin, by ten votes to two, with Zinoviev and Kamenev dissenting. "all this places the armed uprising on the order of the day." (Bolshevik Central Committee resolution, 10 (23) October 1917. Source) The resolution fixed no date, which is why historians dispute how far Lenin imposed his will on the party. On the evening of 24 October he demanded action that night. "The situation is critical in the extreme. In fact it is now absolutely clear that to delay the uprising would be fatal." (V. I. Lenin, letter to Central Committee members, evening of 24 October (6 November) 1917. Source) The same letter subordinated the coming Congress of Soviets to the act itself: "The seizure of power is the business of the uprising; its political purpose will become clear after the seizure." (Lenin, same letter, 24 October 1917. Source) In public the body that would carry out the seizure said the opposite. The Military Revolutionary Committee, or MRC, was the Petrograd Soviet's operational arm. On 6 November it declared: "the Military Revolutionary Committee hereby declares that it exists not to make preparations to seize power but solely to defend the interests of the Petrograd garrison and the democracy against counter revolution and pogroms." (Military Revolutionary Committee declaration, 6 November 1917. Source) Placed beside Lenin's private letter, this is plainly a statement for an audience that included the garrison and the moderate socialists. It tells us what the Committee said, not what it intended. The night in the palace Smolny, a former school used as the Soviet's headquarters, held the MRC's crowded upper room. Anatoly Lunacharsky, a Bolshevik who became the first Commissar of Enlightenment, remembered orders dictated and signed on knees, typists working through the night and couriers leaving with mandates. "The dashing young sailors who came to tell the truth about the fighting then going on around the Winter Palace were listened to in admiration." (Anatoly Lunacharsky, "Smolny on the Night of the Storm," date of writing not stated on the source page. Source) This is an impression written by a participant in power, not a minute of the MRC. Leon Trotsk

title: Bread, Rifles and Fear: The Russian Civil War and War Communism, 1918–1922
description: In June 1918 Nestor Makhno, a Ukrainian anarchist commanding the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine, was shown into the Kremlin to speak with two of the men who had taken power in...
text: In June 1918 Nestor Makhno, a Ukrainian anarchist commanding the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine, was shown into the Kremlin to speak with two of the men who had taken power in October. He recalled Sverdlov assuming that southern peasants were either kulaks, meaning better off peasants, or supporters of the Ukrainian Rada. Makhno's own grievance was military. "The Red Guards, regardless of their numbers, carried on the attack against the enemy by moving along the railroads." (Nestor Makhno, recalling his June 1918 conversation with Lenin; written in exile in the 1930s, translated and published by the Kate Sharpley Library. Source) He wrote a dozen or more years later, for a movement audience, and the editor of the transcription warns that the dialogue cannot be taken as a literal transcript. The complaint still catches the central problem of these years. The revolution had to be defended by armies, and armies had to eat, and the food was in the villages. War Communism, the set of measures adopted from 1918, is usually described from the government's side as nationalisation, a monopoly in grain and compulsory requisitioning. To the people who underwent it, it was a series of struggles over food and authority in villages, railway stations, prison corridors and famine camps. Armies in a broken country After the treaty of Brest Litovsk took Russia out of the war in March 1918, German forces occupied large parts of the country and peasants seized land. The Volunteer Army formed at Novocherkassk from officers, cadets and schoolboys. Its commander, General Anton Denikin, remembered it in a memoir written after defeat: "There were deeds of valour and base depravity; heroism and cruelty; compassion and hatred; social tolerance and class antagonism." (General Anton Denikin, The White Army , 1930; translated from the Russian by Catherine Zvegintzov. Source) His army lived from theft and donations, and he records both the shock of finding mutilated Volunteer prisoners and the fact that his own men shot captured Bolsheviks in revenge. Denikin's political judgement was harsher than his own evidence. "From the very outset the Bolsheviks had summarized the nature of the civil war in a single word: Extermination!" (Denikin, The White Army , 1930; translated by Catherine Zvegintzov. Source) The memoir that makes that claim also documents White reprisals, which is why the record supports a cycle of violence rather than a single origin. The White rear was as hungry as the Red. General Pyotr Wrangel, the last commander of the White forces in the south, described regiments hoarding railway trains, troops living off the population, and requisitioning that damaged the very area the army depended on. "The excessive and disorderly requisitioning by the troops had completed the economic disruption" (General Pyotr Wrangel, memoirs written before his death in 1928; translated from the Russian via the French by Sophie Goulston. Source) He tried to bring soldiers before military courts for murder, pillage and illegal requisitioning, but his criticism was administrative, about discipline, not a challenge to the social programme his side defended. His English text comes through a French edition from which, at his own instruction, accounts of events of purely Russian interest were omitted. On the Red side, Makhno's complaint about the railways was a complaint about a war fought from armoured trains while villages defended themselves. Both armies lived from the country they were trying to govern. Grain and power The grain monopoly and prodrazvyorstka , the compulsory seizure of surplus grain from peasants, were meant to feed the cities and the army. In practice the burden fell unevenly. Arthur Ransome, a British correspondent in Moscow in early 1919 who moved in government circles, reported the Finance Commissar Krestinsky admitting as much. "It was intended to affect the propertied classes only, and thus to weaken the Kulaks (hard fists, rich peasants)

title: Kronstadt 1921: The Sailors and the State
description: Kronstadt was a fortress island in the Gulf of Finland, within sight of Petrograd.
text: Kronstadt was a fortress island in the Gulf of Finland, within sight of Petrograd (Avrich, Kronstadt, 1921 , p. 1). Its sailors had been celebrated as the pride of the revolution since 1917, when they helped the Bolsheviks take power and later served as commissars in the civil war. On the evening of 28 February 1921, the crews of the battleships Petropavlovsk and Sevastopol met to answer a question that had grown through the winter of War Communism, the system of grain requisitioning and military control that kept the cities fed: could a soviet, an elected council of workers' and soldiers' deputies, exist without the Communist Party running it? By 1 March a mass meeting had adopted a resolution drafted from the ship's proposals and chaired by Stepan Petrichenko. Alexander Berkman, writing in 1922 from reports reaching Petrograd, put the assembly at sixteen thousand. Fifteen demands The resolution was political before it was military. It asked for new soviet elections by secret ballot with free agitation beforehand; freedom of speech and press for workers, peasants, anarchists and left socialists; freedom of assembly for unions and peasant organisations; the release of political prisoners; a commission to review prison and camp cases; the abolition of the party's political departments and armed Communist detachments; the removal of the roadblocks that seized food; equal rations; and peasant freedom over land, cattle and handicraft work. "In view of the fact that the present soviets do not express the will of the workers and peasants, immediately to hold new elections by secret ballot, with freedom to carry on agitation beforehand for all workers and peasants" (Petropavlovsk resolution, adopted 1 March 1921. Source). Equal rations matter here, because Trotsky later suggested the sailors wanted privileges. The voting record matters too: the resolution carried with two abstentions, and Kalinin and Vasiliev voted against it. That record appears in the insurgent press and in two accounts written from outside the fortress, which is as close to corroboration as this evidence gets. Two newspapers In Moscow the response came within hours. On 2 March Trotsky, chairman of the Revolutionary War Council, issued a communiqué in Pravda naming an ex Tsarist general, Kozlovsky, as the leader and describing a French counter intelligence plot worked through White Guard leaflets and Socialist Revolutionaries, the peasant oriented party. "Behind the SRs, this time too, stood a Tsarist General." (Leon Trotsky, communiqué, 2 March 1921. Source). Kozlovsky was declared an outlaw, Petrograd was put under a state of siege, and power passed to a defence committee. This was propaganda written by a belligerent, not an investigation, and the claim that Kozlovsky directed the rising is contradicted by the rebels' own account. Their paper, Izvestiia , described a committee formed to hold the town and fortress and anxious to avoid a fight. "The Provisional Committee is deeply concerned that there should not be spilled a single drop of blood." (Provisional Revolutionary Committee of Kronstadt, Izvestiia no. 1, 3 March 1921; translated by Scott Zenkatsu Parker. Source). Its reports of an uprising already under way in Petrograd were false. Each paper is evidence of what its editors wanted readers to believe, not of what was happening elsewhere. The last warning On 5 March Trotsky issued an ultimatum. "Only those who surrender unconditionally may count on the mercy of the Soviet Republic." (Leon Trotsky, "A Last Warning," 5 March 1921. Source). It demanded that the arrested commissars be released and the garrison disarmed, and it assigned responsibility for civilian harm to the insurgents before any assault began. The much repeated phrase about shooting sailors like partridges is not in this signed text; it comes from later retellings. Emma Goldman was in the Tauride Palace on 4 March and heard Zinoviev, Kalinin, an arsenal worker and a sailor speak. She recorded

title: NEP: The Market, the Peasant and the Scissors, 1921–1929
description: On 15 March 1921, with the revolt at Kronstadt still unresolved, Lenin told the Tenth Party Congress that the revolution had to give way to the peasantry.
text: On 15 March 1921, with the revolt at Kronstadt still unresolved, Lenin told the Tenth Party Congress that the revolution had to give way to the peasantry. The New Economic Policy, or NEP, is the name later given to that retreat: a fixed tax in place of requisitioning, and permission for peasants to sell what remained in markets. "The question of substituting a tax for surplus grain appropriation is primarily and mainly a political question, for it is essentially a question of the attitude of the working class to the peasantry." (Vladimir Lenin, speech at the Tenth Party Congress, 15 March 1921, English translation. Source). He admitted that free exchange meant turning back towards capitalism and that the party had gone too far in nationalising local trade. Four days later the All Russian Central Executive Committee made the concession law. "This tax must be less than what the peasant has given up to this time through requisitions." (Tax in Kind decree, 21 March 1921, English translation. Source) The country the policy had to lift The change was made from weakness. J. P. Goodrich, a former governor of Indiana surveying the Volga famine zone for the American Relief Administration, slept in peasants' homes and checked communal records and warehouses, choosing villages away from the railways. "In making my hurried investigation I did not trust to Government statistics, to appearances in the bazaars or on the cities' streets" (J. P. Goodrich, letter to Herbert Hoover, 1 November 1921. Source). He found villagers gathering famine seeds, eating cabbage leaves and melon rinds and butchering dogs; in the German commune of Schilling he listed 25 deaths from cholera, 30 from typhus and 45 from starvation since January. Goodrich was arguing for congressional funds and discounted what he called sensational newspaper reporting, so his figures are a relief advocate's case, but the case rests on houses he entered and records he read. NEP had to work from this baseline. The market and its losers In the cities the retreat was visible first in shop windows. Walter Duranty, the New York Times correspondent in Moscow, watched cafés reopen and traced a Finnish trader who started with a trestle table of relief food packets and within a year had a shop, four salesmen and enough profit to retire. "The first twelve months of NEP. were like the old Roman Saturnalia, when for three days each year slaves and underlings might usurp with impunity the pleasures and privileges of their masters." (Walter Duranty, writing in 1935 about 1921–22. Source). A Nepman, the period's word for a private trader, became a recognisable type within a year or two. The state advertised through avant garde artists and lampooned the same figure as a tax evader; Kardovskii painted NEPmen , Lebedev a NEP Girl , Maliutin a set of NEP Types , and Kustodiev drew the city and village link, the smychka , as an official theme. Fedor Gladkov's novel Cement , published in 1925 and later revised, follows a soldier and factory worker back into a town where shops are opening while rations continue. "An ironical hand had obliterated the first ' not ' in the last of these sentences" (Fedor Gladkov, Cement , 1925, English translation of the 1929 edition. Source). Fiction cannot prove an event, but it records how the return of trade looked to a Bolshevik worker. Not everyone could profit from exchange. Markoosha Fischer, who first visited Russia in 1922 and later worked in child welfare there, recalled that NEP brought unemployment. "NEP brought unemployment. In order to become self supporting, enterprises reduced the number of workers and got rid in the first place of young people without practical experience." (Markoosha Fischer, My Lives in Russia , 1944, recalling 1922. Source). She also remembered former aristocrats hoping for their apartments back, and fathers who disapproved of Nepmen while hoping that NEP meant a return to the good old days. Her book was written after she left the Sovie

The last writings and the end

title: Collectivisation and the Ukrainian famine of 1932–33
description: On 5 April 1932, Oleksandra Radchenko, a teacher in the Kharkiv region, wrote in her diary: 'Famine, artificially created famine is taking on a nightmarish character.' (Oleksandra...
text: On 5 April 1932, Oleksandra Radchenko, a teacher in the Kharkiv region, wrote in her diary: "Famine, artificially created famine is taking on a nightmarish character." (Oleksandra Radchenko, diary, 5 April 1932; translated by Bohdan Klid. Source). She had recorded village life since February 1931: dekulakisation, cattle seizures, meat levies and peasants tried for having too little grain. She was not a peasant and says her own family was not starving, so she observed the worst rather than endured it, and she wrote privately before the outcome was known. Collectivisation, begun in 1929, replaced individual holdings with kolkhozes, collective farms whose land and livestock were held in common and whose grain deliveries the state fixed. The arithmetic of a quota In September 1932 a collective farmer named Shvets wrote to Hryhorii Petrovsky, head of the All Ukrainian Central Executive Committee, from the village of Horozhene. He set out his arithmetic: 600 hectares sown, 1,052 people to feed, a quota of 2,400 poods, a Russian weight of roughly sixteen kilograms, and nothing left for food. He asked "has full agreement been reached with our district authorities to leave our village and cooperative hungry for the whole year" (Y. Shvets to Hryhorii Petrovsky, 13 September 1932. Source). A petition is a rhetorical form, and Shvets wrote in loyal language, even comparing the authorities to former landowners. The letter shows what he thought might move Petrovsky, not what became of him. In the German settlement of Komarivka, Adam and Rosina Ketterling wrote to relatives in North Dakota in April 1933 that their brother had starved, that they had eaten no fat for three months, and that they lived on potato peelings, roots and grass. "Many people are dying of hunger. They swell up and then die." (Adam and Rosina Ketterling, 23 April 1933. Source). The letter reaches us through a newspaper and an edited collection, and its appeal for money shapes what it emphasises. Kiev writes to Moscow On 10 June 1932 Petrovsky told Moscow that after touring Pryluky, Lokhvytsia and other districts he had seen much of the countryside engulfed in famine, with swollen villagers asking why grain had been taken after a good harvest. Vlas Chubar, head of the Ukrainian government, reported hundreds of starving people dying in every village in March and April and children abandoned by their parents. Petrovsky asked for 1.5 to 2 million poods of relief grain and put the villagers' question: "Why did they create an artificial famine? After all, we had a harvest. Why did they take away the seed grain?" (Hryhorii Petrovsky to Molotov and Stalin, 10 June 1932. Source). Both reported to the men who set the quotas and had reason to shift blame; neither letter appeared in the press. Their use of the word famine matters because the leadership denied it publicly. Stalin rejected the appeals on 11 August: "If we do not correct the situation in Ukraine immediately, we could lose Ukraine." (Joseph Stalin to Lazar Kaganovich, 11 August 1932. Source). A month earlier Molotov and Kaganovich, sent to the Ukrainian party conference, had cabled that even Politburo members wanted the plan reduced and that they had refused. They advised on the wording instead. "In order not to give fodder to the foreign press, we deem it necessary to expound on this criticism in our press in moderate tones, without printing facts about the situation in the bad regions." (Molotov and Kaganovich to Stalin, 6 July 1932. Source). This is a decision about publicity, not a full account of what the leadership knew. The black boards The enforcing authority's own orders document the mechanism. A decree of 7 August 1932 made gleaning a crime punishable by imprisonment or execution. On 18 November the Ukrainian party committee subordinated all collective farm reserves, including seed and food, to the procurement plan and blacklisted farms accused of sabotage. "Immediate suspension of delivery of goods and of coo

title: The Moscow Trials
description: On 19 August 1936 sixteen men were brought before the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court in Moscow, the court that heard political cases, in the first of three public proceedings...
text: The transcripts On 19 August 1936 sixteen men were brought before the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court in Moscow, the court that heard political cases, in the first of three public proceedings later grouped together as the Moscow Trials. The state published each proceeding as a book, so the voices of the accused could be read far beyond the courtroom (1936 report). The English text is an abridgement from the People's Commissariat of Justice with no translator named. It shows the architecture of the proceeding and the way confessions were produced: Andrei Vyshinsky, the state attorney, repeatedly put words into a witness's mouth and asked him to confirm them. Questioned on 20 August, Grigori Zinoviev, a former leader of the Communist International, the body that directed communist parties worldwide, accepted that he and Lev Kamenev had practised "double dealing" since the 1920s and that Stalin, Kirov and Voroshilov had been marked for assassination. Asked whether he was telling the whole truth, he replied, "Now I am telling the whole truth to the end." (Zinoviev testimony, 20 August 1936). The record preserves the words, not the conditions in which they were spoken. The last pleas of 23 August read as a contest in self accusation. Kamenev told the court: "For ten years, if not more, I waged a struggle against the Party, against the government of the land of Soviets, and against Stalin personally." (last pleas, 23 August 1936). Zinoviev called Trotskyism "a variety of fascism." Smirnov still denied responsibility for acts after his arrest, and Holtzman's entire printed plea was one sentence denouncing his co defendants. That divergence matters because the editing was severe. Friedrich Adler, a socialist writing from the published report rather than the courtroom, noted that Vyshinsky's speech filled forty nine pages while the last pleas, said to last fourteen hours, were compressed into ten (Adler, The Witchcraft Trial in Moscow , 1936). What was cut cannot be recovered. Bukharin in the dock The last trial, in March 1938, put Nikolai Bukharin, a former Party theorist and one of the Old Bolsheviks, members of the party before 1917, before the same court on charges that a "bloc of Rights and Trotskyites" had acted for foreign intelligence services (1938 trial record). His testimony is the hardest document to read, because confession and rebuttal sit in the same text. He accepted political responsibility for the bloc yet denied the particular acts. Asked on 7 March whether he had sent Slepkov to organise an insurrection, he answered "Yes"; asked whether the plan was his, he said, "I have the right to tell the Court not what you want, but what really happened." (Bukharin interrogation, 7 March 1938). Asked to accept Rykov's or Sharangovich's word as proof, he replied, "If Rykov says it is, I have no grounds for not believing him" (Bukharin interrogation, March 1938). The case was built out of prisoners' statements about one another. His last plea of 12 March combined a sweeping confession with detailed denials. He denied complicity in the deaths of Kirov, Menzhinsky, Kuibyshev, Gorky and Peshkov, denied the 1918 plot to kill Lenin, and called the prosecutor's reasoning tautology, an argument that assumes what it sets out to prove. Explaining his own timing: "For three months I refused to say anything. Then I began to testify. Why? Because while in prison I made a revaluation of my entire past." (last plea, 12 March 1938). He attacked the court's principle: "The confession of the accused is not essential. The confession of the accused is a medieval principle of jurisprudence." (same). And: "I categorically deny that I was connected with foreign intelligence services, that they were my masters and that I acted in accordance with their wishes." (same). Whether this was strategy, damaged memory or the effect of interrogation cannot be settled from the transcript. The plea was also a performance addressed, as Bukharin said, to "We

title: The Archipelago: Forced Labour and the Camps
description: On 14 December 1926 three prisoners returning ill from the camp on the Solovetsky Islands, in the far north, wrote to the Soviet Central Executive Committee.
text: The promise and the petition On 14 December 1926 three prisoners returning ill from the camp on the Solovetsky Islands, in the far north, wrote to the Soviet Central Executive Committee. G. Zheleznov, Vinogradov and F. Belinskii described sixteen hour days, inadequate food and clothing, and punishment handed out to anyone who complained. "People die like flies, i.e., they die a slow and painful death," they wrote (letter from Solovki, 14 December 1926). The letter was a plea for intervention, and its writers had a reason to stress their suffering; the Library of Congress translation notes that the Russian grammar was corrected for clarity. It is a contemporary document nevertheless, sent a decade before the great purges. The Gulag was the system of forced labour camps and exile run by the Soviet secret police, its name an acronym from the Russian for the main camp administration. A decade after the Solovki letter the state published a constitution whose Article 127 read: "Citizens of the U.S.S.R. are guaranteed inviolability of the person. No person may be placed under arrest except by decision of a court or with the sanction of a procurator." (Constitution of the USSR, 5 December 1936). A procurator was the official who sanctioned arrests and supervised the law. The two documents sit easily side by side. One describes arbitrary power at a camp; the other promises that no one can be arrested without legal authority. A constitution records what a state promises, not what its agencies do. The island, the canal and the work Solovki, the monastery island in the White Sea, had become a camp in the 1920s. The White Sea–Baltic canal, dug in the early 1930s, was presented in Soviet propaganda as proof that work could "reforge" prisoners, remaking them into useful members of society. A photograph from 1932 in the collection of Memorial, the Moscow human rights archive, shows women prisoners at the canal works with shovels and wheelbarrows (Belomorkanal construction photograph, 1932). The catalogue names no photographer and cannot establish how many worked there or whether the scene was arranged. A 1933 camp newspaper drove the lesson home to prisoners in other camps: "Camp inmates of Karlag! Learn from the heroe workers of the White Sea Canal construction project how to fight and win." ( Putevka , no. 25 (53), 1933). The spelling "heroe" is the catalogue's. The canal was shallow and narrow, of little later use, but the story of reforging travelled. Inside the camps, work and food were joined. A norm was the quota a prisoner had to meet, and failure cut the ration. Evgeniia Ginzburg, a party official arrested in 1937 and sent to Kolyma in the far east, recalled: "We no longer had the strength to fulfill our output norms. Our rations were steadily reduced." (Ginzburg, "Days and Lives" exhibition). Lev Razgon, who spent years in the camps and later set norms himself, a privileged job known as being a trusty, was blunt: "In fact it was impossible to survive if you were felling timber." (Razgon, "Days and Lives" exhibition). A brigade was the gang of prisoners who worked together, and survival often depended on the job a prisoner held. Varlam Shalamov, who spent sixteen years in Kolyma, wrote after his release about cutting a road across virgin snow; the people who would use it were not the people who made it: "The people on the tractors and horses, however, will be not writers but readers." (Shalamov, "Through the Snow," 1956). In "Rain" he describes standing in prospecting shafts in cold rain: "We couldn't climb out of the shafts, or we would have been shot." (Shalamov, "Rain," Rayfield translation, 2018). These are stories, fiction shaped from what he witnessed, not depositions; the publisher says everything in them was experienced or seen by Shalamov. Hunger and the body Bread was measured in grams. Evfrosiniia Kersnovskaia, deported as a landowner in 1941, remembered the ration falling sharply: "Instead of 350 grams we got barely 120 1

title: Everyday life under Stalin: Stakhanovism and the kolkhoz
description: On the night of 30–31 August 1935 Aleksei Stakhanov, a hewer at a coal mine in the Donbass, cut 102 tons of coal in a single shift.
text: The record On the night of 30–31 August 1935 Aleksei Stakhanov, a hewer at a coal mine in the Donbass, cut 102 tons of coal in a single shift. A hewer is a miner who cuts coal at the working face. The Pravda correspondent who reported it wrote: "During a six hour shift, Stakhanov gave 102 tons of coal, which constitutes 10% of the mine's daily production, and earned 200 rubles." ( Pravda report, 1 September 1935, reproduced in Stakhanov's memoir). The figure became the name of a movement. Stakhanov's own account, published in 1937, complicates the story of the lone hero. He checked his jackhammer, a pneumatic drill, and arranged for two timberers, Shchigolev and Kalinin, to work behind him, with horse drivers and a repair shift moved to serve his face. He told his fellow miners: "There is no secret in the fact that I cut 102 tons of coal. This can be done by every experienced hewer who has mastered the technique of his business, if his labor is divided and he is given the opportunity to cut with a jackhammer the entire shift..." (Stakhanov, The Story of My Life , 1937). Sergo Ordzhonikidze, a member of the leadership, said the same at the Stakhanovite congress in November 1935: "It is sometimes thought that a single man [Stakhanov – N.M.] produced 102 tons. This is not true. These 102 tons were produced by an entire brigade." (Ordzhonikidze, quoted by N. Markin, 1936). Stakhanov's memoir is a partisan official self presentation, and this English text is a machine translation made in 2026; its wording needs checking against the Russian. Even so, the record was collective work. The campaign used the exceptional result to reset expectations. Stalin told about three thousand Stakhanovites in the Kremlin on 17 November 1935 that the movement was "profoundly revolutionary" and had arisen "almost spontaneously... from below, without any pressure whatsoever from the administrators of our enterprises," while ordering party bodies to curb managers and engineers who resisted (Stalin's speech to Stakhanovites, 17 November 1935). He admitted that 102 tons could not become the general norm. He tied the campaign to consumption: "If there is a shortage of bread, a shortage of butter and fats, a shortage of textiles, and if housing conditions are bad, freedom will not carry you very far." (same). And he described the mood he wanted: "Life has improved, comrades. Life has become more joyous. And when life is joyous, work goes well." (same). The rewards were real for the few: 200 rubles for one shift, a new apartment with a telephone and gramophone, orders and promotions in Stakhanov's telling. A Stakhanovite was a worker whose record was held up as an example. A contemporary opponent, N. Markin, collected hostile press reports of resentment, assaults and trials of workers who resisted; he was not in the country and selected his items, so these are a digest, not court records (Markin, "The Stakhanovist Movement," 1936). Both accounts are partial. Stakhanov had genuine skill and real support from mine officials; the conditions he describes were available to very few. Nine girls on the steppe A different picture comes from the land. Sergei Tretiakov, a writer who lived for two years in the countryside, reported in 1935 on a women's tractor brigade in the Don steppe led by Pasha Angelina. A kolkhoz was a collective farm in which land and the main implements were owned jointly and members worked under an elected chairman, usually keeping a small private plot. The male trainees scorned the women; there were no sleeping huts and no fuel, and the brigade shared a four room house. Tretiakov wrote: "The first seven days, when they weren't given anywhere to sleep, they worked without leaving their tractors." (Tretiakov, "Nine Girls," 1935, translated by James von Geldern). He describes twenty hour shifts to honour a promise of 1,200 hectares per tractor, frozen fingers and a gramophone in the field cabin. His reportage was written inside the campaign and

title: The Woman Question in the Soviet Union: Emancipation, the Double Burden and the Family
description: In a Soviet archival file there is a telegram sent to Mikhail Kalinin, the nominal head of state, by an army medical officer in Khabarovsk named Anisimov.
text: In a Soviet archival file there is a telegram sent to Mikhail Kalinin, the nominal head of state, by an army medical officer in Khabarovsk named Anisimov. "Because [of] pregnancy Anisimova left family[.] Request decision terminate pregnancyU restoring family [of] four people [to] normal life[.]" (Anisimov to Kalinin, telegram, GARF f. 7523, op. 23, d. 209, l. 60; OCR artefacts retained, soviethistory.msu.edu). The page gives no date. Anisimova does not speak in the telegram; her husband presents her pregnancy as an administrative fault to be corrected by the leadership. The message belongs to 1936, the year abortion was criminalised across the Soviet Union. It is a small document, and it sits at the end of a long argument about whether the family was a private matter or a public task. A question without a name Socialists had argued about the position of women since the nineteenth century. In 1909 a young Russian Marxist named Alexandra Kollontai, then a Menshevik, wrote that "The followers of historical materialism reject the existence of a special woman question separate from the general social question of our day. Specific economic factors were behind the subordination of women; natural qualities have been a secondary factor in this process." (Alexandra Kollontai, 1909; trans. Alix Holt, marxists.org). By the "woman question" she meant the problem of why women were subordinate and how that might end. She refused to treat it as separate from the question of class, and she attacked bourgeois feminists for seeking legal reform while leaving property relations untouched. The essay was written eight years before the revolution, so it is a statement of a method, not a description of Soviet conditions. Kollontai's point was that changing the law did not move the work. In 1920, by then a Bolshevik and a government minister, she wrote: "Capitalism has placed a crushing burden on woman's shoulders: it has made her a wage worker without having reduced her cares as housekeeper or mother. Woman staggers beneath the weight of this triple load." (Alexandra Kollontai, Communism and the Family , 1920; trans. Alix Holt, marxists.org). This is the "double burden" in its original form, the combined load of paid employment, housekeeping and childrearing. Kollontai's claim was that the burden could not be shifted onto individual women, and that the state, rather than the husband, had to carry it. What the state promised Within months of the seizure of power the new regime tried to make that analysis law. The 1918 Family Code of the Russian Soviet Federated Socialist Republic abolished community of property between spouses: "Marriage does not establish community of property." (Original Family Law of the RSFSR, 17 October 1918, soviethistory.msu.edu). Either spouse could petition for divorce, children born outside marriage were placed on the same footing as others, and a mother could name a father and ask a court to make him share the costs. The purpose was to strip the household of the economic functions that, in the Marxist view, held it together. At the first congress of the Communist International in March 1919, Kollontai introduced a resolution declaring: "The dictatorship of the proletariat can be realized and kept up only through the active and energetic participation of the women of the working class." (Comintern resolution introduced by Kollontai, 6 March 1919, soviethistory.msu.edu). It treated the reform of the family and the socialist rearing of children as central tasks, and asserted that women produced no less than half of all existing values, a figure offered without a stated method. Kollontai put the domestic vision more concretely to an American visitor. "We must build a new society in which women are not expected to drudge all day in kitchens. We must have, in Russia, community restaurants, central kitchens, central laundries — institutions which leave the working woman free to devote her evenings to instructive reading or recreat

title: The National Operations: Ethnicity and the Soviet Purges, 1937–1938
description: Georgios Zacharias was eight years old when militiamen came to his family's home in Odessa.
text: Georgios Zacharias was eight years old when militiamen came to his family's home in Odessa. He remembered the hour for the rest of his life. "21 декабря 1937 года около 2.30 3 часа ночи к нам домой пришли милиционеры и провели обыск." (Georgios Zacharias, memoir written in 2007; Russian text at Greek Martirolog, greek martirolog.com), that is, "Around half past two or three in the morning on 21 December 1937, militiamen came to our home and searched it." His father Dionysios was sentenced in January and shot in Odessa on 2 April 1938. The search was part of an operation named for a nationality. This chapter follows the documents that named the nationalities, and the people who lived under them. A system of categories The Soviet state had spent the 1920s promoting native languages and local officials in its republics. By 1937 the same identities were being read as evidence of disloyalty. The machinery belonged to the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, and it worked through secret operational orders. The first of the national operations in time was Order No. 00439 of 25 July 1937, which named German citizens at military plants, defence workshops and railways. "Начиная с 29 июля с. г. приступить к арестам всех установленных вами германских подданных" (NKVD Order No. 00439, 25 July 1937, Russian text at Russian Wikisource), or "From 29 July, begin arresting all German citizens identified by you." Lists were to be compiled in three days and arrests completed in five. The order targeted citizenship in the first instance; its extension to Soviet citizens of German descent was a later step, documented in the scholarship rather than in this order alone. Five days later came the broader order that historians call the kulak operation, though its reach went well beyond peasants deemed wealthy. NKVD Operational Order No. 00447 of 30 July 1937 assigned numerical quotas to each region and republic and divided victims into two categories. "a) The first category are the most hostile of the enumerated elements. They are subject to immediate arrest, and after their cases have been considered by a three person tribunal [troika] they are TO BE SHOT." (NKVD Operational Order No. 00447, 30 July 1937; English translation by Evan Mawdsley, reproduced by Seventeen Moments in Soviet History, soviethistory.msu.edu). A troika was a three person panel empowered to sentence without a normal trial. The quotas included 500 in the first category and 1,000 in the second for the Armenian republic, and 1,500 and 3,750 for Azerbaijan, which shows that the campaign was administered through the national republics. The target groups also included what the order called non Russian nationalists. The Polish operation followed on 11 August. "(b) all prisoners of war from the Polish Army remaining in the USSR; (c) refugees from Poland regardless of the time of their arrival in the USSR" (NKVD Order No. 00485, 11 August 1937; English translation published by the Institute of National Remembrance / Mieroszewski Centre, operacja polska.pl). The order set a start date of 20 August, a three month timetable and two categories, those to be shot and those to be imprisoned for no less than five to eight years. Lists were approved in batches and results telegraphed every five days. Its claim that a Polish military network existed was the state's allegation, not an established fact. A fourth order, No. 00486 of 15 August, reached into the household. Wives of men labelled spies or enemies of the people were sent for five to eight years to the Temnikov camp for failing to report their husbands, and children were often placed in orphanages or labour camps. Lev Tsel'merovskii, a nineteen year old factory worker and Komsomol member from Petrozavodsk, wrote to the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet in September 1938 from exile in Chimkent. His father had been arrested under Article 58, the clause of the Soviet criminal code used for political offences. "my father (he was arrested and I am exile

title: The Last Year: 1991 and the End of the USSR
description: On 17 March 1991 Soviet citizens were asked whether to preserve 'the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics as a renewed federation of equal sovereign republics in which the rights and...
text: On 17 March 1991 Soviet citizens were asked whether to preserve "the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics as a renewed federation of equal sovereign republics in which the rights and freedom of an individual of any nationality will be fully guaranteed" (Presidential Library of Russia; question reproduced by Michigan State University). The wording mattered: this was a vote for a renewed federation of sovereign republics, not for the centralized state as it stood. Nine of fifteen republics took part and six boycotted. Of 148.5 million participants, 113.5 million, or 76.43 per cent, voted yes. Both sides later claimed the mandate. Novo Ogarevo in clauses The negotiations known as Novo Ogarevo turned the vote into a draft treaty, published on 15 August 1991. "Each republic party to the treaty is a sovereign state." (Draft Treaty on the Union of Sovereign States, 15 August 1991). The Union of Soviet Sovereign Republics would be a federal state to which each republic voluntarily delegated listed powers. Its preamble invoked the March referendum, Article 1 gave republics a right to secede by an agreed procedure, and Article 23 provided that the 1922 treaty on the formation of the USSR would lose effect on signature. This is what "renewed Union" meant to the people drafting it. The text was a working translation of a draft never signed; it records an intention, not an outcome. August: the appeal and the tank On 18 August an eight man State Committee for the State of Emergency (GKChP), headed by Vice President Gennady Yanaev, issued an appeal through the Soviet news agency TASS: "A mortal danger has come to loom large over our great Motherland." (Appeal to the Soviet People, 18 August 1991). The committee claimed constitutional authority, said reform had entered a blind alley and declared that the referendum's results had been "trampled upon". It was issued by men who had detained the president, and its account of popular relief is an assertion, not corroborated fact. Boris Yeltsin, president of the Russian republic, spoke the next day from the parliament building, known as the White House, with a tank outside: "Regardless of the reasons given for his removal, we are dealing with a rightist, reactionary, anti constitutional coup." (Yeltsin, 19 August 1991). He declared the committee's decisions unlawful, said the treaty signing planned for 20 August had been cancelled and called for an unlimited general strike. On 20 August he named individual plotters and held them responsible for inflation, military poverty and bloodshed in the Baltic: "The democratic changes our people struggled for over the past five years have been trampled underfoot." (Yeltsin, 20 August 1991). Each speech was a political act presenting its author as the defender of constitutional order; neither describes the defence of the building. After the putsch Eleven days after his return to Moscow from detention at Foros, Gorbachev told the American senator Sam Nunn that the forces pulling the country together had returned: "First and foremost to exclude any encouragement of any processes of disintegration as our reforms proceed." (conversation with Sam Nunn, 2 September 1991). He said the approaching treaty signing had precipitated the putsch. Asked whether nuclear weapons had stayed under central control during the coup, he answered: "There could be no question about them being out of central control." (Ibid.). This was a Soviet record of a private conversation, translated for the National Security Archive. It preserves Gorbachev's own optimistic reading of his position, which the following months contradicted, and the Archive notes that Nunn was not reassured. At a state dinner in Madrid on 29 October he set out his idea of a "full blooded" union with a common economic space and unified armed forces: "I declare clearly and definitively I am for the union state." (dinner conversation, 29 October 1991). He called Yeltsin "a person who is not always reliable" and identifie
