title: The Revolution That Stopped: Germany, 1918–1919
description: The German revolution began with a refusal.
text: The German revolution began with a refusal. In the last weeks of the war the naval command ordered the fleet at Kiel to put to sea for a final battle against Britain, and sailors refused to go. They and the workers of the port seized the city, released prisoners and formed a soldiers' council, an elected body of sailors and soldiers. On 4 November 1918 the council issued fourteen demands, including freedom of speech and press, an end to mail censorship, the prevention of another fleet sortie, and the election of officers by their units. The leaflet ended with a claim of authority: "These demands are orders of the Soldiers’ Council and are binding for every military person." (Soldiers' Council of Kiel, 4 November 1918; translated by Klaus Kuhl and GHDI staff, germanhistorydocs.org). A demand list is not a record of what was carried out, but it shows how the revolution understood itself at the start. It was a military revolt with a political programme, not a party conspiracy. Two republics and an argument Workers' and soldiers' councils spread through the cities in the days that followed. On 9 November, Philipp Scheidemann of the Social Democratic Party, the largest socialist party, declared a German republic from a window of the Reichstag; Karl Liebknecht proclaimed a socialist republic later the same day. In the weeks before, the shop steward Richard Müller had chaired the executive body of the councils in Berlin. Writing in 1921, he placed the origins of the council movement in wartime strikes and factory committees of 1916 to 1918, not in the Russian example of the previous year: "In November 1918, the revolutionary socialists recognised that the realisation of formal democracy, of political equality, the convening of the National Assembly, was tantamount to the re establishment of the shaken class rule of the bourgeoisie" (Richard Müller, "The Council System in Germany", 1921; translated by Ryan Breeden, historicalmaterialism.org). Müller was a defeated participant writing an argument as well as a memory, and his claim that the revolution was not made sits awkwardly beside his own account of preparing an insurrection. A provisional government, the Council of People's Deputies, brought together three ministers of the Social Democratic Party and three of the Independent Social Democratic Party, a breakaway formed over the war. Its photograph postcard, made for collectors, showed all six with a red flag. Friedrich Ebert, the Social Democratic leader who co chaired it, welcomed nine returning divisions to Berlin on 10 December. He told them that no enemy had overcome them and that the new state would be a "polity of labor": "The socialist republic that welcomes you through me will be a polity of labor." (Friedrich Ebert, address to homecoming troops, 10 December 1918; translated by Pam Selwyn, germanhistorydocs.org). His words joined recognition of the soldiers' sacrifice to a demand that they now lay down their arms. The claim that the army had not been defeated fed the story, current after the war, that it had been betrayed at home. The other half of the arrangement emerged later. Wilhelm Groener, who led the army high command from October 1918, described secret telephone agreements with Ebert, a plan to bring divisions into Berlin, and a threat to resign if the councils' congress was allowed to reorganise the army on its own terms. "All that remained was to muster a volunteer army, which alone could take up the battle against the urban masses of workers." (Wilhelm Groener, memoirs published 1957; translated by Pam Selwyn, germanhistorydocs.org). The arrangement was denied until 1925, and Groener wrote after his death with an interest in presenting the army as the restorer of order. His pages are a memory of conversations, not the pact itself. The argument among socialists was concrete and organisational: whether power belonged in the councils or in a National Assembly, and who would control the army. Rosa Luxemburg, a founde

title: Nine Days in May: The General Strike of 1926 and the Communist Party of Great Britain
description: On the first of May 1926, in the pit village of Pendleton, a miner's wife told a reporter from the Manchester Evening News what a stoppage meant in her kitchen: 'it is the women who have...
text: On the first of May 1926, in the pit village of Pendleton, a miner's wife told a reporter from the Manchester Evening News what a stoppage meant in her kitchen: "it is the women who have to find and put the dumplings in the stew." (1 May 1926, reproduced by the North West Labour History Society; Source: nwlh.org.uk) The sentence came from a newspaper that supported the government, and it survived because a local history society copied it out decades later. It puts the unpaid work of feeding a striking household where most accounts of 1926 leave it out, in the kitchen rather than the negotiating room. What followed was the only general strike Britain has ever known. A general strike is a coordinated stoppage across many industries at once, so that a single trade cannot be isolated and worn down. It ran from 3 to 12 May 1926 and drew roughly three million workers out in support of coal miners who had been locked out of the pits. A lockout is the employer's version of a strike: the workplaces are closed and pay withheld until the men accept terms. The miners were represented by the Miners' Federation of Great Britain, the national body linking the coalfield unions, whose secretary A. J. Cook had made the refusal of wage cuts and longer hours into the strike's watchword. Cook wrote within weeks of the calling off that the stand had reached far beyond Britain: "The whole world is stirred by the miners' struggle, by the refusal of the men or their leaders to compromise on either hours or wages." (A. J. Cook, "The Great Mining Crisis", July 1926; Marxists Internet Archive: mining crisis) The Communist Party of Great Britain (CPGB), a small party formed in 1920 with little influence over the union leadership, printed the demand in its own manifesto: "All Together Behind the Miners Not a Penny off the Pay. Not a Second on the Day." (CPGB, "Fight to Win!" manifesto, May 1926, reproduced by J. T. Murphy; Marxists Internet Archive: strike 04) The miners' own federation gave the same reasoning a harder edge: "from first to last there was never any possibility of the forces arrayed against the miners accepting anything but lower wages, longer hours and district agreements unless compelled to do so by the united strength of the working class." (Miners' Federation of Great Britain, Statement on the General Strike of May 1926 , quoted by National Mining Museum Scotland; Source: nationalminingmuseum.com) In the pit villages that unity had a daily, practical form. Soup kitchens were staffed by miners and their wives, and the CPGB writer Marjorie Pollitt argued that parents should press their children's teachers to act: "In all pit areas, the parents should get the teachers to join them in their demand for free meals for children." (Marjorie Pollitt, June 1926; Marxists Internet Archive: x01) A strike that surprised its own leaders The strike was directed by the General Council of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), the national body that brought Britain's trade unions together. The scale took even its supporters unawares. J. T. Murphy, chairman of the CPGB and involved in the strike's daily direction, recalled that his party was caught by surprise by the union executives' vote, and that workers began packing their tools on 3 May. Jack Tanner, a trade unionist and Communist reporting on rank and file opinion in July 1926, found that the response in the districts he knew exceeded expectations and that non unionists came out alongside union members. Contemporaries disagreed sharply about the numbers because they counted different things: Murphy wrote of three and a half to four million on the first full day, a museum account gives over 1.5 million on 3 May, and later summaries settle around three million across the nine days. None of the first hand sources explains how its figure was reached, so the strike's size is best held as a range rather than a single total. Local organisation mattered as much as national votes. title: Spain 1936–39: War, Revolution and the Retreat
description: In December 1936 George Orwell arrived in Barcelona to join a militia, a part-time citizen army rather than a regular force.
text: In December 1936 George Orwell arrived in Barcelona to join a militia, a part time citizen army rather than a regular force. The English writer had gone to Spain to fight for the Republic against the military rising of that July. What he found was not simply a city preparing for war. "It was the first time that I had ever been in a town where the working class was in the saddle." (George Orwell, Homage to Catalonia , 1938; Marxists Internet Archive: homage catalonia) Shops, transport and even bootblacks had been collectivised, meaning they were run collectively by the people who worked in them rather than by private owners. Tips and formal forms of address had disappeared, and red and black flags hung beside the Republican tricolour. Orwell had joined the militia of the Partido Obrero de Unificación Marxista (POUM), an independent Marxist party in Catalonia that believed the war and the social revolution had to be pursued together. The government Orwell had come to defend was a Popular Front, a coalition of left and liberal parties and trade unions formed to oppose fascism. In July 1936 its best known voice was Dolores Ibárruri, a leader of the Communist Party of Spain (PCE) and a Popular Front deputy, broadcasting from the Ministry of the Interior in Madrid on 19 July: "¡Viva el Frente Popular! ¡Viva la unión de todos los antifascistas! ¡Viva la República del pueblo! ¡Los fascistas no pasarán! ¡No pasarán!" (Marxists Internet Archive: jul 19) The Spanish original is given here; the English gloss, "Long live the Popular Front! Long live the union of all antifascists! Long live the Republic of the people! The fascists shall not pass! They shall not pass!", is not a published translation. The appeal named workers, peasants, women and soldiers, and the closing words, "they shall not pass", became the Republic's watchword. A poster of the same weeks showed two men and a woman firing over a fallen comrade while reinforcements arrived, one man wearing the cap of the anarcho syndicalist CNT FAI federation, the other that of the socialist UGT union. The image made the alliance look like a single fighting force. A coalition under fire The alliance was never as solid as its posters suggested. The military rising had split Spain, and in Toledo the Nationalists, as the rebel forces were called, held the Alcázar fortress. José Moscardó, the commander there, kept an official diary from 18 July to 28 September 1936 recording bombardments, casualty lists, requisitions of food, the mapping of a suspected mine and the dropping of supplies by rebel aircraft. On 23 July he noted, in restrained military language, that the commander of the Republican militias had telephoned to say he held Moscardó's son and would shoot him unless the fortress surrendered. The relief of the garrison on 28 September made the siege a founding story of the Francoist cause, and later commemoration built a myth around an exchange the diary itself does not narrate in the famous terms. The log tells us what one officer recorded for his superiors; it says nothing about the disposition or losses of the besiegers. Guernica On 26 April 1937 German and Italian aircraft flying for the Nationalists attacked Guernica, a small Basque market town well behind the front. Three reporters reached it independently and left accounts that corroborate one another in outline. Elizabeth Wilkinson of the Daily Worker was in the town before the raid: "Yesterday at about 1.30 pm I arrived in Guernica, the ancient capital of the Basque country. It was a peaceful town, with no factories, no munition works and no troops stationed there." (Elizabeth Wilkinson, Daily Worker , 27 April 1937; Source: spartacus educational.com) George Steer of The Times walked the ruins after midnight and again the following afternoon: "Guernica was not a military objective. A factory producing war material lay outside the town and was untouched. So were two barracks some distance from the town." (George Steer, The Time

title: The Popular Front: Unity Against Fascism and the Shadow of Moscow, 1934–1938
description: In June 1936, with a socialist government in power in France, metalworkers in Paris occupied their factories rather than merely walking out.
text: In June 1936, with a socialist government in power in France, metalworkers in Paris occupied their factories rather than merely walking out. Simone Weil, a philosopher who had worked in Renault and Alsthom plants in 1934 and 1935, wrote about the strike wave from the workers' side under the pen name S. Galois. She rejected the two conspiracy theories then current, that Communists had provoked the occupations to embarrass the government and that employers had staged them, and said no provocation was needed. What she recorded was a change in the balance of feeling on the shop floor. "Indépendamment des revendications, cette grève est en elle même une joie. Une joie pure. Une joie sans mélange." (Simone Weil, "La vie et la grève des ouvrières métallos", 10 June 1936; Source: fr.wikisource.org) The strike was a joy in itself, quite apart from the demands. Weil had left wage work by then and wrote as a sympathetic observer of women metalworkers, not as one of them, but her account supplies the grievance that the official settlement does not: the pace of the line, the threat of dismissal, hunger, an unheated changing room, and the sense that with a socialist in power a worker was no longer automatically the weaker party before his employer. The Popular Front was the coalition that had brought that government to office. It joined socialists, Communists, radicals and liberals against fascism, the far right movement that had taken power in Italy and Germany and promised to destroy left wing politics by force. In France the coalition won the election of 1936, and workers answered with one of the largest strike waves in the country's history up to that date. The turn and the minimum programme The new line had been stated publicly a year earlier. On 2 August 1935 Georgi Dimitrov, recently released from Nazi custody after the Leipzig trial and by then a leading official of the Communist International, the body that coordinated communist parties across countries, addressed its Seventh Congress. He defined the enemy in economic terms: "Fascism is the power of finance capital itself. It is the organization of terrorist vengeance against the working class and the revolutionary section of the peasantry and intelligentsia." (Georgi Dimitrov, report to the Seventh Comintern Congress, 2 August 1935, translated from the Sofia Press Selected Works edition, 1972; Marxists Internet Archive: 08 02) He blamed the Social Democrats' willingness to cooperate with capitalist parties for the defeats in Germany, Austria and Spain, and called for a "united front" and an "anti fascist people's front", including a section headed "A United Front government". His insistence that the road could be blocked was a claim about political will: "Yes, comrades, the road to fascism can be blocked. It is quite possible. It depends on ourselves on the workers, the peasants and all working people." (same report and translation; Marxists Internet Archive: 08 02) This was doctrine announced from a congress platform, not a record of private instructions to the French or Spanish parties. What such a front meant in practice can be read in the Spanish pact of 16 January 1936, signed by republican parties, the Socialist Party with its trade union UGT, the Communist Party, a syndicalist party and the POUM. Its promises were amnesty for political offences since November 1933, reinstatement of dismissed workers, compensation for victims of repression, restored constitutional guarantees, agrarian measures, public works and labour courts. The signatories agreed "sin perjuicio de dejar a salvo los postulados de sus doctrinas, han llegado ha comprometer un plan político común" ("without prejudice to preserving the tenets of their doctrines, they have agreed a common political plan"; the "ha" is in the transcription). (Spanish Popular Front pact, 16 January 1936; Source: fuenterrebollo.com) The republican parties expressly refused the Socialist demands for nationalisation of land with free

title: Budapest 1956: The Revolution and the Workers' Councils
description: On 22 October 1956, students at the Building Industry Technological University in Budapest printed sixteen demands as leaflets.
text: On 22 October 1956, students at the Building Industry Technological University in Budapest printed sixteen demands as leaflets. They survive in a translation reproduced in a United Nations report, and they matter because the demands were political and economic before any fighting began. "We demand the immediate withdrawal of all Soviet troops in accordance with the provisions of the Peace Treaty." (students of the Building Industry Technological University, 22 October 1956) The students asked for secret ballot elections, a government led by Imre Nagy and an end to the one party system. "We demand complete freedom of opinion and expression, freedom of the Press and a free Radio" (same resolution, 22 October 1956). They also wanted revised work norms, a minimum wage and the removal of the Stalin statue. The last point called a demonstration for the next day and invited factory workers to join it. This was a programme of specific claims, issued as the authorities began loosening the rigid controls of Stalin's rule after his death, a shift known as de Stalinisation. The demands before the fighting The demonstration of 23 October drew students, workers and soldiers. A delegation went to the Radio Building to ask that all sixteen points be broadcast and was refused; the ÁVH, the state security police, fired on the crowd, and the first weapons came from soldiers and factory stores. The UN Special Committee, which heard 111 refugees in five cities in early 1957, concluded: "What took place in Hungary was a spontaneous national uprising, caused by long standing grievances." (UN Special Committee on the Problem of Hungary, findings, June 1957) An anonymous professor of philosophy told the committee: "that the Hungarian revolution had no leaders. It was not organized; it was not centrally directed." (anonymous witness heard by the UN Special Committee, 1957) Peter Fryer, correspondent of the British Communist Daily Worker , reached Budapest on 31 October and recorded the same pattern of security police shootings in the provinces. The committee was denied entry to Hungary and Fryer was a communist breaking with his party; their agreement on the sequence carries weight. Nagy's five days Imre Nagy was a communist prime minister, not an opponent of the regime. His broadcasts show a position shifting under pressure. On 28 October he still spoke of a "great national democratic movement" while warning that "criminal elements" had used it; by 30 October he had abolished the one party system and named a coalition cabinet. On 1 November he declared neutrality, meaning Hungary would leave the Soviet led military alliance, the Warsaw Pact: "The Hungarian people desire the consolidation and further development of the achievements of its national revolution without joining any power blocs." (Imre Nagy, declaration of neutrality, 1 November 1956) On 4 November, as Soviet troops returned, he said: "Our troops are fighting. The Government is in its place." (Imre Nagy, radio broadcast, 4 November 1956) A variant text of his last address, with no recording or named translator, has him saying "it is possible that I shall only be able to stay at my post for one or two hours" (Imre Nagy, "Last Message", 4 November 1956). He asked leaders to leave the country if they could. The two English versions disagree, so the exact final wording is unsettled. What Moscow decided Budapest could not see the decision that sealed the revolt. On 31 October the Soviet leadership reversed its own decision to withdraw. Khrushchev told the Presidium: "We should reexamine our assessment and should not withdraw our troops from Hungary and Budapest. We should take the initiative in restoring order in Hungary." (Nikita Khrushchev, CPSU Presidium, 31 October 1956) The notes show a plan to install a provisional government under János Kádár before any Kádár government existed. At five in the morning on 4 November, Soviet guns opened on the city. The American legation telexed Washington

title: Socialism with a Human Face: The Prague Spring and the Invasion of 1968
description: In January 1968 the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia replaced Antonín Novotný with Alexander Dubček.
text: In January 1968 the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia replaced Antonín Novotný with Alexander Dubček. In April its Central Committee adopted the Action Programme, which named the "personality cult", the exaggerated praise of one leader, and directive planning, in which officials fixed targets for every enterprise, as obstacles. It promised free speech and assembly, an end to censorship, equal standing for Czechs and Slovaks in a federal state, and a new constitution. Western journalists called the project "socialism with a human face", a phrase the sociologist Radovan Richta had used, according to Zdeněk Mlynář, one of its principal drafters. The programme insisted the party kept its leading role, its sole right to govern: "The Communist Party enjoys the voluntary support of the people; it does not practice its leading role by ruling the society but by most devotedly serving its free, progressive socialist development." (Central Committee of the KSČ, Action Programme, adopted 5 April 1968, translated by Zdravko Saveski) This was a statement of intent, not a record of change. A programme from within The reforms began inside the party. Nine weeks after the programme, on 27 June, the writer Ludvík Vaculík published a manifesto, "Two Thousand Words", in four Prague newspapers. He attacked the apparatus of officials who ran the farms and factories, called for workers' councils and warned that their adversaries would not take a summer holiday: "The spring is over and will never return. By winter we will know all." (Ludvík Vaculík, "Two Thousand Words", 27 June 1968) The five allied parties that later intervened read this one intellectual's intervention as proof of counter revolution, a return to the old order. That was their reading, not a neutral description. The party pressed from both sides Moscow and four allies answered in a letter of 15 July, released by the Soviet news agency TASS on 18 July. The Warsaw Letter told the Czechoslovak leaders the reforms were no longer their own affair: "This is something more than your cause. It is the common cause of our countries, which have joined in the Warsaw Pact ..." (Warsaw Letter, TASS release 18 July 1968). It demanded that the party retake the press, radio and television. The pressure was not only external. In August five senior Czechoslovak officials, Indra, Kolder, Kapek, Švestka and Bil'ak, wrote secretly to Brezhnev in Russian: "The very existence of socialism in our country is under threat." (Indra, Kolder, Kapek, Švestka and Bil'ak, secret letter to Brezhnev, August 1968, translated by Mark Kramer). They said the press was in right wing hands and the leadership paralysed. The letter gave the invasion domestic sponsors, though its authors had reason to exaggerate. On 13 August Brezhnev telephoned Dubček. A KGB transcript, released in 1994, brackets places where the transcriber summarised Dubček's replies. Brezhnev accused him of deceit, demanded the dismissal of named reformers and warned of new, independent measures. Dubček answered: "If you believe that we're deceiving you, then take the measures you regard as appropriate." (Alexander Dubček in the KGB recorded telephone conversation with Brezhnev, 13 August 1968). He argued that decisions needed a plenum and time; the editors leave open whether Moscow took this as permission. The public case came in a Soviet newspaper article whose author and date the two holding repositories give differently: "The sovereignty of each socialist country cannot be opposed to the interests of the world of socialism, of the world revolutionary movement." (official Soviet doctrinal article, 1968, translated by Novosti). The name "Brezhnev Doctrine" was attached later; Brezhnev denied a formal doctrine existed. The night the transmitters went silent On the night of 20–21 August 1968, Warsaw Pact troops entered Czechoslovakia. title: Solidarność: The Union That Broke the Bloc, 1980–1989
description: On 31 August 1980, the day the Gdańsk Agreement was signed, Krzysztof Korczyński photographed two plywood boards mounted by Gate No.
text: On 31 August 1980, the day the Gdańsk Agreement was signed, Krzysztof Korczyński photographed two plywood boards mounted by Gate No. 2 of the Lenin Shipyard. They carried twenty one demands painted for the strike that had shut the yard. The image, held by the European Solidarity Centre, shows the list as a public claim addressed to people beyond the factory. The first demand was the one that mattered most: "Akceptacja niezależnych od partii i pracodawców wolnych związków zawodowych, wynikająca z ratyfikowanej przez PRL Konwencji nr 87 Międzynarodowej Organizacji Pracy dotyczącej wolności związkowych." (The 21 Demands, point 1, Gdańsk, 16–17 August 1980). In translation: "Acceptance of free trade unions independent of the party and employers, arising from ILO Convention No. 87 ratified by the PRL, concerning freedom of association." The reference was to an international treaty on freedom of association Poland had ratified. The boards at Gate No. 2 The strike was a workplace occupation with an explicit political programme. The Inter Factory Strike Committee, the MKS, drew the list from demands sent in by striking workplaces. With free unions went a right to strike, free publication, the reinstatement of workers dismissed after the strikes of 1970 and 1976, and the release of named political prisoners. Economic demands sat beside these: a 2,000 złoty rise, food supply, cheaper meat and free Saturdays. Arkadiusz Rybicki, who helped paint the boards, recalled years later: "Do komisji wpłynęło około 700 postulatów" (Arkadiusz Rybicki, interviewed by Polskie Radio, published 17 August 2012), rendered as "About 700 demands reached the commission." The final twenty one were a narrowing of a wider set that included leaving the Soviet led alliance; the number is a recollection, not a minute. The protocol shows what was conceded and deferred. Officials accepted unions outside the state trade union register, the CRZZ, and promised no discrimination. The MKS declared the unions would not act as a political party and affirmed "socialist" ownership and the leading role of the PZPR, the ruling communist party. The right to strike, censorship reform and the five day week were all put off to future bills. The record fixes the strike's end at five on 31 August and notes that Andrzej Gwiazda did not sign. Deadlines are evidence of what was left for later, not of delivery. Fifteen months For fifteen months Solidarity existed legally. It published a national weekly, the first issue on 3 April 1981, and at its September congress delegates addressed workers in other communist ruled countries, drawing condemnation from several allied leaderships. Lech Wałęsa, the electrician who chaired the strike committee, described the agreement from Oslo when he accepted the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983: "Addressing you, as the winner of the 1983 Nobel Peace Prize, is a Polish worker from the Gdansk Shipyard, one of the founders of the independent trade union movement in Poland." (Lech Wałęsa, Nobel lecture, 11 December 1983, Nobel Foundation English translation, read by Bogdan Cywinski). He called the agreement a charter of workers' rights and insisted Solidarity had not sought power: "During the 15 months of 'Solidarity's' legal existence nobody was killed or wounded as a result of its activities." (Lech Wałęsa, Nobel lecture, 11 December 1983). That was his claim, not a checked statistic, and the lecture was self defence delivered while he was interned. Of what followed he said, "Let the veil of silence fall presently over what happened afterwards. Silence, too, can speak out." (Lech Wałęsa, Nobel lecture, 11 December 1983). On 12–13 December 1981 the government imposed martial law, rule by the military with strict controls. title: The Wall and the Workers: East Germany, 1953–1989
description: On 16 June 1953 the Politburo of the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED), the ruling party of the German Democratic Republic (GDR, East Germany), used its central newspaper to retreat...
text: On 16 June 1953 the Politburo of the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED), the ruling party of the German Democratic Republic (GDR, East Germany), used its central newspaper to retreat from a decision taken in May. It had raised the work quota, the output a worker had to produce for full pay, by ten per cent. Builders on the Stalinallee housing site in East Berlin had found the change in their pay packets, stopped work and marched. The Politburo declared: "The increase in work quotas cannot and must not be carried out through administrative methods. It can only be based on conviction and voluntary action." (statement of 16 June 1953). The concession followed the strike, still defended higher productivity, and said nothing about the demands made the next day. The streets in June On 17 June the walkout spread and the party leadership was evacuated to Karlshorst. In a secret report to Molotov and Bulganin dated 24 June, the Soviet military and diplomatic leadership wrote: "The main role in the dispersion of the demonstrations and in the liquidation of street unrest in Berlin was played by the Soviet forces." (Sokolovskii, Semyonov and Yudin, 24 June 1953). The report put some 66,000 demonstrators in East Berlin and listed the demands: lower norms, lower shop prices, the government's resignation and free elections. It recorded interruptions in fat, meat and sugar and a 10 to 15 per cent rise in ration coupon meat prices. It called 17 June "X day" and blamed Western intelligence, yet its own facts pointed to the quota policy. The government printed a different account on 18 June: "The unrest that ensued is the work of agents provocateurs and fascist agents of foreign powers and their accomplices from German capitalist monopolies." (GDR government statement, 17 June 1953). Marion Gräfin Dönhoff, writing from West Germany in Die Zeit on 25 June, described "With no weapons, only sticks and stones, the workers faced off against the Russian tanks." (Dönhoff, 25 June 1953). She relayed events outside Berlin second hand and wanted 17 June made a German national day, a proposal the Bundestag adopted on 3 July. Both accounts were partisan, but they agree on the scale of the protest. In Magdeburg the gardener Ernst Jennrich was accused of shooting a People's Police officer on 17 June. At his trial on 25 August he said in his last words: "I know for a fact that I never fired a shot at a member of the People's Police" (Jennrich, 25 August 1953). He was sentenced to life imprisonment; after the Justice Minister demanded death, a fifteen minute retrial imposed a death sentence. He was executed in March 1954 and acquitted in 1991. Shelves and the sealed border Six months after the uprising the Politburo ordered a campaign against emigration: "Above all, the enemy's work to recruit skilled workers and members of the technical intelligentsia from industrial enterprises must be quashed." (SED Politburo resolution, 15 December 1953). It named RIAS, the American backed radio station in West Berlin, and ordered proceedings against "recruiters". It was an order, not a report on results. A photograph from 25 July 1953 shows "bursting" shelves in an East Berlin delicatessen a month after the revolt; the "New Course" brought Soviet food deliveries but did not reverse the May quotas. In May 1979 an internal SED report still recorded: "All the first class goods produced by our republic are either exported or sold in special stores [Exquisitläden] that ordinary people cannot afford." (SED internal report, 15 May 1979). It listed rising prices, goods "under the table" and missing Trabant spare parts, and framed complaints as rumours to be countered. It shows that criticism was reported, not how widespread it was. On 13 August 1961 Radio DDR asked citizens about the sealing of the border. title: The Yugoslav Experiment: Workers' Councils, Tito and the National Question
description: In November 1948, months after the Soviet-led Cominform, the association of communist parties through which Moscow directed the others, expelled Yugoslavia, Josip Broz Tito told the...
text: In November 1948, months after the Soviet led Cominform, the association of communist parties through which Moscow directed the others, expelled Yugoslavia, Josip Broz Tito told the Slovene Academy of Arts and Sciences: "Socialism does not require of us that we renounce our love for our socialist country, that we renounce our love for our own people." (Tito, 26 November 1948). His subject was the charge of nationalism. In his account the break was a defence of the right of a smaller socialist country to take its own road. That claim has to be weighed against what he did with the independence, and against what people inside Yugoslavia later made of it. The break and the national question The case was put in principle by Boris Ziherl, a Yugoslav party ideologist, in 1949: "in addition to the Soviet Union, there is today a series of states whose working populations also quite rightfully consider them as their socialist fatherland" (Ziherl, Communism and Fatherland , 1949). The wartime liberation struggle, he argued, had proved the communists were the truest sons of their own countries. The vocabulary was that of 1949 propaganda and the booklet says nothing about conditions inside Yugoslav factories or republics, but it shows how the leadership wanted the split understood: as a question of equality between socialist states. Tito put the same case to the French journalist Louis Dalmas in answers dated December 1949: "it is not only possible, but also very useful for small nations to pursue a genuinely principled policy in the settlement of international questions" (Tito, interview with Dalmas). He said the difference between parties "was later transformed – because it could not be otherwise – into differences between the USSR and the Federative People's Republic" (Ibid.). The interview also shows the limit of the break: asked whether the Soviet show trials of 1936 and 1937 could have been staged, he declined to answer. It reached English through a French bulletin and was reprinted by Trotskyist opponents whose editorial note is not evidence, though the unanswered question is. Tito's 1948 speech claimed that the national question had been settled through the common liberation war, naming Macedonia, Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina as republics that had gained equality, and describing personnel sent from Slovenia, Croatia and Serbia to assist the "backward" republics. That is a leader's assertion of success. The later history of the federation makes it a claim to test, and the record here holds no testimony from people living in those republics about whether they experienced equality. The factory question and the 1950 law On 26 June 1950 Tito introduced a bill to the Federal Assembly: "The adoption of this bill will be the most significant historic act of the Federal Assembly next to the Law on Nationalization of the Means of Production." (Tito, 26 June 1950). State ownership, he said, had not delivered "the factories for the workers"; directors were still appointed from above, and the party had copied Soviet methods "uncritically". The transfer would be gradual: "The state functions in the management of economy are not yet ceasing completely, but they are no longer the exclusive factor." (Ibid.). He named Bosnia, Sandzak, Macedonia, Kosovo and Metohiya, Lika and Montenegro as regions where new factories would turn poor peasants into industrial workers. The Basic Law passed that day supplies the machinery. "The workers' councils of the enterprises and of the higher economic associations are to be elected and recalled by the workers' collectives." (Basic Law of 26 June 1950). Councils were to meet at least once in six weeks, choose management boards, approve plans and distribute retained accumulation. At least three quarters of board members had to be production workers, serving without pay while keeping their jobs. title: The Long March and the Chinese Civil War
description: In the autumn of 1936 Edgar Snow sat with Mao Tse-tung in Pao-an, the small town in the Communist-held Northwest that served as the Party's base.
text: In the autumn of 1936 Edgar Snow sat with Mao Tse tung in Pao an, the small town in the Communist held Northwest that served as the Party's base. They worked at night. Snow wrote Mao's answers in English, an interpreter read them back in Chinese, and Mao corrected the result. Snow described the method himself: "My interviews were written in full in English, and then re translated into Chinese and corrected by Mao, who is noted for his insistence upon accuracy of detail." (Edgar Snow, interviews written July–September 1936, published November 1936) This is the closest surviving thing to a participant's voice at the end of the march, and it reaches us through two languages, an editor and a foreigner's choice of questions. It was said before the retreat had hardened into a legend. The retreat in contemporary words Weeks after the First Front Army reached northern Shensi, Mao addressed Party activists at Wayaopao. He conceded that the old base areas were gone and that the army had been considerably weakened, then refused the word defeat. "the Long March is the first of its kind in the annals of history, that it is a manifesto, a propaganda force, a seeding machine." (Mao Tse tung, "On Tactics Against Japanese Imperialism," 27 December 1935) In the same report he gave the distance in his own idiom: "by using our two legs we swept across a distance of more than twenty thousand li through the length and breadth of eleven provinces." (same report, 27 December 1935) A li is roughly a third of a mile. Snow, who was not on the march but interviewed survivors and read their handouts within a year of the arrival, supplied the texture that a leadership speech leaves out. He recorded a First Army Corps itinerary of 18,088 li , heavy losses before Guizhou, distraction marches through the province, a forced night march to an unguarded ferry on the Jinsha River, and the rush to an iron chain bridge over the Tatu. P'eng Teh huai put the stakes in a sentence Snow kept: "'Victory was life,' said P'eng Teh huai; 'defeat was certain death.'" (P'eng Teh huai, quoted by Edgar Snow, Red Star Over China , "The Heroes of Tatu," written 1936–37) Mao's own explanation of survival was blunter and more political. "Tactics are important, but we could not exist if the majority of the people did not support us. We are nothing but the fist of the people beating their oppressors!" (Mao Tse tung, autobiographical interview recorded 1936, English translation in Red Star Over China ) Each of these statements was made in public by a man with a stake in the outcome. They are evidence of what participants chose to say, not a neutral measurement of the road. Zunyi and the numbers that do not agree The Party's own chronicle dates the meeting at Zunyi, a town in Guizhou province, to 15 and 17 January 1935. It records that the army fell from more than 86,000 at the start of the year to just over 30,000 after the fighting at the Xiang River, that Mao was co opted onto the Standing Committee, and that a three man group of Mao, Zhou Enlai and Wang Jiaxiang was formed. The chronicle calls the meeting a turning point that saved the Party. Historians working with the same fragmentary record read it differently. Benjamin Yang argued that Mao's rise was gradual and that the Communists moved from revolutionary idealism to political realism on the road. Thomas Kampen, using a 1983 Party investigation report and participant memoirs, qualified that account: Mao was neither party chairman nor chairman of the military commission when the meeting ended. The dispute is over how much one meeting could have decided, not over whether it was held. The distances and losses resist consolidation in the same way. Snow took 18,088 li from a First Army Corps itinerary and noted that the Reds themselves spoke of a "25,000 li March." Mao said "more than twenty thousand li " through eleven provinces in December 1935. A Xinhua report published in 2026 used roughly 12,500 kilometres. The Party chronicle

title: Land to the Tiller: The Chinese Countryside in Its Own Words, 1927–1964
description: In the winter of 1927 Mao Zedong spent thirty-two days travelling through five counties of Hunan, trying to answer critics inside and outside the Communist Party who said the peasant...
text: In the winter of 1927 Mao Zedong spent thirty two days travelling through five counties of Hunan, trying to answer critics inside and outside the Communist Party who said the peasant movement had gone too far. He did not rely on official reports. "I called together fact finding conferences in villages and county towns, which were attended by experienced peasants and by comrades working in the peasant movement" (Mao Zedong, Hunan investigation, January–February 1927, written up March 1927; translated in Selected Works ). What came back was a record of village activity assembled by an investigator who had a case to make, not a survey of every household. Read for its detail rather than its famous phrases, it shows a countryside already in motion. The associations and the rent campaign A peasant association was a village organisation formed to challenge landlord power. Mao recorded that by November 1926 such organisations with a total membership of 1,367,727 had been set up in thirty seven of Hunan's seventy five counties, and that by January 1927 the movement claimed roughly two million members and a following of about ten million. He broke the rural population down by class: "According to the survey of Changsha County, the poor peasants comprise 70 per cent, the middle peasants 20 per cent, and the landlords and the rich peasants 10 per cent of the population in the rural areas." (Mao Zedong, same report, March 1927; Selected Works translation) Poor peasants held nearly all the chairmanships and committee seats at township level. His list of fourteen achievements describes what associations did: checking landlords' accounts, imposing fines, parading offenders, banning grain exports and rent increases, and pressing for lower rents and deposits. "From November onwards, as the peasants have gained ascendancy over the landlords they have taken the further step of agitating for reduced rents and deposits." (Mao Zedong, same report, section "Hitting the Landlords Economically," March 1927; Selected Works translation) The class percentages came from surveys whose method Mao did not give. Nearly twenty years later, in a village John Hersey called Crow Village in the Shansi Chahar Hopei Border Region, the same issue reached the level of individual households. Hersey attended a "Clearing the Accounts" meeting in 1945–46 at which nine landlords were fined and a new village head elected. A flat 25 per cent rent cut was applied with some retroactive claims, alongside a sliding "Reasonable Burden Tax." Afterward a farmer named Wang described what the campaign had meant in grain: "They gave me back thirty piculs of red and yellow [sorghum and millet] and reduced the rent on my water land from twelve piculs a mow to eight." (Farmer Wang, Crow Village, interviewed by John Hersey, 1946; recorded in Hersey's English with the help of a Chinese interpreter) A picul was a measure of grain weight and a mou a measure of land area. The landlord Hsi was less impressed. "I don't feel that things are any better or any worse now than they were under the Japanese. Things are just going along." (Landlord Hsi, Crow Village, to John Hersey, 1946; rendered in Hersey's English. The following passage in Hersey makes clear that Hsi then described his losses in detail.) He went on to speak of mortgaging 130 of his 300 mou and trying side deals to win back the reduction. Hersey found that Hsi and other landlords remained materially comfortable and that the gap between them and poor peasants was narrowing, not gone. He stayed only a few days, and Wang's and Hsi's words reach us in his English through an interpreter. Classification and the land to the tiller law The daily experience of rent reduction came before the confiscation of land. The change is marked in the Draft Agrarian Law of the Communist Party, announced on 28 December 1947 and reproduced by William Hinton. title: The Cultural Revolution: The Movement in Its Own Words
description: In October 1966 a schoolgirl named Sung Yao-wu described a rally in Peking where she found herself near Mao Tse-tung.
text: In October 1966 a schoolgirl named Sung Yao wu described a rally in Peking where she found herself near Mao Tse tung. A Red Guard of the Girls' Middle School at Peking Normal University, she put an arm band on the leader's sleeve and reported the feeling in a state magazine: "We have risen to rebel, to fight!" (Sung Yao wu, Red Guard, China Reconstructs , October 1966; from a poor scan, short phrase only) The sentence was printed for foreign readers under official editorial control, so it tells us how a participant was invited to describe herself rather than what she privately thought. It is still a useful entry point, because the rebellion she announced had been authorised, step by step, in documents that can be read today. The documents that launched it The movement did not begin with an undefined social mood. On 16 May 1966 the Central Committee issued a circular dissolving the existing Five Person Group and its February "Outline Report" and replacing them with a Cultural Revolution Group under the Politburo Standing Committee. It accused Peng Chen of acting behind the leadership's back. The circular was a victorious faction's indictment, and its charges are its own claims. Nine days later, on 25 May, the philosophy teacher Nie Yuanzi and six colleagues put up a big character poster at Peking University. A big character poster was a large handwritten sheet displayed in public for all to read. "But here in Beida [Beijing University] the masses are being kept immobilised." (Nie Yuanzi and six colleagues, big character poster, 25 May 1966; bracketed gloss is the editor's) Mao singled the poster out for praise twice, which corroborates its importance at the launch. On 1 August he wrote to a named school group, the Red Guards of Tsinghua University Middle School: "You say it is right to rebel against reactionaries; I enthusiastically support you." (Mao Tse tung, letter to Red Guards of Tsinghua University Middle School, 1 August 1966) The same letter asked them to unite with all who could be united with and to give those who had made mistakes a way out. On 5 August, in "Bombard the Headquarters," he turned on officials who had tried to restrain the students. "But in the last fifty days or so some leading comrades from the central down to the local levels have acted in a diametrically opposite way." (Mao Tse tung, "Bombard the Headquarters," 5 August 1966) The decision adopted on 8 August, known from its sixteen clauses as the Sixteen Points, gave the movement its rules. "The main target of the present movement is those within the Party who are in authority and are taking the capitalist road." (Central Committee of the CPC, decision adopted 8 August 1966 (the "Sixteen Points"), translated in Peking Review , 12 August 1966) Those in authority taking the capitalist road meant senior officials accused of steering the Party back toward market relations. Another clause urged, "Trust the masses, rely on them and respect their initiative. Cast out fear. Don't be afraid of disturbances." (same decision, section 4) The contradiction sits in the text without any historian's help. The same decision that tells the masses to cast out fear also says disputes must be settled by reasoning, not by coercion or force, and that the great majority of cadres and masses must be united behind the movement. The press repeated the warning in September 1966 and again in December. The existence of those warnings is contemporary evidence that coercion was already a recognised problem. The rebels were not of one mind The word Red Guard covers people with quite different grievances. Hsu Chien hua, a twenty year old kindergarten staff member in Peking, wrote in a rebel periodical in January 1967 about a work team sent into her workplace after staff put up posters attacking the principal. A work team was a group dispatched to take charge of a unit's campaign. "All the members of my family were so moved that we broke down in tears, because we were all victims of

title: Tiananmen: The Square and the Verdict
description: On 18 April 1989, students holding a sit-in outside the Great Hall of the People, the state's ceremonial hall in Beijing, presented seven demands.
text: On 18 April 1989, students holding a sit in outside the Great Hall of the People, the state's ceremonial hall in Beijing, presented seven demands. They were mourning Hu Yaobang, the former party leader who had died three days earlier, but the mourning had become a programme. Among the demands, preserved in a disputed translated collection, were calls to "publish information on the income of state leaders and their family members; end the ban on privately run newspapers and permit freedom of speech" (seven student demands, 18 April 1989). Published as The Tiananmen Papers , the collection is contested and no original was examined, so the wording is not a settled transcription. Even so it shows how far the students had moved in three days: from grief to elections, a free press and an end to restrictions on demonstrations. "Turmoil" and the hunger strike On 26 April the Party's official newspaper, the People's Daily , called the protests "turmoil", casting the students as a threat to order. Their answer came on 13 May, when a hunger strike began in Tiananmen Square, the ceremonial space at the centre of Beijing where the state held its founding ceremony in 1949. The declaration issued that afternoon named inflation, official profiteering and corruption as reasons for the fast, and insisted the students were patriots. Its most quoted line was "Democracy is not a task for a few; it takes generations." (hunger strike declaration, 13 May 1989). The text survives as an edited extract with unnamed translators, and its authors cannot be identified. At about 5:40 p.m. Wang Dan announced the fast and read a declaration asking for equal dialogue and a fair judgement of the movement as patriotic and democratic. Students swore an oath: "For the democratization of China, and for the prosperity of the motherland, I willingly go on hunger strike." (oath recorded at the Square, 13 May 1989). Banners read "Hunger can be tolerated, but a lack of democracy cannot." (banner recorded at the Square, 13 May 1989). Compiled by a memorial museum from later memoirs rather than a contemporary recording, the words are probably close to what was said, but the crowd's size and the residents' behaviour cannot be checked. The argument at the top The most vivid account of the leadership's divisions is also the least secure. A purported record of the Politburo Standing Committee meeting of 16 May, the small group of senior leaders who took day to day decisions, has Zhao Ziyang saying: "We have to revise the April 26 editorial, find ways to dispel the sense of confrontation between us and the students, and get things settled down as soon as possible." (purported minutes of 16 May 1989). Li Peng replies that the key phrases came from Deng and cannot be changed. The editors, Andrew Nathan and Perry Link, never saw originals and describe the minutes as reconstructions from aides' notes. Alfred Chan argued in The China Quarterly in 2004 that such texts were stitched together from public sources and fiction; Nathan replied that the volume of named detail made fabrication implausible. The exchange is unresolved, so the passage is evidence that a split was claimed, not proof of the exact words. The occupation and its witnesses Through late May the Square stayed occupied. Chai Ling, who commanded the Hunger Strike Headquarters, recorded a videotaped interview with Philip Cunningham on 28 May and asked that it be released abroad in case she was arrested. She said she had known from the start that the fast would not win results. One line became the centre of a later dispute: "Only when the Square is awash with blood will the people of China open their eyes." (Chai Ling, interview of 28 May 1989). Chai later said the Chinese word had been mistranslated and the idea came from Li Lu; other leaders accused the filmmakers of manipulation. The footage is genuine but its interpretation contested: it shows desperation and a strategy of holding the Square, not a plan for bloodshed.

title: The Korean War: Voices from Three Armies and a Divided Peninsula
description: On 2 October 1950, days before China committed its army to Korea, Mao Zedong warned Stalin that the step might be a mistake.
text: On 2 October 1950, two days before China committed its army to Korea, Mao Zedong warned Stalin that the step might be a mistake. The message passed through Nikolai Roshchin, the Soviet ambassador in Beijing, who relayed Mao's words to Moscow in a coded telegram. "we now consider that such actions may entail extremely serious consequences." (Mao to Stalin, 2 October 1950, relayed 3 October, translated by Kathryn Weathersby and Alexandre Mansourov). Mao listed the reasons: his divisions were poorly equipped, an attack might bring war with the United States, it might draw in the Soviet Union, and China was exhausted after its civil war. He proposed waiting and preparing. This is not the language of an unbroken march to war, and it sits uneasily beside later Chinese accounts of a firm, early decision. The decision and the order By 8 October the decision had been taken. Mao told Stalin that Peng Dehuai had been appointed commander and that "The troops might begin to cross into Korean territory by about 15 October." (Mao to Stalin, 8 October 1950). His order of the same day created the Chinese People's Volunteers. The order states no reason for the name. "I herewith order the Chinese People's Volunteers to march speedily to Korea and join the Korean comrades in fighting the aggressors and winning a glorious victory." (Mao's order, 8 October 1950). In January 1951 he instructed those troops to "take not a single needle or a single thread from the Korean people" (Mao's directive, 19 January 1951). A separate set of political rules told them to "Strictly follow the political commands of the Korean government" (four principles for unity, October 1950), defining solidarity as obedience to the host party. That text comes from a 1968 internal compilation and a museum display, so its wording may reflect a later context, and an instruction states an intended standard rather than what happened in villages. The historian Chen Jian, using both Russian and Chinese records, notes that the 2 October telegram does not match the Chinese published version of the decision, a warning against treating either text as the whole story. The hidden air war Soviet air power was committed only from November 1950, after an abortive air war plan, and the engagement was kept secret. On 15 November 1950 Mao wrote to Stalin: "Thanks to the courage and efforts of the Soviet air force men in battle, in the past 12 days 23 invading American planes have been shot down." (Mao to Stalin, 15 November 1950, translated by Jingxia Yang and Douglas Stiffler). The number is Mao's report to Stalin, not an independently verified loss count. Porfiriy Ovsyannikov, a Soviet pilot flying MiG 15 jet fighters, recalled decades later that Soviet airmen flew from bases in China, were told to limit Russian radio talk, and trained Chinese and Korean pilots. "But when we began to fly with the Chinese, some of them fainted from the G forces. From hunger." (Ovsyannikov interview, published 2019, translated by James F. Gebhardt). The editor's footnotes repeatedly challenge the pilot's victory claims against American records, so his recollection is evidence of what a pilot believed, not of enemy losses. It also links the secret air war to the material condition of China's own air force. The soldiers' war British, American and Commonwealth veterans describe a war of sudden attacks and long stagnation. A speaker in the Imperial War Museums' "Voices of the Korean War" collection remembers the fighting of September 1950: "The end of the day we had ninety casualties and it just decimated them two platoons." (IWM oral history). Another recalls an officer's order to a bugler, "Play anything you like bar a retreat." (recalled by Private Anthony Eagles, IWM). Marguerite Higgins, a war correspondent, said of the opening weeks, "I saw my countrymen mauled and humiliated" (American RadioWorks transcript, 2003). Billy J. title: The Vietnamese revolution, 1919–1954: from petition to Điện Biên Phủ
description: In 1919 a Vietnamese nationalist appeared at the Paris Peace Conference, where the Allies were settling the end of the First World War, and asked for civil rights inside the French...
text: In 1919 a Vietnamese nationalist appeared at the Paris Peace Conference, where the Allies were settling the end of the First World War, and asked for civil rights inside the French empire rather than independence. Nguyễn Ái Quoc, later known as Ho Chi Minh, presented claims on behalf of Vietnamese patriots. One was "Complete amnesty of Vietnamese political prisoners." (List of Claims of the Annamese People, 1919). He also asked for equal legal treatment with Europeans, freedom of press and opinion, technical schools, the rule of law instead of decrees, and a Vietnamese representative in the French Parliament. Addressed to an audience that could grant reforms, the petition's moderation reflects that audience as much as his convictions. It is the starting point of a revolution that changed its programme more than once. From petition to party, 1919 to 1930 At the Fifth Congress of the Communist International in 1924, the Moscow directed body that guided communist parties abroad, Nguyễn Ái Quoc argued that colonial liberation belonged to the working class revolution. He criticised the French and British parties for neglecting colonial questions and described plantations of 20,000 to 25,000 hectares, forced labour and a land tax raised by 30 percent after floods. "Ninety five per cent of the population are peasants." (report to the Fifth Comintern Congress, 8 July 1924) was his summary of the French colonies, though his figures elsewhere were second hand. In 1930, convening the founding meeting in Hong Kong, he announced: "The Indochinese Communist Party has been founded. It is the Party of the working class. It will help the proletariat lead the revolution waged for the sake of all oppressed and exploited people." (founding appeal, 18 February 1930). Proletariat means the industrial working class. The ten slogans included an eight hour day, universal education, equality between women and men, and land for poor peasants. Looking back in 1960, Ho described reading Lenin's thesis on colonies: "This is what we need, this is the path to our liberation!" ( The Path Which Led Me to Leninism , first published April 1960). That account is retrospective, written thirty years later. Prison poems, 1942 to 1943 Between 1942 and 1943 Ho was held by Chiang Kai shek's police while travelling towards Chongqing. He wrote poems in classical Chinese because his jailers would have found Vietnamese suspicious, filling a worn notebook with what the editor of the published edition calls a hundred odd quatrains. The sequence records shackles, transfer through thirteen districts of Guangxi and eighteen prisons, meagre rice, scabies, cold, and the death of a fellow prisoner from hunger. "Four months of a subhuman life, it appears, / Have aged me even more than ten years." ( Four Months Have Passed , 1942–43). Elsewhere: "Thy body is in jail. / But thy spirit, never." ( Prison Diary , 1942–43). These are verses, not reportage, and they reach the reader through an unnamed translator in a 1972 Hanoi edition whose printed text has scanning errors. They are the closest surviving record of Ho's private experience between the 1930s and the insurrection of 1945. The August Revolution of 1945 Trường Chinh, the party's general secretary, wrote within a year of the insurrection and revised the account twelve years later. Local uprisings began on 11 and 13 August, before the general order of the night of 13 August. A congress at Tân Trạo followed on 16 August, demonstrations in Hanoi on 17 and 18 August, and the seizure of the capital on 19 August: "On August 19, the entire capital rose up." (Trường Chinh, The August Revolution , written 1946, revised 1958). He explains the rush: an earlier rising would have been crushed, a later one might have left a Japanese backed or restored French administration in power. "Hundreds of thousands of people starved beside granaries full of rice kept by the Japanese and French." (same work). The party had dropped the agrarian revoluti

title: Year Zero: Cambodia, 1975–1979
description: On 17 April 1975 the correspondent Sydney Schanberg stayed in Phnom Penh after the American staff left.
text: On 17 April 1975 the correspondent Sydney Schanberg stayed in Phnom Penh after the American staff left. The Khmer Rouge, as the soldiers and cadres of the Communist Party of Kampuchea were called, were entering the city. In testimony to the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, the international tribunal set up to try the regime's leaders, Schanberg described more than two million people driven out, hospitals emptied and patients abandoned. The tribunal's summary of his evidence records: "[T]here was an air of panic and fear." The state these soldiers proclaimed, Democratic Kampuchea, lasted until 1979. Its revolution left an unusual archive: its own constitution, assembly minutes, prison rules, confessions and slogans. Read against the people who lived under them, those documents are the subject of this chapter. The first hand record 1. "All workers are the masters of their factories. All peasants are the masters of the rice paddies and fields. All other labourers have the right to work. title: The Party That Was Erased: Indonesia, 1965–66
description: In the early hours of 1 October 1965 a group of officers led by Lieutenant Colonel Untung seized radio and communications facilities in Jakarta, killed six senior generals, and announced...
text: In the early hours of 1 October 1965 a group of officers led by Lieutenant Colonel Untung seized radio and communications facilities in Jakarta, killed six senior generals, and announced a "30 September Movement" that claimed to be forestalling a pro American coup by the generals (FRUS 1964–1968, vol. XXVI, docs. 149 and 161; CIA, Office of Current Intelligence, 6 October 1965). The CIA's Office of Current Intelligence, writing days later from broadcasts and reports, recorded that President Sukarno told the generals to "leave the political settlement to me." Within a day the army under General Suharto had crushed the movement. The destruction of the Communist Party of Indonesia, the PKI, followed over the next months and was still under way in 1966. It was the largest communist party outside the Soviet bloc and China, with millions of members, a trade union federation, a peasant front, a women's organisation and a press. The surviving record consists chiefly of the papers of the people who planned, watched and encouraged that destruction, because the party's own documents are almost entirely missing. The first hand record 1. "leave the political settlement to me." — Sukarno, reported by the CIA Office of Current Intelligence, 6 October 1965. Source: history.state.gov 2. "But it is impossible that there is no connection with this affair among elements of the air force." — General Suharto, public statement of about 4 October 1965, as quoted in the CIA memorandum of 6 October 1965. Source: history.state.gov 3. "odds seem overwhelming that, at very least, Sukarno knew what was afoot and had given tacit blessing to seizure of the generals" — Ambassador Marshall Green, telegram 1184, 26 October 1965. Source: history.state.gov 4. "In the life and death struggle which has finally been joined with the PKI, the Army deserves our support." — David Cuthell, State Department memorandum, 3 November 1965. Source: history.state.gov 5. "Attitude Pemuda Pantjasila leaders can only be described as bloodthirsty." — US Consulate, Medan, telegram 65, 16 November 1965. Source: history.state.gov 6. "we continue receive reports PKI being slaughtered by Ansor many areas East Java" — US Consulate, Surabaya, telegram 183, 24 November 1965. Source: nsarchive.gwu.edu 7. Source: nsarchive.gwu.edu 8. "G.30.S adalah satu 'complete overrompeling' bagi saya." — Sukarno, Pelengkap Nawaksara , 10 January 1967. My translation: "G.30.S was a complete surprise to me." There was no Leo." — Leo Mulyono, interview published 26 July 2015. Internet Archive snapshot: leo mulyono 11. "Fifty years is already too long." — Adi Rukun, interview with Sean O'Hagan, 7 June 2015. title: Hunger and the Village: Communism in India, 1943–1969
description: First-hand sources on Hunger and the Village: Communism in India, 1943–1969: first-hand documents, the evidence, scholarly interpretations and the limits of the record.
text: In October 1943 T. G. Narayanan, a correspondent for The Hindu , tried to get an ambulance for an old woman lying near Ballygunge station in Calcutta. He recorded what happened: "Hundreds of people passed by her. Not one cared enough to telephone for an ambulance. Before the ambulance I asked for came she was gone." Narayanan had been sent to the famine areas of Bengal, and his reports, later collected as Famine Over Bengal , were written by a man who watched destitutes arrive in the city. The Bengal famine of 1943 killed between one and two million people, according to the official inquiry, and left about six million seriously affected. It was the first of three events that shaped Indian communism in this period; the others were the peasant revolts of 1946 to 1951 and the uprising at Naxalbari in 1967. This chapter follows the witnesses to all three. The first hand record 1. "Hundreds of people passed by her. Not one cared enough to telephone for an ambulance. Before the ambulance I asked for came she was gone." — T. G. Narayanan, describing an old woman near Ballygunge station, October 1943, in Famine Over Bengal (March 1944). Internet Archive: famine over bengal 1 djvu 2. Internet Archive: 26318 Famine Inquiry Commission Report On Bengal djvu 4. "There was a feeling of tenseness and expectancy in Calcutta. Calcutta was largely empty. Houses were vacant." — witness to the Famine Inquiry Commission, quoted in Report on Bengal , 1945; the witness is unnamed in the published text. They've lost their nerve after the hat hartal." — reported by Somnath Hore at a sharecroppers' meeting in Badgachha, 19 December 1946; translated from Bengali by Somnath Zutshi. title: Two Archipelagos: Communist Movements in the Philippines and Japan, 1942–1972
description: On the rice plain of central Luzon during the Japanese occupation, a song passed among the Hukbalahap, the peasant movement that took up arms in 1942.
text: On the rice plain of central Luzon during the Japanese occupation, a song passed among the Hukbalahap, the peasant movement that took up arms in 1942. Its English version begins: "We are what they call mere peasants; / Who were created by God in sincere love; / We who live by our own toil," — Huk peasant song "We Are Peasants", English version reproduced by Benedict Kerkvliet, translator not named, reproduced by Rodney Azama, 1985 (Source: globalsecurity.org). It speaks of hunger, usury and a country that would go hungry if the peasants stopped, giving the land question a voice that party documents do not. An American Army counterinsurgency study reprinted it in 1985. Founded on 29 March 1942, the movement built a local administration while fighting the Japanese; Luis Taruc, based at Mount Arayat from December 1941, became its best known commander. After the war its programme of rent reduction and land met a restored landlord state. What the rebels asked for In February 1947 Taruc gave a journalist his minimum terms of peace: democratic rights restored, charges from 1946 dropped, local officials and the police command in central Luzon replaced, the six Democratic Alliance congressmen elected in 1946 seated, and land reform toward the abolition of tenancy (Kerkvliet, The Huk Rebellion , 1977, p. 171, citing the Manila Chronicle , 7 February 1947). A top secret State Department paper for National Security Council staff, dated 20 June 1950, called the Huks a serious military problem rooted in the rice plain and recorded that the army and constabulary had mistreated the population while the rebels gained by their conduct: "In marked contrast to the Philippine army and constabulary, which has usually mistreated and oppressed the population in areas where they have operated, the Huks have increased their popular support by correct behavior." — US Department of State draft paper for NSC staff, 20 June 1950 (Source: history.state.gov). It argued for American military advice to "insure the liquidation of the military phase" and called the leadership "totally captured by the Communists". It was a policy paper written to secure a decision. Its value is the convergence: a rebel song and a hostile intelligence estimate point to the same source of support. The Army chronology supplies the skeleton: insurrection in May 1947, the name HMB in November 1948, a raid on the Politburo, the party's top leadership body, in October 1950, resettlement under a programme known as EDCOR in February 1951, Taruc's surrender in May 1954. Written to draw lessons for future counterinsurgency, its foreword celebrates the defeat; it concedes that time pressure limited primary research and that General Lansdale, who helped shape the campaign, reviewed the draft. Whether reform or force defeated the rebels remains disputed, and the rebel sources do not address it. A party rebuilt Two decades later the countryside became the objective of a new party. The Communist Party of the Philippines was re established on 26 December 1968: "The Communist Party of the Philippines is now re established and rebuilt as a party of Mao Tse tung's thought." — Communist Party of the Philippines, "Programme for a People's Democratic Revolution", ratified 26 December 1968, quoted by Azama, 1985 (Source: globalsecurity.org). This was Maoism in its Philippine form, revolution from rural base areas rather than city strikes, with "armed struggle and the national united front", an alliance of political groups, as its two weapons. It broke with the older pro Moscow party, whose leaders it called revisionist, and its authors were teachers and students around Manila rather than peasants. The founding resolution, drafted by Jose Maria Sison as Amado Guerrero, put the break more sharply: "What we need to rebuild in the Philippines today is a proletarian revolutionary party that is armed with Mao Tsetung Thought." — "Rectify Errors, Rebuild the Party!", CPP, 26 December 1968 (Source: philippinere

title: Che Guevara
description: Full biography, all available writings and his theory of guerrilla warfare, the "new man" and internationalism.
text: Ernesto Guevara de la Serna was born in Rosario, Argentina, in 1928 and was killed in Bolivia in 1967. Between those dates he became a doctor, a commander in the Cuban revolutionary war, a minister in the Cuban government, a banker, and the most widely read theorist of rural guerrilla war in Latin America. His life and his writings are treated together here because he repeatedly joined a military decision to a political or ethical argument. The evidence comes from his own diaries, letters, essays and speeches, from the recollections of those who fought beside him, and from historians who have assessed what his ideas achieved in practice. Argentina, the journey, and Guatemala Pathfinder Press describes him as "Ernesto Che Guevara (1928 to 1967) was an Argentine born central leader of the Cuban Revolution" (Pathfinder Press, Ernesto Che Guevara author page). The Marxists Internet Archive encyclopedia calls him "Argentinian doctor; joined Castro in Mexico … a leader of the 1956 59 Cuban Revolution. Che served as president of Cuba's national bank and as Cuba's minister of industry in the period immediately following the Cuban Revolution" (MIA Encyclopedia of Marxism, "Guevara, Che (1928 1967)"). He wrote little about his childhood, and his own retrospective accounts are deliberately brief. Writing to Guillermo Lorentzen in May 1963 he reduced the whole of his life before the Cuban Revolution to a single sentence: "I was born in Argentina, I fought in Cuba, and I began to be a revolutionary in Guatemala." Source: Che Guevara, letter to Guillermo Lorentzen, Havana, 4 May 1963 The young man who appears in The Motorcycle Diaries is literate, self ironising and medically trained. He warned his readers against the heroic pose before he had begun the journey: "This is not a story of heroic feats, or merely the narrative of a cynic; at least I do not mean it to be. It is a glimpse of two lives running parallel for a time, with similar hopes and convergent dreams." Source: The Motorcycle Diaries , "So we understand each other" He described his method as that of a witness: "Man, the measure of all things, speaks here through my mouth and narrates in my own language that which my eyes have seen." He also marked the distance between the person who wrote the notes and the person who revised them years later: "The person who wrote these notes passed away the moment his feet touched Argentine soil again. The person who reorganizes and polishes them, me, is no longer, at least I am not the person I once was. All this wandering around 'Our America with a capital A' has changed me more than I thought." Source: Ibid. The journey of 1951 to 1952 took him through the Chilean nitrate fields, the Andes, the Amazon and a leper colony. Its political education appears less as doctrine than as a series of encounters with poor people. Staying with farm labourers in Chile, he recorded that "in general they didn't try to communicate with us, as is typical of the subjugated Araucanian race who maintain a deep suspicion of the white man who in the past has brought them so much misfortune and now continues to exploit them" ( The Motorcycle Diaries , chapter 6). At that point he still described himself as a drifter whose "destiny is to travel" (chapter 7). The "Our America" of the diary was not an abstraction. It was the America of the Araucanian labourer and the Quechua speaking peasant, and its unity would later be defined as "language, habits, religion, a common foreign master" ( Message to the Tricontinental ). The authorized Ocean Press edition of 2005, with its map, itinerary and appendix reproducing the 1960 speech to medical students, explicitly links the young traveller to the mature revolutionary (MIA, The Motorcycle Diaries index). Asthma appears in Che's own account of the war. In his account of the Granma aftermath he records that on 5 December 1956 he asked for an inferior rifle because "I was in very poor physical condition due to an attack of asthm
