title: Fidel Castro
description: Full biography from Moncada to the Update, with "History Will Absolve Me", the Havana Declarations and his complete writings.
text: Fidel Castro was born on 13 August 1926 at Birán, in the eastern province then called Oriente, and died in Havana on 25 November 2016. Between those dates he became the central figure of a revolution that overthrew a dictatorship, changed the ownership of land and industry, aligned Cuba with the Soviet bloc, and outlived the collapse of that bloc by decades. He also left an enormous body of speeches, declarations, interviews and reflections. Those texts are the starting point for any study of the Revolution, because they show what its leaders wanted the world to believe about it. They need to be read with care. A courtroom plea written by a defendant is an argument, not a neutral record. A party newspaper is an institution with an interest. A speech delivered twenty years after an event is evidence of how a leader later understood that event, not necessarily of what happened at the time. Historians have spent decades checking the movement's founding stories against court records, interviews with participants and the testimony of people who lived through the changes. This chapter follows the life and the arguments together, and marks where the official account and the independent evidence part company. Student politics and the road to Moncada Castro entered the University of Havana in 1945 and became a student leader there. In 1947 he joined the founding of the Orthodox Party ( Partido Ortodoxo ), the party built around Eduardo Chibás, whose radio broadcasts attacked corruption and whose death in 1951 made him a martyr for a generation of students. The biographical note published by Pathfinder Press, a United States movement publisher that issues collected editions of Castro's speeches, records the sequence: "A student leader at the University of Havana from 1945. Founding member of the Orthodox Party in 1947 and central organizer of its revolutionary minded youth" (Pathfinder Press). In History Will Absolve Me Castro quoted Chibás as an authority on the abuses of the regime: "How right Eduardo Chibás was in his last radio speech, when he said that Batista was encouraging the return of the colonels, castor oil and the law of the fugitive!" ( History Will Absolve Me , 16 October 1953). The official Cuban constitutional history presents the same period as a constitutionalist one. When General Fulgencio Batista seized power on 10 March 1952, "the first [person] who went to a court to denounce the coup d'état of Batista and the repeal of the Constitution of 1940 was Fidel Castro Ruz. The second was Armando Hart," and the University Students' Federation, the FEU, "carried out the burial of the Constitution" (Cuban National Assembly, Historia Constitucional Cubana ). Castro's own retrospective account, given in 1961, stresses method rather than doctrine. His generation "went about recruiting young people, picking from the youthful elements ... those who were more serious, more willing, more involved and had a more sincere revolutionary inclination," and when rival student groups arrived "with a machine gun," his own organisation "didn't have machine guns" and won cadres by political explanation instead (Speech on Marxism Leninism, 2 December 1961). The decision to organise a revolutionary movement came only "until we became convinced that the people were really being deceived and that it was all madness, all that madness" (Ibid.). This is a retrospective self description, valuable for what the mature Castro wanted to say about his own formation and not a contemporary record of the 1940s. He described that formation in deliberately unflattering terms. In the 1961 address he recalled that when he left university "I had already been greatly influenced — I wouldn't say that I was a Marxist Leninist, far from it. It is possible that I had two million petit bourgeois prejudices and a string of ideas that I'm glad not to have anymore" (1961 Marxism Leninism speech). He added a detail that is itself a piece of autobiographical evidence: "it

title: The Black Panther Party
description: Full history, the Ten-Point Program, survival programmes, internal debates and the Party's own publications.
text: The Black Panther Party was founded in Oakland, California, in October 1966 by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale. Its original name was the Black Panther Party for Self Defense. The Marxists Internet Archive's Party history says the Panthers "practiced militant self defense of minority communities against the U.S. government, and fought to establish revolutionary socialism through mass organizing and community based programs" (MIA, History of the Black Panther Party). Newton's autobiography gives the same date and place ( Revolutionary Suicide ). For a long time the Party's own publications were the main body of evidence available, and they remain central: its newspaper, its Ten Point Program, its rules, and the books and speeches of Newton, Seale, Eldridge Cleaver and Fred Hampton. Historians have since widened the base. Donna Jean Murch's Living for the City drew on oral history and untapped archives to show that the Party grew out of a study group formed by young black southern migrants at Merritt College, and that the gun carrying image was neither universal inside the organisation nor the main reason many people joined (University of North Carolina Press, 2010). Alondra Nelson's Body and Soul used archival research and interviews with former members to show that health care was not a side issue but central to the Party's political philosophy (University of Minnesota Press, 2011). This chapter uses the Party's texts, but reads them as the interested and often brilliant documents of a political organisation, and sets beside them the accounts of ordinary members and the work of these historians. Founding: Oakland, October 1966 Newton and Seale met at Merritt College, then Oakland City College. Seale's account is direct: "I met Huey P. Newton in the early Sixties, during the Cuban blockade when there were numerous street rallies going on around Merritt Junior College in West Oakland" (Seale, Seize the Time ). What drew them together was impatience with existing organisations. Newton recalled that "these sessions at Bobby's house were our political education classes, and the Party sort of grew out of them" ( Revolutionary Suicide ). Seale said the organisation was built for "the brothers off the block", and that Newton had shown him that the man on the block was ten men "when politically educated, and if you got him organized" ( Seize the Time ). Murch's research gives this social setting a harder edge. Oakland was a city of recent southern migrants, many of them from east Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma, and the study group that produced the Panthers also included people who later took very different political paths, among them the cultural nationalist Maulana Karenga and the future congressman Ron Dellums (University of North Carolina Press; interview with Murch). The name and symbol came from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization in Alabama, whose electoral mark was a black panther. Newton's account is precise. He had read a pamphlet about voter registration in Mississippi and about how people in Lowndes County had armed themselves against violence. Their political group used a black panther as its symbol. He suggested the name to Seale, reasoning that the panther does not attack until it is cornered and then strikes out. "The image seemed appropriate, and Bobby agreed without discussion" ( Revolutionary Suicide ). Seale independently remembered how the symbol was explained to sceptics at a poverty centre. When people asked why they wanted to be a vicious animal, Newton answered that the panther never attacks, but if attacked or cornered it wipes out the aggressor "absolutely, resolutely, wholly, thoroughly, and completely" ( Seize the Time ). Newton later rejected Stokely Carmichael's claim that Carmichael's permission had been sought. The founders had chosen the name themselves, he wrote, and were organised before they met him ( Revolutionary Suicide ). The archive preserves the names of the original six, photographed in Nov

title: Malcolm X
description: Life, the OAAU, the Pan-African and anti-imperialist turn, and all of his available speeches and writings.
text: Malcolm X was born Malcolm Little in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1925 and was shot dead in the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem on 21 February 1965, aged thirty nine ( New York Times , 22 February 1965; National Archives, "Malcolm X"). In the twelve years before his death he moved through several distinct roles: a street hustler and prison convert, a minister of the Nation of Islam, the breakaway founder of two new organisations, and, in the last year of his life, a Black nationalist and internationalist who argued that the struggle of Black Americans belonged before the United Nations. His ideas changed, and the record of that change survives in speeches, interviews, letters and one famous book. The Autobiography of Malcolm X , told to the journalist Alex Haley, was published in 1965, nine months after the assassination, and has shaped nearly every later account of the man. It is also a collaborative and retrospective text, assembled under conditions that historians have only recently begun to reconstruct. This chapter follows the documented sequence of Malcolm's positions and uses the Autobiography for what it is: an extraordinary source that must be read alongside the speeches and the scholarship. The written record on which this account rests has one unusual feature. Many of Malcolm's speeches survive in the Malcolm X Files, an activist transcript archive published as a blog with no stated editorial procedure. Where a text also exists in the Marxists Internet Archive, the Internet Archive, the Malcolm X.org document collection, or the Columbia University Malcolm X Project, those versions are cited here as well. For a number of the shorter talks and interviews the blog transcription is the only version readily available, and the reader should treat those transcripts as one witness rather than as a settled text. Dates given for undated items follow the archive's own index. Omaha, the Littles, and Garveyism The Autobiography opens with a threat rather than a birth date. Malcolm wrote that when his mother was pregnant with him, "a party of hooded Ku Klux Klan riders galloped up to our home in Omaha, Nebraska, one night. Surrounding the house, brandishing their shotguns and rifles, they shouted for my father to come out." The Klansmen had come because his father was "spreading trouble" among Black people in Omaha with "the 'back to Africa' preachings of Marcus Garvey" ( The Autobiography of Malcolm X , Chapter One, "Nightmare"). Garveyism was the movement founded by Marcus Garvey, which urged people of African descent to build their own institutions, take pride in African identity and consider Africa a homeland. It was a framework of Black self organisation that reached this family before any contact with the Nation of Islam. Malcolm identified his father as a Baptist minister and a Garvey organiser: "My father, the Reverend Earl Little, was a Baptist minister, a dedicated organizer for Marcus Aurelius Garvey's U.N.I.A. (Universal Negro Improvement Association)" (Ibid., Chapter One). His mother is named in the same chapter: "My mother was twenty eight when I was born on May 19, 1925, in an Omaha hospital" and "Louise Little, my mother, who was born in Grenada, in the British West Indies, looked like a white woman. Her father was white" (Ibid.). Attallah Shabazz's foreword to the 1996 edition spells the family name "Louisa" and describes both grandparents as "crusaders for Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association, acting as chapter president and writer/translator for more than a decade" (Ibid., Foreword). Malcolm's narrative uses "Louise"; the foreword uses "Louisa". Both spellings appear in the book. The Autobiography records the murder of Earl Little and the breakup of the household. Malcolm states his family's conviction that "my father was finally himself to die by the white man's hands," and he expected the same fate: "It has always been my belief that I, too, will die by violence. I have done all that I can to be prepared

title: W. E. B. Du Bois and Paul Robeson
description: Black Reconstruction, the CPUSA, Here I Stand, the Pan-African Congresses and complete bibliographies.
text: W. E. B. Du Bois and Paul Robeson left different kinds of records. Du Bois wrote books, essays, editorials and an autobiography; Robeson left articles, speeches, greetings to conferences and a long answer to a congressional committee (Du Bois, Dusk of Dawn ; MIA index of The Crisis ; MIA Robeson archive). Both men used what they wrote to argue that the liberation of Black people could not be separated from the struggle against capitalism, racism and war. This chapter follows those records in roughly the order their authors produced them, then asks what the two bodies of work share and where they differ. It treats each text as an argument made at a particular moment, not as a transparent report of what its author saw or did. The chief witnesses are the two men themselves. Du Bois's published work spans more than six decades and changes markedly over that span, so a sentence from 1903 cannot simply be joined to a sentence from 1935 as if the author had never revised his views. Robeson's most vivid account of Soviet life is a newspaper article written within weeks of a reception in Moscow and published by a party newspaper, a document that tells us much about his reception and almost nothing independent about conditions in the Soviet Union. For both men, later memorial articles written by political associates are a third category: useful evidence of how the movement remembered them, not neutral biography. Independent scholarly work is used here to set these claims beside the findings of historians who were not participants. W. E. B. Du Bois, 1868 to 1963 A scholar formed in New England and Berlin Du Bois grew up in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, a New England village where racial inequality existed but had not yet hardened into the all powerful system he would later study in the South (Lewis, Biography of a Race , 1993, ch. 1). That difference shaped the early work. He approached what contemporaries called the Negro problem as a question of citizenship and nationhood, and his first major book was not a memoir but a piece of empirical social research. His education took him from Fisk to Harvard and then to the University of Berlin, where he encountered German social science and the historical school of economics (Lewis, Biography of a Race , 1993, chs. 2–3). Those studies did not make him a Marxist in the 1890s, but they gave him the habit of treating racial inequality as a historical and economic problem rather than a moral failing of individuals. The first decisive publication was The Conservation of Races , a paper delivered to the American Negro Academy in 1897. Its announcement described the educated minority's responsibility to "take concerted steps" for the uplift of the race, the idea later known as the Talented Tenth. The stress in that phrasing falls on agency and on a duty to act rather than on charity. It also locates the agency in a small educated stratum, and Du Bois spent much of the next thirty years testing and revising that claim. The Philadelphia Negro (1899) was a door to door study of the city's Black population ( The Philadelphia Negro , 1899). Du Bois did not simply write about Black people; he counted, interviewed and mapped them, making their conditions visible to a discipline that had largely ignored them. The method established his reputation as a sociologist of Black urban life and prepared the way for the much larger historical argument of Black Reconstruction . David Levering Lewis's two volume biography, W. E. B. Du Bois: Biography of a Race, 1868–1919 (1993) and W. E. B. Du Bois: The Fight for Equality and the American Century, 1919–1963 (2000), remains the standard scholarly account of how that reputation and that argument developed. The Souls of Black Folk and the color line The Souls of Black Folk appeared in 1903. Its short "Forethought" ends with the sentence that gave Du Bois his lifelong theme: "the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color line." He was making a claim ab

title: Black Women Communists: Jones, Davis, Shakur
description: Claudia Jones's triple exploitation thesis, Angela Davis's Marxist feminism and Assata Shakur's writings.
text: Claudia Jones, Angela Davis and Assata Shakur wrote in different decades and from different organizations. Jones published her central essay on Black women in the Communist Party's theoretical journal in 1949 ( Political Affairs , June 1949), then wrote about peace, imprisonment and the Caribbean diaspora until her death in 1964 (MIA Claudia Jones archive). Davis wrote an autobiography in 1974 ( Angela Davis: An Autobiography ), edited a collection on political prisoners in 1971 ( If They Come in the Morning ) and developed an analysis of housework and imprisonment over the following three decades ( Women, Race and Class ; Are Prisons Obsolete? ). Shakur published an autobiography in 1987 ( Assata ) and a series of letters from exile in the 1990s and 2010s (1998 letter; 2014 letter). Reading them together means comparing arguments made in distinct settings, not smoothing those settings away. Each woman is a witness to her own life, and each account has a purpose. Jones's 1953 court statement is a declaration of principle addressed to a judge who had already sentenced her; her 1956 prison account was written for a party newspaper after her deportation. Davis's autobiography is a retrospective book, her prison interviews are political statements made while she was in custody, and her 1998 television interview looks back over twenty five years. Shakur's account of a 1973 traffic stop was written more than a decade later and is a work of political autobiography, not a police report. Where a court record or a contemporary report exists, it is set beside that account. Donald Hines, who worked with Jones in London, is the one participant writing about someone else's life, and his recollections were published in 2008, more than forty years after the events he describes. Claudia Jones, 1915 to 1964 A journalist in the Communist Party Claudia Jones was born in Port of Spain, Trinidad, on 21 February 1915 and joined her parents in Harlem in 1924. She entered the Communist Party in 1936, partly in response to its defence of the Scottsboro defendants, and by 1937 was on the editorial staff of the Daily Worker . These details come from a participant account by Donald Hines, first published in Race & Class in 2008. Hines worked with Jones at the West Indian Gazette and writes as a colleague and admirer. His chronology is the fullest available, but his purpose was to recover a neglected figure, not to provide a detached assessment. The MIA Claudia Jones archive preserves her bylines and makes the shape of her early work visible. She wrote on NAACP youth delegates in July 1937, on "Negro Youth Pamphlet" in June 1938, and on the party's youth leadership in a piece titled "Young Communist Leader Lauds Workers School Value as Educator" in January 1941. Her 1942 title was "Lift Every Voice For Victory!" In 1940 she published the pamphlet "Jim Crow in Uniform." The bylines show her working on two fronts from the start: defending Black youth against discrimination and building the organizational life of the party and its youth league. By the mid 1940s she was writing on what the party called the Negro Question. A discussion article on the draft resolution appeared in Political Affairs in August 1945, and in January 1946 she published "On the Right to Self Determination for the Negro People in the Black Belt" in the same journal. Her 1946 Daily Worker articles covered the filibuster against fair employment legislation, a CIO packing house campaign against Jim Crow, and mass action against lynching. The theoretical argument was attached to specific campaigns from the beginning. The turn to Black women as a distinct subject came in 1948 and 1949. "For New Approaches to Our Work among Women" appeared in Political Affairs in August 1948. The landmark "An End to the Neglect of the Problems of the Negro Woman!" appeared in the same journal in June 1949, volume 28, number 6, on pages 51 to 67. "We Seek Full Equality for Women" followed in the Daily Worker o

title: US Black Communist Leaders: Haywood, Ford, Hampton
description: The Black Belt thesis, The Negro and the Communist Party, and Hampton's Rainbow Coalition.
text: Between the late 1920s and the end of the 1960s, three American radicals argued that the freedom of Black people could not be separated from the struggle against capitalism. All three were communists. By that they meant that they belonged to organisations which took the writings of Karl Marx and Vladimir Lenin as their guide and which aimed to replace private ownership of the main industries with public control. Harry Haywood, James W. Ford and Fred Hampton worked in different periods and different organisations, and they disagreed about strategy. Yet each returned to the same claim: that racism was rooted in an economic system, that Black liberation required mass organisation rather than appeals to goodwill, and that the state would resist those who said so. Their published words survive in their movements' presses and in the pages of the Communist Party's newspapers. Read carefully, and with the limits of those sources in mind, they show how an American revolutionary tradition was made and how it was met. Harry Haywood and the invention of the Black Belt nation Harry Haywood was born in 1898 and grew up in the world of railway work and the sea. The biographical notice attached to his archive says that in the early 1920s he worked as a trainman and maritime seaman before entering the circle around the African Blood Brotherhood, an early organisation of Black radicals. His own account places his political education abroad. He travelled to Moscow in 1926 and studied at KUTVA, the university established for workers from the East, where he joined the internal arguments of the Soviet party. He later recalled that he and the other Black students supported Stalin against Trotsky because they read Stalin's policies as the continuation of Lenin's. In his autobiography he wrote that those who used the word Stalinist as an insult were avoiding the real question, which was whether Stalin and the Central Committee had been right. He believed history had shown that they had. (MIA Encyclopedia, "Haywood, Harry"; Haywood, "Trotsky's Day in Court") That formation mattered because the theory for which Haywood became known was built with the concepts of the Communist International, the Moscow based body that coordinated communist parties in different countries. The Communist Party of the United States, usually shortened to CPUSA, was the American member. Haywood served on its Central Committee and, in the early 1930s, on its Politburo, the small group of senior leaders who took decisions between full committee meetings. He spent more than four years in the Soviet Union and helped draft the resolutions on the "Negro question" adopted by the Communist International in 1928 and 1930. He also fought in the Abraham Lincoln Brigade in Spain during the Spanish Civil War, and in the 1960s he became associated with the Maoist New Communist Movement, a current that looked to Mao's China rather than to Moscow. A movement obituary described him as a worker intellectual who had transformed himself from a railwayman and seaman into a theorist of Black liberation. (Beal, "'Black Bolshevik' Harry Haywood Dies at 87," 1985) Haywood's central proposition was that Black people in the Southern Black Belt formed an oppressed nation, not simply a racial minority. The Black Belt was the band of counties across the cotton growing South where Black people formed a large share of the population. In his 1948 book Negro Liberation he argued that what was called racial persecution was in fact a form of national oppression, and that within the borders of the United States there existed two nations, one dominant and white, the other subject and Black. He set out the case with the criteria then standard in Marxist writing. A nation, in that scheme, needed a shared territory, a common economic life, a division of labour, and a culture. Haywood claimed all of these for the Black Belt. He described a region of roughly 470 counties containing five million Black people, with its o

title: The Chilean Road: Popular Unity, the Coup and the Voices It Left
description: On the morning after the vote of 4 September 1970, Salvador Allende stepped onto the balcony of the University of Chile Students' Federation building in Santiago.
text: On the morning after the vote of 4 September 1970, Salvador Allende stepped onto the balcony of the University of Chile Students' Federation building in Santiago. Popular Unity, the coalition that had won, had campaigned under a song whose chorus ran: "Venceremos, venceremos, con Allende en septiembre a vencer." — Popular Unity anthem "Venceremos", quoted by Memoria Chilena, National Library of Chile, "El gobierno de la Unidad Popular (1970–1973)" (Source: memoriachilena.gob.cl). Allende promised to respect the rights of all Chileans and not to trade away the programme. The song was the sung form of a written platform agreed the previous December: "La única alternativa verdaderamente popular [...] es terminar con el dominio de los imperialistas, de los monopolios, de la oligarquía terrateniente." — Popular Unity Basic Programme, 17 December 1969 (ellipsis marks my omission). Marxists Internet Archive: diciembre17 The Basic Programme of 17 December 1969 named the industries to be taken into state hands, copper, iron, nitrates, banking, foreign trade and strategic industry; promised agrarian reform and a "social area" of state ownership with worker representation on public sector boards; and pledged to preserve democratic freedoms and not use the armed forces against the people. That last claim was tested within three years. A road built in law Allende's transition preserved legality while transferring ownership. In a message to Congress on 21 May 1971 he set out a second, democratic model of revolution: "Vamos al socialismo por el rechazo voluntario, a través del voto popular, del sistema capitalista y dependiente." — Salvador Allende, speech to Congress, 21 May 1971. Marxists Internet Archive: 21 5 71 There would be a plurality of parties and institutions preserved while ownership changed, with a socialist constitution later. He argued that a social revolution takes years, not weeks. His confidence that the armed forces would defend the constitutional order was an assumption, not a finding. The Statute of Democratic Guarantees, Law 17.398, promulgated on 30 December 1970 with Justice Minister Lisandro Cruz, protected organisation, expression, assembly, teaching and the press, banned prior censorship and extended social rights. It defined the armed forces and the Carabineros, the police force, as professional, hierarchical, disciplined, obedient and non deliberative bodies. Its existence does not prove enforcement, but it fixes the settlement the coup destroyed. Copper nationalisation was the central economic act; Allende maintained it was lawful and approved unanimously by Congress. The most concrete content given to "workers' control" came in a draft law of 15 July 1972 on a National System of Self Management, whose first article stated its purpose was: "cuyo objetivo será acentuar el proceso de control de la economía por los trabajadores" — Draft law on the National System of Self Management, Article 1, 15 July 1972. Marxists Internet Archive: julio15 Capital in a self managed firm belonged to the state development corporation, management to the workforce. An Assembly of Workers, one vote per permanent worker and no proxies, would elect a five member Management Council to appoint the manager. The state fixed plans, pay and a compulsory levy on surplus, and workers could not divide the capital. More precise than the slogan, it was a draft, not an enacted law, and no minutes of an actual assembly survive. The local industrial bodies known as CORD were the intended channel, but the record holds no account from a factory council. Blockade and rehearsal The government's case was that it was being strangled from outside. In an open letter to President Nixon on 20 August 1971, Allende listed the withdrawal of a scientific mission from Easter Island, cancellation of the warship Enterprise 's visit, opposition to Santiago hosting the third UN Conference on Trade and Development, and suspension of Export Import Bank credits after copp

title: Nicaragua: Insurrection, Literacy and War, 1979–1990
description: Within two or three years of the Sandinista victory of July 1979, the commanders who had made it were asked to explain how.
text: Within two or three years of the Sandinista victory of July 1979, the commanders who had made it were asked to explain how. Marta Harnecker, a Chilean journalist, interviewed Dora María Téllez, who led the seizure of the National Palace in 1978 and the rising in León ( Pueblos en Armas ). Téllez described insurrection as something assembled patiently: "la insurrección es una telaraña que hay que tejer" — Dora María Téllez, FSLN commander, interview first published March 1981, in Marta Harnecker, Pueblos en Armas . Original Spanish; my translation: "the insurrection is a spiderweb that has to be woven". Marxists Internet Archive: harnecker 89861 The FSLN, the Sandinista National Liberation Front, overthrew the dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza, weakened by the 1972 earthquake that destroyed much of Managua and by a broad opposition coalition. The interviews preserve the victors' own account, close enough to be specific and early enough to be candid: "En 1961, de la conjugación de varios grupos armados, surge el Frente Sandinista" — Humberto Ortega, FSLN commander, interview 1980–82. Original Spanish; my translation: "In 1961, from the combination of several armed groups, the Sandinista Front arose". Marxists Internet Archive: harnecker 89861 Ortega, a National Directorate member and commander of the final offensive, placed the Front's creation in several armed groups and described its split into three tendencies in 1976 and 1977 as a failure of organisation under repression. The rising of September 1978 failed militarily, but Téllez said it taught the movement what the web required: "las masas nunca se te van a levantar si no creen que van a tomar el poder" — Dora María Téllez, interview first published March 1981. Original Spanish; my translation: "the masses will never rise unless they believe they are going to take power". Marxists Internet Archive: harnecker 89861 She argued that militias, communications and hospitals had to be woven together before the 1979 offensive, and that in Monimbó, an indigenous community, crowds rose spontaneously in response to killings before the party could direct them. All the interviewees were winning commanders; opponents, peasants and ordinary fighters do not appear. Governing and teaching Two later interviews show how the movement tried to govern. Luis Carrión, a National Directorate member and Vice Minister of the Interior, traced Christian participation to Vatican II and Medellín; where other popular organisation was repressed, small Catholic base communities became centres of local leadership: "comienzan a hablar, no sólo de temas cristianos, sino de los problemas económicos y sociales que los están agobiando" — Luis Carrión, FSLN National Directorate member, interview 14 November 1986. Original Spanish; my translation: "they begin to speak not only of Christian matters but of the economic and social problems weighing on them". Marxists Internet Archive: harnecker 90187 Carlos Carrión described a later effort to replace vertical command with mass participation under the pressure of war. Both were senior officials justifying party policy, and no critical Christian or bishops' voice appears. The best documented social programme was the National Literacy Crusade of 1980, whose aim included concientización , the raising of political consciousness. The official record gives 95,582 participants, 406,056 people taught and 59 literacy workers dead, and states the result as: "reduciendo la tasa de analfabetismo de un 50.35% a un 12.96%" — Nicaragua Ministry of Education, official page on the National Literacy Crusade. Original Spanish; my translation: "reducing the illiteracy rate from 50.35% to 12.96%". Source: mined.gob.ni José Luis Rocha, a former brigadista, recalled a Popular Literacy Army of about 100,000, of whom 60,000 went to the mountains, working five months: "The National Literacy Crusade turned into an intensive five month course—from March 23 to August 23, 1980." — José Luis Rocha, f

title: El Salvador: The War We Were Told Was Not Happening
description: On 23 March 1980, three days before his death, Óscar Romero, Archbishop of San Salvador, stood in his cathedral and addressed the army, the National Guard and the police on Radio YSAX.
text: On 23 March 1980, three days before his death, Óscar Romero, Archbishop of San Salvador, stood in his cathedral and addressed the army, the National Guard and the police on Radio YSAX. He told them they were killing their own campesinos, poor rural farmers, and that no soldier had to obey an order against the law of God. He ended with a command: "I beg you, I beseech you, I order you in the name of God: stop the repression." Source: Óscar Romero, homily, 23 March 1980, published English translation, Archbishop Romero Trust (translator not named on the page) Romero was shot the next afternoon while celebrating mass. The church and the security forces The United Nations Commission on the Truth for El Salvador, set up under the peace accords to investigate rather than prosecute, later identified who had given the order. It described a "death squad", an unofficial group of killers working with official protection: "Former Major Roberto DAubuisson gave the order to assassinate the Archbishop and gave precise instructions to members of his security service, acting as a 'death squad', to organize and supervise the assassination." Source: UN Commission on the Truth, From Madness to Hope , 15 March 1993 The Commission also found that the Supreme Court helped those involved escape punishment. Jean Donovan, an American lay missionary, a church worker without clerical status, in La Libertad wrote to Senator Edward Kennedy on 30 November 1980 about a twelve year old boy she believed had been macheted by ORDEN, a paramilitary force allied to the army. Witnesses had told her that men searching the refugee centre looked and spoke like Americans: "As a North American, one of the hardest things to see is how the people are suffering here because of actions of our government." Source: Jean Donovan, letter to Senator Edward Kennedy, 30 November 1980, quoted in a UPI report of 13 December 1980 She was killed three days later with three other churchwomen. Her account of the men was hearsay, which she flagged; the letter survives in excerpts found with the possessions returned in her coffin. The river and the village In March 1981 families fled towards the Lempa river, pursued by troops and helicopters. María Isidora Leiva remembered the crossing in a sworn statement given decades later: "They cornered us on the banks of the river and we had to throw ourselves into the water, whether we could swim or not." Source: María Isidora Leiva, sworn statement, 2013, published English translation, University of Washington Center for Human Rights (translator not named) The dead were swept away, so no count is reliable. The Commission recorded twenty to thirty killed and 189 missing against press estimates of 200. Declassified cables show US diplomats privately accepted that Salvadoran forces fired on civilians while disputing the word "massacre". At El Mozote in Morazán, soldiers of the Atlacatl battalion, an elite unit trained by American advisers, killed villagers and their neighbours in December 1981. Rufina Amaya, the only adult survivor, told Raymond Bonner of the New York Times, who entered rebel held territory in January 1982: "It was a great massacre. They left nothing." Source: Rufina Amaya to Raymond Bonner, January 1982, two sentences from one interview joined for brevity, reproduced in the Columbia University case study Bonner found charred skulls beneath burned roofs and heard thirteen peasants name the battalion. Alma Guillermoprieto of the Washington Post entered Morazán at the same time. In a later testimony Amaya recalled: "A las doce del mediodía ya habían terminado de matar a todos los hombres." ("By noon they had already finished killing all the men." My gloss.) Source: Rufina Amaya, in Luciérnagas en El Mozote (1996), reproduced by BBC Mundo The Argentine Forensic Anthropology Unit excavated the convent in 1992. title: Guatemala 1944–1954: The Revolution That Was Stopped
description: On 27 June 1954 President Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán went on the government radio station and read a speech written by his secretary, Manuel Fortuny.
text: On 27 June 1954 President Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán went on the government radio station and read a speech written by his secretary, Manuel Fortuny. The audio is lost; the text survives in a later transcription. Exile aircraft were flying over the country. Árbenz told listeners what he thought was happening: "No me han acorralado los argumentos del enemigo, sino los medios materiales con lo que cuenta para la destrucción de Guatemala." Source: Jacobo Árbenz, resignation broadcast, 27 June 1954, transcription no. 0020, HistoriaGT He named the United Fruit Company, the American corporation that dominated the banana trade and the railway to the coast, and American "monopolies": "Han tomado pretexto al comunismo. La verdad es muy otra. La verdad hay que buscar en los intereses financieros de la compañía frutera." Source: Jacobo Árbenz, resignation broadcast, 27 June 1954, HistoriaGT He handed power to Colonel Carlos Enrique Díaz rather than let the country be destroyed. It was the end of the only democratically elected government Guatemala knew before 1996. The land question The government had come to power after the October Revolution of 1944, an uprising that toppled the junta of Jorge Ubico's successor Federico Ponce Vaides. Guatemala elected two civilian presidents, wrote a constitution and legalised unions and a communist party. Its central promise was land. Decree 900 of 17 June 1952 abolished the forms of forced labour that bound rural workers to estates: "Quedan abolidas todas las formas de servidumbre y esclavitud, y por consiguiente prohibidas las prestaciones personales gratuitas de los campesinos" Source: Decree 900, Agrarian Reform Law, Article 2, 17 June 1952 It exempted holdings of roughly ninety hectares, protected indigenous communal land, defined large uncultivated or rented estates as subject to expropriation with twenty five year bonds, and gave the peasant confederation seats on the agrarian committees. A law is not proof of implementation, but the Commission for Historical Clarification, the truth commission set up under the 1994 peace agreement, later recorded that by 1954 more than 138,000 peasant families, mostly indigenous, had benefited. Washington's decision The reform alarmed Washington. CIA meetings began in November 1951. An internal paper of 4 September 1953 recorded that an earlier plan to arm exiles led by Carlos Castillo Armas had failed when the State Department refused an export licence: "All went well until the shipment had actually left the warehouse en route to New Orleans. The Department of State refused an export license" Source: CIA draft paper, 4 September 1953, quoted in FRUS 1952–1954, Guatemala The replacement operation, PBSUCCESS, was large and mostly political. A CIA memorandum of 1975 listed 85 trained exiles, clandestine radio, a three million dollar budget and nearly eighty air missions in a fortnight: "There were approximately 80 missions flown during the 14–29 June 1954 period, by various type aircraft such as C–47's, F–47's and Cessnas" Source: CIA memorandum, "CIA's Role in the Overthrow of Arbenz", 12 May 1975, FRUS 1952–1954, Guatemala, document 287 Declassified files also show preparation for political killing. The agency's training material included a practical guide: "A hammer, axe, wrench, screw driver, fire poker, kitchen knife, lamp stand, or anything hard, heavy and handy will suffice." Source: CIA, "A Study of Assassination", undated, declassified 1997, quoted by the National Security Archive It warned: "no assassination instructions should ever be written or recorded" Source: CIA, "A Study of Assassination", undated, National Security Archive A memorandum of 31 March 1954 asked for a list of government leaders, party members and people of tactical importance whose removal was judged necessary for military action. Another split targets between those to be killed and those to be imprisoned or exiled. Every name on the released copies was deleted, so the lists prove a targ

title: Bolivia 1952: The Revolution the Miners Made
description: In November 1946, six years before the insurrection, the country's mine workers met at Pulacayo and adopted a programme.
text: In November 1946, six years before the insurrection, the country's mine workers met at Pulacayo and adopted a programme. The Federación Sindical de Trabajadores Mineros de Bolivia, or FSTMB, the federation of mine unions, was organising around a demand beyond wages: "If we wish to avoid a repeat of the massacre of Catavi we must arm the workers." Source: FSTMB, Thesis of Pulacayo , 8 November 1946, English text published 2019, translator not named The Catavi massacre it invoked was an attack on striking miners in 1942. The thesis called for a living wage, a forty hour week, occupation of mines threatened with closure, and workers' control, meaning management by committees elected in the mines. It rejected the ballot and cooperation with employers. If companies closed their mines: "If the capitalists respond to all demands with the threat of closing their mines, there is no option open to the workers other than seizing the mines and organizing production ourselves." Source: FSTMB, Thesis of Pulacayo , 8 November 1946 This was a programme, not a record of events, and its authorship was disputed even among Bolivian Trotskyists. Its importance is that it shows what the miners wanted before the revolution, so the later argument over nationalisation can be read as a conflict between two positions. The world the miners lived in The camps were company property. Domitila Barrios de Chungara, who grew up at Pulacayo and Siglo XX and later organised in the Catavi Housewives' Committee, recalled that a miner could wait five or ten years for a house, that a room was four by five or six metres with no water or sanitation, and that a widow had ninety days to leave. These are recollections from the 1970s, not contemporary records, but they describe the world the thesis was written for. April 1952 In April 1952 the state's ability to coerce its own people collapsed. The Movimiento Nacionalista Revolucionario, or MNR, the nationalist party that had won the 1951 election, rose on 9 April with the national police and much of organised labour. Dean Acheson, the US Secretary of State, wrote to President Truman six weeks later: "the uprising of April 9 constituted to a large extent a spontaneous expression of public sentiment" Source: Dean Acheson, memorandum to the President, 22 May 1952, FRUS 1952–1954, The American Republics, volume IV, document 136 His memorandum sought a decision on recognition and stressed the junta's lack of control: the army in the La Paz area had been badly damaged, civilians kept the rifles they had seized, and Víctor Paz Estenssoro did not return from six years in exile until 15 April. It has no Bolivian popular voice, but on the failure of the army it is clear. Domitila's family story puts miners in the fighting away from the capital. She was fifteen in 1952, so this is community memory: "It participated actively in the revolution of April 9, 1952, disarming the government forces of Uyuni." Source: Domitila Barrios de Chungara, on Pulacayo, oral testimony recorded in the mid 1970s, translated by Victoria Ortiz A correspondent for the American paper Labor Action recorded the new leaders' language. Hernán Siles Zuazo, soon vice president, promised: "our government will not only be one of reform, but it will be a government of political, social and economic transformation" Source: Hernán Siles Zuazo, first official declaration, reported late April 1952, rendered in English by Labor Action , translator uncredited Juan Lechín, head of the mine workers' union and soon Minister of Mines, promised nationalisation. The correspondent, a partisan anti Stalinist, drew the division: the workers fought for a social revolution, the MNR for a reform of Bolivian capitalism. That was his interpretation, but the next months show the argument was real. title: After the Victory: Ordinary Cubans and the Social Revolution, 1959–1971
description: In 1961 Felo Rojas was thirteen years old.
text: In 1961 Felo Rojas was thirteen years old. He slept in a hammock in a peasant house in the Cuban countryside, beneath a roof of leaves, on an earth floor, with water drawn from a well. He had been sent there to teach adults to read. "I was sleeping in a hammock. The house had a dirt floor, no running water — water came from a well — and the roof was made of leaves." He recalled it when a radio producer interviewed him in Havana fifty four years later (Felo Rojas, interviewed by Brian Kahn, broadcast 22 March 2015; English wording as published by Montana Public Radio, translator not stated). That hut, and thousands like it, was where the revolution's most durable claim was lived out: that it had carried literacy and a new dignity to people the old order had left behind. At a May Day rally in Havana that year, Fidel Castro pointed to the same effort from a platform. He told the crowd that "the volunteer teachers paraded and also representatives of the 100,000 young people on their way to the interior to wipe out illiteracy" (Fidel Castro, May Day speech, 1 May 1961; English transcription in the Castro Internet Archive). The parade measured the campaign in tens of thousands. Rojas's hammock measures what it felt like to the young people who did the work. Teaching by lantern The volunteers were often children. Rosa Hernández Acosta was ten in 1961. "Well, imagine! I was born in 1951 and the Campaign started 1961, so I was 10 years old." That was how she introduced herself in an interview sixty years later (Rosa Hernández Acosta, interview by Kian Seara Rey, 6 February 2021; translated from Spanish by the interviewer). When the assigned teacher could not stay in her village, she took on three or four adult pupils herself. She taught by kerosene lantern and waited until eight or nine at night for a pupil who worked in the fields to return. Afterwards the adults called at her house to show her that they could read the newspaper. Marietta Biosca, nineteen in 1961, kept a stricter timetable: "We arrived at their houses at four in the afternoon and taught them till ten at night." (Marietta Biosca, interviewed by Brian Kahn, 22 March 2015; English wording as published by Montana Public Radio, translator not stated). Not everyone wanted to learn. Pamela Rios was ten, and she met adults who turned her away. "Some said, 'I'm too old to learn to read and write.' I explained that reading would allow them to understand what was happening in the entire country, not just in their towns." She remembered the conversation (Pamela Rios, interviewed by Brian Kahn, 22 March 2015; English wording as published by Montana Public Radio, translator not stated). The material conditions were as bare as the houses. A volunteer interviewed by Timoteo Delgado remembered that "where we were there was not potable water, there was not light, there were not sanitary services." (unnamed brigadista, quoted by Timoteo Delgado, 6 June 2019). Another told Delgado she had received a death threat from an anti revolutionary group, knowing that another volunteer had been killed, and that supervisors advised her to go home, but she refused; the government then issued her a gun for self protection. Joanne Elvy's oral histories record the names of two volunteers who were killed, Conrado Benítez and Manuel Ascunce Domenech (Joanne C. Elvy, "Photos from a Cuban Diary," 10 September 2005). The work was a schoolroom and a political front line at once. Angelica Martiz gave the reason simply: "I wanted to help spread literacy because it was something the country needed." (Angelica Martiz, quoted by Timoteo Delgado, 6 June 2019). A change in themselves More than half the volunteers were young women, and many had never previously left home without an escort. In their own accounts the campaign is remembered less as a teaching exercise than as a change in how they understood their own lives. title: The Dirty War: Argentina, 1973–1983
description: On 24 March 1977, the first anniversary of the military coup, Rodolfo Walsh sat down to write an open letter to the junta.
text: On 24 March 1977, the first anniversary of the military coup, Rodolfo Walsh sat down to write an open letter to the junta. Walsh was a writer and journalist who had worked for the CGT news service, had later joined the Montoneros, and had lost a daughter in combat. He was writing from inside Argentina as a man who expected to be arrested, and he circulated the letter clandestinely rather than submitting it to the censors. He opened with a count: "Quince mil desaparecidos, diez mil presos, cuatro mil muertos, decenas de miles de desterrados son la cifra desnuda de ese terror." Fifteen thousand disappeared, ten thousand prisoners, four thousand dead, tens of thousands exiled: that was the bare figure of the terror, as he saw it in the regime's first year (Rodolfo Walsh, Carta abierta de un escritor a la Junta Militar , 24 March 1977). He knew the letter might cost him his life: "sin esperanza de ser escuchado, con la certeza de ser perseguido, pero fiel al compromiso que asumí hace mucho tiempo de dar testimonio en momentos difíciles." He was declaring himself without hope of being heard, certain of being hunted, but faithful to a pledge to bear witness in hard times (Walsh, same letter). The desaparecidos , the disappeared, were people seized by the security forces and never acknowledged to be in custody. Their families could not prove they were alive or dead. The Argentine state called what it was doing a war against subversion and described itself as anti communist and "occidental y cristiano," Western and Christian. The armed turn To understand why Walsh wrote as he did, it is necessary to go back to the movements that preceded the dictatorship. Juan Perón was overthrown by a coup in 1955, and Peronism, the political movement built around him, was banned. A generation of activists concluded that constitutional politics had been closed to them. Among them was the Montoneros. On 1 June 1970 the organisation issued a communiqué of four sentences. "The leadership of the MONTONEROS communicates that at 7:00 today Pedro Eugenio Aramburu was executed." (Montoneros Communiqué No. 4, 1 June 1970; translated by Mitchell Abidor). Aramburu was a former president; the 1955 coup against Perón had been led by Lonardi, whom Aramburu replaced on 13 November 1955. The terse notice, addressed over the heads of the government to "the people of the nation," set the movement's early public tone: ritualised, formal, and insistent that it spoke for the country. Later that year the Montoneros defined themselves more fully. "Only by fighting will we succeed in recovering what is ours. The Montoneros call for armed resistance for a Free, Just and Sovereign Fatherland." (Montoneros, "The Montoneros: Armed Wing of Peronism," September 1970; translated by Mitchell Abidor). The claim to be the armed wing of Peronism was contested inside Peronism and later by Perón himself; the document records the claim, not its acceptance. A second current, the ERP, or Ejército Revolucionario del Pueblo, the People's Revolutionary Army, was the armed wing of the Revolutionary Workers' Party, a Trotskyist party influenced by Che Guevara. Its newspaper El Combatiente announced on 28 July 1976 that Mario Roberto Santucho, known as Comandante Carlos, had been killed with Domingo Menna and Captain Benito Urteaga in a firefight at a flat in Villa Martelli after their ammunition ran out (PRT ERP, "Comandante Carlos ¡Hasta la victoria siempre!," El Combatiente No. 226, 28 July 1976; text signed by Luis Mattini). This was a eulogy by the surviving leadership, not an independent account of how the security forces found the flat. On 12 October 1973, the day Perón resumed the presidency, the Montoneros and the FAR, the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias, recorded their merger: "A partir de la fecha ambas organizaciones se fusionan pasando a constituir una sola y quedando unificadas definitivamente todas sus estructuras y mandos;" (FAR–Montoneros, Acta de Unidad , 12 October 1973). title: The Zapatistas: Indigenous Rebellion and Another Politics
description: On 1 January 1994, the day the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect, indigenous rebels in the southern Mexican state of Chiapas seized six towns and declared war on the...
text: On 1 January 1994, the day the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect, indigenous rebels in the southern Mexican state of Chiapas seized six towns and declared war on the federal army. The document they released that morning was the First Declaration of the Lacandon Jungle, dated 1993 and issued in the name of the General Command of the EZLN, the Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional, or Zapatista Army of National Liberation, named after the revolutionary Emiliano Zapata. It invoked Article 39 of the Mexican Constitution, the people's right to alter their government, and it ended with a claim of ancestry: "Pero nosotros HOY DECIMOS ¡BASTA!, somos los herederos de los verdaderos forjadores de nuestra nacionalidad" (EZLN General Command, First Declaration of the Lacandon Jungle, 1993, released 1 January 1994). But today we say enough, the declaration continued in this English rendering, we are the heirs of the true builders of our nationality. The uprising was the first major armed rebellion against a neoliberal state in Latin America after the collapse of governments calling themselves socialist in Europe, and it refused the model those governments had followed. The EZLN did not set out to capture the state. It insisted on mandar obedeciendo , leading by obeying, and built autonomous municipalities in the years that followed. Eleven demands and a twelve day war The First Declaration was a list of demands as well as a declaration of war. It set out eleven of them in a single line: "apoyando este plan del pueblo mexicano que lucha por trabajo, tierra, techo, alimentación, salud, educación, independencia, libertad, democracia, justicia y paz" (First Declaration of the Lacandon Jungle). Work, land, housing, food, health, education, independence, liberty, democracy, justice and peace. The text named the PRI, the Partido Revolucionario Institucional or Institutional Revolutionary Party, which had governed Mexico since 1929, and President Carlos Salinas de Gortari as its enemy. It claimed the heritage of five hundred years of indigenous and Mexican struggle and set out six military orders. After twelve days of fighting, mass demonstrations in Mexico City helped bring about a ceasefire. On 10 June 1994 the EZLN extended that ceasefire unilaterally, said its base communities had rejected the government's peace proposals, and explained why it would not lay down its arms: "Chiapas no tendrá solución real si no se soluciona México." (Second Declaration of the Lacandon Jungle, 10 June 1994). Chiapas would have no real solution without a solution for Mexico. The declaration opened with a 1914 speech attributed to Zapata at the Aguascalientes convention, which is where the movement later built a gathering place of that name. The claim to have consulted the base communities is the movement's own account of its procedure, with no independent record attached. Another politics In August 1994 the EZLN built a convention centre in the Chiapas jungle and called it Aguascalientes, after the revolutionary convention of 1914. Comandante Tacho, speaking for the clandestine indigenous leadership, formally handed it over to the National Democratic Convention at 8.20 in the morning of 3 August: "A partir de hoy, Aguascalientes ya no es del EZLN, ahora es de su propiedad de la Convención Nacional Democrática." (Comandante Tacho, speech at Aguascalientes, 3 August 1994). From today, he said, Aguascalientes was no longer the EZLN's but belonged to the Convention. The handover was a political act: transferring a site to civil society does not by itself establish who controlled it in practice. It was also a statement of what the movement meant by another politics. Subcomandante Marcos, its best known spokesperson, wrote in an open letter in 1996 that the Zapatistas were not trying to take power. "Nosotros no luchamos por tomar el poder; luchamos por democracia, libertad y justicia." (Marcos, "Lo que nos hace diferentes es nuestra propuesta política

title: The ABC Strikes and the Workers' Party: Brazil's Labour Road to the Presidency
description: On 18 April 1980 the metalworkers' newspaper Movimento described the industrial town of São Bernardo do Campo in the middle of a general strike: 'a cidade se transforma numa verdadeira...
text: On 18 April 1980 the metalworkers' newspaper Movimento described the industrial town of São Bernardo do Campo in the middle of a general strike: "a cidade se transforma numa verdadeira praça de guerra, com quase 4 horas de escaramuças onde os operários, sem direção nenhuma, reagem à violência policial com pedradas." (the city becomes a veritable square of war, with nearly four hours of skirmishes in which the workers, leaderless, answer police violence with stones, my rendering). The line appeared in Movimento no. 255 of 19–25 May 1980 and is reproduced in the Fundação Perseu Abramo's chronology of the strike. Brazil was then under military rule, which banned strikes and supervised the unions. The action had begun on 1 April after weeks of mass meetings at Vila Euclides, the football stadium where workers from the ABC belt gathered. The ABC is the cluster of industrial municipalities around São Bernardo do Campo and São Paulo where the car and metal plants were concentrated. On 14 April a regional labour court declared the strike illegal, on 17 April the government intervened in the union and removed forty two of its directors, and on 19 April police arrested the union president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and twelve other leaders without a judicial warrant. A march on 1 May was reported at about 100,000 people; the strike ended on 12 May and the prisoners were released on 20 May. The crowd figures come from the organizers and the police, not from independent measurement. That ban on strikes is why the dispute reached beyond wages. Through the 1970s the military government held down real wages, a squeeze known as the arrocho , while an official union structure kept independent organizing out of the plants. In the ABC a current of organizers known as the new unionism worked around that structure through factory assemblies and a popular newspaper, ABCD Jornal , founded in 1975. Its surviving 1977 cover tells workers not to work overtime, not to accept shift changes and not to trust the bulletin of the intervenor, the official appointed to run the union. The strike wave began with a stoppage at the Scania truck plant on 12 May 1978 and grew through 1979 into the mass meetings at Vila Euclides. A photographic exhibition drawn from those years records Lula speaking from tables in the rain while the crowd repeated his words back through the stadium, a caption written decades later rather than a contemporary report. The historian John D. French argues, from police reports, oral histories and newspaper reporting, that Lula's authority was made in those assemblies rather than brought to them, rejecting both the great man account and older Marxist accounts that treated him as merely an expression of the ranks. Attendance at Vila Euclides was estimated by the police and the union, not counted. The step from strike to party was stated plainly by Lélia Abramo, an actor and trade unionist who was among the first to sign the founding documents. Recalling the strikes some twenty years later, she said: "No decorrer das memoráveis greves de 1978 80, todos os que participavam do movimento começaram a perceber a necessidade de sair das lutas puramente reivindicatórias e estendê las para o campo político." (during the memorable strikes of 1978–80, all who took part came to see the need to leave purely wage demands and extend the struggle into politics, my rendering). This is retrospective testimony by a committed activist, published 24 April 2006 (Fundação Perseu Abramo). On 10 February 1980, at the Colégio Sion school in São Paulo, supporters gathered the 101 signatures required by law to form a party, with delegates from seventeen states. Raul Pont, Paulo Skromov and Paul Singer, interviewed in 1994, described how the Movimento Pró PT added a letter to become the Partido dos Trabalhadores, the Workers' Party, known as the PT. title: The War Inside: Sendero Luminoso and Peru, 1980–2000
description: On 17 May 1980 members of the Partido Comunista del Perú burned ballot boxes at Chuschi, a highland town, and began a war against the state that lasted twenty years.
text: On 17 May 1980 members of the Partido Comunista del Perú burned ballot boxes at Chuschi, a highland town, and began a war against the state that lasted twenty years (CVR, Informe Final , 2003). The party was better known by its other name, Sendero Luminoso, or Shining Path. Its own documents set out a doctrine that historians call Maoism, after Mao Zedong, and that the party called Marxism Leninism Maoism. It claimed that "the scientific ideology of the proletariat, all powerful because it is true, has three stages or landmarks in its dialectical process of development" (Communist Party of Peru, "On Marxism Leninism Maoism", 1988, in Fundamental Documents , an English translation whose translator is not named; Foreign Languages Press). The claim was that Mao had completed what Marx and Lenin had started. Carlos Iván Degregori traced the party's first cadres to a free education movement of 1969 in Ayacucho and to regional inequality, with the university and the teaching profession as the main recruiting ground. The war that followed was fought chiefly in the countryside. Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, the CVR, found that 79 percent of reported victims lived in rural areas and that 75 percent spoke Quechua or another native language as their mother tongue, against 16 percent of the population. Quechua is an Indigenous language of the Andes. Those percentages give the conflict its shape: the people who bore it were mostly poor and Indigenous. In the highlands the two sides fought through villages. Sendero had governed parts of Ayacucho through surveillance and compulsory attendance; at Lucanamarca, after local people killed party cadres, the party killed community members on 3 April 1983. The CVR's own chapter gives two different totals, 69 in one paragraph and 67 in another. Abimael Guzmán, the party's leader, put the number higher and described the killing in an interview of July 1988: "ahí fueron aniquilados más de 80, eso es lo real; y lo decimos, ahí hubo exceso" (there more than 80 were wiped out, that is the reality; and we say it, there was an excess there, my rendering). The words are the commission's transcription of a newspaper interview, not the newspaper itself (Abimael Guzmán, interview with El Diario , Lima, July 1988, transcribed in the CVR's Lucanamarca chapter; CVR final report, Tomo V). It is unusual for a movement's leader to concede in his own words that an action went beyond what he would defend, though Guzmán framed the attack as a necessary blow with an unfortunate side effect. At Uchuraccay, on 26 January 1983, eight journalists, their guide and a community member were killed. A commission set up that year explained the killings as a cultural misunderstanding; it had no Quechua speaker, visited once and never published its assembly transcript. The CVR later called this the "indigenista paradigm". Its own account uses twenty one testimonies and a list, compiled in two assemblies in 2002, naming 135 residents of Uchuraccay killed in the wider violence. Saturnina Figueroa, widow of Severino Morales, told the CVR in February 2002: "Si me matan, mátenme con mis hijos, sino quién los va a criar. ¡Traigan a todos mis hijos y mátennos!" (if they kill me, kill me with my children, otherwise who will raise them? Bring all my children and kill us too, my rendering). Her words were spoken nineteen years after the event, and the report does not say whether they were translated from Quechua or by whom (Saturnina Figueroa, interviewed at Uchuraccay 9 February 2002, quoted in the CVR's Uchuraccay chapter; CVR final report, Tomo V). A local Sendero commander using the name "Suni Puni" wrote in March 1985 that "Desde 1981, Uchuraccay, Iquicha y Huaychao eran bases de apoyo donde existían ya pelotones de la fuerza local y unidades guerrilleras." (since 1981 Uchuraccay, Iquicha and Huaychao were support bases where local defence squads and guerrilla units already existed, my rendering). The manuscript survives i

title: Before and After the Panthers: RAM, the Black Liberation Army and the Black Radical Congress
description: In 1957, in Monroe, North Carolina, members of the local NAACP branch took up guns to defend Black homes against Ku Klux Klan violence.
text: In 1957, in Monroe, North Carolina, members of the local NAACP branch took up guns to defend Black homes against Ku Klux Klan violence. Its president, Robert F. Williams, later accepted responsibility. The sentence that opened his 1962 book Negroes with Guns was direct: "Because a Negro community in the South took up guns in self defense against racist violence — and used them." (Robert F. Williams, Prologue, Negroes with Guns , 1962). The book was assembled in exile from a Havana taped interview while he was wanted on a kidnapping charge: a defence of his own conduct, not a neutral record. Williams said he was not opposed to Martin Luther King's nonviolence, only to what he called the lack of flexibility in pacifist commitments; when law and order broke down, citizens might defend themselves. "It is remarkable how easily and quickly state and local police control and disperse lawless mobs when the Negro is ready to defend himself with arms." (Robert F. Williams, Prologue, 1962). That was his account of police behaviour, not an independent finding, and the book's dates needed an errata page. The argument was already whole in 1962: armed self defence, a rejection of gradualism, and the claim that the state protected the wrong people. "UNITE or PERISH" Three years later the Revolutionary Action Movement, a small clandestine organisation, printed its own version in the Summer–Fall 1965 issue of its journal Black America , with Williams listed as chairman in Exile. The journal said its purpose was to bring "clarity and direction in revolutionary struggle" and unite "Black America with the Bandung world" of Asia, Africa and Latin America. It ended with "UNITE or PERISH WE WILL WIN." (RAM, Black America , Summer–Fall 1965, statement of purpose). Under "Revolutionary Black Internationalism" it argued that the United States contained two nations: a white America and a captive colonial Black America, and that the vanguard was the sub proletariat of exploited races rather than the industrial working class. It rejected civil rights liberalism as "bourgeois reformism" and Black capitalism and separatist cultural politics as "bourgeois nationalism". The scan drops letters, so exact wording needs checking against page images; it preserves a programme, not a record of what members did, and its language about white people was the movement's own. RAM predated the Panthers, founded in Oakland in 1966, but the connection is argued rather than settled. Seale had been involved with RAM, and Umoja and Jones argue that it shaped the vocabulary of Newton and Seale while recording a tactical disagreement: RAM treated the vanguard as underground, the Panthers built a party in the open. The Party's own account has Newton insisting the founders chose the name. Scholars agree that repression shaped the turn to clandestine work; they disagree on how much RAM organised and whether armed struggle was a rational response or a strategic error. The underground after 1971 After the Panthers' internal crisis and the split of 1971, a clandestine formation called the Black Liberation Army carried part of that programme forward. Jalil Abdul Muntaqim, a former Panther imprisoned from 1971, wrote in 1979: "The Black Liberation Army is a politico military organization, whose primary objective is to fight for the independence and self determination of Afrikan people in the United States." (Jalil Muntaqim, "On the Black Liberation Army", written 18 September 1979). He dated the underground to 1968 or 1969 and the split to 1971. Assata Shakur, quoted by Umoja, described autonomous collectives rather than a central organisation; Umoja argues that repression replenished its ranks from the Panthers while conceding the idea predated the party. The record cannot adjudicate. Its Study Guide '77–78 , reproduced in a 2023 collection, stated: "We identify the enemies of the Black Nation not as white people per se, but as the monopoly capitalist class and its agents, be they Black

title: Thomas Sankara and the Burkina Faso Revolution
description: The Democratic and Popular Revolution, women's emancipation, self-reliance and Sankara's collected speeches.
text: Thomas Isidore Noël Sankara was born on 21 December 1949 at Yako in Upper Volta, then a French colony in West Africa. He was an army captain when he became head of state on 4 August 1983, and he was killed in office on 15 October 1987. The four years between those dates are known as the Democratic and Popular Revolution, or RDP from its French name, Révolution démocratique et populaire. The body that held power was the National Council of the Revolution, usually called the CNR, and the mass organisations it called into being were the Committees for the Defence of the Revolution, the CDRs. These are not neutral descriptions. They are the names the revolution gave itself, and any account of the period has to keep them distinct from the judgements of later writers. The surviving record is unusually rich in the revolution's own voice. The Marxists Internet Archive preserves twelve dated texts by Sankara, including his radio proclamation of 4 August 1983 and his speech to the Organisation of African Unity on debt in 1987 (Thomas Sankara Archive). The site thomassankara.net, maintained by people who identify with the movement, publishes the ordinances, the chronology, the speeches and interviews with participants (official site). Pathfinder Press issued a collected volume, Thomas Sankara Speaks , in English and French editions (Pathfinder, English edition; French edition). These are primary sources, and they are indispensable. They are also interested witnesses, so historians have had to put them alongside other evidence. Brian J. Peterson's Thomas Sankara: A Revolutionary in Cold War Africa drew on government archives and more than a hundred interviews with family, friends and colleagues, and treats Sankara as a polarising figure rather than a consensual hero (Indiana University Press, 2021). Ernest Harsch, who reported from Burkina Faso during the revolution and met Sankara, wrote both a short biography and a wider national history (Ohio University Press, 2014; Zed Books, 2017). The 2018 collection A Certain Amount of Madness , edited by Amber Murrey, brings together scholars who examine the revolution's limits as well as its appeal, including its difficult relations with trade unions (Pluto Press). James E. Genova has studied the revolution's use of film as political education (Michigan State University Press, 2022). This chapter uses the movement's documents as evidence, and sets beside them the testimony of participants and the judgements of these historians where they help to explain what happened. The making of an officer, 1949 to 1983 The date and place of Sankara's birth appear in both the archive headnote and the movement's chronology, whose first entry reads: "21/12/49. Naissance de Thomas Sankara à Yako," meaning "21 December 1949. Birth of Thomas Sankara at Yako." (MIA archive index; official chronology). The official site reproduces a biographical note issued by the Union pour la Renaissance, Mouvement Patriotique Sankariste, or UNIR MPS, for the seventy sixth anniversary of his birth. It gives the movement's account of his upbringing and education. He spent his early childhood at Gaoua, where his father was a soldier, and went to secondary school at the Lycée Ouezzin Coulibaly in Bobo Dioulasso, studying Greek and Latin. As a schoolboy at the moment of independence he replaced a colonial flag with that of the future Upper Volta. The note names his history and geography teacher, Adama Abdoulaye Touré, who introduced him to the idea of class struggle and to the underground literature of the African Independence Party, the PAI, and the Patriotic League for Development, LIPAD (UNIR MPS declaration, 19 December 2025). Such a note is a piece of movement memory, written long after the events, and it reads Sankara's childhood in the light of what he later became. The chronology supplies the institutional stages. Sankara won a place at the Prytanée Militaire de Kadiogo in 1966, entered the Military Academy at Antsirabé in Mada

title: Kwame Nkrumah and Patrice Lumumba
description: Consciencism, Neo-Colonialism, the Convention People's Party and the Congo crisis from African sources.
text: Kwame Nkrumah led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana in 1957 and was overthrown in 1966 (Official Ghanaian Biographical Sketch , 1962; Nkrumah, The Dark Days in Ghana , 1968). Patrice Lumumba became the first prime minister of the independent Congo in 1960 and was killed seven months later (Patrice Lumumba, 1984 biography). Both men argued that a flag and a national anthem were not enough. Both believed that political freedom had to be completed by economic control and by the unity of the whole continent. And both wrote their last major texts in exile or confinement, addressing the question of how their defeats would be remembered. The idea that connected them was Pan Africanism. In its simplest form this was the belief that people of African descent everywhere shared a common political destiny, and that the separate states of Africa should act together rather than compete. For Nkrumah it became a programme of continental institutions. For Lumumba it was a security doctrine: if the Congo fell, he argued, every independent African state would be exposed. Both were working during the Cold War, the long contest between the United States and its allies and the Soviet Union and its allies that shaped politics from the late 1940s until the early 1990s. Neither man wanted Ghana or the Congo to become a client of either side. Their speeches and letters, preserved in the movements' publications, show what that refusal meant in practice, and where their hopes ran up against the limits of their power. Kwame Nkrumah: from mission school to the Pan African Congress The official Ghanaian Biographical Sketch issued by the Ghana Information and Trade Center on 9 April 1962 records the basic facts. Nkrumah was born on 21 September 1909 at Nkroful, in what was then the Western Province of the Gold Coast, the son of a goldsmith. He attended mission schools and trained as a teacher at Prince of Wales College at Achimota. He went to the United States in 1935 to study at Lincoln University in Pennsylvania, majored in economics and sociology, and graduated in 1939. He then studied theology and education at the University of Pennsylvania and taught philosophy, Negro history and Greek at Lincoln while working towards a doctorate. To pay his way he worked in shipyards, went to sea as a steward during vacations and preached in Black churches in Pennsylvania and New York. (Official Biographical Sketch, 1962) A movement biography published in Moscow in 1984 gives a compatible account, adding that he trained at Accra and Achimota after Catholic primary school and began his career teaching in Catholic schools at Elmina and Axim. It says that in the United States he studied Marx, Engels and Lenin alongside Black American writers and educationalists. The agreement between a government sketch and a movement biography on this point is significant, because it means the broad outline of his formation is not in serious dispute. He was a mission educated Gold Coast teacher who had worked with his hands and acquired a wide reading in the United States before he entered politics. ( Kwame Nkrumah , in Fighters for National Liberation , 1984) In 1945 Nkrumah left the United States for Britain to study at the London School of Economics, joined Gray's Inn to read law and served from 1945 to 1947 as general secretary of the West African National Secretariat, an organisation set up to work for a united Africa. His own account of 1945 is the founding document of his Pan Africanism. In Africa Must Unite he wrote that Pan Africanism and African nationalism took concrete expression when the Fifth Pan African Congress met in Manchester. More than two hundred delegates attended, and he and George Padmore had been joint secretaries of the organising committee. The congress addressed a declaration to the colonial peoples of the world. It called on intellectuals and professionals to awaken to their responsibilities, told them that liberties would be won through trade union rig
