title: Amílcar Cabral and Walter Rodney
description: The Weapon of Theory, national liberation and culture, and How Europe Underdeveloped Africa.
text: Amílcar Cabral and Walter Rodney both wrote about revolution while taking part in one. Cabral led the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde, known as the PAIGC, through a war against Portuguese rule in Guinea Bissau and died months before victory. Rodney was a Guyanese historian whose How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) became a standard reference for a generation of scholars, and who then returned home to organise workers against an authoritarian government (MIA Encyclopedia, "Rodney, Walter"; How Europe Underdeveloped Africa ). Neither treated ideas as a separate activity from politics. Cabral argued that a revolution could not succeed without a theory of its own society. Rodney argued that the history of Africa had to be written as a weapon in a present struggle. Their lives ended violently within eight years of each other (MIA Encyclopedia, "Cabral, Amilcar"; "Rodney, Walter"), and the movements they served preserved their words in the institutions they had helped to build. The two men are usually placed in the same broad current of anti colonial Marxism, but the connection between them is narrower and easier to document than that label suggests. Rodney read Cabral, adopted some of his categories and cited him in public. There is no evidence in the surviving documents that Cabral read Rodney. What they shared was a problem: how to make a revolution in societies where the class that European Marxism treated as the agent of change was barely formed, and where the state inherited at independence could be turned against the people who had fought for it. Their answers converged on culture, on the educated middle group that inherited colonial power, and on the need for intellectuals to become answerable to ordinary working people. Cabral's formation and the founding of the PAIGC Amílcar Cabral was born on 12 September 1924 at Bafatá in Portuguese Guinea, the son of an employee of the colonial administration. He was educated at the lyceum on São Vicente and entered the Lisbon Higher Institute of Agronomy in 1945, qualifying as an engineer agronomist in 1952. As a student he took part in Portugal's democratic opposition. He returned to Guinea in 1953 to work at the Pessuba experimental station and was dismissed in 1955 for anti colonial activity and expelled from the territory. That year and the next he worked as an agronomist on sugar plantations in Angola and joined Agostinho Neto and others in building the Movement for the Liberation of Angola, better known by its Portuguese initials, MPLA. His training as an agronomist mattered later. Cabral surveyed crops and soils across Guinea, and the habit of direct observation shaped the way he analysed its society (MIA hosted movement biography, Fighters for National Liberation , Progress Publishers, 1984). On 19 September 1956 he founded the African Party for the Independence and Union of the Peoples of Guinea and Cape Verde, renamed in 1960 the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde, or PAIGC. In Lisbon in 1957 he helped establish the Anti Colonial Movement, described in the movement biography as the first illegal organisation of Africans in Portugal to make the struggle against colonialism its objective. From the middle of 1960 he directed the party's bureau in Conakry, and in April 1961 he became deputy general secretary of the Conference of National Liberation Organisations of the Portuguese Colonies. The party began armed operations in 1963 and within two years held liberated zones in which it effectively governed. Cabral argued in 1971 for a National People's Assembly, which was created in 1972 on the basis of popular vote in the liberated territories (MIA Encyclopedia of Marxism, "Cabral, Amilcar (1924 to 1973)"). Cabral was careful to say that his movement had not copied a foreign model. Asked in New York in October 1972 how the struggle had been prepared, he replied that when the party began, its members had not known the writings

title: Nyerere, Neto, Machel and Mandela
description: Ujamaa and the Arusha Declaration, the MPLA and FRELIMO, and the ANC Freedom Charter tradition.
text: Julius Nyerere, Agostinho Neto, Samora Machel and Nelson Mandela led four different movements in four different countries. Nyerere governed Tanganyika after independence and then the United Republic of Tanzania. Neto led the Movement for the Liberation of Angola, known as the MPLA, through war and into power. Machel commanded the Mozambique Liberation Front, known as FRELIMO, and became the first president of independent Mozambique. Mandela became the public face of the struggle against apartheid in South Africa and its first democratically elected president. Each used the language of socialism, but each meant something specific by it, and each defined the power of the people in a different way. Their own texts remain the best evidence for what they intended. The work of later historians shows how far those intentions diverged from what their governments did. Nyerere's early life and the idea of ujamaa Julius Kambarage Nyerere was born on 13 April 1922 at Butiama, on the eastern shore of Lake Victoria in north west Tanganyika, the son of the chief of a small Zanaki community. He began school at twelve, walking the twenty six miles to Musoma, went on to Tabora Government Secondary School and trained as a teacher at Makerere University in Kampala with help from the Roman Catholic priests who taught him. After three years of teaching he took a government scholarship to study history and political economy at the University of Edinburgh. There, partly through the gradual socialism of the British Fabian Society, he began to connect socialist ideas with African communal life (MIA biography of Nyerere). Nyerere described himself as a schoolmaster by choice and a politician by accident. In 1954 he brought the nationalist factions together in the Tanganyika African National Union, or TANU, and led it until 1977. He entered the Legislative Council in 1958, became chief minister in 1960 and premier under internal self government. Tanganyika became independent in December 1961, and he was elected president in 1962. After the Zanzibar revolution of 1964 he negotiated the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar that created Tanzania. He retired from the presidency in 1985, remained chair of Chama Cha Mapinduzi, or CCM, the party formed from TANU and the Zanzibari party, until 1990, and served as chief mediator in the Burundi conflict in 1996. He died of leukaemia in a London hospital on 14 October 1999 (MIA biography). His founding text, "Ujamaa: The Basis of African Socialism," appeared in 1962. The Swahili word ujamaa is usually rendered as familyhood, and Nyerere used it for the extended family principle of shared responsibility, which he argued should be extended from kinship to the nation as a whole. The idea was to make the values and obligations of the family the basis of a national community. Nyerere held that humanness rather than the creation of wealth must come first, and that societies improved through the development of people rather than through the expansion of output. He collected the essays in Ujamaa: Essays on Socialism , published by Oxford University Press in 1968, and reprinted much of the material in Freedom and Unity and Freedom and Socialism ( Ujamaa: Essays on Socialism , 1968; Freedom and Unity ; Freedom and Socialism ). The Arusha Declaration of 5 February 1967 Nyerere wrote the Arusha Declaration and TANU's Policy on Socialism and Self Reliance for his party, and TANU published it on 5 February 1967. Its creed stated that all human beings were equal, that every citizen had a right to take an equal part in government at local, regional and national level, that citizens held the natural resources of the country in trust for their descendants, and that the state must control the principal means of production in order to prevent exploitation and the accumulation of wealth inconsistent with a classless society. title: Manchester 1945: The Congress That Changed the Language of Empire
description: In October 1945, in a town hall in Manchester, a Gold Coast railway worker stood up to describe the kind of politics the gathering wanted.
text: In October 1945, in a town hall in Manchester, a Gold Coast railway worker stood up to describe the kind of politics the gathering wanted. He was J. S. Annan, an officer of the Gold Coast Railway African Employees' Union, and he told the congress that what it needed was "a man who wields tools, a man who knows no colour." (J. S. Annan, Gold Coast Railway Civil Servants and Technical Works' Union, 16 October 1945; 1947 proceedings). The Fifth Pan African Congress had met in Manchester from 15 October to 21 October. A Pan African congress is a meeting of organisations and individuals from Africa, the Americas and the Caribbean who hold that people of African descent share a common political cause. The first was held in London in 1900. This one is remembered for the famous men who attended, W. E. B. Du Bois, George Padmore, Kwame Nkrumah and Jomo Kenyatta, but the published proceedings show a meeting built around trade unions and colonial organisations, with figures who never became heads of state doing most of the speaking. Peter Abrahams, the congress's publicity secretary, reported "some two hundred delegates holding mandates"; there is no independent roll against which to check that figure, and Abrahams dates the congress from 13 October while the session headings give 15 October. The meeting grew out of another conference. In February 1945 colonial delegates to the World Trade Union Conference in London, the first international labour forum where colonial workers had been able to speak, were invited to Manchester. Padmore, who organised the congress, presided over its Standing Orders Committee and signed the preface to the proceedings, recorded a debate in which colonial delegates challenged a telegram to Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin that applied self determination only to Europe. I. T. A. Wallace Johnson, a Sierra Leonean trade unionist, supported an amendment that all peoples be allowed to choose their own form of government; the telegram was redrafted to include the Atlantic Charter principle. Wallace Johnson put the stakes in terms that joined race and class: "Imperialism is for the Colonial workers as great a menace as Fascism is to the workers of the metropolitan countries of Europe." (I. T. A. Wallace Johnson, February 1945, quoted by Padmore in his foreword to The Voice of Coloured Labour ; Marxists Internet Archive). That foreword is Padmore's selection of speeches, not the conference minutes. Back in Manchester, Padmore, Peter Milliard, T. R. Makonnen, Kenyatta, Wallace Johnson and others issued the call through the Pan African Federation, a British organisation of Black groups, including an open letter to the prime minister, Clement Attlee, and a proposal for a "Colonial and Coloured Peoples' Freedom Front". The sessions moved between life in Britain and conditions in the colonies. The opening session on 15 October dealt with the colour bar, the informal exclusion of Black people from jobs, housing and ordinary social life: the insecurity of Black seamen, children of American servicemen turned away by white homes, and discrimination in Liverpool, Cardiff and Hull. Milliard, president of the Pan African Federation, called the congress "Dr Du Bois's child". The North and West Africa sessions gave the gathering its working class character. Annan proposed a permanent London office and said his members would spend their last penny on it. Chief A. Soyemi Coker of the Nigerian Trades Union Congress asked for living wages, cooperatives and the nationalisation of transport and mines, and referred to a strike involving 500,000 people, a delegate's claim rather than an audited total. Nkrumah, acting as rapporteur, set out political and economic trends and called imperialism a major cause of war. Kenyatta reported on six East African territories and described the kipande , a certificate African workers had to wear around their necks, linking low wages to the impossibility of building a standard of living that could sustain

title: The Algerian War: Independence and Its Witnesses
description: On the night of 1 November 1954 the National Liberation Front, or FLN, made a peace offer at the moment it declared war.
text: On the night of 1 November 1954 the National Liberation Front, or FLN, made a peace offer at the moment it declared war. Its Secretariat wrote that "our action is directly solely against colonialism, our only blind and obstinate enemy, which has always refused to grant the least freedom by peaceful means" (proclamation, 1 November 1954, trans. Mitch Abidor). It asked for talks on Algerian sovereignty, the release of political prisoners, an end to emergency measures and recognition of Algerian nationality, and promised to respect French interests and to let Europeans in Algeria choose their nationality. Armed attacks began the same night. Charles Robert Ageron, who dates the text 31 October, found that most of these terms reappeared in the settlement of March 1962. The distance between the offer and the violence that delivered it runs through the war. Who the movement said it was The FLN's newspaper El Moudjahid said in 1956 that "It is about time that an organ of resistance fighters comes to be, to fill a certain void" ( El Moudjahid , first issue, 1956, trans. Mitch Abidor). It argued that jihad , often read as religious war, meant self defence, and counted the soldier of the National Liberation Army, or ALN, the activist, the liaison agent, the shepherd, the housewife in the Casbah and the striking schoolchild as fighters. The Casbah was the old walled quarter of Algiers. Some who joined were Europeans born in Algeria. Henri Maillot, a former army cadet who defected and stole arms for the FLN, wrote to the French press in April 1956: "I'm not Muslim, but I am Algerian of European origin. I consider Algeria to be my homeland." (Maillot, April 1956, trans. Mitchell Abidor from the El Watan republication of 18 June 2007). Fernand Iveton, a European born communist and FLN member, wrote days before his execution in February 1957 that "morale is good" and that he had found "a fair amount of understanding and even, from some of them, sympathy" among his guards (Iveton, 8 February 1957, trans. Mitch Abidor). The Algerian Communist Party, allied to the FLN, told settlers in 1957: "The Algerians aren't making war on the French people or the Europeans of Algeria, but on FRENCH COLONIALISTS." (PCA leaflet, 7 October 1957, trans. Mitch Abidor). These were different messages to different audiences in one war. The Casbah and the cell Saadi Yacef commanded the FLN in the Battle of Algiers and recalled the Casbah from inside it. He described roofs linked by hidden passages, a mason's skill turned to escape routes, and FLN "justice" against informers. Entering one family's room, he found the wife and children hidden behind a curtain: "I had never had the occasion to see such terrible poverty laid out before me." (Yacef, Souvenirs de la Bataille d'Alger , 1962, trans. Mitchell Abidor). The movement bought the family a house, which he said "considerably reinforced the authority of the Front among the little people of the Casbah". The memoir was written a few years later and gives no voice to those the Front sentenced. Henri Alleg, editor of Alger Républicain , was arrested by paratroopers in Algiers in June 1957 and held a month at El Biar. The Question , written four months later, gives a first person account of interrogation and torture. "But it was necessary for me to tell what I know." That is how he explains his purpose (Alleg, The Question , November 1957). The book closes with the words "But they must know what is done IN THEIR NAME." (same edition). The publisher said it was seized after two weeks; Sartre wrote that "torture is a systematised form of hatred that creates its own instruments" (Sartre, preface to The Wretched of the Earth , 1961). Omar Hamadi, a captured ALN fighter, wrote to his lawyer in December 1960: "We arrived June 20, 1959 and as is usual at Berrouaghia, as soon as we arrived the beatings began, and without reason." (Hamadi, 5 December 1960, trans. Mitch Abidor). He named guards and described a rubber pipe filled wi

title: Nasser and the Revolution from Above: Egypt, 1952–1970
description: The broadcast of 23 July 1952 was careful to sound like an instruction rather than a coup.
text: The broadcast of 23 July 1952 was careful to sound like an instruction rather than a coup. The Free Officers said in the name of the army: "Egypt has recently been going through a period marked by corruption, bribery, and governmental instability." (Statement of the Revolution, 23 July 1952, English translation on the Bibliotheca Alexandrina site). The Free Officers were a group of army officers who took power in the name of reform. They assured Egyptians that detained officers were unharmed, warned against violence and promised foreign residents that the army would protect them. The statement shows how deliberately they presented themselves as disciplined guardians. Within months their chairman, Gamal Abdel Nasser, was writing an explanation of why they had acted. Two revolutions Nasser wrote The Philosophy of the Revolution in 1953 and 1954, after the officers had consolidated power. He treated the Abdeen Palace incident of 1942, the war of 1948 and the scandal of defective arms as accelerants rather than causes. The old parties, in his telling, had forfeited any right to lead. "I can now say that we are at present in the throes of two revolutions and not one." ( The Philosophy of the Revolution , written 1953–54, translator unnamed in the scanned edition). Political liberation and social revolution were to be carried out together by the same officers in the same decade. He recorded his shock that crowds did not rise behind the vanguard after Farouk's abdication. In letters to his friend Hassan El Nashar written before the revolution, the young officer said the army had stopped talking about "women and amusement" and had begun talking about "sacrifice and dignity" (letters, including that of 16 February 1942). This is a participant's retrospective and a set of edited extracts from a family linked archive. The claim that the masses were absent is contested. The canal and the invasion On 26 July 1956 Nasser told a crowd in Manshiya Square, Alexandria, that the Suez Canal Company had always been an Egyptian company. The canal was the waterway linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, and the company that operated it was the focus of Egyptian grievance. "Everything which was stolen from us by that imperialist company, that state within a state, when we were dying of hunger, we are going to take back" (nationalisation speech, 26 July 1956, retranslated from the Arabic by Anne Alexander, 2006). The name de Lesseps was the signal that started the seizure of the company's offices. A decree read that evening set up an Egyptian authority under the Ministry of Commerce, ordered employees to stay at their posts and promised compensation at the previous day's Paris Bourse price. The US State Department's record of the same day notes that officials took over the administration while Nasser spoke (Foreign Relations of the United States, 1955–1957, vol. XVI, document 1). In September, with invasion still ahead, he said: "Egypt insists her sovereignty must remain intact and refuses to give up any part of that sovereignty for the sake of money." (speech of 15 September 1956, official US State Department translation). Israel attacked Egypt on 29 October 1956, Anglo French bombing began on 31 October, and British and French troops landed on 5 November. The voices that survive from the resistance are not only those of the president. Fathallah Mahrus, a factory worker and trade unionist, recalled: "So the popular resistance against the invasion was led by the people of Port Said – women and children as well – armed with cooking pans, kitchen knives, walking sticks and anything they could find." (interviewed in Cairo, 25 March 2006, translated in Anne Alexander's article). Layla al Shal, a Cairo University student and activist, said: "We set up women's resistance committees across the capital. We had military style training; how to defuse a bomb, how to shoot a rifle and so on." (interviewed 31 March 2006). Communist activists trained workers in a

title: The Party and the Spear: Communists, Workers and the South African Liberation Struggle, 1921–1964
description: The Communist Party of South Africa was founded in Cape Town on 30 July 1921 by a merger of socialist bodies.
text: The Communist Party of South Africa was founded in Cape Town on 30 July 1921 by a merger of socialist bodies. Its manifesto "makes its appeal to all South African workers, organised and unorganised, white and black, to join in promoting the overthrow of the capitalist system..." (founding manifesto, 30 July 1921). It sought a Commonwealth of Workers, anticipated repression and linked black labour to the world capitalist system. The years that followed show how hard that appeal was to hold. The Native Republic argument In 1928 the Executive Committee of the Communist International, the body that directed communist parties across the world, called South Africa a colony of a special kind. It noted that the CPSA was then predominantly African in composition, with about 1,750 members, and told the party to join daily racial demands to "the slogan of an independent native South African republic as a stage towards a workers' and peasants' republic, with full equal rights for all races, black, coloured and white" (ECCI resolution, 1928). This was the "Native Republic" line: a national democratic revolution had to precede socialism. The line was contested. E. R. Roux, just back from Moscow, wrote to the general secretary Douglas Wolton on 5 September 1928: "It is equally necessary to say 'natives unite; unite as black men to free yourselves from slavery'." (Roux to Wolton, 5 September 1928). He wanted a workers' and peasants' republic as the basis for a government of the native majority, argued that a blunt Black Republic slogan would cost the party its footing in white trade unions, and complained that the framers refused even an editorial change. The letter proves the instruction was disputed, not how widely. The two stage idea survived. The SACP's clandestine programme of 1962, The Road to South African Freedom , named "colonialism of a special type" as the condition to defeat: "The destruction of colonialism and the winning of national freedom is the essential condition and the key for future advance to the supreme aim of the Communist Party: the establishment of a socialist South Africa" (SACP programme, 1962). It rejected "African Socialism" as a substitute for Marxism Leninism. The continuity from 1928 to 1962 is in the party's own words. A programme states doctrine, not which members read it. Wages, land and care Economic demands were never an afterthought. In 1943 the African National Congress, or ANC, the principal African nationalist organisation, adopted claims for universal suffrage, the repeal of the pass laws, land and equal pay, including "the statutory recognition of the right of the African worker to collective bargaining under the Industrial Conciliation Act." (ANC claims, 16 December 1943). The colour bar, rules reserving skilled jobs for white workers, was what organisers met. Billy Nair, a Durban trade unionist and MK member, recalled the 1922 miners' rebellion and its slogan "Workers of the World unite for a White South Africa". "The slogan 'Workers of the World unite for a White South Africa' does violence to the militancy and heroism displayed by the workers." (Nair, "Through the Eyes of the Workers"). His essay is a later polemic. The Women's Charter of 17 April 1954 joined national liberation to the subordination of women. It began: "We women share with our menfolk the cares and anxieties imposed by poverty and its evils." (Women's Charter, FEDSAW, 17 April 1954). It demanded equal pay, property and marriage rights, free compulsory education, maternity homes and creches, and named the burdens on women left in towns and on farms while husbands worked in the mines. FEDSAW was the Federation of South African Women. Frances Baard remembered building it from a meeting of forty or fifty women in Port Elizabeth in 1953 and the conference of about 150 delegates that adopted the Charter in 1954. title: Land, Terror and the National Question: Ethiopia's Revolution, 1974–1991
description: In November 1969 a fourth-year arts student at Addis Ababa University published an article in the student journal Struggle asking whether Ethiopia was one country or several.
text: In November 1969 a fourth year arts student at Addis Ababa University published an article in the student journal Struggle asking whether Ethiopia was one country or several. Walleligne Mekonnen argued that the unity proclaimed by the monarchy was a fiction maintained by the dominance of one people. "What is this fake Nationalism? Is it not simply Amhara and to a certain extent Amhara Tigre supremacy?" he wrote. He named Oromo, Tigray, Amhara, Gurage, Sidama, Wolayta, Harari and Somali nations, held that secession could be progressive if workers and peasants led it, and rejected a military coup as the answer (Walleligne Mekonnen, "On the Question of Nationalities in Ethiopia," 17 November 1969). Five years before the officers' Provisional Military Administrative Council, known as the Derg, took power, the national question was already being argued in the students' own words. The students and the claim to the revolution Walleligne wrote for a student audience; his Leninist frame was his own, not every student's view. The internal history of the movement survives in a retrospective account by Alem Habtu, who sat on the executive of the Ethiopian Students Union in North America between 1965 and 1970. He wrote in 2015, recalling events forty four years earlier: "My discussion will, therefore, rely on my first hand or insider knowledge." (Alem Habtu, "The Ethiopian Student Movement: My Experiences in ESUNA, 1964–1971," 25 February 2015). Habtu dates the break from embassy funding to 1965, the shift from reform to anti feudal politics to 1966 to 1968, and two occupations of the Ethiopian embassy in Washington to 1969. He defends his own part in the settlement, so the chronology is a participant's with an interest in it. The Ethiopian Peoples' Revolutionary Party, or EPRP, formed from a merger of currents that included the Ethiopian People's Liberation Organisation, claimed descent from this student radicalism. Its clandestine programme of 1975 called the February uprising incomplete, accused the officers who had seized power of riding a revolutionary tide they had not made, and demanded a provisional peoples' government and a national congress. It promised the unrestricted right of nations to self determination and declared that it would not bow to whoever held a gun. Its claim to represent the working class was stated in one sentence: "The E.P.R.P. is the party of the working class." (Ethiopian Peoples' Revolutionary Party, programme, 1975). The programme was written before the killings that put that claim to the test. The February 1974 uprising itself appears in another participant's words. Senay Likke led the Waz League, an underground group that trained military cadres and worked with the Derg. He described the revolt in the vocabulary the officers adopted: "After age old oppression under an archaic autocratic and monarchical rule, the Ethiopian people rose in revolt in February of 1974." (Senay Likke, The Ethiopian Revolution , mid 1970s). Likke argued that the officer corps was carrying the same revolution forward. He was killed in a shootout with the Derg in February 1977, so his pamphlet cannot speak to what came after. Alongside the EPRP document it shows two incompatible accounts of who owned the revolution, written in the same language of feudalism, imperialism, the people and the vanguard, the revolutionary party that claimed to lead the working class. The All Ethiopia Socialist Movement, known as MEISON, was another civilian current that worked with the Derg before the regime turned on it; its own programme survives only as an unreadable scan. The cleaning up campaign Mengistu Haile Mariam, then chairman of the Derg, addressed a May Day crowd in Addis Ababa in 1977 in the language of the revolution's defenders. He announced that workers and peasants were being armed, that the neighbourhood associations known as kebeles were forming defence squads, and that the campaign against the EPRP and its allies would continue. title: The Carnation Revolution and the End of Portuguese Africa, 1974–1988
description: On 27 April 1974, two days after a coup by middle-ranking officers ended Portugal's dictatorship, the central committee of the Mozambique Liberation Front, known as FRELIMO, issued a...
text: On 27 April 1974, two days after a coup by middle ranking officers ended Portugal's dictatorship, the central committee of the Mozambique Liberation Front, known as FRELIMO, issued a statement from the war. The leaders had learned of the events in Lisbon from radio broadcasts. They hailed the Portuguese democratic forces but refused any settlement short of independence, and insisted that the colonial system, not the Portuguese people, was the enemy. "We are not fighting to become Portuguese with black skins. We are fighting to affirm ourselves as Mozambicans" (FRELIMO Central Committee, "The Coup d'Etat of April 25," 27 April 1974, English translation, translator not named). The claim that the liberation wars had forced the coup was an argument, not a demonstrated finding, but it fixed the movements' reading of events before any negotiation began. The coup and the movements' reply Agostinho Neto, president of the Movement for the Liberation of Angola, or MPLA, answered from Lusaka on 1 May. He listed the colonial wars, inflation, emigration and military desertion as the crisis behind the coup. He rejected the federation proposed by General Spínola, the Portuguese officer who hoped to keep a common system, because Portugal would have the final say. His statement "does not agree to a federation as proposed by General Spinola, that is a federation in which Portugal would have the last word" (Agostinho Neto, statement on the Portuguese coup, 1 May 1974, MPLA translation). Neto insisted on complete independence as the only basis for cooperation, while declaring that the MPLA was prepared to negotiate. This was a public position from the movement's own information department, not a record of its internal debate. British residents in Lisbon and Angola remembered the same weeks differently. In reminiscences compiled by the British Historical Society of Portugal, witnesses recalled the end of censorship, armed young men stopping cars in Lisbon, the congestion at Luanda's port as expatriates left, the RAF airlift, and the arrival of roughly a million retornados in Lisbon, some housed in former prisons and one in the Ritz. The compiler warns that these accounts were written more than thirty years afterwards and came from a narrow group of businesspeople and landowners. They are memories of decolonisation from the settler side, not contemporary documents. The MFA, the Armed Forces Movement that made the coup, appears here only as the liberators named by the movements. Alvor and the two ceremonies Nine months after Neto's statement, the Portuguese state and the three Angolan movements, the MPLA, the FNLA and UNITA, met at Alvor in the Algarve and signed an agreement on 15 January 1975. It recognised the three as "the only and the legitimate representatives of the people of Angola", fixed a date for independence and set up a transitional government under a High Commissioner and a presidential college of three members, one from each movement. "The independence and the complete sovereignty of Angola shall be solemnly proclaimed on the 11th of November 1975" (Alvor Agreement, Article 4, signed 15 January 1975, English translation). Article 6 recorded a ceasefire already observed in practice, Article 15 made coordination rather than majority rule the college's task, and Article 17 required two thirds majorities. Each movement's forces stayed where they were stationed. The settlement was built to manage rivalry rather than end it. Neto spoke at the signing for all three movements, and his words caught the brief optimism of the moment. He called the talks an attempt to take decisions about ending colonial rule, credited the Armed Forces Movement with freeing Portugal from fascism, and thanked the Portuguese security police and armed forces for keeping calm at the meeting. title: Bandung to Havana: The Afro-Asian Left, 1955–1966
description: On 18 April 1955 Sukarno, the host of the Asian-African Conference at Bandung, opened a meeting of delegates from twenty-nine Asian and African states.
text: On 18 April 1955 Sukarno, the host of the Asian African Conference at Bandung, opened a meeting of delegates from twenty nine Asian and African states. He spoke of nuclear fear and of a colonialism that had not ended with the fall of empires. It survived, he said, in a modern dress of economic, intellectual and physical control by a small alien community within a nation. He offered "Unity in Diversity" and "live and let live" as the principles that could hold the gathering together. "We are united by a common detestation of colonialism in whatever form it appears. We are united by a common detestation of racialism." (Sukarno, opening speech to the Asian African Conference, 18 April 1955). The English text comes from an Indonesian government publication and is an excerpt, so the phrasing carries editorial choices as well as Sukarno's own claim to lead the "New Emerging Forces". Two readings of Bandung The delegates were not there to form an alliance. Jawaharlal Nehru, India's prime minister, argued in the political committee that joining either Cold War bloc meant surrendering the identity of a country that had just won independence. "I belong to neither and I propose to belong to neither whatever happens in the world." (Jawaharlal Nehru, speech to the Bandung Conference Political Committee, April 1955). This was the case for non alignment, the policy of refusing to take sides between the American and Soviet blocs, made as a claim about national identity rather than tactics. He held that the unaligned area reduced the risk of war and that the moral force of Asia and Africa counted despite the bombs of the great powers. His words record a position in committee, not the conference's decisions. Three days after the conference, Tito, the president of Yugoslavia, told Radio Belgrade that the results had been a pleasant surprise. "matters have reached an historical turning point, in that the people of the two continents are determined to decide their own future for themselves." (Josip Broz Tito, statement to Radio Belgrade, 27 April 1955). He added that the conception which prevailed at Bandung was in harmony with his own. That is the earliest documentary link between the conference and the movement that took shape at Belgrade in 1961, but it is a favourable answer to a sympathetic questioner and a political appropriation. Bandung style Afro Asianism and Belgrade style non alignment were not the same project. Paul Robeson read the meeting from a distance. Barred from travelling abroad as a Black American activist, he sent a greeting that appeared in Spotlight on Africa in April 1955. "the very fact of the convening of the Conference of Asian and African nations at Bandung, Indonesia, in itself will be recorded as an historic turning point in all world affairs." (Paul Robeson, "Message of Greetings to the Bandung Conference," April 1955). He named the Ganges, Nile, Yangtze and Niger, linked peace to sovereign rights for the nations of Asia, and connected Korea, Kenya, North Africa and South Africa. The greeting was written before or during the meeting, not after, and its praise of the Soviet Union is his own commitment. His "spirit of Bandung" was the breaking of the colour line; Tito's was a concordat between governments. The phrase never named one programme. From states to peoples The second project began in Cairo in December 1957 at the First Afro Asian People's Solidarity Conference, the founding meeting of the Afro Asian Peoples' Solidarity Organization, or AAPSO. Anwar el Sadat, then an Egyptian minister, said the gathering met for two reasons. "Today this people's Conference of ours meets, partly in honour of the spirit of Bandung and as a reminder of the principles and ideals it stands for, and partly to push it a step forward." (Anwar el Sadat, address to the First Afro Asian People's Solidarity Conference, 26 December 1957). The distinction was institutional. title: Oppressed Peoples and Oppressed Nations, Unite!: Anti-Colonial Internationalism, 1919–1952
description: On the morning of 10 February 1927, in the Palais d'Egmont in Brussels, a delegate from the Chinese Nationalist Party, or Kuomintang, addressed a congress that had gathered anticolonial...
text: On the morning of 10 February 1927, in the Palais d'Egmont in Brussels, a delegate from the Chinese Nationalist Party, or Kuomintang, addressed a congress that had gathered anticolonial activists from across the world. Liao Huanxing told the hall: "Our relations to the imperialists to day are so critical, that the latter are using all means with which to attack us. We must form ourselves strongly and firmly into an international united front against world imperialism." (Liao Huanxing, Kuomintang, Brussels, 10 February 1927, as translated in Inprecorr. Source: revolutionsnewsstand.com) A directory of delegates listed thirty Chinese, Koreans, Indo Chinese and Dutch East Indians, alongside Africans and Latin Americans. A reporter for the New York Daily Worker called the gathering "the long hoped for and long dreaded coming together of oppressed peoples with workers of the oppressing nations": "The long hoped for and long dreaded coming together of oppressed peoples with workers of the oppressing nations has become a world wide reality." (Manuel Gomez, Daily Worker , 10 March 1927. Source: revolutionsnewsstand.com) To see how such a room could exist, it is necessary to go back to the years just after the First World War, when two different ways of linking socialism to anticolonial politics were being worked out. The colonial question enters the programme The Communist International, the body founded in 1919 to coordinate communist parties, put the colonies on its agenda at its second congress in 1920. Lenin's draft theses of 5 June placed oppressed and oppressor nations at the centre of the argument: "The real meaning of the demand for equality consists in its being a demand for the abolition of classes." (V. I. Lenin, draft theses, 5 June 1920, translation by Julius Katzer. Marxists Internet Archive: jun 05) He called for support for bourgeois democratic liberation movements in backward countries while insisting that communists keep their own organisation, and he warned against Pan Islamism. The argument that super profits from the colonies helped sustain reformism among workers in the imperialist countries belongs to Lenin's Imperialism and to Roy's supplementary theses, not to the draft theses of 5 June. "The Communist International must enter into a temporary alliance with bourgeois democracy in the colonial and backward countries" (V. I. Lenin, draft theses, 5 June 1920, translation by Julius Katzer. Marxists Internet Archive: jun 05), but only on those terms. The text was contested from the start. M. N. Roy, an Indian revolutionary who had helped found communist parties in India and Mexico, put supplementary theses on 25 July from the standpoint of India and the other large Asian peoples: "The super profits made in the colonies form one of the main sources of the resources of contemporary capitalism." (M. N. Roy, supplementary theses, 25 July 1920, translator unnamed in the edition. Source: redsails.org) Roy wanted communists to build workers' and peasants' organisations rather than follow the national bourgeoisie, the native middle class that led the independence movements. Lenin called his theses important. The two documents therefore record an argument inside the International, not a single settled line. They come to us in translations of differing provenance, and the edition that prints Roy's text carries its own political commentary; the wording must not be merged with the Soviet published translation of Lenin's draft. The theses also reached people far from the congress. Hồ Chí Minh recalled in 1960 how, as a young man in Paris, he had joined the French Socialist Party and asked which International sided with colonial peoples: "If you do not condemn colonialism, if you do not side with the colonial people, what kind of revolution are you waging?" (Hồ Chí Minh, 1960, recalling the 1920s, translator unnamed. Source: redsails.org) He said a comrade gave him Lenin's theses, printed in L'Humanité , and that reading them rep

title: Marxist-Leninist Parties Worldwide
description: A regional directory of communist and socialist parties, ruling parties in detail, and international coordinating bodies.
text: This chapter is a reference directory of communist, Marxist Leninist and socialist parties. It records what each party says about itself in the documents it publishes, on its own website, or in its own newspaper or other publication, called its official organ below. A party's own name is used throughout. If a party calls itself Marxist Leninist, scientific socialist, communist or Trotskyist, that is the label reported here, even where an outsider would classify it differently. Where a party states no label, the entry gives the name alone. The purpose is to show how these organisations present themselves, not to decide which label is correct. Three rules shape the entries. First, a party's own published words take priority. Where a programme or constitution was available, it is the basis of the entry. Where it was not, the entry rests on an official website or organ, and the source column says so. Second, for parties with no official site, the directory uses their listing in the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties (IMCWP), a recurring forum of communist and workers' parties whose meetings are indexed by its information service, Solidnet. A listing there establishes that a party exists and calls itself communist, but gives no founding date, membership figure or election result. Third, the status labels are descriptive. Ruling means the party leads the government, alone or as the dominant partner. Opposition means it contests elections and has held seats in parliament. Extra parliamentary means it is organised but has no seats in parliament. Banned means the party says it operates under a legal ban. These labels describe, they do not approve. Where no official source was available online, the entry leaves the founding date blank and names the basis in the source column. A small number of well known parties have thinner entries for that reason. Dates appear only when an official source states them. Nothing here is a verdict on a party's size, support or truthfulness. The five ruling parties in detail Five parties rule states that officially describe themselves as socialist: China, Korea, Vietnam, Cuba and Laos. The accounts below use each party's own constitutional and congress language, and describe it as the party's claim. Communist Party of China The party's official name is 中国共产党 (Zhōngguó Gòngchǎndǎng), the Communist Party of China (CPC). Its report to the 20th National Congress, delivered on 16 October 2022, says that "the Communist Party of China has walked a hundred year course of struggle" (中国共产党已走过百年奋斗历程), which puts the hundredth anniversary in 2022. The report was published in full by the State Council's official portal (gov.cn, report to the 20th National Congress). The party runs an official website, 共产党员网 / CPC Member Network, operated by its Central Organisation Department. The name and information at the top of the site, its masthead, presents the party's rules and a database of its regulations, the 党内法规库. The Party Constitution, 2022 edition, has a General Programme and eleven chapters covering members, the organisational system, central and local bodies, grassroots bodies, cadres (trained party officials), discipline, the bodies that check party discipline, party groups, relations with the Communist Youth League, and the party emblem and flag. It also carries the 20th Congress resolution on the constitutional amendment and an audio version. The 20th Congress report records that over the preceding decade the party "upheld Marxism Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Theory of Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development, and fully implemented the Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era" (坚持马克思列宁主义、毛泽东思想、邓小平理论、"三个代表"重要思想、科学发展观，全面贯彻新时代中国特色社会主义思想) (official report text). title: Movement Media Outlets
description: Podcasts, channels, periodicals, publishers and official party media that promote Marxism-Leninism and socialism.
text: Movement media are the podcasts, journals, websites, presses and video channels that socialist and communist organisations run themselves. This chapter records projects that describe themselves as Marxist, Marxist Leninist, communist or socialist. The word outlet is used here to mean a publication, channel or press. Each project is presented through its own about page, published articles, episode pages, catalogue, official social links, or information in its own header and settings. Self descriptions are quoted or closely paraphrased, and are reported as claims the outlet makes about itself. The projects described below assign themselves four overlapping functions: teaching theory, preserving historical documents, communicating within an organisation, and expressing solidarity with movements elsewhere. Several outlets attack each other in print, and those disputes remain unresolved; they are recorded here only as the outlets' own positions. A social media link proves that an outlet chose to publish there. It does not prove the outlet's size or the truth of its claims. What counts as movement media The chapter covers podcasts, video channels, independent news and analysis websites, periodicals, book publishers and printers, zine and newsletter projects, and documentary style video operations. It also includes, briefly, official party and state publications. The dividing line is not always sharp. A podcast may be published as a video, a publisher may run a video channel, and a party newspaper may host a film unit. The sections below group projects by their main form, and note where the forms overlap. title: Video and Audiovisual Sources
description: A directory of video and audio material hosted by the movements and states that made it, with access limitations disclosed.
text: This chapter is a directory of video and sound material produced by the movements and states that made it, or hosted by their own organisations. A recording counts as the speaker's own when the speaker, the organisation in whose name it was made, or a movement archive that holds the figure's recorded material distributes it. This includes the official site of a party or state body and a movement's own film or audio unit. It also includes state broadcasters that host their own material. The directory does not rank films or recommend documentaries for their cinematic merit. It records what exists, topic by topic and figure by figure, and sets that material apart from recordings made by news agencies and by other people. An official website may show a video from another site inside its own page, a practice called embedding. Such a video remains a recording made by whoever uploaded it, even when a party or museum page displays it. Where a speech survives only on audio, the directory lists it as audio. Where no official source is available, the entry says so. The material is spread unevenly. Marx and Engels left none, because they died before sound recording and film were in use. Lenin survives in a silent film compilation held by the Marxists Internet Archive (MIA), a volunteer run library of Marxist writing and related material. Mao's founding ceremony is held by China Central Television, the state broadcaster. The fullest corpora are the official Fidel Castro archive, which organises dozens of indexed pages of video, and the official Thomas Sankara site, which separates audio, video, film and documentary material into distinct sections. The written primary sources remain the foundation of the book; audiovisual material supplements them. Founders and classical Marxism Marx and Engels: no audiovisual source exists Karl Marx, who lived from 1818 to 1883, and Friedrich Engels, who lived from 1820 to 1895, died before sound recording was commercially available and long before film production (MIA Encyclopedia, "Marx, Karl"; "Engels, Friedrich"). There is no film of either speaking and no recorded voice. Later films portray them as dramatizations. The book's treatment rests on their written texts: the Manuscripts of 1844 , the Theses on Feuerbach , the Communist Manifesto , the 1859 Preface , Capital , Anti Dühring , Ludwig Feuerbach , the letters and the MIA's editorial introductory notes. title: The New Left in the West: From 1956 to the Years of Lead
description: First-hand sources on The New Left in the West: From 1956 to the Years of Lead: first-hand documents, the evidence, scholarly interpretations and the limits of the record.
text: In the summer of 1957, E. P. Thompson, a historian and a communist who had broken with the party, put an open letter in the first issue of a small journal called The New Reasoner . His subject was what socialists should say about Stalinism, the system of rule and doctrine built under Stalin in the Soviet Union. He argued that it had to be understood as an ideology that could win assent, not merely as hypocrisy by men who knew better. "It is humanist because it places once again real men and women at the centre of socialist theory and aspiration" (E. P. Thompson, "Socialist Humanism: An Epistle to the Philistines", The New Reasoner no. 1, Summer 1957. Marxists Internet Archive: sochum). The current he was naming became known as socialist humanism: socialism defined by actual people rather than by abstractions such as "Marxism Leninism Stalinism". The generation after 1956 Two years later Thompson described the current he belonged to. "It is a generation which never looked upon the Soviet Union as a weak but heroic Workers' State; but, rather, as the nation of the Great Purges and of Stalingrad" (E. P. Thompson, "The New Left", 20 May 1959. Marxists Internet Archive: newleft). He wrote before New Left Review existed and admitted that in Britain this "New Left" was scarcely identifiable as an organisation. He proposed journals, clubs and education instead of a new party, and attacked what he called demonism, economism and parasitic factionalism among the older left. The name described a convergence of dissident communists, left socialists and the postwar generation, not a membership card. The same break showed up in the campaign against nuclear weapons. The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, or CND, pressed for Britain to give up its bombs unilaterally, whatever other states did. Thompson defended that position in the summer of 1958, linking it to a break with NATO, the Western military alliance, and to what he called active neutrality in Europe. "This is what the Aldermaston marchers thought they were marching about; not only against the Bomb but also against all crooked attitudes of power which permit the Bomb to be used as an instrument of policy." (E. P. Thompson, "NATO, Neutralism and Survival", Summer 1958. Marxists Internet Archive: nato) He reported that British Communist Party leaders regarded CND as a "pathetic illusion". He conceded that some of his own assumptions could not be proved; his piece is an argument about what the marches meant, not a survey of the marchers. In France the corresponding rupture came through the war in Algeria, France's colonial war against the movement for Algerian independence. On 6 September 1960 (the press release was issued on 5 September), the day before the trial of the Jeanson network, 121 intellectuals and public figures, among them Simone de Beauvoir, Jean Paul Sartre, André Breton and Henri Lefebvre, declared a right of insubordination. "The cause of the Algerian people, which contributes decisively to the ruin of the colonial system, is the cause of all free men and women." (The Manifesto of the 121, 5 September 1960. Marxists Internet Archive: manifesto 121) A journal that printed the text was censored and left two blank pages. The manifesto broke with the official Communist Party's cautious peace campaign. It was written by intellectuals, not by Algerians or soldiers, and the publisher stopped at 121 signatures because the number sounded nice. May 1968 in Paris At Nanterre, a student group called the March 22 Movement issued a leaflet calling a demonstration for 10 May 1968. It rejected what it called a "dialogue" about decisions already taken and refused the role of "complicitous managers and beneficiaries of the exploitation of the workers". "We don't want to be capitalism's watchdogs." (March 22 Movement leaflet, "1000 Wounded 3 dead Combat Gas", 10 May 1968. Marxists Internet Archive: 1000 wounded) The casualty figure in the heading was the movement's own, not an independent c

title: Half the Sky? Women in the Socialist States and Movements
description: In 1920 Alexandra Kollontai, a Bolshevik and People's Commissar for Social Welfare, gave a name to a burden the revolution had promised to lift.
text: In 1920 Alexandra Kollontai, a Bolshevik and People's Commissar for Social Welfare, gave a name to a burden the revolution had promised to lift. Capitalism, she wrote, had added wage work without removing the older loads: "Capitalism has placed a crushing burden on woman's shoulders: it has made her a wage worker without having reduced her cares as housekeeper or mother. Woman staggers beneath the weight of this triple load." (Alexandra Kollontai, "Communism and the Family", 1920; translated by Alix Holt). The "triple load" meant paid employment, housework and child rearing. She proposed communal kitchens, laundries, creches and collective child rearing, and pointed to the 1917 divorce decree as a gain for working women. This was a programme by a senior official with a polemical purpose, not a report on what had been built; the English is a 1977 translation. Looking back in 1926, Kollontai recalled being the only woman in the first Bolshevik cabinet and the isolation she felt when she first pressed the party on the woman question. "I am also the first woman ever to have been appointed ambassadress, a post which I occupied for three years and from which I resigned of my own free will." (Alexandra Kollontai, autobiography written 1926; translated by Salvator Attansio). She also remembered the six week strike of women laundry workers in 1917. The autobiography was written nine years later and shaped as self justification; its published text restores passages she crossed out in proof under what the prefatory note calls the gradually sharpening Stalinist control. The claim to be the first woman in a cabinet is her own. The woman question before the party The woman question entered revolutionary writing before Marxism did. In 1919, working as a young journalist in Changsha, Mao Zedong treated a young woman's suicide as a social fact. She had been trapped by three "iron nets": Chinese society, her own family and her betrothed's family. "It happened because of the shameful system of arranged marriages, because of the darkness of the social system, the negation of the individual will, and the absence of the freedom to choose one's own mate." (Mao Zedong, "Miss Chao's Suicide," 1919; translation, translator not credited on the page). Mao did not witness the suicide, gave no original venue, and used the event as an argument. In Paris in 1922 the Vietnamese anti colonial journalist Ho Chi Minh joined the question to empire: "Colonization is in itself an act of violence of the stronger against the weaker. This violence becomes still more odious when it is exercised upon women and children." (Ho Chi Minh, "Annamese Women and French Domination," 1 August 1922; translation, translator not credited on the page). He said he was recounting facts seen and described by witnesses, so he did not claim to have seen the atrocity he quoted. The article is polemical and speaks about Vietnamese women rather than recording their own organising. That difference between speaking for and speaking with runs through the record. Labour as liberation In his 1927 investigation of the peasant movement in Hunan, Mao observed rural women forming associations and the "authority of the husband" weakening: "With the rise of the peasant movement, the women in many places have now begun to organize rural women's associations; the opportunity has come for them to lift up their heads, and the authority of the husband is getting shakier every day." (Mao Zedong, Hunan report, March 1927; translated in Selected Works ). His explanation was material: poor peasant women had more say in family decisions because economic necessity forced them into manual labour. The report is advocacy as well as investigation, and this is an excerpt selected for the Little Red Book. The productivist core was stated in 1955: "China's women are a vast reserve of labour power. This reserve should be tapped in the struggle to build a great socialist country." (Mao Zedong, introductory note, 1955; tra

title: The Red Scarf and the Oath: Children and Youth in Revolutionary Movements
description: On 2 October 1920 Lenin stood before the Third All-Russia Congress of the Russian Young Communist League, the Komsomol, and reduced its purpose to one word.
text: On 2 October 1920 Lenin stood before the Third All Russia Congress of the Russian Young Communist League, the Komsomol, and reduced its purpose to one word. "the tasks of the youth in general, and of the Young Communist Leagues and all other organisations in particular, might be summed up in a single word: learn." (V. I. Lenin, speech to the Third All Russia Congress of the Russian Young Communist League, 2 October 1920, translated in the Collected Works edition). Learning did not mean memorising slogans. He tied it at once to practical work: abolishing illiteracy, tending suburban vegetable gardens, organising public hygiene and food distribution, and taking part in subbotniks , voluntary work parties. He warned that young people who only learned phrases by rote became "communist text jugglers". The speech appeared in Pravda five days later. It is a leader's address to a congress, not a record of what members did, and its claim of half a million members is the speaker's. Mao addressed the young differently. In a 1957 Moscow talk, preserved in the "Youth" chapter of Quotations from Chairman Mao , he said: "The world is yours, as well as ours, but in the last analysis, it is yours. You young people, full of vigor and vitality, are in the bloom of life, like the sun at eight or nine in the morning. Our hope is placed on you." (Mao Zedong, "Talk at a meeting with Chinese students and trainees in Moscow", 17 November 1957, as quoted in Quotations from Chairman Mao , chapter 30, official Foreign Languages Press translation). Revolutionary standing was conditional: youth had to integrate with workers and peasants. Another item tells Youth League organisations to attend to "recreation, sport and rest" as well as study and work. The quotations were selected for instruction, stripped of context and translated by the state publisher. They show how the leadership addressed the young, not how the young received it. The oath and the object The Soviet Young Pioneers, the organisation for younger children, turned that relationship into words a child could memorise at initiation. The 1922 oath read: "Честным словом обещаю, что буду верен рабочему классу, буду ежедневно помогать своим трудовым собратьям, знаю законы пионеров и буду им повиноваться." (Young Pioneer oath, 1922 version; translation mine: "I promise on my word of honour that I will be faithful to the working class, will help my working brothers every day, know the laws of the pioneers and will obey them.") (1922 version). The wording changed across six recorded versions from 1922 to 1986. Early promises spoke of fidelity to the working class, a 1924 version pledged to uphold "the behests of Ilyich", and late versions promised to love and cherish the Motherland. The same rite was adapted to three political moments. The pledge also entered the home: a 1960 colour postcard in a set called "The Laws of the Young Pioneers" was printed in a run of 175,000 and sold for 20 kopecks. The catalogue record was verified but its text was not transcribed; the oaths come from a reference site rather than the Soviet publications it cites, and the translations are provisional. Reciting an oath does not establish what a nine year old believed. The Artek camp archives include a "Personal notebook of the Young Pioneer, solemn promise, and regulations of the Soviet Young Pioneers" and draft regulations, documents dated 1944 to 1967. The catalogue records are verified; the notebooks are behind a paywall and were not read. Artek was an elite showcase camp and cannot represent an ordinary school. A secular confirmation In East Germany the Socialist Unity Party, the SED, decided in March 1954 to introduce a Jugendweihe , a secular coming of age ceremony, because no secular ritual marked the transition to adulthood. The first promise, published on 17 February 1955, put a question to fourteen year olds: "Seid Ihr bereit, alle Eure Kräfte für ein glückliches Leben der werktätigen Menschen und für den Fortschr

title: Faith and the Socialist Claim
description: On 2 November 1850 the first issue of a London periodical put a claim on the table that neither clergy nor radicals found comfortable.
text: On 2 November 1850 the first issue of a London periodical put a claim on the table that neither clergy nor radicals found comfortable. The Christian Socialist , edited by the barrister John Malcolm Forbes Ludlow and shaped by the clergyman Frederick Denison Maurice and Charles Kingsley, argued that Christianity and socialism were allies rather than enemies. Socialism was "the livery of the nineteenth century", the journal said, as Protestantism had been the livery of the sixteenth. The editors backed the claim with institutions: cooperative workshops and a college for working men. The opening number went further, insisting that "even the strangest and most monstrous forms of Socialism are at bottom but Christian heresies." So wrote the first issue of The Christian Socialist , 2 November 1850, as transcribed at Source: spartacus educational.com The starting point Whatever one makes of that claim, the argument had to begin with a text written a few years earlier in Paris. In an introduction composed in December 1843 and January 1844 and first published on 7 and 10 February 1844, Karl Marx set down the line that would shadow every later discussion: "Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, and the soul of soulless conditions. It is the opium of the people." (Karl Marx, introduction written December 1843 – January 1844, first published 7 and 10 February 1844. Marxists Internet Archive: intro) Marx's point was not simply that religion was an illusion. He argued that the criticism of heaven turns into the criticism of earth, and that the state and society which need religious consolation must themselves be examined. His own chapter in this book sets out the reasoning in full. What concerns us here is what other socialists did with the relation between faith and politics. The Christian Socialists took the opposite course. They did not wait for religion to wither; they tried to build a just order inside it. That programme was contested from within socialism almost at once. In January 1884 the British Marxist E. Belfort Bax attacked Kingsley and Maurice in a polemic called "Unscientific Socialism": "It was undoubtedly some scheme of co operation, we may observe, that the 'old', 'original' Christian Socialists in this country, Kingsley and Maurice, had in view." (E. Belfort Bax, "Unscientific Socialism", January 1884. Marxists Internet Archive: unscisoc) Bax argued that their practical programme was trade cooperation, or industrial partnership, and so stayed within the ideas of the bourgeois system he wanted to replace. He called their guild a red herring and dismissed their ethics. His account is useful as evidence of a quarrel, not as a neutral description: he wrote to discredit a rival, and he expounded a prejudice about "Semitic ethics" that must be rejected rather than repeated. One further caution: Kingsley later described the Bible as an "opium dose for keeping beasts of burden patient"; the two phrases should not be merged. Marx published his line earlier. Faith as a resource The Victorian argument was one version of a wider attempt to use religious tradition for egalitarian ends. At Medellín in 1968, 145 Latin American bishops declared that "Peace is, above all, a work of justice. It presupposes and requires the establishment of a just order in which men can fulfill themselves as men, where their dignity is respected." (Latin American bishops, Medellín, 6 September 1968, English text at Source: we are church.org) They described underdevelopment as an unjust situation that bred tension, named institutionalised violence, and instructed pastors to defend the poor and to encourage grassroots organisation. They warned that those who held privilege by force would be answerable for "explosive revolutions of despair". The phrase that came to summarise this shift, the "preferential option for the poor", the choice to put poor people first, was still being formed. The Peruvian theologian Gustavo Gut

title: The Private and the Political: LGBTQ+ People in Socialist Movements and States
description: In May 1934 a Scottish-born journalist working in Moscow sat down to write to Stalin.
text: In May 1934 a Scottish born journalist working in Moscow sat down to write to Stalin. Harry Otter Whyte was a member of the Communist Party of Great Britain and an editor at the Moscow Daily News , and he was a gay man. The Soviet government had issued a decree on 7 March making sodomy a crime. Whyte asked how the new law could be reconciled with the ideas it claimed to defend: "The question is as follows: can a homosexual be considered someone worthy of membership in the Communist Party?" (Harry Whyte, letter to Stalin, May 1934; English translation by Jeff Meek. Source: blog.historicenvironment.scot) He did not abandon socialism. He used Stalin's own attacks on the levelling of personal life, and comparisons with women, colonised peoples and Jews under Hitler, to argue that the decree was wrong. He said he had asked secret police officials, psychiatrists and his editor for a clear answer and had received contradictory replies. Stalin never answered. A marginal note attributed to him dismissed the letter as the work of an idiot and a degenerate, and it was filed. The law and the letter Whyte's question only makes sense against an earlier change. The Soviet criminal codes of 1922 and 1926 had removed penalties for same sex relations between consenting adults. Historians working from newly opened Soviet archives have argued that this was a deliberate revolutionary project, not an oversight, and that the 1934 decree reversed it. The reversal turned a private matter into a matter of state order. Whyte's argument, the clearest surviving contemporary case by a gay communist that the new law contradicted Marxism, stayed inside the language of his time. He wrote of a "constitutional" minority, offered a two percent estimate, and distinguished between people born homosexual and those who acquired the condition. Those claims belong to the assumptions of the 1930s and should not be repeated as findings. What endures is his method: a party member holding his own movement to its stated principles, and finding that it would not answer. Sugar and the new man In Cuba the argument took a harsher form. The government's UMAP camps, a network of forced labour sites, joined work in the sugar fields to an attempt to manufacture a particular kind of militant, masculine "new man". The camps were not secret. Castro spoke of them at the University of Havana in March 1966, and a historian counting the press found a dozen articles in 1966 and 1967 carrying photographs and interviews with cheerful internees. He also found that eleven pieces in Granma and Verde Olivo referred to the camps without once mentioning homosexuals, because propaganda had to protect their reputation. Scholarship disagrees about what they were for. One reading treats them as social engineering, a deliberate remaking of gender and labour; another argues they served economic and security goals, varied from camp to camp, and were not a single uniform institution, with Jehovah's Witnesses among the worst treated. Neither reading makes the experience of the people held there harmless. José Rolando Valdés was sent to the Primero de Enero camp, where gay men and Christians were held together. He recalled being picked up after an incident at his naval camp, refusing the uniform, being beaten and kept in his underwear in a cell for four days. He described a sergeant putting "effeminate" boys naked into a cold water tank, a start at half past five or six in the morning, roughly twelve hours in the cane field, evening political study, seven pesos a month, and a machete wound he had to work through. "Aunque salgas con vida, a un lugar así no sobrevives del todo." (José Rolando Valdés, interview published December 2019. Source: washingtonblade.com; my translation: "Even if you leave alive, you never fully survive a place like that.") He said he did not speak of it for more than fifty years out of shame, later lived under another name, married and emigrated in 2002. His is one retrospective acc

title: One Big Union: The IWW in the United States, 1905–1920
description: On 18 November 1915, a man awaiting execution wrote a will in his cell.
text: On 18 November 1915, a man awaiting execution wrote a will in his cell. "My will is easy to decide, / For there is nothing to divide." (Joe Hill, written in his cell, 18 November 1915. Source: en.wikisource.org) Hill had no property to dispose of. He asked that his body be cremated and his ashes scattered, and ended with an instruction to organise rather than mourn. He was an organiser and songwriter for the Industrial Workers of the World, a union that carried its politics in verses printed on cheap paper. The songbook that preserved his will also printed the union's constitution, its membership fees and the address of its general secretary treasurer, William D. Haywood. A member could carry the argument in a pocket. The union in the songbook The Industrial Workers of the World was founded in Chicago in 1905. Its preamble opened with a claim that left no room for gradualism: "The working class and the employing class have nothing in common." (IWW preamble, printed in Songs of the Workers , ninth edition, March 1916. Source: en.wikisource.org) The union organised by industry rather than by craft. A craft union brings together workers who share one skilled trade; an industrial union brings together everyone in a factory or an industry, including the unskilled. The IWW admitted foreign born and migratory workers whom the American Federation of Labor largely left outside. Its stated aim was not only better wages but the abolition of the wage system, summed up in the phrase "one big union". The ninth edition of the songbook was printed in Cleveland in March 1916. Alongside the preamble it carried songs by Ralph Chaplin and Joe Hill, and its index listed "Come Join the One Big Union", "Solidarity Forever", "The Preacher and the Slave" and "John Golden and the Lawrence Strike". Its advertising pages described the union's newspaper, Solidarity , as carrying first hand reports from strikes. Songs were not decoration. For members who were often newly arrived, poorly paid and working long hours, they were the main way the union explained itself. The argument over one big union On 11 January 1912, ten days before the Lawrence strike began, Haywood and Morris Hillquit debated at Cooper Union in New York before a Socialist Party audience. Haywood read the preamble aloud and said that "One Big Union" should be the slogan of every socialist agitator, on the platform and in the workshop. (William D. Haywood, Cooper Union debate, 11 January 1912. Internet Archive: 120111 hillquithaywood nycdebate) He attacked craft unions as "job trusts" and called industrial unionism "socialism with its working clothes on". Hillquit conceded that industrial organisation was superior in the abstract, but argued that the form of the union mattered less than class consciousness and that a rival union would split the socialist movement. The argument was not settled doctrine. One speaker treated the union as the shape socialism would take; the other feared it would divide those who already called themselves socialists. The debate survives in a modern edited transcription rather than a contemporary verbatim report, and the editor's introduction is not a participant's words. On the picket line In Lawrence, Massachusetts, the immediate cause of the 1912 strike was a cut in hours from 56 to 54 a week without a matching adjustment in pay. The federal investigation reported: "During the first few days of the strike approximately 14,000 employees withdrew from their work, later accessions increased the number on strike to approximately 23,000" (Charles P. Neill, official report, 1912. Internet Archive). It recorded 296 strike related arrests producing 355 court cases, and a settlement giving roughly 30,000 workers increases of between 5 and 20 per cent. Justus Ebert's IWW account describes a strike committee organised through nationality groups and the difficulty of turning a spontaneous walkout into an industrial strike. title: The Workshop and the Union: Workers' Control from the Clyde to Chile
description: At the congress of the Confédération générale du travail at Amiens in 1906, the vote on a charter was 830 for, eight against and one abstention.
text: At the congress of the Confédération générale du travail at Amiens in 1906, the vote on a charter was 830 for, eight against and one abstention. Roughly forty names were appended with their trades. The document declared that the CGT, the French General Confederation of Labour, stood outside "all political schools" and united workers "conscious of the fight to be carried out for the disappearance of the salaried and of employers". It said that "economic action must be carried out directly against the bosses, the confederated organizations not having to involve themselves, as a union group, with parties and sects" (Charter of Amiens, CGT, 1906, translated by Mitch Abidor. Marxists Internet Archive: charter amiens). It committed the union to immediate improvements and to complete emancipation through the expropriation of the capitalists and the general strike, a strike extended across whole industries rather than one workplace. On the union's future role it concluded: "it advocates as a method of action the general strike; and it considers that the union, today a resistance group will be, in the future, a group for production and redistribution" (Charter of Amiens, CGT, 1906, translated by Mitch Abidor. Marxists Internet Archive: charter amiens). This was syndicalism: the belief that trade unions, rather than political parties, were the instrument of workers' emancipation. It was a statement of principle, not a handbook for running production, and the CGT's later participation in wartime and postwar bodies is a separate question. The English wording is a volunteer translation and would need checking against the French. "We will act independently" In the Clyde region of Scotland during the First World War, shop stewards built a different institution. A shop steward is a worker elected by fellow workers to represent them at the workplace. A strike in February 1915 and the imprisonment of three Govan shipwrights led to the Clyde Workers' Committee, a body of delegates from all trades. A leaflet signed by its president, William Gallacher, and secretary, J. M. Messer, set out the committee's position: "We will support the officials just 'so long as they rightly represent the workers, but we will act independently immediately they misrepresent them." (William Gallacher, president, and J. M. Messer, secretary, Clyde Workers' Committee leaflet, issued June–August 1915. Marxists Internet Archive: clyde committee) It listed ten trades, from toolmakers to school teachers, and claimed to represent the rank and file. The officials in question led the ASE, the engineers' craft union, whose leaders had supported the Munitions Act. "The support given to the Munitions Act by the Officials was an act of Treachery to the Working Class." (same leaflet, 1915. Marxists Internet Archive: clyde committee) The dispute centred on dilution, the wartime relaxation of craft rules that let less trained workers into jobs previously reserved for skilled men. Gallacher wrote that "the workers were left with the impression that the 'dilution of Labour' was simply a pretext for the 'deluding of Labour'" (William Gallacher, "Prepare for Action", The Worker no. 1, 8 January 1916. Marxists Internet Archive: prepare action). He reported that 20 of 24 or 25 invited unions refused to pack Lloyd George's meeting at St Andrew's Hall, and that when the committee put an alternative scheme of industrial organisation to the minister, he replied: "It would be a revolution... and it can't be done." (William Gallacher, "Prepare for Action", The Worker no. 1, 8 January 1916. Marxists Internet Archive: prepare action) In a second article Gallacher stated the positive aim: "the ultimate aim of the Clyde Workers' Committee is to weld these unions into one powerful organisation that will place the workers in complete control of the industry" (William Gallacher, "A Call to All Workers", The Worker no. 4, 29 January 1916. Marxists Internet Archive: call workers). The committee was cons
