title: The Cooperative Idea: Rochdale, the Commonwealth and the Commune
description: On 21 December 1844 a group of weavers and artisans—traditionally said to number twenty-eight—opened a shop in Toad Lane, Rochdale, in the north of England.
text: On 21 December 1844 a group of weavers and artisans—traditionally said to number twenty eight—opened a shop in Toad Lane, Rochdale, in the north of England (Rochdale Pioneers Museum (archived)). Its first stock was flour, butter, sugar and oatmeal. They owned it themselves, having gathered twopence at a time until they held enough to take a lease at £10 a year; the traditional figure for their capital is about £28. A consumer cooperative is a shop owned by the people who use it: they pool money to buy in bulk and receive any surplus in proportion to what they spend, rather than paying a return to outside shareholders. The founders did not mean to stop at a grocery. Their rules set out a much longer journey. George Jacob Holyoake knew the Rochdale socialists and Chartists and later printed the Society's own minutes. He described how the idea had begun among working people: "a few poor weavers out of employ, and nearly out of food and quite out of heart with the social state, met together to discover what they could do to better their industrial condition." Source: George Jacob Holyoake, The History of the Rochdale Pioneers , first published from 1857 The trigger was a failed strike of flannel weavers in 1843. The arguments continued on Sundays in the Temperance or Chartist Reading Room. Chartists, who wanted political rights for ordinary men, debated there with teetotalers and followers of Robert Owen, who held that character was formed by circumstance and communities could be organised cooperatively. John Kershaw, a coal miner and one of the founders, remembered the conditions: "Distress was far and widespread. People were badly fed and badly clothed. The hand loom weavers seemed to be the worst off of any of the working class." Source: John Kershaw, Rochdale Pioneer, in the Co operative News , 9 April 1893, reproduced in John Samuel, 1894 Kershaw had begun in a mill at seven and gone into the mine at eight. His memory reaches us through Holyoake and a pamphlet written to persuade American workers, a participant's account at two removes. The Society's 1864 annual report, reproduced in that pamphlet, says it was formed after working men despaired of success in a strike. The rules show how far the founders meant to go. Alongside the store they listed housing, manufacture to employ members laid off by wage cuts, and land to be cultivated by the unemployed. Then came the clause that gave them their wider name: "That, as soon as practicable, this society shall proceed to arrange the powers of production, distribution, education, and government, or in other words, to establish a self supporting home colony of united interests." Source: The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers, rules, 1844 Most of the larger objects were never carried out. What survived was a discipline about money: limited interest on shares, meaning a cap on the return paid to anyone's capital, and a surplus divided according to purchases. The shop was to be a business that could not be captured for private gain. The rules that outlived the colony The Society survived the Lancashire cotton famine. Holyoake's history records that during the four years of the crisis members drew out £83,000, the Society gave £750 in relief and spent £1,840 on self education (Holyoake, The History of the Rochdale Pioneers , 1893, pp. 152–153). The Co operative Wholesale Society, founded in 1863, was owned by the retail societies it supplied; its customers were its member societies (Redfern, The Story of the C.W.S. , 1913). A cooperative was answerable to its own customers. By 1966 the International Co operative Alliance had turned Rochdale practice into six principles: "Members of primary societies should enjoy equal rights of voting (one member, one vote) and participation in decisions affecting their societies." Source: International Co operative Alliance, Co operative Principles, 1966 The others limited interest on capital, declared the surplus to belong to members, required memb

title: The Cost of the Promise: Socialism and the Environment
description: Friedrich Engels walked the industrial districts of Manchester in the 1840s and wrote down what he saw.
text: Friedrich Engels walked the industrial districts of Manchester in the 1840s and wrote down what he saw. The river below the town was not scenery but a consequence of how production was organised: "At the bottom flows, or rather stagnates, the Irk, a narrow, coal black, foul smelling stream, full of debris and refuse, which it deposits on the shallower right bank." Source: Friedrich Engels, The Condition of the Working Class in England , written 1844–45, English edition 1887 Engels was a young businessman living in the city, and his book mixes his own observation with official reports. It is a witness's polemic, not a measurement. Marx, in Capital , described work as a process in which people and nature act on one another, an exchange of matter that goes on in every society (Marx, Capital , Volume I, Chapter 7). In an unfinished essay written in 1876 Engels warned that interventions in nature bring unforeseen consequences, from deforestation to lost soil, and connected that warning to the way production is organised: "Let us not, however, flatter ourselves overmuch on account of our human victories over nature. For each such victory nature takes its revenge on us." Source: Frederick Engels, "The Part Played by Labour in the Transition from Ape to Man", written 1876, translated by Clemens Dutt (1934) None of this describes an actually existing socialist state. These are nineteenth century texts, translated and selectively written, which later readers used to argue that pollution was structural rather than accidental. Whether they amount to a theory of ecology is still disputed. Water, fish and a sea that disappeared Cotton did more damage to the Aral Sea than any single factory. Irrigation diverted the rivers that fed it, and a fishing economy at Muynak came apart. Jasmurad Kenesbay, a fisherman and state farm member, remembered the record catch of 1957 and the end of commercial fishing by 1982. A state farm is a farm owned and run by the government. "I don't think I will ever fish again," ... "As the sea dies, so does this village. Our entire economy has been destroyed and so have our lives." Source: Jasmurad Kenesbay, fisherman at Muynak, quoted by Don Hinrichsen, 1995. Ellipsis marks the reporter's intervening words The reporter recorded exposed seabed, salt and pesticide dust, and a cannery still processing frozen fish shipped in from the Baltic. Almas Tolvashev had been a captain at Moynaq: "I was the first Muslim captain in Moynaq and my ship was the Volga... There were 250 ships here. I used to catch 600 700 kilos of fish every day. Now there is no sea." Source: Almas Tolvashev, former fishing captain, interviewed by the BBC, 2018. Ellipsis marks omitted words Soviet authorities denied that the sea was disappearing until the USSR broke up, according to the same report. Both men speak decades after the events, through journalists, and neither is a measurement of the catch. Criticism also came from inside the system. Soviet scientists and writers campaigned to protect Lake Baikal, and Douglas Weiner's archival study shows that scientist led nature societies survived from the Stalin years onward, insisting they were patriots rather than dissidents. The campaigning letters and decrees themselves were not opened for this account; they reach us only in Weiner's English translation, and are not quoted here as primary text. By 1989 the shrinking Aral, dead sturgeon in the Volga and effluent from the Baikal pulp mill were being reported in the Soviet press. Fyodor Morgun, chairman of the new State Committee for Environmental Protection, said: "We have started too late," Morgun told the group. "Our air is not up to the proper mark, our soil is polluted, and our forests are affected." Source: Fyodor Morgun, chairman of Goskompriroda, quoted by Dick Thompson, TIME, 2 January 1989 New fines, criminal proceedings and public protests were appearing under glasnost, the late Soviet policy that permitted open criticism. title: The Science of Control: Cybernetics, Genetics and the Socialist Plan
description: Norbert Wiener coined the word cybernetics for a study of control and communication in machines and living things.
text: Norbert Wiener coined the word cybernetics for a study of control and communication in machines and living things (Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics: or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine , MIT Press, 1948). Feedback, the idea at its centre, means feeding information about the result of an action back into the system so that it can adjust. Wiener had worked on anti aircraft fire control during the war, and in 1943 he and two colleagues proposed that the human nervous system and a machine could be discussed in one vocabulary. He wrote: "It is these boundary regions of science which offer the richest opportunities to the qualified investigator." Source: Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics , 1948 (read in the 1961 second edition) That proposal was a research tool, not a finished doctrine. In the Soviet Union it became a philosophical argument conducted in Marxist terms. A 1960 exchange, translated the following year by the U.S. Joint Publications Research Service, set two philosophers against each other. Borshchev, Rokhlin and Il'in held that a machine might in principle develop a quality analogous to consciousness without contradicting dialectical materialism. M. N. Andryushchenko replied that thinking belonged to highly organised living matter and that a model of a reflex was not a reflex. Her objection turned on a toy that could be taught to avoid an obstacle: the machine followed a purpose given from outside. "Man predetermined the character of the reaction." Source: M. N. Andryushchenko, "Reply to Comrades Borshchev, Il'in and Rokhlin", 1960, translated by the U.S. Joint Publications Research Service Both writers treated cybernetics as a live question. Neither simply repeated a ban. The science that could not be wrong Biology in the same state took a different path. Mendelian genetics is the theory of heredity based on Gregor Mendel's laws, in which traits pass between generations through units we now call genes. Trofim Lysenko, president of the Lenin All Union Academy of Agricultural Sciences, rejected it. At a session of the academy in July and August 1948 he told his audience that heredity was a property of the whole organism and its conditions of life, that acquired characters were inherited, and that chromosome theory was idealist. The transcript records applause and ovations. At the close of the session on 5 August he said: "the Central Committee of the Party has examined my report and approved it." Source: T. D. Lysenko, concluding remarks, 5 August 1948, translated "We do not recognize the chromosome theory of heredity; we do not recognize Mendelism Morganism." Source: T. D. Lysenko, concluding remarks, 5 August 1948, translated In his full report of 31 July he named the practical objection he had against the geneticists, that they taught a theory students could learn while offering nothing to the fields: "Morganism Mendelism (the chromosome theory of heredity) is to this day taught, in a number of versions, in all colleges of biology and agronomy, whereas the study of Michurin genetics has in fact not been introduced at all." Source: T. D. Lysenko, report, 31 July 1948, translated The session endorsed the report and geneticists were dismissed. Vavilov had been arrested in 1940 and died in prison in 1943. Zhores Medvedev, a biologist who was an onlooker in the earlier phase and a participant in the struggle against Lysenkoism in the 1960s, described his own changing role: "in the first as historian; in the second as an onlooker; and in the third as participant" Source: Zhores Medvedev, preface dated January 1967, translated by I. Michael Lerner He reports that a petition signed by more than three hundred scientists asked for Lysenko's removal from the academy presidency by the end of 1955, and that it succeeded: "By the end of 1955 more than three hundred scientists had signed a petition requesting Lysenko's removal from the post of LAAAS president" Source: Zhores Medvedev, The Rise and Fall of T. D. Lysenko ,

title: Living in Truth: Dissent and Samizdat in the Soviet Bloc, 1962–1989
description: Every morning a greengrocer in Czechoslovakia placed a printed notice in his shop window, the revolutionary slogan that shopkeepers were expected to display.
text: In an essay written in October 1978 the playwright Václav Havel constructed an example: a greengrocer in Czechoslovakia placed a printed notice in his shop window, the revolutionary slogan shopkeepers were expected to display. Havel's greengrocer did not put it there out of conviction. He put it there because the authorities expected it, and because the alternative was to lose his shop, or worse. Havel made that ordinary act the key to understanding power in a state that called itself socialist. The regime did not rule chiefly by terror, he argued. It ruled by making people repeat its formulas, and each repetition rebuilt the thing it obeyed: "For by this very fact, individuals confirm the system, fulfill the system, make the system, are the system." Havel called the greengrocer's bargain "living within the lie" and named its opposite "living within the truth". He described Czechoslovakia as "post totalitarian", meaning that power worked mainly through ritual and ideology rather than through open violence. Of a man who breaks the ritual he wrote: "He has said that the emperor is naked." (Václav Havel, "The Power of the Powerless," October 1978) Havel's essay did not appear in an ordinary journal. It was typed and copied in samizdat , the name for the underground practice of reproducing uncensored writing on typewriters and carbon paper and passing it from reader to reader. To publish in samizdat was to break the state's monopoly on the printed word; to be caught with a duplicated text could mean prison. The writing that survived this way came from famous dissidents and from people whose names never travelled beyond their own city. A text in print, and the silence around it In November 1962 the Soviet literary journal Novy Mir published Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's novella One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich . It was fiction drawn from the author's eight years in the camps, but it described a prisoner's working day with a detail official writing had refused to supply. An old prisoner in the story tells the others, "It's the law of the taiga here, men. But a man can live here, just like anywhere else." The narrator counts the moments when a convict belongs to himself: "Apart from sleep, an old lag can call his life his own only for ten minutes at breakfast time, five at lunchtime, and five more at suppertime." (old prisoner Kuzyomin and the narrator, quoted in Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich , 1962) The novella was a breach in the official silence about the camps. Readers' letters to the journal, studied later by Miriam Dobson, show that the response was more divided than a simple quarrel between liberals and conservatives. Solzhenitsyn was expelled from the Writers' Union, and his later books circulated in typescript. In his 1970 Nobel lecture, delivered only to the Swedish Academy, he put the matter in two sentences: "Woe to that nation whose literature is disturbed by the intervention of power." And, "ONE WORD OF TRUTH SHALL OUTWEIGH THE WHOLE WORLD." (Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, Nobel literature lecture, 1970) Copies passed from hand to hand The alternative press carried news that the official papers suppressed. A Chronicle of Current Events , an illegal human rights periodical, summarised what was circulating in March 1975 in its thirty fifth issue. It described Bukovsky and Gluzman's "A Manual on Psychiatry for Dissenters", written from prison and a labour camp, listed the contents of underground journals, and recorded searches and KGB interrogations. On the manual's account of prisoners who publicly recanted, the Chronicle noted that "it is precisely this fear and helplessness that the authors consider to be the reason behind recent unexpected 'repentances' and 'repudiations'". ( A Chronicle of Current Events , no. 35, section 35.12, 31 May 1975, Peter Reddaway translation) The same issue preserved a real disagreement among exiles. title: The Cell and the Page: Prison and Exile Testimony
description: In an Odessa prison, a blacksmith welded iron rings onto Leo Deutsch's ankles.
text: In an Odessa prison, a blacksmith welded iron rings onto Leo Deutsch's ankles. Deutsch was a founder of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, and he was being prepared for the long journey to Siberia. "Every stroke of the hammer made my heart sink, as I realised that a new existence was beginning for me." (Leo Deutsch, Sixteen Years in Siberia , describing the welding of his fetters, translated by Helen Chisholm (1903)) His translator noted the quiet tone and the absence of sensationalism, and advised reading between the lines. Deutsch was marched through Moscow in chains, with half his head shaved; the convict dress and chains were meant to mark him as "deprived of all rights". This chapter asks what a text like that can establish. Prison writing is the book's richest store of first hand evidence, but a memoir proves that one person experienced something; it does not give a rate. Four kinds of writing are used here: retrospective memoirs, letters smuggled out at the time, poems written in custody, and interviews recorded long after release. Each tells us something different, and each has its own limits. The nineteenth century inheritance A literature of confinement existed before Marx. Alfred Dreyfus, a French artillery captain convicted of treason in 1894, described his public degradation on 5 January 1895: "Soldiers, they are degrading an innocent man. Soldiers, they are dishonoring an innocent man. Vive la France, vive l'armée!" (Alfred Dreyfus, "The Degradation," 1895, translated by August F. Jaccaci (1901)) He was held on Devil's Island in French Guiana. The Communards deported after 1871 went chiefly to New Caledonia, a different place which should not be confused with it. Dreyfus was not a socialist; he supplies the liberal case of a man wrongly convicted, and he had to reclaim his own words in writing after a gendarmerie captain turned his protests into a legend of confession. Louise Michel, a Communard, schoolmistress and anarchist, wrote her memoirs inside Saint Lazare prison, using a rule that allowed attorneys to receive sealed letters to get her pages past the gate. "Many brave hearts are found among those unfortunate prisoners whom people despise. People must see things as they are, and only someone who has lived through such experiences knows." (Louise Michel, memoirs written at Saint Lazare, 1883–86, translated by Lowry and Gunter) Her translators state that the words are hers and the arrangement is theirs, and they record her own inaccuracies about her age and her past. What these three accounts establish is the experience of punishment meant to mark the body and strip honour. Writing under censorship Rosa Luxemburg wrote from Wronke to Sophie Liebknecht, the wife of Karl Liebknecht, under rigid censorship. She was allowed two letters a month, and delivery could take from four days to three weeks. Time itself changed in prison: "As during the siege of Sebastopol, every month seems a year." (Rosa Luxemburg to Sophie Liebknecht, Wronke, 21 November 1916) She watched a wryneck, then the disappearance of songbirds, then a beetle eaten by ants; she said she felt more at home with birds than at a party congress, while holding to her purpose: "You know that I really hope to die at my post, in a street fight or in prison." (Rosa Luxemburg, letter to Sophie Liebknecht, Wronke, 2 May 1917, translated by Eden and Cedar Paul) Antonio Gramsci, founder of the Italian Communist Party, wrote his notebooks in a Fascist prison between 1929 and 1935. Censorship entered the language itself. Where the Marxist meaning of "class" would be obvious, he substituted "social group"; his editors record the fact in a footnote: "Gramsci tends, for reasons of censorship, to avoid using the word class in contexts where its Marxist overtones would be apparent." (Editors' footnote, Hoare and Nowell Smith, on Gramsci's terminology, not Gramsci's words) His argument survived the substitution: "All men are intellectuals, one could therefore

title: The 'state capitalist' debate and the theory of transition
description: In 1918 Rosa Luxemburg sat in Wronki prison, writing a book she did not live to finish.
text: In 1918 Rosa Luxemburg sat in Wronki prison, writing a book she did not live to finish. A supporter of the Bolsheviks, she accepted that the Russian Revolution needed a dictatorship, meaning rule by the working class rather than by the old propertied classes. But she insisted that this rule had to belong to the whole class and to the public life of the country. "Freedom only for the supporters of the government, only for the members of one party – however numerous they may be – is no freedom at all. Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently." (Rosa Luxemburg, The Russian Revolution , ch. VI "The Problem of Dictatorship", written 1918, first published 1922, English translation by Bertram Wolfe, 1940) She was writing from a cell, without full information about the decisions of the soviet, and her manuscript was pieced together after her death. Yet the sentence is not a footnote to a settled doctrine. It is one answer, spoken at the time, to a question socialists were arguing about while the institutions were being built: what did the transition from capitalism to socialism actually require? Marx had placed a distinct period between the two. The "transition" here means that period of revolutionary transformation, in which the working class was expected to take power and begin to reshape property and production. Lenin, in hiding from the Provisional Government in August and September 1917, quoted Marx to place it precisely: "Between capitalist and communist society lies the period of the revolutionary transformation of the one into the other... the state can be nothing but the revolutionary dictatorship of the proletariat." (V. I. Lenin, The State and Revolution , ch. V, written 1917, first published 1918, English from the Soviet Collected Works ; translator not named in the online headnote; ellipsis marks an omitted passage) This was a scheme written before the seizure of power, not a description of institutions that existed. The planned seventh chapter was never written. The text was also a polemic, and Chapter VI attacked Kautsky and named the Dutch theorist Anton Pannekoek, so the later council communist critique was already a live target in 1917. Reforms, democracy and the party Luxemburg's starting point had been an argument within German social democracy about whether reforms could replace revolution. In 1899 she wrote that giving up the expectation of capitalism's collapse led by stages to giving up the socialist aim itself: "Without the collapse of capitalism the expropriation of the capitalist class is impossible. Bernstein therefore renounces expropriation and chooses a progressive realisation of the 'co operative principle' as the aim of the labour movement." (Rosa Luxemburg, Reform or Revolution , ch. IX, 1899 (revised 1908), English translation by Integer, Militant Publications, 1986) That was before any workers' state existed, so it says nothing about how a transition government should be organised. Her 1918 manuscript supplies the organisational claim. Socialism could not be decreed, because its concrete measures were not contained in any party programme. Democracy had to begin at the seizure of power, with "unlimited democracy": "Socialist democracy begins simultaneously with the beginnings of the destruction of class rule and of the construction of socialism." (Rosa Luxemburg, The Russian Revolution , ch. VIII "Democracy and Dictatorship", written 1918, Bertram Wolfe translation) She called the Bolsheviks' work an "immortal historical service" and blamed the distortions she saw on isolation, German occupation and the failure of the German revolution, so this is not a simple denunciation. Some passages are only rough notes which the translator rendered literally. Lenin's answer developed in the other direction. title: Why Revolutions Succeeded
description: The victories came in Russia, China, Vietnam and Cuba rather than in the advanced industrial societies some Marxists expected. This chapter sets out what the book's evidence supports and what it cannot prove.
text: In 1919 Nguyễn Ái Quoc asked the Paris Peace Conference for civil rights inside the French empire, among them "Complete amnesty of Vietnamese political prisoners" (claim). In 1945 his movement took power in Hanoi in the gap after Japan's surrender (Trường Chinh). The puzzle is that Marx and Engels wrote for industrial capitalism, with the proletariat defined in Engels's 1888 footnote as "the class of modern wage labourers who, having no means of production of their own, are reduced to selling their labour power in order to live" ( Manifesto , ch. I), while the victorious movements worked chiefly where that class was small. Marx's 1859 preface warned that "no social order is ever destroyed before all the productive forces for which it is sufficient have been developed"; productive forces means the labour, tools, techniques and knowledge available (preface). The Manifesto said its ten measures would apply "in most advanced countries" ( Manifesto , ch. II). Lenin's answer was uneven development: monopoly capitalism, the division of the world among the great powers, and revolution possible in one country ( Imperialism , ch. VII). Stalin wrote in 1924 that Russia "was the focus of all these contradictions of imperialism" ( Foundations of Leninism , ch. I). These are arguments within a tradition, not findings about why particular revolts won. The weight of the countryside is the first common feature. Ho told the Comintern in 1924 that "Ninety five per cent of the population are peasants" in the French colonies (Ho). In Hunan in 1927 Mao reported poor peasants at 70 per cent, middle peasants at 20 and landlords and rich peasants at 10, and claimed 1,367,727 members in peasant associations across thirty seven counties (Mao). His class percentages came from surveys whose method he did not give, but any movement seeking rural support had to address rent and land. In Crow Village in 1946 farmer Wang told John Hersey that a "Clearing the Accounts" meeting returned thirty piculs of grain and cut his rent from twelve piculs a mow to eight; the landlord Hsi described mortgaging 130 of his 300 mou (Hersey). The 1947 Draft Agrarian Law declared the "feudal and semi feudal" system abolished and "land to the tiller" established. Hinton, sympathetic to the revolution, recorded a dozen people beaten to death and small holders wrongly dispossessed, and warned that Long Bow was atypical (Hinton). Land hunger was a force to be mobilised, not a uniform grievance that movements simply expressed. Castro's 1953 defence counted "the five hundred thousand farm laborers who live in miserable shacks, who work four months of the year and starve the rest" and 100,000 small farmers working land that was not theirs ( History Will Absolve Me ). The 1959 agrarian law broke the large estates while forbidding "spontaneous seizures" (Castro). In Vietnam, Trường Chinh wrote that "Hundreds of thousands of people starved beside granaries full of rice kept by the Japanese and French" (Trường Chinh). The 1953 to 1956 land reform remains a gap: Giáp called it a source of army strength, while a RAND study based on prisoner interviews gave four incompatible death estimates and called its evidence "meager" (Giáp; RAND). War broke old states. Russia's February Revolution produced dual power, two authorities neither strong enough to displace the other, and Lenin's April Theses refused support to the Provisional Government (dual power; April Theses). China's Long March left the Red Army weakened; Mao claimed "more than twenty thousand li " through eleven provinces (Mao). The Japanese invasion and Chiang's detention at Xi'an in December 1936 pushed the struggle towards a united front. The American ambassador cabled that he lacked information from Xi'an as to the generals' purposes, while Mao claimed Communist mediation was decisive (Johnson; Mao). Cuba's courts had already failed Batista's opponent: Castro filed a writ in 1952 and found that "Days and months passed... The accused

title: Why States Centralised
description: From Kronstadt to the Prague Spring, revolutionary governments concentrated authority. Structural pressure, institutional design and deliberate coercion have to be separated.
text: On 28 February 1921 the crews of two battleships at Kronstadt met to ask whether a soviet, an elected council of workers' and soldiers' deputies, could exist without the Communist Party running it. Their resolution of 1 March demanded new soviet elections "by secret ballot, with freedom to carry on agitation beforehand for all workers and peasants", equal rations and peasant freedom over land (resolution). Red troops crossed the ice on 16 and 17 March. On 16 March the Tenth Congress adopted "On Party Unity", citing the uprising as proof that a faction, an organised group within the party campaigning for a distinct programme, helped counter revolution (congress resolution; Kronstadt ). Some centralisation answered war and hunger. Some was written into rules and institutions by people who chose it. Some was imposed by force on socialists who objected. The material pressures were real. Civil war armies lived off the country they were trying to govern: Makhno complained that Red Guards advanced along railways while villages defended themselves, and the White general Wrangel recorded that "The excessive and disorderly requisitioning by the troops had completed the economic disruption" (Makhno; Wrangel). Compulsory grain requisitioning was meant to feed cities and soldiers but fell unevenly. Krestinsky told Arthur Ransome it was intended for "the propertied classes only", while some districts assessed "rich and poor peasants" alike (Ransome). Ethel Snowden heard peasants call Lenin "a name with which to conjure out of both rich and poor peasant the stocks of food they are believed to be hiding" (Snowden). Famine and peasant resistance forced the tax in kind that replaced requisitioning in 1921 (Mann; Beeuwkes). In 1930 a secret police report from Dnipropetrovsk recorded a worker saying "All our newspapers lie about the gains of collectivization. In practice, everything is falling apart" (REESOURCES). Elsewhere the pattern was war and siege: the Chinese Red Army survived the Long March with heavy losses (Mao); Trường Chinh justified the haste of Vietnam's 1945 rising by the risk of a restored French administration (Trường Chinh); Cuba faced blockade, invasion and the October missile crisis (Castro; Ocasio). These conditions explain why leaders valued command. They do not explain the forms command took. Centralisation was also designed. Democratic centralism, the rule that local bodies may discuss policy but must carry out central decisions, was written into the Soviet constitution, which "combines central leadership with local initiative and creative activity" (Article 3). Lenin grounded "iron discipline" and "absolute centralisation" in small property, which "engenders capitalism and the bourgeoisie continuously, daily, hourly, spontaneously, and on a mass scale" (Lenin). Stalin stated the operating rule: nothing important was decided without "guiding directives from the Party", and "In the U.S.S.R. there is ground only for one party, the Communist Party" (Stalin 1926; Stalin 1936). The official textbook called planned development "an economic law of socialism" ( Political Economy ). The security apparatus was an institution: the Cheka issued decrees ordering named numbers of hostages shot in 1918, and NKVD Order 00447 of 30 July 1937 gave each region quotas, dividing victims between shooting and eight to ten years in camp (Melgunov; Order 00447). Cuba merged its revolutionary organisations into the ORI, then PURS, then the Communist Party; the 1976 Constitution made the party the "superior leading force of society and the state" in Article 5 (Castro 1961; Castro 1965; Raúl Castro 2021). In Budapest the ÁVH fired on a crowd at the Radio Building on 23 October 1956 (UN report). Prague's Action Programme of April 1968 kept the party's leading role, while five senior officials wrote secretly to Brezhnev that "The very existence of socialism in our country is under threat" (Action Programme; secret letter). title: Who Controlled the Workplace?
description: Election of councils, appointment of directors, plan targets and wage systems: the gap between a right on paper and authority over production.
text: The rules of the Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers in 1844 promised that the society would "arrange the powers of production, distribution, education, and government, or in other words, to establish a self supporting home colony of united interests" (rules). Most of those objects were never carried out; what survived was limited interest on shares and surplus divided according to purchases ( The Cooperative Idea ). The governing standard of this book draws a line across that gap: "Distinguish theory, intention, implementation, experience, outcome, and interpretation. Stated ambition is not evidence of success" (research/MASTER STANDARD.md). Applying it means asking separately who was elected, who appointed directors, who set the plan and who decided the wage. Yugoslavia built the most elaborate formal answer. The Basic Law of 26 June 1950 provided that state enterprises be managed by workers' collectives "in the name of the community, within the scope of the state economic plan", through elected and recallable workers' councils and management boards; at least three quarters of board members had to be production workers (Basic Law). The director, however, was appointed by a higher state or economic organ, sat on the board, hired workers and could delay decisions contrary to the plan ( The Yugoslav Experiment ). Tito told the First Congress of Workers' Councils in 1957 that "more than six hundred thousand workers and employees" participated in management, a figure with no stated method, and in the same speech conceded that "certain people in leading positions in the enterprises deny these rights to the workers councils" (Tito). In March 1969 a worker told the student paper Student : "That's only on paper. When the managers choose their people, workers have to obey" (worker). One unnamed person in a hostile compilation cannot stand for every factory, but the remark corroborates the sponsor's admission. The 1974 Constitution later institutionalised associated labour and delegates' assemblies ( Global Survey ). Soviet workplaces offered a different settlement. The 1935 kolkhoz statute set land in perpetuity to the farm and paid wages in "working days" entered in a labour book, with piecework norms and penalties from a public blackboard to dismissal (statute). Delegates argued over private plots, and Stalin enlarged them against the claim that "0.12 hectares is not enough" (debate). The official formula, "From each according to his ability, to each according to his work", was the equality of labour that Marx had called "a bourgeois right" (1936 constitution; Gotha Programme ). Stakhanovism showed the distance between a record and a norm: Stakhanov cut 102 tons in 1935 with two timberers, horse drivers and a repair shift serving his face, and Ordzhonikidze told the Stakhanovite congress that "These 102 tons were produced by an entire brigade" (Stakhanov; Markin). Stalin called the movement "profoundly revolutionary" and "almost spontaneously... from below", while ordering party bodies to curb resistant managers (Stalin). The exceptional result was used to raise norms. A hostile press digest collected reports of resentment, but its editor selected the items (Markin). Letters show the boundary of authority. P. I. Voronov asked in 1936 for work days to be entered every ten days and complained that the chairman, brigade leader and clerk did no work (Voronov). V. A. Sychov reported that his brigade was "all barefoot because we have noware to buy" and that the milk plan fell to 55 to 60 per cent for want of water (Sychov). These are plan fulfilling workers using the plan's language. Rationing set another limit: Ksenia Chekina, stripped of her internal passport, wrote "I have been without a job, without shelter, without a piece of bread for seven months already" (Chekina). China's household registration regulation of 9 January 1958 required one permanent residence and made a move to a city conditional on an employment certificate, scho

title: Why Markets Returned
description: Why centrally planned economies brought back trade, prices and private enterprise, and what the surviving evidence can and cannot show.
text: On 15 March 1921, with the revolt at Kronstadt still unresolved, Lenin told the Tenth Party Congress that the revolution had to give way to the peasantry. The New Economic Policy, or NEP, is the name later given to that retreat: a fixed tax in place of requisitioning, and permission for peasants to sell what remained in markets. "The question of substituting a tax for surplus grain appropriation is primarily and mainly a political question, for it is essentially a question of the attitude of the working class to the peasantry." J. P. Goodrich, surveying the Volga famine zone for the American Relief Administration, chose villages away from the railways and found people eating cabbage leaves and melon rinds (Lenin at the Tenth Party Congress; Goodrich's report). Lenin's official case was that state ownership and management could serve a workers' government. "State capitalism would be a step forward as compared with the present state of affairs in our Soviet Republic," he wrote in April 1921, naming concessions, co operatives, commission agents and leases. That was a justification of a retreat, not a neutral analysis. Pannekoek and Bordiga read the same institutions from the opposite end, one calling Soviet industry state capitalism, the other holding that wherever commodities and wage labour circulate the economy is capitalist (Lenin, The Tax in Kind ; Pannekoek, 1936; Bordiga, 1952). The Soviet precedent: crisis, retreat and argument Walter Duranty watched cafes reopen and traced a Finnish trader who moved from a trestle table to a shop. A Nepman, the period's word for a private trader, became a recognisable type, though Markoosha Fischer remembered that NEP also brought unemployment, with young workers shed first. By October 1923 industrial prices stood at 276 per cent of their 1913 level against 89 per cent for agricultural prices, a historian's calculation known as the scissors because the two lines pulled apart. Trotsky demanded cheaper nails, cloth and matches rather than a repeat of the slogan of the smychka , the bond between town and country; Bukharin replied that conflict between worker and peasant was possible rather than inevitable (Duranty; Fischer; Siegelbaum; Trotsky; Bukharin). Lenin's last article "On Cooperation" conceded that "by adopting NEP we made a concession to the peasant as a trader, to the principal of private trade". Whether NEP was a temporary concession or a new route was left unsettled, and Moshe Lewin's study of Lenin's final months tests that question. Broad agreement holds that NEP was a retreat forced by crisis, that Nepmen reappeared because the state could not supply exchange, and that the worker peasant alliance was the central political problem. Historians still disagree over whether the last articles reorient strategy and whether the scissors was mainly a pricing failure or a structural imbalance (Lenin, "On Cooperation"; Lewin; Ball). Yugoslavia: decentralisation without private trade After the Cominform expelled the Yugoslav party in 1948, Tito told the Federal Assembly in June 1950 that state ownership had not delivered "the factories for the workers" and that directors were still appointed from above. The Basic Law passed that day provided for workers' councils elected by the workers' collectives, Yet the state plan remained in force and the appointed director sat on the board, hired workers and represented the enterprise. In 1957 Tito claimed that more than six hundred thousand workers, about a third of those employed, had taken part in management, while also recording that enterprise officials denied councils their rights. Perlman argued that self management masked bureaucratic power; Hoxha called it capitalist in practice. Neither reading can be tested here, because no council minutes or price series are available (Tito, 1950; Basic Law; Tito, 1957; Perlman; Hoxha). title: Why Movements Fragmented
description: The arguments that divided socialists from the First International to the New Left, and what the documentary record can settle about them.
text: At the Hague Congress of September 1872 the International Working Men's Association voted to make the formation of a working class into a political party indispensable. "The conquest of political power has therefore become the great duty of the working class," ran the new Article 7a. It passed by 29 votes to 5 with 8 abstentions; Mikhail Bakunin was expelled by 27 votes to 6. Marx's Inaugural Address of 1864 had already said that "to conquer political power has, therefore, become the great duty of the working classes". Bakunin, who argued for the abolition of the state and of coercive authority, an outlook later called anarchism, answered that "the basic unity of the International has been fractured". He claimed a managed majority; the vote counts cannot confirm or refute that claim. Engels, without naming him, argued that a cotton mill, a railway and a ship at sea all require coordination: "Wanting to abolish authority in large scale industry is tantamount to wanting to abolish industry itself, to destroy the power loom in order to return to the spinning wheel" (Inaugural Address; Hague resolutions; Bakunin's reply; Engels, On Authority ). This was a division over means and organisation, not yet over the ownership of property. Historians read it differently. Stekloff's Marxist history treats the split as a real division with its own later life; Nicolaievsky and Maenchen Helfen stress Marx's conduct and motives; Joll and Avrich set the conflict within the wider history of anarchism. The documentary case against the Alliance was made by one party, drawn partly from rules supplied by dissidents, and was never tested adversarially. The votes are facts; the weight to give them is interpretation (First International; Joll). Reform, revolution and the party The next division concerned whether capitalism could be voted away. Luxemburg wrote in 1899 that "without the collapse of capitalism the expropriation of the capitalist class is impossible. Bernstein therefore renounces expropriation and chooses a progressive realisation of the 'co operative principle' as the aim of the labour movement." She was answering Eduard Bernstein, who argued that capitalism could be reformed through parliamentary and trade union gains; her text was written before any workers' state existed, so it says nothing about how a transition government should be organised. The German revolution of 1918 made that question practical. Workers' and soldiers' councils, elected bodies of workers and soldiers, spread through the cities; on 9 November Scheidemann declared a republic and Liebknecht proclaimed a socialist republic later the same day. Luxemburg wrote that the choice lay between a National Assembly and "all power to the Workers' and Soldiers' Councils", yet at the KPD founding congress thirteen days later she urged entering the assembly elections, and the congress rejected her. She was murdered with Liebknecht in January 1919 (Luxemburg, Reform or Revolution ; German revolution; Kollwitz's diary). Luxemburg's dispute with Lenin was over the agent as well as the form. From prison in 1918 she wrote that "freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently" and that socialist democracy had to begin at the seizure of power. Lenin answered from the other direction: "small scale production engenders capitalism and the bourgeoisie continuously, daily, hourly, spontaneously, and on a mass scale," which grounded "iron discipline" and "absolute centralisation". His What Is To Be Done? held that workers develop only trade union consciousness by their own efforts, so socialist consciousness had to be brought from without. Inside the Russian party the Workers' Opposition wanted unions rather than appointed managers to run production; Kollontai wrote that "bureaucracy is a direct negation of mass self activity". These texts are arguments with audiences. They establish what leaders said, not what rank and file members thought, and each was written u

title: What History Establishes
description: A concluding synthesis organized around ideas, power, institutions, outcomes and transformation, with an explicit account of the book's epistemic limits.
text: This book has kept four things apart: what thinkers wrote, what revolutionaries intended, what states declared, and what happened to the people who lived under them. A constitution can declare that an economy works in a certain way without establishing that it does (Marx, 1859 preface). Ideas: what socialists believed and why Historical materialism holds that social existence shapes consciousness and that productive forces eventually conflict with existing relations of production. Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme set a lower phase, distribution according to work, and a higher phase, distribution according to needs; Lenin read the first as socialism. Mao made contradiction central, Juche asserted national self reliance in revolution, and Cabral insisted that theory must grow from a country's own social reality. These are arguments by named writers, not evidence that the society described was achieved (Gotha Programme; Soviet Political Economy ; Cabral, 1966). Power: who controlled decisions The vanguard is the most politically organised section of a movement. Lenin held that workers develop only trade union consciousness by themselves, while democratic centralism means that members discuss policy but carry out the central decision. Luxemburg replied that freedom for one party alone is no freedom; Kollontai called bureaucracy a negation of mass self activity. The constitutional texts agree on formal authority: the 1977 Soviet constitution made the party the directing force, and China's Article 1, Vietnam's Article 4 and Cuba's Article 5 all give it the leading role. Yugoslav councils were elected, but the plan and appointed director remained. The decisions that ended the USSR were taken by a few ministers and republican leaders (Lenin, 1902; Luxemburg, 1918; Kollontai; Basic Law, Yugoslavia, 1950; Belovezh Accords). Institutions: how principles were implemented Planning was taught as an "economic law of socialism". The instruments changed: requisitioning gave way to the tax in kind and markets under NEP; workers' councils replaced direct state administration in Yugoslavia; China's constitution admitted a socialist market economy; Vietnam named a socialist oriented market economy; Cuba's Reordering Task unified currencies while keeping public ownership of the main means of production. Stalin's 1936 remark that a programme speaks of the future while a constitution should speak of the present is a warning in reverse: constitutional claims have to be checked (Stalin on the draft constitution; China's constitution; Vietnam's constitution). Outcomes: what happened and to whom Outcomes were distributed unequally. Cuba's literacy campaign sharply reduced illiteracy and its volunteers remembered it as a change in their own lives; the same years saw camps for homosexuals, religious believers and political nonconformists (Felo Rojas; Elvy). Collectivisation and requisitioning were followed by the Ukrainian famine; demographers put excess deaths at about 3.9 million, with estimates from 2.6 to 5 million, while concealment is documented and intent contested (Rudnytskyi and others; Davies and Wheatcroft). China's Great Leap famine has been estimated at about 30 million premature deaths, with weather and policy weighed differently (Ashton and others; Bernstein). North Korean death estimates range from hundreds of thousands to two and a half million (Haggard and Noland). These are estimates from different methods and baselines, not a single count; the chapter on North Korea sets out the underlying figures. The Chinese and North Korean figures are not measured on the same basis as the Ukrainian demographic series. East German workers marched in 1953 over work quotas; Soviet industry damaged the Aral Sea, and Chernobyl's liquidators were not told their doses (Morgun; Kramarevskyy). Chinese officials report 98.99 million rural residents lifted out of poverty by 2020, measured against China's own poverty line (Chinese white paper). Transforma

title: Prices Without Markets: The Calculation Question
description: Stalin allowed that the law of value operated under socialism while denying that it regulated production. The sources assembled here show what that distinction meant in practice.
text: Economic calculation means comparing the cost of different uses of a scarce resource in order to choose between them. In an economy with capital markets, meaning markets in which savers lend to firms and receive a price called interest, the prices of factories and raw materials carry much of that comparison. Socialist economies largely abolished such markets in the means of production. How, then, did a planner decide whether steel should go into a bridge or a lathe? They answer unevenly, with official doctrine, a Chilean computer experiment and admissions of failure. They do not contain the classic books on the subject. That absence shapes what can be said. The Soviet textbook tradition treated planning as a law rather than a choice. "Social, socialist ownership of the means of production, and large scale socialist production both in industry and in agriculture, make the planned, proportional development of the whole economy objectively possible and necessary," the Academy of Sciences textbook stated, calling planning "an economic law of socialism" and "the regulator of socialist industry" ( Political Economy , chapter 30). Stalin's 1952 Economic Problems drew a harder distinction. Commodity production means making goods for sale rather than for direct use. Where it existed, "the law of value must also exist". That is the rule that goods tend to exchange according to the labour socially necessary to produce them. But "the law of value has no regulating function in our socialist production, but it nevertheless influences production, and this fact cannot be ignored when directing production" (Stalin, Economic Problems , §3). Mao criticized the textbook from the other side, complaining that it "is not concerned with people; it considers things, not people" (Mao, "Critique of Stalin's Economic Problems of Socialism in the USSR "). These are arguments about what ought to govern allocation, not measurements of prices at work. The textbook did allow a practical device. Economic accounting meant comparing inputs and outputs in money terms to check profitability. It was "a method of planned economic management in socialist enterprises, based on the operation of the law of value" ( Political Economy , chapter 34). Money prices were used inside enterprises but denied the role of allocating investment between industries. Stalin defined the aim as "the securing of the maximum satisfaction of the constantly rising material and cultural requirements of the whole of society through the continuous expansion and perfection of socialist production on the basis of higher techniques" ( Economic Problems , chapter 8), a target with no account of how it is to be calculated. The textbook also claimed that under socialism "capital, surplus value, capitalist profit, price of production, wage labour" would cease to exist ( Political Economy , chapter 29). That is a claim about a future society, not a finding about one. Information and its limits The book's most direct attempt to solve the information problem is cybernetics, the study of control and communication in machines and living things. Norbert Wiener, who coined the word, described feedback as feeding information about the result of an action back into a system so that it could adjust: "It is these boundary regions of science which offer the richest opportunities to the qualified investigator" (Wiener, Cybernetics , 1948). In the Soviet Union the idea became a philosophical argument. Andryushchenko insisted that "Man predetermined the character of the reaction," because the purpose came from outside (Andryushchenko, 1960). Whether cybernetics was reformist language or administrative power is contested: Gerovitch reads it as a discourse absorbed by orthodoxy, while Peters gives more weight to bureaucratic obstacles in the failed Soviet computer network (Gerovitch; Peters). No primary text by the network's chief architect was opened. In Allende's Chile the problem was tackled in factories rather th

title: The Plan and the Shortage: Targets, Responses and Scarcity
description: A miner's record, a ten per cent quota rise and a party report on empty shelves: how plans were made, how they were answered and why goods remained scarce.
text: On the night of 30 to 31 August 1935 Aleksei Stakhanov, a hewer, meaning a miner who cuts coal at the working face, produced 102 tons in a single shift, ten per cent of the mine's daily output ( Pravda report, 1 September 1935, reproduced in Stakhanov's memoir). A Stakhanovite was a worker whose record was held up as an example. Stalin called it "profoundly revolutionary" and "almost spontaneously... from below," while ordering party bodies to curb resisting managers (Stalin, speech to Stakhanovites, 17 November 1935). He conceded 102 tons could not become the general norm, the output expected of an ordinary worker for full pay, yet it was used to raise expectations. The record was collective work. Stakhanov described arranging timberers, horse drivers and a repair shift, and wrote: "There is no secret in the fact that I cut 102 tons of coal" (Stakhanov, The Story of My Life , 1937). Sergo Ordzhonikidze told the Stakhanovite congress: "These 102 tons were produced by an entire brigade" (Ordzhonikidze, quoted by Markin, 1936). The memoir is an official self presentation in a machine translation; Markin's hostile digest of resentment and assaults is selected press cuttings, not court records (Markin, 1936). Both agree the figure depended on help most miners lacked. In May 1953 the Socialist Unity Party, ruling party of the German Democratic Republic, raised the work quota by ten per cent. Builders on the Stalinallee site in East Berlin found the change in their pay packets, stopped work and marched. On 16 June the Politburo retreated: "The increase in work quotas cannot and must not be carried out through administrative methods. It can only be based on conviction and voluntary action" (SED statement, 16 June 1953). The concession followed the strike but kept the productivity goal. A secret Soviet report of 24 June put 66,000 demonstrators in East Berlin, listed lower norms and prices, recorded food interruptions, and blamed Western intelligence while calling 17 June "X day" (Sokolovskii, Semyonov and Yudin, 24 June 1953). Its own facts point to the quota policy: the target was raised, workers stopped work, and the leadership withdrew the method while keeping the aim. How the plan was answered Letters from Soviet workers show what happened when targets met material conditions. V. A. Sychov, a prize winning herdsman at a sovkhoz, a state farm owned and run by the government, wrote in September 1935 that his brigade was "all barefoot because we have noware to buy... We have nothing not even matches." The milk plan fell to fifty five to sixty per cent because there was no water and the herd had to be driven seven kilometres (Sychov letter, 13 September 1935). A kolkhoz was a collective farm where land and implements were owned jointly and members worked under an elected chairman. P. I. Voronov wrote in 1936 for a village meeting asking for "an uninterrupted supply of goods for sale in our villages, especially flour," noting that "for bread kolkhoz farmers have to travel thirty kilometers" (Voronov letter, 1936). He complained that the chairman, brigade leader and clerk did no work and asked that work days, units of recorded collective farm labour, be entered every ten days. These are plan fulfilling workers demanding the means to fulfil the plan. Tretiakov's 1935 report on Pasha Angelina's women's tractor brigade described twenty hour shifts for a promised 1,200 hectares per tractor and seven days without somewhere to sleep (Tretiakov, "Nine Girls", 1935). Written inside the campaign, its praise is the author's; it records a brigade winning authority under conditions the plan did not provide. Why scarcity returned Shortage outlived the famine years. A photograph of 25 July 1953 showed "bursting" shelves a month after the East Berlin revolt (photograph entry). title: Who Owned What: Legal Title, Control and the Meaning of Social Ownership
description: Constitutions named the owner. Statutes and letters show who hired, who invested and who could overrule a workplace.
text: Ownership is a bundle of rights: legal title, the power to decide how an asset is used, to hire and dismiss workers, to invest surplus and to dispose of output. A share certificate, a collective farm statute and a workers' council can all be called ownership while distributing those powers differently. The book's editorial standard draws a line between theory, intention, implementation, experience, outcome and interpretation, and warns that "stated ambition is not evidence of success". A constitution declaring the means of production publicly owned establishes a legal claim; it does not say who appointed the director. Stalin made the same point in reverse when presenting the 1936 Soviet constitution. A programme, he said, "speaks of that which does not yet exist," whereas a constitution "must speak of that which already exists" (Stalin, report on the draft constitution, 25 November 1936). Article 12 then declared: "The principle applied in the U.S.S.R. is that of socialism: 'From each according to his ability, to each according to his work'" (Constitution of the USSR, 5 December 1936). The claim was not that abundance had arrived, but that the owning relation had changed. The Soviet textbook described socialism as based on "social ownership of the means of production in its two forms": state property and co operative or collective farm property ( Political Economy , chapter 26). Both were called socialist, and the textbook stressed what they shared: no private ownership of the large factories and banks. Whether state ownership was socialism at all was the question of the transition debate. Lenin argued in 1921 that "state capitalism would be a step forward as compared with the present state of affairs in our Soviet Republic," naming concessions, co operatives, commission agents and leases (Lenin, The Tax in Kind , 21 April 1921). State capitalism here meant state ownership and management with profits taken as state income. Pannekoek used the same words as a verdict: "the work is planned, financed and managed by the state; the directors of industry are appointed by the state and profits are considered the income of the state" (Pannekoek, State Capitalism and Dictatorship , 1936). Bordiga went further, defining any system of commodity production, meaning goods made for sale, combined with wage labour as capitalist (Bordiga, Dialogue with Stalin , 1952). Luxemburg framed the issue as one of public life rather than title: "freedom only for the supporters of the government... is no freedom at all" (Luxemburg, The Russian Revolution , ch. VIII, 1918). The Workers' Opposition made it an industrial demand: "Professional and production unions are to be built on the basis of workers democracy, the elective principle and accountability of all organs from the bottom to the top" (Shliapnikov and signatories, Theses of the Workers Opposition , 18 December 1920). Kollontai put the objection in a sentence: "Bureaucracy is a direct negation of mass self activity" (Kollontai, The Workers' Opposition , ch. III, 1921). These texts dispute who should exercise the rights ownership conveys; they do not show who did. The cooperative form The 1935 kolkhoz statute shows a legal form that was both concession and discipline. A kolkhoz was a collective farm whose land and implements were owned jointly. The statute set land in perpetuity to the artel, the farm, allowed private plots of a quarter to a half hectare and up to a hectare in some districts, and permitted privately owned cows, pigs, sheep and hives. Wages were paid in "working days," units entered in a labour book monthly, with piecework norms setting the rate. Penalties ran from a public blackboard through fines of up to five working days to dismissal, and pilfering was called "a betrayal of the kolkhoz cause" (Kolkhoz Statute, 17 February 1935). title: Authors and Intellectual Traditions
description: A research collection of socialist thinkers, political economists, historians and critics of capitalism, with profiles, bibliographies and verified sources.
text: Authors and Intellectual Traditions The historical chapters of this book explain what happened. This collection asks what particular thinkers argued about why it happened. It brings together socialist intellectuals, political economists, historians, anti imperialist writers and critics of capitalism, and it records where they agree, where they disagree and what can be said for their claims with evidence. A profile here is not a verdict. A writer's political interpretation is reported as their interpretation. Where a writer is a professional historian or economist, the method and evidence behind the work are described as well as the conclusion. Polemical writers sit beside archival historians and empirical economists, and the difference is stated rather than hidden. This follows the book's Editorial & Source Policy. How a profile is built Every author profile uses the same thirteen sections: biography; intellectual tradition; major contributions; analysis of capitalism; analysis of socialism; complete bibliography; recommended reading; selected lectures and interviews; intellectual influences; influence and legacy; criticisms and controversies; related thinkers; and sources cited grouped by evidentiary tier. The recommended reading section selects three to five starting points and is kept separate from the complete bibliography, so a reader can see both where to begin and what the author published. The full rule is in research/AUTHOR PROFILES STANDARD.md in the repository. Each profile is written from a research dossier in research/authors/ . The dossier records which primary sources were opened, which facts could not be verified and where a claim comes from a secondary writer rather than the author. Profiles are marked research stage until that check is complete. Nothing in this collection uses Wikipedia, Goodreads, Scribd or Google Books as evidence. Traditions represented The collection is organised by argument, not by loyalty to a single tradition. The headings below describe the ground the collection is intended to cover; not every heading has a published profile yet. Classical Marxism — Marx, Engels and the writers who developed or revised their theory. Marxism Leninism — the tradition of Lenin, Stalin and Mao, and its later interpreters. Western Marxism — Lukács, Gramsci, Adorno, Horkheimer and the critical theory current. Democratic socialism and social democracy — parliamentary and reformist traditions. Libertarian socialism and anarchism — Bakunin, Kropotkin, Goldman, Bookchin and their critics. Anti imperialist thought — Fanon, Rodney, Cabral, Nkrumah, Amin and the dependency writers. Socialist political economy — value, accumulation, monopoly, finance and the labour process. Socialist feminism — domestic labour, social reproduction and racial capitalism. Black radical thought — Du Bois, Robeson, Davis, Cedric Robinson and the prison abolitionists. Ecological socialism — the metabolic rift, fossil capital and degrowth. Contemporary critical thought — media, ideology, platform capital and the claim that alternatives are unthinkable. title: Crossing Between Systems: Transition as an Economic and Political Process
description: NEP, doi moi, Chinese reform, the Cuban Reordering Task and the collapse of 1989 to 1991, read through the sources the book already holds.
text: On 15 March 1921, with the revolt at Kronstadt unresolved, Lenin told the Tenth Party Congress that the revolution had to give way to the peasantry. The New Economic Policy, or NEP, was that retreat: a fixed tax replacing requisitioning and permission to sell what remained. Lenin called the tax measure "primarily and mainly a political question", essentially about "the attitude of the working class to the peasantry" (Lenin at the Tenth Party Congress, 15 March 1921). The decree of 21 March specified that "This tax must be less than what the peasant has given up to this time through requisitions" (Tax in Kind decree). The change was made from weakness. J. P. Goodrich, surveying the Volga famine zone for the American Relief Administration, chose villages away from railways and found people eating cabbage leaves and melon rinds (Goodrich, 1 November 1921). His figures were a relief advocate's case, but rested on houses he entered. Every later transition began in crisis and decided which groups the state would favour. NEP made the political content visible. Lenin argued that state ownership could serve a workers' government: "State capitalism would be a step forward as compared with the present state of affairs in our Soviet Republic" (Lenin, The Tax in Kind , 21 April 1921). A Nepman, the word for a private trader, became a recognisable type, while Fischer remembered young workers shed first (Fischer, 1944). By 1923 industrial prices were 276 per cent of 1913 levels against 89 per cent for farm prices, a gap called the scissors (Siegelbaum). Trotsky demanded "cheaper nails, cloth and matches" instead of repeating the smychka slogan, the bond between town and country (Trotsky, 1923). Bukharin replied that conflict between worker and peasant was "only possible," not inevitable (Bukharin, 1924). Lenin left the question open: "By adopting NEP we made a concession to the peasant as a trader" (Lenin, "On Cooperation"; Lenin, "Better Fewer, But Better"). Lewin tests whether the last articles reorient strategy (Lewin). The end came through everyday machinery: villagers asked how many cattle they could have before being called kulaks, peasants deemed class enemies, and after 1929 Nepmen were disenfranchised (Ball). Yugoslavia: a transition without private trade The Yugoslav transition began with an international rupture, not a market crisis. After the Soviet led Cominform expelled the party in 1948, Tito told the Slovene Academy that "Socialism does not require of us that we renounce our love for our socialist country" (Tito, 26 November 1948). In June 1950 he introduced a law because state ownership had not delivered "the factories for the workers" (Tito, 26 June 1950). The Basic Law put enterprises under workers' collectives "in the name of the community, within the scope of the state economic plan," with elected councils but an appointed director who hired workers and could delay decisions contrary to the plan (Basic Law, 26 June 1950). This was decentralisation inside a plan. Tito claimed in 1957 that over six hundred thousand workers participated in management while admitting officials denied councils their rights (Tito, 25 June 1957). Perlman argued that self management masked bureaucratic power; Hoxha called it capitalist (Perlman, 1969; Hoxha, 1978). No council minutes or price series decide between them. A change in formal owner can be a political realignment without a change in allocation. Vietnam and China: crisis and the party's timetable Đổi Mới, meaning renewal, was adopted at Vietnam's Sixth Party Congress in December 1986 in response to crisis. Fforde records inflation above 700 percent, exports of about US$500 million against US$1,221 million in imports, and areas near famine. Output contracts let households keep a surplus; Contract 10 of 1988 gave land rights, ended central targets and allowed open sales (Fforde, 1997). Transition reached the household. title: Michael Parenti: Class Power, Imperialism and the Politics of Anti-Communism
description: A research profile of the American political scientist: his class analysis, media critique, account of fascism and defence of existing socialist states, with his critics.
text: Michael Parenti wrote about power in a plain, direct way that made him one of the most widely read left wing authors in the United States. He argued that democratic institutions could not be understood apart from the property interests they protected, that mass media served their owners rather than the public, and that the standard account of twentieth century communism ignored both the pressures socialist states faced and the material gains they made. Those arguments made him influential and controversial. This profile sets out what he claimed, what can be checked in his published texts, and where historians and other socialists objected. Biography Parenti was raised in an Italian American working class family in New York City. After high school he worked for several years, then returned to study, earning a BA from City College of New York, an MA from Brown University and a PhD in political science from Yale University (Michael Parenti Political Archive, biography). His own biography gives no birth year; obituary reporting gives 30 September 1933, and this should be read as reported by obituaries rather than confirmed by his archive. He taught at colleges and universities in the United States and abroad, with fellowships from the Ford Foundation, the Social Science Research Council and other bodies, and a visiting fellowship at the Institute for Policy Studies in Washington. According to a memoir by Christopher D. Cook, his teaching career was disrupted in 1970 after he was struck by police while protesting the shootings at Kent State; he left the University of Illinois, moved to the University of Vermont and was dismissed there after a conviction connected with the protest (Cook, The Progressive , 2026). He then worked mainly as a writer and lecturer, and stood for Congress in Vermont in 1974 on the Liberty Union ticket. His archive records a Certificate of Special Congressional Recognition in 2007 and an American Book Award lifetime achievement award in 2014 (archive biography). He died on 24 January 2026 in Amherst, Massachusetts, aged ninety two (Democracy Now!, 2026). Intellectual tradition Parenti wrote as a Marxist political scientist and public intellectual rather than as a university based scholar after the early 1970s. His archive does not state a party affiliation, and this profile makes no claim about one. Cook places his formation in the Old Left of the 1930s to 1960s rather than the student New Left; that is Cook's interpretation, not a fact established by Parenti's own records. His arguments were built against three targets. The first was liberal accounts of American politics that treat government as a neutral referee. The second was what he called left anti communism: the habit, as he saw it, of judging communist states by standards that critics did not apply to capitalist ones. The third was the study of fascism that described its ideology but avoided questions about who benefited from its class policies. In an excerpt from Blackshirts and Reds he wrote that most literature on fascism "say[s] little if anything about the class policies of fascist Italy and Nazi Germany. How did these regimes deal with social services, taxes, business, and the conditions of labor? For whose benefit and at whose expense?" (Parenti, "Rational Fascism"). He shared Chomsky's interest in media and foreign policy but rejected the libertarian conclusion that existing socialist states were not worth defending. That disagreement is part of the record and is not smoothed over here. Major contributions Five arguments recur in the work. First, Democracy for the Few , first published in 1974, connected political institutions to accumulated wealth. Cook quotes the book: "The close relationship between politics and economics is neither neutral nor coincidental. Large governments evolve through history in order to protect large accumulations of property and wealth" (Cook, 2026). The book itself was not opened for this profile, so the words ar

title: Domenico Losurdo: Liberalism, Class Struggle and the Communist Question
description: A research profile of the Italian Marxist historian's counter-history of liberalism, his defence of existing socialism and the criticism it drew.
text: Domenico Losurdo (1941–2018) was an Italian Marxist philosopher and historian of ideas who built his work by turning the history of liberalism against itself. Liberalism, the political tradition that puts individual liberty, rights and limits on government at the centre of public life, was for him not a set of ideas to admire in the abstract but a set of institutions to examine in practice. His best known book, Liberalism: A Counter History , is a counter history: an account written against the way a movement describes itself, showing how liberal societies actually worked and who was left outside them. Losurdo argued that the "community of the free" was defined against slaves, colonial peoples, wage workers and women. He also widened class struggle, the conflict between social groups over wealth and power, to cover colonial, racial and gender conflicts, and he defended the communist states of the twentieth century against what he saw as a one sided verdict. Those arguments won him a wide readership and drew sharp objections from historians and other socialists. This profile sets out what he claimed, what can be checked in the texts, and where his critics disagreed. Biography Verso's author page gives Losurdo's dates as 14 November 1941 to 28 June 2018 and describes him as Professor of Philosophy at the University of Urbino (Verso author page). The translators of the English edition of his Stalin book add that he was born in Sannicandro di Bari and that a tumour took his life in 2018 (Iskra translation foreword, in the Stalin PDF). Angelo d'Orsi, writing in La Repubblica and reprinted by Verso, gives the same birthplace and year and says he died of a brain tumour after a short illness; David Broder's obituary in Jacobin also reports a brain tumour (Verso obituary by d'Orsi; Broder, Jacobin ). Broder calls him seventy seven, which does not sit with the 1941–2018 dates; the dates on the Verso page are the safer record. His university training and teaching career are only partly documented. Guido Liguori, in an obituary published by Verso, says he studied under Pasquale Salvucci at Urbino and then taught the history of philosophy there for many years (Verso obituary by Liguori). Springer's author note for Class Struggle calls him Emeritus Professor at Urbino, and Verso confirms the professorship (Springer book record; Verso author page). The University of Urbino keeps a personal page listing him as Professore Emerito and an institutional CV. Both were located in search results, but the CV downloaded as a fifteen page scan with no text layer and the personal page was not opened directly. The often repeated details that he graduated in 1963, wrote a thesis on Johann Karl Rodbertus and led the Internationale Gesellschaft Hegel Marx from 1988 could not be independently verified from those records and remain unconfirmed here. His political development is described consistently in three obituaries. Liguori records that he was first a militant and leader in the Italian Communist Party (PCI), then in Rifondazione Comunista (PRC), then in the PdCI and the effort to refound a PCI after 2016, and that he was president of the Associazione Marx XXI (Verso obituary by Liguori). Broder, writing in New Left Review in 2017, gives a fuller sequence: as a young militant in the 1960s Losurdo sided with the Chinese position in the Sino Soviet split and welcomed the Cultural Revolution; in the 1980s he wrote for the PCI daily l'Unità and joined the party; after the PCI changed its name in 1991 he went with those who formed Rifondazione Comunista; from 2016 he joined the attempt to recreate a PCI (Broder, New Left Review 107). d'Orsi confirms that Losurdo was an "unrepentant communist" who joined the small party that became the PdCI and helped launch a new Italian Communist Party, and says the two men disagreed significantly about Stalin (Verso obituary by d'Orsi). title: Noam Chomsky: State Power, propaganda and Libertarian Socialism
description: A research profile of the linguist and political writer's critique of US foreign policy, media propaganda and his libertarian socialist alternative.
text: Noam Chomsky wrote in two fields that this collection reads together: linguistics, and a body of political essays and talks about war, media and concentrated power. The political work is not a rival system to Marxism. It is a sustained argument that private and state power together narrow democratic life, that official accounts of foreign policy cannot be taken at face value, and that ordinary people already possess the habits of mind needed to see through them. His positive alternative, libertarian socialism — the view that the people who do the work and are affected by it should control institutions directly, rather than private owners or a state bureaucracy doing it on their behalf — placed him at odds with liberal capitalism and with Leninist and state socialist currents on the left alike. This profile reports what Chomsky argued and what his critics objected to. It does not convert his polemics into established history. Biography Chomsky was born on 7 December 1928 in Philadelphia. The biographical note his own website reproduces from MIT gives the date and city, and the note reproduced from the University of Arizona gives the same.
