Both describe a career divided between linguistics and political writing, but they differ in emphasis: the MIT note lists linguistic publications and named lectures, while the Arizona note calls him the founder of modern linguistics and one of the most cited scholars in modern history (chomsky.info, 2002; University of Arizona, 2017). He studied at the University of Pennsylvania, taking his BA and PhD there; the PhD was awarded in 1955. His dissertation was titled "Transformational Analysis", and its central claims appeared in the 1957 monograph Syntactic Structures . From 1951 to 1955 he was a Junior Fellow of the Harvard Society of Fellows. He joined MIT in 1955, became a full professor in 1961, held the Ferrari P. Ward Professorship from 1966 to 1976 and was appointed Institute Professor in 1976. He spent 1958–59 at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and delivered the John Locke Lectures at Oxford in 1969, the Bertrand Russell Memorial Lecture at Cambridge in 1970, the Nehru Memorial Lecture in New Delhi in 1972 and the Huizinga Lecture in Leiden in 1977 (chomsky.info, 2002). MIT's linguistics page now lists him as Institute Professor and Professor of Linguistics emeritus (MIT Linguistics). The Arizona record says he joined that university in autumn 2017 after his long MIT career (University of Arizona, 2017). His own account of how he became political is more particular than these institutional summaries. In an interview excerpted from The Chomsky Reader he recalls an experimental, Deweyite school he attended until about the age of twelve, where there was no ranking of pupils and "the sense was that everyone was doing something important". High school was the opposite: he found he was a good student, disliked the competition and regimentation, and remembered almost nothing of the classes. At Pennsylvania he planned to leave after two years for political interests. The philosophy course of C. West Churchman, Arabic classes connected partly to politics and partly to his father's work in Hebrew, and the antifascist exile Giorgio Levi Della Vida mattered to him. Through these interests he met the linguist Zellig Harris, whose broad political and intellectual circle drew him into graduate work in linguistics and philosophy; Nelson Goodman recommended him for the Society of Fellows (Chomsky, "Personal influences"). The same interview gives the political background. Chomsky describes his teenage politics as "anarchist or left wing (anti Leninist) Marxist", combined with a socialist, binationalist view of Palestine and support for the kibbutzim and cooperative labour institutions of the pre state Jewish settlement. He was "strongly anti Bolshevik" and could find no organised group that shared his views. An uncle ran a newsstand at Seventy second Street and Broadway that served as a mee

title: Edward S. Herman: The Propaganda Model and Corporate Media
description: A research profile of the political economist's account of corporate media, the propaganda model and double standards in reporting, with the debate around it.
text: Edward S. Herman was an American economist and media analyst who argued that news in the United States is shaped by the corporate interests that own and fund the media. His central idea, developed with Noam Chomsky, is the propaganda model: the claim that news is filtered before it reaches the public, not by one controller issuing orders, but by several pressures that reinforce one another. The model names five such filters. The first is the size, concentrated ownership, wealth and profit orientation of the dominant media firms. The second is advertising as the main source of income. The third is reliance on information supplied by government, business and experts funded or approved by them. The fourth is "flak", organised complaints that discipline media organisations. The fifth is anticommunism, later widened to include market ideology, treated as a national belief that marks some views as unacceptable. News has to pass through each filter, and what survives is the reporting that fits established interests. This profile sets out what Herman argued, what can be checked in his published texts, and where critics objected. Biography Edward Samuel Herman was born in Philadelphia into a family of liberal Democrats. The University of Pennsylvania's own record says he studied economics at Penn, taking bachelor's and master's degrees, and found a mentor in Robert A. Brady, a Berkeley professor who studied the economic systems of fascist societies. He completed a doctorate in economics at Berkeley in 1953, joined Penn as a lecturer in 1958, became an associate professor in 1961 and a professor in 1970, and retired as professor emeritus in 1989. The same record describes him as an economist and media analyst specialising in corporate and regulatory issues and political economy. He died on 11 November 2017, aged 92 (Penn Almanac, 5 December 2017). The precise birth date of 7 April 1925 appears in the author biography attached to his articles at ZNetwork and in an Open Library authority record; it was not confirmed from an institutional record opened for this profile and should be treated as unverified. Before the media books his working life was that of a finance academic with a taste for regulatory conflict. In a 2012 interview with Paul Jay he said his doctoral work at Berkeley studied the Bank of America system and the Transamerica Corporation, that he moved from Penn State to Wharton after being recruited for a study of branch banking in Pennsylvania, and that at Wharton he worked on an early Securities and Exchange Commission study of mutual funds and on a Federal Home Loan Bank Board study of savings and loan associations. The conflict of interest paper from the second study, he recalled, was the one the industry hated and publicly denounced. A grant from the Twentieth Century Fund let him update Berle and Means's The Modern Corporation and Private Property ; the result was Corporate Control, Corporate Power (1981). He placed the start of his collaboration with Chomsky in the early 1970s antiwar movement, their first joint article being on Saigon, and described both men's entry into media analysis as a natural extension of their work on corporate power (The Real News Network interview, 1 July 2012; RePEc/Cambridge book record). Two details in the Penn obituary need care. It groups The Washington Connection and Third World Fascism and After the Cataclysm under 2015, although Herman's and Chomsky's own records and later publisher biographies place the original two volume The Political Economy of Human Rights in 1979; the 2015 dates are best read as later editions, a point that was not independently verified. It also describes The Myth of the Liberal Media as being "with Robert W. McChesney", while the Peter Lang publisher page lists Herman alone as author. Neither discrepancy changes the central biography, but neither should be repeated as settled (Penn Almanac; Peter Lang publisher page). The same notice records that Herman's wife

title: Michael Hudson: Rent, Debt and Financial Empire
description: A research profile of the economist's critique of rentier capitalism, US financial empire and debt, with his institutional proposals and critics.
text: Michael Hudson is an economist whose work joins a critique of rentier capitalism to the history of debt and to the structure of American financial power abroad. His central claim is that economies divide between a productive sector and a rent extracting one. Economic rent means income obtained by owning an asset rather than by producing goods or services, and a rentier is someone who lives from that income. Hudson argues that finance, insurance and real estate have become rent seeking sectors, that American empire works chiefly through the dollar and the recycling of foreign surpluses into United States government debt, and that the cancellation of debts has a far longer history than standard economics textbooks allow. This profile sets out those arguments, the evidence Hudson offers for them, and the objections made against them. It does not treat his claims as established findings. Biography Hudson was born and raised in Minneapolis in a household shaped by the American Trotskyist movement. In an autobiography interview conducted at Peking University on 7 May 2018 by Lau Kin Chi, he said that his father was one of the leaders of the Minneapolis general strikes of 1934 to 1936 and was jailed under the Smith Act when Hudson was three years old, and that his parents had worked with Leon Trotsky in Mexico. He said that visitors to the family home included veterans of the Russian Revolution and that he grew up expecting, in his words, to "lead a revolution if conditions were right." The same interview records his claim that after Trotsky's widow Natalia died, the executor Max Schachtman assigned him the copyrights to Trotsky's writings and identified him as Trotsky's godson. These are Hudson's own retrospective statements, not independently corroborated records. A separate interview by D. L. Jacobs for Platypus Review , conducted on 15 July 2022 and published in November 2022, repeats the account of a Marxist household and a father among the "Minneapolis 17." No exact birth date was verified from an admissible source, and none is given here (Life & Thought: An Autobiography; Platypus Review interview). He says that his early interests lay in physics, chemistry and music rather than politics. He studied piano and trained as a conductor, and at the University of Chicago he combined a degree in Germanic philology and the history of culture with full time music study. His own biography page gives the formal academic record: a B.A. at Chicago in 1959 in philology with a minor in history; an M.A. at New York University in 1963 in economics, with a thesis on the World Bank's philosophy of development; and a Ph.D. at New York University in 1968 in economics, with a dissertation on nineteenth century American economic and technological thought. A conflicting M.A. date appears in tertiary material that is not admissible evidence for this profile, so 1963 is reported as Hudson's own record rather than as a settled external fact (Biography). His working life moved between banking and academia. He worked at the Savings Banks Trust Company from 1962 to 1964, at Chase Manhattan Bank as a balance of payments economist from 1964 to 1967, at Arthur Andersen from 1968 to 1969, at Continental Oil from 1970 to 1971, and at the Hudson Institute from 1972 to 1976, where he published studies on monetary reform with Herman Kahn. He taught at the graduate faculty of the New School for Social Research from 1969 to 1972. From 1985 to 1998 he was a research associate at Harvard's Peabody Museum and a visiting scholar at New York University, organising colloquia on the ancient Near East. He became president of the Institute for the Study of Long Term Economic Trends (ISLET) in 1996 and Distinguished Research Professor of Economics at the University of Missouri–Kansas City in 2002, and is listed as a research associate by the Levy Economics Institute and a fellow by the Democracy Collaborative (Biography; Levy Economics Institute; Democracy Collaborative). Two

title: Richard D. Wolff: Exploitation, Class and Democracy at Work
description: A research profile of the Marxian economist's account of exploitation, workplace democracy and the crises of capitalism, with his critics.
text: Richard D. Wolff is a Marxian economist whose work begins with a question that economics textbooks often leave aside: who decides what happens inside a firm? His answer rests on three linked ideas. Surplus means the output that workers produce beyond what they are paid and what the physical inputs cost. Exploitation means that this surplus is received and distributed by people other than those who produced it. "Democracy at work" means that the people who do the work also make the decisions normally reserved for shareholders and directors: what to produce, how, where, and what to do with the surplus. Wolff argues that capitalism depends on keeping those decisions away from the great majority of workers, and that a socialist alternative does not require equating socialism with state ownership. This profile sets out what he has argued, which claims can be traced to sources that were opened, and where other economists have objected. Biography Richard David Wolff was born in Youngstown, Ohio, on 1 April 1942. The finding aid for his papers at the University of Massachusetts Amherst says that his parents, Max and Lieselotte Wolff, had emigrated from Germany during the Second World War and later lived near New York, and that his mother wrote a manuscript about her escape from Germany (UMass Amherst finding aid). He took a BA in history at Harvard in 1963, an MA in economics at Stanford in 1964, an MA in economics at Yale in 1966, an MA in history at Yale in 1967, and a PhD in economics at Yale in 1969. His dissertation was titled "Economic Aspects of British Colonialism in Kenya, 1895–1930". There is a small discrepancy between the records here: Wolff's own site lists the Harvard, Stanford and Yale history and doctorate degrees but omits the 1966 Yale economics MA (Wolff, About). He taught at Yale while a graduate student from 1967 to 1969, then at City College of the City University of New York from 1969 to 1973. UMass Amherst hired him in 1973 as part of a "radical package" of economists that included Samuel Bowles, Herbert Gintis, Richard Edwards and Stephen A. Resnick. He became a full professor in 1981, won a UMass Distinguished Teaching Award in 1981, and taught there until he retired in 2008, when he was named professor emeritus. He has also been a visiting professor in the Graduate Program in International Affairs at The New School in New York. In 1979–80 he spent a sabbatical in Paris studying with the Marxist philosopher Louis Althusser. He was a founding member of the New Haven Green Party and ran unsuccessfully for mayor of New Haven in 1985 (UMass finding aid; Wolff, About). He lives in New York with his wife, the psychotherapist Harriet Fraad; they have two adult children (Democracy at Work, The Progressive interview). In 2012 he co founded the nonprofit Democracy at Work, which produces Economic Update , a bi monthly Global Capitalism lecture, the Ask Prof Wolff series and books. Wolff says that he donates his work on several books so that the sales revenue goes to the organisation (Wolff, About; Democracy at Work, Understanding Marxism). Intellectual tradition Wolff works in Marxian political economy, but his version differs from both Soviet style orthodoxy and from Marxists who give the economy a determining role. In his own summary, the approach he developed with Stephen Resnick "retains and systematically elaborates the Marxist notion of class as surplus labor" while it "rejects the economic determinism typical of most schools of economics and usually associated with Marxism as well". Two ideas define it. Class, understood as the production, appropriation and distribution of surplus labour, is used as an "entry point" for social analysis. "Overdetermination" supplies the logic of a non determinist analysis: no single factor, including the economy, determines the others, because each part of a social formation shapes the rest (Wolff, About). That position places him in the "Amherst School" of heterodox economics, a

title: Samir Amin: Unequal Development, Delinking and Eurocentrism
description: A research profile of the Egyptian Marxist economist's account of global capitalism, dependency and the struggle against Eurocentrism, with his critics.
text: Samir Amin was an Egyptian Marxist economist whose work reshaped how the left understood global capitalism. He argued that poverty in the poorer countries was not an early stage that capitalism would eventually overcome but a result of capitalism itself. He called the mechanism "unequal exchange" — the exchange of goods whose production involves greater differences in wages than in productivity — and held that the rich countries drew value from the poor ones. His best known political idea was "delinking", by which he meant refusing to adjust a country's development to the needs of capitalist global expansion and pursuing an independent strategy instead. He also argued that Eurocentrism, a systematic distortion in dominant social theories that treats Europe as the centre of world history, had to be fought inside social theory itself. This profile reports those arguments as arguments, sets out the evidence his interpreters used, and records the objections made against them. Biography Amin was born in Egypt in 1931 and died in Paris on 12 August 2018, aged 86 (Tricontinental 2018; Global Dialogue 2020; Developing Economics 2021). Tricontinental and the Arab Council for the Social Sciences give Cairo as his birthplace, while the New Socialist obituary says he lived in Port Said until 1946 and then moved to Paris, and the Arab Council records secondary education at a French lycée in 1947 (ACSS; New Socialist 2018). These details are compatible but come from different institutions. No birth certificate or equivalent official record was found for this profile. His own account of his political formation comes from a 2017 interview with Leo Zeilig for Review of African Political Economy . Amin said he considered himself a communist already at secondary school, understanding the word to mean equality between people and between nations and taking the Russian Revolution as his example. After secondary school he contacted the Egyptian Communist Party and joined it. As a student in France he joined the French Communist Party, following what he called an internationalist rule that communists belonged to the party of the country where they lived. He returned to Egypt in 1957, during Nasser's rule, and disagreed with Soviet advice that communists should accept the "non capitalist road" and support Nasser without an independent party. He was in the minority and moved to Mali in 1960 (ROAPE interview, 2017). This first person account is the strongest evidence for his early political development. Most scholarly and memorial sources date his doctorate to 1957 (New Socialist 2018; Global Dialogue 2020; Valiani 2021). Tricontinental's introduction to his last interview says "1956", and in the interview itself Amin speaks of his PhD dissertation of "1956" (Tricontinental 2018). The discrepancy is not resolved here. What the sources agree on is that the dissertation studied underdevelopment and the mechanisms that produced it, and that it became the basis of Accumulation on a World Scale . Tricontinental records that Amin worked in Nasser's Institute for Economic Management in Cairo from 1957 to 1960 and then as an adviser in the Ministry of Planning in Bamako from 1960 to 1963. Amin confirmed the Cairo period in the ROAPE interview and described sitting on the boards of public companies, where he saw a state apparatus being used to build what he called a "bourgeois caste" of private interests inside public enterprises (Tricontinental 2018; ROAPE interview, 2017). He later headed the African Institute for Economic Development and Planning (IDEP) in Dakar and directed the Third World Forum there. In 2017 he listed his continuing affiliations as the Third World Forum, the World Forum for Alternatives and the Arab Centre for Research in Cairo. Global Dialogue credits him with co founding the Council for the Development of Social Science Research in Africa (CODESRIA) in 1973 and serving as its first executive secretary; other sources say more cautiously t

title: David Harvey: Accumulation, Neoliberalism and the Right to the City
description: A research profile of the geographer's account of capital accumulation, the spatial fix, neoliberalism and urban struggle, with scholarly objections.
text: David Harvey is a geographer who rebuilt Marxist political economy around space, the city and the built environment. His best known arguments treat urbanisation as a way capitalism absorbs surplus and postpones crisis, and treat dispossession as a continuing part of accumulation rather than a distant prehistory. He has taught Marx's Capital for more than fifty years and writes in the Marxist tradition, but in an argumentative rather than a devotional mode. This profile sets out what he has argued, what can be checked in the sources opened for it, and where other scholars, including other Marxists, have objected. Biography Harvey's own curriculum vitae supplies the basic record. It lists a B.A. with first class honours in geography from St John's College, Cambridge, in 1957, and an M.A. and Ph.D. in geography from the same college in 1962. It then gives his permanent positions in sequence: lecturer in geography at the University of Bristol from 1961 to 1969; associate professor at Johns Hopkins from 1969 to 1973; professor there from 1973 to 1989; Halford Mackinder Professor of Geography at Oxford from 1987 to 1993; professor at Johns Hopkins again from 1993 to 2001; and Distinguished Professor at the City University of New York Graduate Center from 2001 onward (Harvey, Curriculum Vitae ). His author site describes him as Distinguished Professor of Anthropology and Geography at the CUNY Graduate Center, Director of Research at the Center for Place, Culture and Politics, and a teacher of Marx's Capital for more than fifty years (davidharvey.org, About). A post on that site dated 24 September 2021 adds that he was a Miliband Fellow at the London School of Economics and Halford Mackinder Professor at Oxford (author post, 2021). The CV records honours that help date his standing in the discipline: the Gill Memorial of the Royal Geographical Society in 1973, the Anders Retzius Gold Medal in 1989, the Patron's Medal of the Royal Geographical Society and the Vautrin Lud International Prize in 1995, election as a corresponding fellow of the British Academy in 1998, election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2007, and honorary doctorates from Buenos Aires and Roskilde in 1997, Uppsala in 2000, Ohio State in 2004 and Lund in 2008 (Harvey, Curriculum Vitae ). The CV appears to date from around 2008, since it lists a New Left Review article as forthcoming and its publication list ends there. Several biographical details remain unverified. His exact birth date was not confirmed from any primary source opened here. A CUNY faculty page and a CUNY news release appeared in search results but returned access denied responses when fetched, so no biographical detail has been taken from them. A date of 1961 for the doctorate appears in tertiary search results, but the author's own CV says 1962, which is the figure used here. Intellectual tradition Harvey works in Marxist geography and in what he calls a historical geographical materialism: an attempt to rebuild Marx's theory of accumulation with space, place and the production of the built environment treated as central rather than incidental. Explaining where his most influential idea came from, he says it "initially came out of attempts to reconstruct Marx's theory of the geography of capitalist accumulation" (Harvey, "Globalization and the 'Spatial Fix'", p. 25). Bob Jessop, writing in 2004, describes the deeper project as "to reconstruct theory with space (and the 'relation to nature') clearly integrated within it as foundational elements", and notes that Harvey sought to overcome the privilege conventional dialectics give to time over space (Jessop, 2004). His relation to the Marxist tradition is argumentative. The 2004 Antipode symposium on The Limits to Capital included Jessop's "On the Limits of The Limits to Capital " and Erica Schoenberger's "The Spatial Fix Revisited"; a 2006 Historical Materialism symposium produced Robert Brenner's "What Is, and What Is Not, Imperialism?"

title: Walter Rodney: How Europe Underdeveloped Africa
description: A research profile of the Guyanese historian's account of colonial extraction, underdevelopment and Black Power, with scholarly debate over his work.
text: Walter Rodney argued that Africa's poverty was made, not inherited. By underdevelopment he meant neither a stage of backwardness nor a plain absence of development: every people had developed in some way, and the word described a comparison produced by uneven development and, more importantly, a relationship in which the surplus of one country was transferred to another. Dependency, in his usage, was the resulting reliance of the poorer economy on the metropolitan capitalist economies that drew that surplus away. This profile sets out his argument in the sources opened for it, the method behind it, and the objections made to it. It does not convert his claims into settled fact. Biography The chapter on Cabral and Rodney already tells the story of Rodney's life, his exclusion from Jamaica, the writing of How Europe Underdeveloped Africa , his organising in Guyana and the disputed circumstances of his death; this profile keeps the biography to what bears on the work and adds an account of his arguments, his method and the scholarly debate around them. Walter Anthony Rodney was born in Georgetown, British Guiana, on 23 March 1942, the second of six children of Percival Edward Rodney, a tailor, and Pauline Worrell Rodney, a seamstress and home maker. The Atlanta University Center finding aid records that his father was involved in the People's Progressive Party, the multi racial anti colonial party that included Marxists and socialists. This is an institutional record, not Rodney's own retrospective account (AUC finding aid). He won a scholarship to Queen's College in Georgetown and then to the University of the West Indies at Mona, Jamaica, where he took a first class bachelor's degree in history in 1963. A further scholarship took him to the School of Oriental and African Studies in London. He married Patricia Henry in London in January 1965; they had three children, Shaka, Kanini and Asha. He received his doctorate in African history in 1966, at twenty four, with a dissertation on the Upper Guinea Coast that became his first book (AUC finding aid). His first teaching post was at University College, Dar es Salaam, from 1966 to 1968. He returned to the University of the West Indies in Jamaica in 1968, taught African history and spoke outside the university to students, workers and people in poor districts of Kingston, making contact with Rastafarians. While he was in Montreal for the Congress of Black Writers in October 1968, the Jamaican government of Hugh Shearer barred him from re entering the country. The finding aid records student demonstrations, the closure of the university for two weeks, unrest that spread beyond the campus, deaths and injuries, extensive debate in Parliament and heavy property damage. Those are the archive's words; the scale is not independently measured here. The talks he gave in Jamaica and Montreal were published in 1969 as The Groundings with My Brothers (AUC finding aid; 2019 Verso edition_djvu.txt)). Rodney went back to Dar es Salaam, where he was senior lecturer from 1969 to 1972 and associate professor from 1972 to 1974. He spent February to June 1972 as a visiting professor at the University of Michigan's Center for Afro American and African Studies, and the first months of 1975 teaching at Cornell University's African Studies and Research Center. In 1974 the University of Guyana offered him the chair of history; the government rescinded the appointment after he returned. He remained in Guyana, worked in the leadership of the Working People's Alliance, founded in 1974 and constituted as a party in 1979, and became the main national figure opposing Forbes Burnham's People's National Congress government. He and seven others were charged with arson in July 1979 after two government offices burned. His trial began on 2 June 1980 and was adjourned a week later (AUC finding aid). He was killed in Georgetown on 13 June 1980, a week after his last public speech, at the age of thirty eight. The finding

title: Frantz Fanon: Colonial Violence, Liberation and the National Bourgeoisie
description: A research profile of the psychiatrist and anti-colonial writer's account of colonial domination, its psychological effects and the pitfalls of national liberation.
text: Frantz Fanon wrote about what colonial rule did to people and about what survived its end. He argued that colonial domination rests on force from the beginning, that the struggle to end it is itself violent, and that a local elite can take over the colonial economy after the flags change. By colonial violence he meant the force that sets up and holds together rule over another people, from conquest to policing, not only the fighting that brings that rule to an end. By the national bourgeoisie he meant the local class of business owners, officials and intermediaries who step into the positions settlers left behind after independence. His writing on the native intellectual and on that class made him a lasting point of reference in anti colonial debate. This profile sets out those arguments from his own texts, records what his publishers and libraries establish about the books, and reports the objections made against him. Biography The chapter on Empire and Underdevelopment already covers Fanon's claim that the national middle class becomes a "transmission line between the nation and a capitalism, rampant though camouflaged, which today puts on the masque of neocolonialism", and notes that his examples were his own selections; this profile adds his arguments about violence, the native intellectual, the internal structure of that class critique and what he thought should replace colonial rule, without retelling the history of decolonisation. Grove Atlantic's own author note, repeated on its pages for all four of his books, says Fanon was born in Martinique in 1925, served in the French Army during the Second World War, studied medicine and psychiatry in France, published his first book Black Skin, White Masks in 1952, joined the Algerian Nationalist Movement in the mid 1950s, and published The Wretched of the Earth shortly before dying of leukaemia in December 1961 (Grove Atlantic, product pages). Éditions La Découverte, which now issues the French editions first published by François Maspero, describes him as "né antillais et mort algérien (1925–1961)", a psychiatrist and FLN militant who died at 36 (La Découverte). The Bibliothèque nationale de France authority heading on its catalogue records gives the years 1925–1961 and the identifier 12016577. The exact day and month of his birth, and the place and date of his death, were not verified from any primary record opened for this profile; the publisher's phrase "December 1961" is the most precise death date confirmed. No institutional record of his medical training, his post at the Blida psychiatric hospital, his expulsion from Algeria or his diplomatic posting was opened, so none of those episodes is asserted here. The two books dated 1952 and 1961 and the FLN connection rest on the publisher and library records above. Intellectual tradition Fanon wrote as a psychiatrist and a political theorist, and the two roles are hard to separate in the texts. In the opening chapter of Black Skin, White Masks , as reprinted by Grove Atlantic in Richard Philcox's translation, he moves between clinical observation, philosophy and politics, citing Césaire, Sartre's Black Orpheus , the anthropologist Westermann, Michel Leiris, André Breton, Piaget and the linguists Damourette and Pichon, and saying he had read Cheikh Anta Diop's linguistic work "with great interest". He treats Sartre's claim that the black poet turns against the French language as a position he partly accepts and partly qualifies for Antilleans (Grove Atlantic, Black Skin, White Masks ). The preface Sartre later wrote for Les damnés de la terre is itself a primary theoretical text. It reads Fanon as an "ex native" who addresses the colonised rather than Europeans, and argues that "in order to triumph, the national revolution must be socialist" (Sartre, preface, 1961). That sentence is Sartre's formulation of what he took Fanon to be arguing, not a sentence Fanon wrote. His relation to Marxism was contested even among Marxists. T

title: William Blum: Killing Hope and the Record of US Intervention
description: A research profile of the journalist's catalogue of US interventions, his anti-imperialist argument and the scholarly criticism of his method.
text: William Blum collected evidence of what the United States government did in other countries and argued that the actions served a single imperial purpose. His books reached readers well outside universities, while reviewers in academic journals and in the CIA's own professional publication accepted the scale of his documentation but objected to the way he selected and interpreted it. This profile keeps those two things apart: the operations that can be shown in official records, and Blum's account of why they happened. Biography William Henry Blum was born on 6 March 1933 in Brooklyn and died on 9 December 2018 in Virginia, aged 85. The dates come from the Library of Congress name authority record as it appeared in search results; a direct fetch of that record returned a 403 error. His death date is confirmed on his own website, which posted a farewell saying "Bill died on December 9th, 2018" and reproducing Louis Wolf's account of a fall in his apartment on 4 October 2018, a 65 day fight for life, and kidney failure as the immediate cause. No birth certificate was opened for this research, and details carried in obituaries that were not opened, such as hospital and parentage, were not independently verified (Primary Official — LC authority record; Primary Theoretical — Blum site, farewell). Blum's own account of his political development is brief and consistent. He worked with computers, including for IBM and then for the State Department, and left the State Department in 1967 because he opposed what the United States was doing in Vietnam. He abandoned an ambition to become a Foreign Service officer, then helped found and edit the Washington Free Press , described on his site as the first alternative newspaper in the capital. He worked as a freelance journalist in the United States, Europe and South America. A period in Chile in 1972–73, writing about the Allende government's "socialist experiment" and what he called its "tragic overthrow in a CIA designed coup", made the question of intervention — the use of military, intelligence or political power to change or suppress another country's government — a permanent subject for him. In the mid 1970s he worked in London with the former CIA officer Philip Agee and Agee's associates on projects exposing CIA personnel and operations (Primary Theoretical — About William Blum). The memoir West Bloc Dissident gives this period from the inside. Its publisher description says Blum spent four years at IBM and more than two at the State Department before the Vietnam War and the 1960s moved him into anti war and counter cultural politics, and that it recounts the underground press, government informers, his life in Chile under Allende, and an unsuccessful Hollywood documentary project with Oliver Stone. The book's opening line, quoted on his author page, places the reader at CIA headquarters in Langley on 4 August 1969, where he began recording employees' licence plates. That is his retrospective account, not an independent record of the events (Primary Theoretical — West Bloc Dissident book page). From 2002 to 2003 he wrote a regular column for The Ecologist . From 2003 until shortly before his death he published the free monthly newsletter The Anti Empire Report ; his site lists 160 issues, the last dated 20 September 2018. He also gave talks and radio and television interviews (Primary Theoretical — About; Primary Theoretical — Anti Empire Report 160). Intellectual tradition Blum wrote from anti imperialist journalism rather than from academic history or party theory. He called himself a "historian" on his own site, but his training was in accounting and his method was that of an investigative reporter assembling a documentary record against official denials. In an interview he said plainly, "I'm a socialist", while adding that an American form of socialism would not arrive in his lifetime or his son's. For the foreseeable future he thought the realistic demand was the "highly increased

title: Howard Zinn: History From the Bottom Up
description: A research profile of the historian's method, his political commitments, A People's History of the United States and the scholarly objections to it.
text: Howard Zinn wrote history from the standpoint of people usually absent from history books: workers, women, Black and Indigenous Americans, immigrants and soldiers. The phrase "history from below" is a description used by Bish Sanyal, the MIT professor who introduced Zinn at a lecture in 2005. It means telling the past through the lives of ordinary people rather than through rulers and governments. Zinn himself did not use that phrase; he and his publishers said "from the bottom up." His best known book, A People's History of the United States: 1492–Present , made that approach familiar to a large audience. His refusal to present himself as a neutral historian became part of the argument about his work. This profile sets out what he argued, what the sources show and where historians objected (what history establishes). Biography Howard Zinn was born in Brooklyn on 24 August 1922 and died in Santa Monica on 27 January 2010. His own website describes a working class immigrant household; the Tamiment Library finding aid for his papers adds that he was one of four sons of Edward and Jennie (Rabinowitz) Zinn. He worked from the age of fourteen, graduated from Thomas Jefferson High School and served an apprenticeship as a ship fitter at the Brooklyn Navy Yard. He joined the Army Air Corps in early 1943, trained as a bombardier and flew combat and humanitarian missions in Europe. He married Roslyn Shechter in 1944. Under the GI Bill he took a bachelor's degree at New York University in 1951, then an MA at Columbia in 1952 and a PhD in 1958; the Tamiment finding aid records a post doctoral year in East Asian Studies at Harvard in 1960–61 (biography; Tamiment finding aid). He taught part time at Upsala College in New Jersey from 1953 to 1956, then moved to Spelman College in Atlanta in 1956 as chair of history and social sciences. Spelman was a historically Black college for women. There Zinn became involved in the civil rights movement, advised the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), wrote for The Nation and Harper's , and mentored students including Marian Wright Edelman, Alice Walker and Bernice Johnson Reagon. Spelman's president dismissed him in 1963. Zinn recalled the reason in his own words: "I was fired for insubordination. Which happened to be true." He took a post at Boston University, where he taught until retiring in 1988 and became a leading critic of the Vietnam War. In 2005 Spelman invited him to deliver the commencement address and awarded him an honorary doctorate. His awards included the Lannan Foundation Literary Award for Nonfiction, the Eugene V. Debs Award and the Ridenhour Courage Prize (biography; Tamiment finding aid). One date is unsettled. Zinn's own bibliography dates You Can't Be Neutral on a Moving Train to Beacon Press, 1994, with later editions in 2002 and 2018, and Beacon currently lists a 2002 paperback and a 2025 cloth edition. The Tamiment finding aid calls it a "1995 autobiography." That discrepancy is not resolved here (bibliography; Beacon paperback; Beacon cloth; Tamiment finding aid). Intellectual tradition Zinn belonged to the New Left and to the tradition of history written from the side of ordinary people, but he stood apart from the professional institutions of radical history. In a 2013 essay the Rutgers historian David Greenberg noted that Zinn never wrote for Studies on the Left or Radical History Review and, according to Martin Duberman's biography, did not join the Radical Historians Caucus of the American Historical Association. Zinn's own writing explains why. In a 1999 book festival talk he said he "didn't want to be a historian who went into the past and got lost," but wanted "to see what I could find and come out and apply it to what was going on in the world" (Greenberg; Book TV transcript). He rejected the label of neutral scholar. In the foreword he wrote for the 2018 edition of his memoir, quoted on his own website, he said he did not "pretend to an objectivity tha

title: Vijay Prashad: The Third World Project and the Global South
description: A research profile of the historian's account of Third World internationalism, imperialism and contemporary struggle, with his critics.
text: Vijay Prashad is an Indian born historian and journalist whose work explains how countries emerging from colonial rule tried to act together in world politics. Three terms need a plain definition before his arguments can be followed. "Third World" in his usage is not a place on a map but a political project: the countries of Africa, Asia and Latin America that asserted national liberation and non alignment rather than joining either Cold War bloc. "Global South" is, in his publisher's formulation, not a geographical space but "a concatenation of protests against neoliberalism". "Internationalism" means the belief that working people and movements in different countries should cooperate across borders; Prashad calls the nationalism he studies "an internationalist nationalism". This profile sets out what he has argued, what can be checked in published and institutional records, and where historians and other socialists have objected. Biography Tricontinental's own staff page, the strongest institutional record available for this profile, says Vijay Prashad was born in 1967 in Calcutta, India. It describes him as a historian and journalist and as the director of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research, though elsewhere on the same page he is called executive director. The institute describes itself as an inter movement research institute of the Global South associated with the International Peoples' Assembly, claims that his weekly newsletter reaches almost two million people, says he has written more than forty books, and says that two of his histories, The Darker Nations (2007) and The Poorer Nations (2013), won awards and that he has twice received the Muzaffar Ahmed Prize. These are the institute's own figures and claims, not independently counted here (Tricontinental, "The Team"). The New Press author biography adds that Prashad is editor of LeftWord Books and chief correspondent for Globetrotter, that The Darker Nations was chosen as a Best Nonfiction Book of the Year by the Asian American Writers' Workshop and won the Muzaffar Ahmad Book Prize, and that he lives in Santiago, Chile, and Northampton, Massachusetts (The New Press, The Darker Nations ). Monthly Review's author page calls him executive director of Tricontinental, chief editor at LeftWord Books and a regular writer for Frontline , The Hindu , Alternet and BirGun (Monthly Review, "Vijay Prashad"). An older institutional page records an earlier stage of the same career. The University of Oklahoma says Prashad was the George and Martha Kellner Professor of South Asian History and director of the International Studies Program at Trinity College in Hartford, that he earned a PhD in history at the University of Chicago in 1994, and that he had previously taught at Syracuse and Cornell. It identifies him as the 2007 NCORE keynote speaker, lists board service with the Center for Third World Organizing, United for a Fair Economy and the National Priorities Project (University of Oklahoma, NCORE page). Some commonly cited biographical details could not be verified here. A University of Chicago International House event listing described him as "PhD'94" and the George and Martha Kellner Chair, but its URL returned a 404 when opened. An UNCTAD notice gave a BA from Pomona College (1989), an MA from Chicago (1990) and a PhD from Chicago (1994), but that page returned HTTP 403, so the earlier degrees are not confirmed in this profile. The domain vijayprashad.org now serves unrelated casino material and cdn.vijayprashad.org returned a transport error; neither can be used as a first party record. Intellectual tradition Prashad works in the tradition that Tricontinental calls "national liberation Marxism". The institute's history page says its name joins two sources: the Tricontinental Conference held in Cuba in January 1966, which brought together revolutionary movements from Africa, Asia and Latin America with an orientation of national liberation, non alignment and soci

title: John Pilger: Investigative Journalism Against Empire
description: A research profile of the journalist's reporting on Cambodia, East Timor and Western foreign policy, his documentary method and his critics.
text: John Pilger (1939–2023) was an Australian born reporter and documentary maker who worked mainly in British newspapers and television. He made the victims of war, sanctions and authoritarian allies the subjects of mass market reporting, and argued that news organisations helped those in power by repeating official accounts and dropping stories that did not fit them. This profile sets out what he claimed, the evidence he offered and the objections raised against him. It treats his work as a record of arguments and contested events, not as settled history. His method was investigative journalism: reporting that starts from documents and witnesses gathered by the reporter rather than from official briefings, and publishes facts that governments would rather keep hidden. Biography John Richard Pilger was born in Sydney on 9 October 1939 and died in London on 30 December 2023, aged 84. The Guardian obituary by Anthony Hayward names his parents as Elsie (née Marheine), a teacher, and Claude Pilger, a carpenter, and says he attended Sydney Boys' High School. His own biography says he was born and grew up in Bondi, launched a newspaper at Sydney High School and completed a four year cadetship with Australian Consolidated Press. The two accounts agree on the outline but use slightly different school names, so the precise institution should not be stated more narrowly than the sources allow (Guardian obituary, 1 January 2024; official biography). According to the Guardian, he joined Australian Consolidated Press in 1958, worked on the Sydney Sun and then the Daily and Sunday Telegraph , freelanced in Italy, moved to Britain in 1962, joined Reuters as a subeditor and moved to the Daily Mirror in 1963. His own career summary gives the same sequence with different boundaries: 1958–62 reporter and sub editor in Sydney; 1962 freelance correspondent in Italy; 1962–63 on the Middle East desk at Reuters; 1963–86 reporter and chief foreign correspondent at the Daily Mirror ; 1986–88 editor in chief and a founder of News on Sunday ; 1969–71 reporter for World in Action at Granada; and from 1974 to 2023 an independent documentary maker working largely with ITV. These are first party and obituary records, not audited personnel files. The Guardian reports that the apartheid government banned him from South Africa in 1967 and that he was metres away when Robert Kennedy was assassinated in Los Angeles in 1968; his own biography puts him "in the same room". He covered Vietnam, Cambodia, Bangladesh, Biafra and the Middle East, and reported from the United States during the 1960s and 1970s. The Guardian says he won the British Press Awards' Journalist of the Year title twice, first for Vietnam and second for Cambodia, and received the United Nations media peace prize. His own list adds the 1991 Richard Dimbleby Award from BAFTA, an Emmy, the 2003 Sophie Prize, the 2009 Sydney Peace Prize and the 2017 Order of Timor Leste. The Guardian gives pulmonary fibrosis as the cause of death; the BBC report of 31 December 2023 confirms the date and place but gives no cause. He was survived by his partner Jane Hill, a son Sam and a daughter Zoe (BBC News). Two disputes shaped his public standing and belong here. After his first film, The Quiet Mutiny (1970), the US ambassador in London complained to the Independent Television Authority, which reprimanded Granada. The regulator's successor, the IBA, required his films to be introduced as a "personal view". Pilger called the regulator's chief programme officer David Glencross "commercial television's chief censor" and regarded demands for objectivity, balance and impartiality as "code for the establishment view of the world, against which most perspectives are measured". Separately, his claim in Cambodia: The Betrayal (1990) that SAS members had trained Khmer Rouge guerrillas led Pilger and Central Television to lose a libel action. Oliver Kamm says the case was settled at substantial cost; the court record was not ope

title: Antonio Gramsci: Cultural Hegemony and the Modern Prince
description: A research profile of the Italian Marxist's account of hegemony, the party, and the dispute over how his Prison Notebooks were edited and used.
text: Antonio Gramsci wrote most of what he is famous for in prison, in notes that he never arranged into a book. He was a Marxist and a founder of the Communist Party of Italy who spent his last years under fascist imprisonment. His notes set out how a ruling class holds power by winning consent as well as by using force, and how a party might build the collective will needed to replace it. Those ideas became some of the most used and most disputed concepts in twentieth century left wing thought. This profile sets out what Gramsci wrote, what later editors made of his notes, and where scholars disagree. Biography Antonio Gramsci was born at Ales in Sardinia on 22 January 1891, the fourth of seven children of Francesco Gramsci, a civil servant in the local registry office, and Giuseppina Marcias. The family moved to Ghilarza after his father was arrested and imprisoned for an administrative irregularity. Gramsci finished elementary school in 1903 with the highest marks and then, because the family had little money, worked for two years in the tax office before resuming his studies. He attended the lyceum at Cagliari and in 1911 won a scholarship to the University of Turin, where he enrolled in letters and studied linguistics under Matteo Bartoli. His health was fragile and he stopped taking examinations; his last examination was in April 1915. He had already begun journalism, writing for Il Grido del popolo , and in December 1915 he joined the Turin editorial staff of the Socialist Party daily Avanti! (Casa Museo Antonio Gramsci, biography and chronology; International Gramsci Society, chronology). After the Turin uprising of August 1917, when the authorities arrested most of the city's socialist leaders, Gramsci became secretary of the Turin section of the Italian Socialist Party. In 1919 he and Angelo Tasca, Palmiro Togliatti and Umberto Terracini founded the weekly L'Ordine nuovo ( The New Order ), the first issue appearing on 1 May 1919. The journal joined Socialist culture to the factory council movement in Turin. Gramsci took part in the Livorno congress of January 1921 at which the Communist Party of Italy was founded, and joined its central committee. In 1922 he went to Moscow as the party's representative to the Communist International, met Giulia Schucht there, and, according to the two institutional chronologies opened for this profile, met Lenin on 25 October 1922. Mussolini became prime minister that same month, and an arrest warrant prevented Gramsci from returning to Italy. He worked in Vienna from December 1923, was elected to parliament in April 1924, returned to Italy in May, and became general secretary of the Communist Party in August 1924. His only speech in parliament was on 16 May 1925, against a law on secret societies (Fondazione Gramsci, biography; Casa Museo, chronology; IGS, chronology; Gramsci, "Speech to the Italian parliament", 16 May 1925). Fascist authorities arrested him in Rome on the evening of 8 November 1926 despite his parliamentary immunity. He was held at Regina Coeli, sentenced to five years of internal exile, and sent to Ustica in December. A military court in Milan issued a new warrant in January 1927 and he was imprisoned there. The Special Tribunal for the Defence of the State tried him in Rome between 28 May and 4 June 1928 with twenty one other Communist leaders, and on 4 June sentenced him to twenty years, four months and five days. Because of his health he was sent to the special prison at Turi near Bari. He received permission to write in his cell in January 1929 and began the first of his prison notebooks on 8 February 1929. An amnesty reduced the sentence to twelve years and four months in 1932. Serious illness led to his transfer to a clinic at Formia in November 1933, to conditional freedom in October 1934, and to the Quisisana clinic in Rome in August 1935. His sentence expired on 21 April 1937. He suffered a cerebral haemorrhage on the evening of 25 April and died early on 27

title: Eric Hobsbawm: Social History, Capitalism and the Short Twentieth Century
description: A research profile of the Marxist historian's periodisation, labour history and membership of the Communist Party, with scholarly objections.
text: Eric Hobsbawm was a Marxist historian whose books made two schemes of dates familiar to a wide readership: the long nineteenth century, meaning the span from the dual revolution — industrial in Britain, political in France — to 1914, and the short twentieth century, from 1914 to the collapse of the Soviet Union. The idea of a long nineteenth century existed before him; he made it standard. He wrote social history, meaning history that starts from the working lives, customs and institutions of ordinary people rather than from rulers, wars and high politics alone, and he argued that workers' own practices belonged at the centre of the account. He was also a member of the Communist Party of Great Britain from 1936 until the party dissolved in 1991, and his refusal to leave it after 1956 became the most contested part of his legacy. This profile sets out what he argued, what his sources could support, and where historians and other socialists objected. Biography Eric John Ernest Hobsbawm was born in Alexandria on 9 June 1917, the son of Leopold Percy Hobsbaum, a British postal official whose family name had been altered by an immigration officer, and Nelly Grün, from a Viennese Jewish family. The family moved to Vienna after the First World War. His father died of a heart attack in 1929 and his mother of tuberculosis in 1931. The orphaned boy and his sister moved to Berlin, where he entered a Gymnasium and joined a communist school students' organisation in 1932. He took part in the last Communist demonstration in Berlin in January 1933. His uncle moved the family to Britain shortly afterwards. Hobsbawm was a British citizen who came to England for financial reasons at the same time as the Nazis took power, and he later rejected the description of himself as a refugee from Nazism. That distinction is his own, and is reported here as such. He won a scholarship to King's College, Cambridge, and went up in October 1936, joining the student branch of the Communist Party of Great Britain on arrival. He edited Granta , was elected to the Cambridge Apostles, and in 1940 co wrote a pamphlet with Raymond Williams defending the Soviet position in the war against Finland. After war service in the Royal Engineers and the Army Educational Corps he returned to Cambridge for doctoral work and was appointed a lecturer at Birkbeck College, London, in 1947. He stayed at Birkbeck until retiring in 1982, then taught one semester a year at the New School for Social Research in New York until 1997. He was elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 1978 and died in London in 2012, aged 95. The party membership needs careful handling. The Edinburgh bibliography says he identified with communism as a teenager in Berlin but joined the party formally in 1936 at Cambridge and remained a member until it dissolved in 1991. Richard Evans's British Academy memoir gives the same sequence and adds what followed 1956. After Khrushchev's secret speech and the Soviet invasion of Hungary, Hobsbawm signed a protest letter which the Daily Worker refused and which appeared in the New Statesman on 18 November 1956. He then stopped all active work inside the party but refused to resign. He explained the refusal later as loyalty "to a great cause and to all those who had sacrificed their lives for it", and said he wanted to succeed as a known Communist despite the damage to his career. Evans records that the party hierarchy treated him as unreliable, that MI5 monitored him, and that the Foreign Office tried to block a UNESCO lecture in 1970. In later life he moved towards the Italian Communist Party and Eurocommunism, then towards social democracy, while still describing himself as at the "tail end of the first generation of communists". Intellectual tradition Hobsbawm worked inside Marxist historiography but was never its official theorist. He was a central member of the Communist Party Historians' Group, founded as the Marxist Historians' Group in 1938 and reconstituted i

title: Harry Braverman: Deskilling and the Capitalist Labour Process
description: A research profile of the Marxist economist's account of scientific management, the separation of conception from execution and the degradation of work.
text: Harry Braverman put the organisation of work itself at the centre of Marxist political economy. He argued that under capitalism the control of how work is done passes from the people who do it to the people who employ them, and that this transfer reshapes factory, office and service jobs alike. His book Labor and Monopoly Capital became one of the most cited works of post war social science and also one of the most contested. This profile sets out what Braverman argued, what can be checked in the texts opened for this research and where later scholars objected. It reports his claims as claims, not as settled findings about every workplace. Biography The fullest checked account comes from John Bellamy Foster's introduction to the 1998 edition of Labor and Monopoly Capital . Braverman was born on 9 December 1920 in New York City, the son of Morris Braverman, a shoeworker, and Sarah Wolf Braverman. He entered Brooklyn College but left after about a year because of the Depression. From 1937, according to Foster, he apprenticed at the Brooklyn Naval Shipyard as a coppersmith, moved into pipefitting and eventually supervised a team of eighteen to twenty workers refitting pipes on docked ships. He was drafted in 1945 and, as an army sergeant at Cheyenne, Wyoming, taught and supervised locomotive pipefitting. In 1947 he and his wife Miriam settled in Youngstown, Ohio, where he worked in steel layout and fitting at Republic Steel, William B. Pollock Co. and Owen Structural Steel. Foster says he was dismissed from Republic Steel at the instigation of the FBI. Chris Smith and Paul Thompson, writing in Contributions to Political Economy in 2024, give a slightly different chronology: a four year coppersmith apprenticeship from 1938 to 1942, three further years at the shipyard supervising up to twenty men, then military service and steel fabrication work. The two accounts agree on the substance and differ by about a year over the starting date. Neither difference is resolved here. Smith and Thompson divide his working life into skilled manual work from 1938 to 1951 and journalism and publishing from 1952 to 1976, while cautioning that most of his working life was actually white collar. Foster records that he joined Grove Press as an editor in 1960, became vice president and general manager, was credited with publishing The Autobiography of Malcolm X and completed a B.A. at the New School for Social Research during those years. In 1967 he became director of Monthly Review Press, a post he held until his death on 2 August 1976. The Monthly Review Press book page confirms that he was director of the press at the time of his death; the Marxists' Internet Archive biography says he died of cancer in August 1976. Foster describes him as identifying with socialism from his teenage years in Brooklyn, first in the Young People's Socialist League and then in the Socialist Workers Party, part of the American Trotskyist movement. During the 1940s and early 1950s he wrote frequently for SWP publications under the party name Harry Frankel. The Marxists' Internet Archive index says he used that name for Fourth International and The Militant until 1952, which can be checked against the archived bylines: the May 1944 review "A Defamer of Marxism" and the September 1952 essay "Capitalism and Democracy" are headed "Harry Frankel", while the October 1955 article "Automation: Promise and Menace" is headed "Harry Braverman". Foster says that in 1953 he broke with the SWP, left the steel industry and founded an independent periodical, The American Socialist , with Bert Cochran. Foster dates the magazine to 1960, while the Marxists' Internet Archive biography says it lasted until 1959. Both dates are recorded here without choosing between them. Intellectual tradition Braverman wrote from within American Trotskyism and then from the orbit of Monthly Review Marxism. The 1944 Frankel review is a defence of Trotsky's analysis of the Soviet Union as a "degenerated worke

title: Ellen Meiksins Wood: Capitalism, Democracy and Empire
description: A research profile of the historian's account of capitalism's distinct social relations, its origins and its relation to democracy and empire.
text: Ellen Meiksins Wood spent her career arguing that capitalism must be understood as a distinct social form, not as the natural flowering of trade. By "social relations of production" she meant the social rules that settle who owns and controls the means of production, how people have to obtain a living, and how the surplus they create is taken, used and reinvested. Her claim was that these rules differ sharply between capitalist and pre capitalist societies. Markets existed long before capitalism, but became an imperative rather than an opportunity only when producers and appropriators alike lost non market access to the means of their own reproduction. That argument shaped the current known as political Marxism and led her into debates about democracy, empire and the possibility of socialism. This profile sets out what she argued, what can be checked in the texts opened for it, and where critics objected. Biography Ellen Meiksins Wood was born in New York City on 12 April 1942, the daughter of Latvian Jewish parents who had been active in the Bund, the Jewish socialist organisation, and who had fled Latvia as political refugees. She told Christopher Phelps in 1998 that her parents arrived in the United States in 1941, after her father, a leader of a socialist youth organisation, was about to be arrested as Latvia's indigenous fascists came to power. A granduncle edited the Jewish socialist magazine Der Vecker , and her mother later worked for the Jewish Labor Committee and the United Nations relief effort. Robert Brenner, her friend and co thinker, adds that her parents fled Latvia for Paris in 1940 and then went from France to Portugal before reaching the United States, and that her father worked as a chief interpreter at the United Nations and described himself as a Marxist, a Menshevik and a radical analyst (Monthly Review interview; York University obituary; Brenner tribute). She received a BA in Slavic languages from the University of California, Berkeley in 1962 and a PhD in political science from UCLA in 1970. She arrived in Canada in 1967 with her first husband, Neal Wood, and taught political science at York University in Toronto until 1996. She later said that York's political science department became, "for some peculiar reason", probably the most Marxist department in North America, and that she could not have done her work in an American university. She served on the editorial committee of New Left Review from 1984 to 1993 and, after leaving it, joined Monthly Review as coeditor in March 1997 with Harry Magdoff and Paul Sweezy, becoming its first new editor in thirty years. She was inducted into the Royal Society of Canada in 1996. Neal Wood died in 2003; she married Ed Broadbent, the former New Democratic Party leader, in 2014. She died of cancer at her home in Ottawa on 14 January 2016, aged 73 (York University obituary; Monthly Review Press notice; Monthly Review interview). There is a date conflict worth recording. Both the York obituary and the 1999 interview give 1988 for the Isaac Deutscher Memorial Prize for The Retreat from Class . A tertiary summary gives 1986; that source is not used here as evidence. The 1988 date is the one supported by the opened first party records. Intellectual tradition Wood's sustained project was to separate capitalism from the longer history of markets, commerce and "modernity". In the 1999 interview she said: "If there has been one single project in all my intellectual work and in my teaching, it has been to identify the specificity of capitalism." She wanted readers to absorb the idea that capitalism is "a historically specific social form, which means that it has a beginning and an end." The same interview describes her as "closer to an earlier left" than to her own generation. She found the British first New Left of E. P. Thompson and John Saville, and the Monthly Review of Sweezy and Magdoff, more convincing than the second New Left or the later postmodernist left, because

title: Silvia Federici: Unpaid Labour, Enclosure and the Witch Hunts
description: A research profile of the feminist theorist's account of social reproduction, primitive accumulation and the commons, with scholarly objections.
text: Silvia Federici is an Italian born Marxist feminist whose writing put unpaid women's work at the centre of how capitalism sustains itself. Three linked ideas carry through her work. Social reproduction is the everyday work of bearing and raising children, cooking, cleaning and caring for the sick and elderly that keeps a workforce fed and renewed; Federici argues that most of it is done by women without pay. Primitive accumulation is the violent process by which capitalism first gathered wealth, driving people off the land, colonising other countries and enslaving people, and she argues that it never really stopped. The commons are resources such as land, forests and water that a community holds and governs together rather than as private property. Her best known book, Caliban and the Witch , argues that the witch hunts of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries were part of that process. This profile sets out what she claimed, what can be checked in her published texts, and where historians and other socialists objected. Biography Federici was born in Parma, Italy, in 1942. In an interview with Rachel Andrews for The White Review she recalled that her earliest years were spent on a farm because Parma was being bombed at night, that her mother was pregnant with her sister when Mussolini declared war, and that her father, a philosophy teacher, was stopped by a Nazi squad in 1943 and released after giving his profession. She described Parma as a centre of anti fascist resistance and said a communist high school teacher was one of her strongest early influences. She read for a degree in modern languages and literature, then enrolled in philosophy; a summer school in Edinburgh in 1966 led American students to urge her to apply to Buffalo, and she went to the University of Buffalo in 1967 on a Fulbright scholarship, stating that she wanted to leave the restrictions of her family in Italy (White Review interview). The finding aid for her papers at Brown University records that her doctorate at the State University of New York at Buffalo was titled The Development of Lukács' Realism ; the dissertation itself was not opened for this profile. Hofstra's faculty profile confirms a PhD and MA from SUNY Buffalo and a BA from the Università degli Studi di Bologna (RIAMCO finding aid; Hofstra faculty profile). She travelled to Mexico in 1968 shortly after the Tlatelolco massacre and wrote her first article in English about it. She moved to New York in 1970, began organising with feminist groups in Buffalo in 1970–71, and read Mariarosa Dalla Costa's Women and the Subversion of the Community (1971), which she calls the foundation document of the Wages for Housework campaign. She attended the Padua meeting in 1972 at which the International Feminist Collective was formed and worked with the New York Wages for Housework Committee from 1972 to 1977. In the White Review interview she described opening a small storefront in Brooklyn in autumn 1975, and said the committee dissolved two years after New York City's 1975 bankruptcy and the austerity that followed (White Review interview; Viewpoint interview; Interference Archive event record). In the preface to Caliban and the Witch she writes that shortly after the 1984 publication of Il Grande Calibano she left the United States for a teaching post in Nigeria and remained nearly three years. She dates the decisive period to 1984–86, when the debt crisis and negotiations with the IMF and World Bank brought structural adjustment, what she calls a "War Against Indiscipline", and a campaign denouncing women's "vanity and excessive demands". She credits the encounter with Women in Nigeria, the country's first feminist organisation, with helping her understand Nigerian women's defence of their resources (Caliban and the Witch, Preface). Institutional biographies place her at the University of Port Harcourt and record that she co founded the Committee for Academic Freedom in Africa in 1991 and helped found

title: Angela Davis: Race, Class, Gender and Abolition
description: A research profile of the Marxist feminist's analysis of race, class, imprisonment and abolition, with her major works and critics.
text: Angela Davis argued that racism, sexism and class exploitation form one system, and that imprisonment is one of the ways that system defends itself. This profile sets out those arguments in her own words, records the sources behind them, and reports the objections made by other scholars, including writers who broadly share her concerns. It is a profile of claims, not a substitute for the historical chapters of this book. Biography The existing chapter on Black Women Communists covers Davis's childhood in Birmingham, her study with Herbert Marcuse, her entry into the Communist Party and the Che Lumumba Club, the courthouse event of 7 August 1970, her flight, FBI listing, arrest on 13 October 1970, sixteen months in custody, trial and acquittal on 4 June 1972, and it quotes her prison interviews; this profile adds a check of the publication record, a connected account of her arguments about race, class, gender and imprisonment, her own statements about influences, socialism and communism, and the scholarly criticism those arguments have received. Angela Yvonne Davis was born in Birmingham, Alabama, on 26 January 1944. The National Archives biographical page and the European Graduate School faculty biography both give that date and place, and both describe a middle class family with long standing links to communist and labour organisers. The National Archives notes that her mother, Sallye Bell Davis, worked for the Southern Negro Youth Congress, an organisation associated with the Communist Party. The two institutional records agree on the main sequence of her education: a B.A. at Brandeis in 1965, where she studied with Herbert Marcuse; study in Frankfurt; an M.A. at the University of California, San Diego; and a doctorate at Humboldt University in Berlin. Neither page gives a year for the doctorate, and the University of Alabama's Alabama Authors entry, checked only as a search endpoint, also names Humboldt without supplying a year. No year is given here. Davis joined the Communist Party USA in 1968, according to the European Graduate School biography and Joy James's introduction to The Angela Y. Davis Reader . James, a political theorist and the editor of that collection, places her in the Che Lumumba Club, one of the party's all Black collectives, and describes her party work as lasting more than twenty years, including service on the Central Committee. That is James's account rather than an independently audited party record. The European Graduate School confirms the 1968 membership and her two candidacies for the vice presidency in 1980 and 1984. She was appointed to teach philosophy at UCLA in 1969 and dismissed in 1970 after her party membership became public; the University of California's own faculty page, checked only as a search endpoint, says she was removed because of her activism and her Communist Party membership. The federal record fixes the dates of the manhunt more tightly than many retrospective accounts. The FBI's chronological list of the Ten Most Wanted fugitives records "Angela Yvonne Davis" as number 309, placed on the list on 18 August 1970 and located on 13 October 1970, and says she was arrested in a motel room in New York. A separate FBI image caption gives "January 13, 1970", which contradicts the Bureau's own table and the contemporary New York Times report of 5 June 1972; the table and the contemporary report are preferred here. The European Graduate School and the National Archives agree that she spent sixteen months in custody and was acquitted in 1972. The New York Times report, filed from San Jose on 4 June and published on 5 June, records that an all white jury found her not guilty on three counts after thirteen hours of deliberation. It also records the prosecution's argument that the guns registered in her name were supplied for the courthouse action, and the defence's answer that they were for the Soledad Brothers' defence headquarters. Those are positions stated at trial, not findings of f

title: Mark Fisher: Capitalist Realism and Cultural Power
description: A research profile of the cultural theorist's claim that capitalism has become unthinkable to replace, its sources and the criticisms it drew.
text: Mark Fisher was a cultural theorist whose central claim was that capitalism had become the unquestioned frame of reality. He called this capitalist realism and defined it in the opening chapter of his 2009 book as "the widespread sense that not only is capitalism the only viable political and economic system, but also that it is now impossible even to imagine a coherent alternative to it" (Fisher, Capitalist Realism , 2009). The claim belongs to the study of ideology: here, a set of ideas that makes the existing social order appear natural and inevitable, rather than something people made and could change. Fisher asked how that order is lived in work, education, culture and mental health, and where its openings might be. This profile reports his arguments as arguments, records the sources on which they rest, and sets out the objections other writers made. Biography Mark Fisher was born in Leicester on 11 July 1968 and died on 13 January 2017, aged 48. Repeater Books, his publisher, gives the years 1968–2017, and The Wire 's obituary supplies the full dates. The research brief for this profile gave 1967 as the birth year. Every source opened for the dossier that states a birth date gives 1968, including The Wire , Simon Reynolds's memorial in The Guardian and Repeater's author biography, and the 1967 date could not be verified. It is flagged here as a discrepancy in the brief and is not used. Reynolds said Fisher took his own life after an intermittently severe struggle with depression. Carl Freedman reported that Fisher's widow, Zoë, had stated the date of death, and that Fisher left a wife and a young son; the LARB memorial names the son as George. These are contemporaneous recollections by colleagues rather than a civil record; no birth or death certificate was examined (The Wire, 16 January 2017; Freedman and others, LARB, 11 March 2017). Fisher's education and early career ran through the philosophy department at the University of Warwick. The Wire reports that he made music in the early 1990s with the group D Generation, which released a twelve inch record called Entropy In The UK , and that he entered the orbit of the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU) in the middle of that decade. The CCRU was conceived by Sadie Plant and Nick Land and, according to The Wire , was never formally founded or dissolved; after Plant left, Fisher became one of its driving forces. He completed a PhD in 1999 titled Flatline Constructs: Gothic Materialism And Cybernetic Theory Fiction . Simon & Schuster's current publisher record describes the thesis as completed in 1999 during the CCRU period and lists a published edition dated 1 April 2025. He then worked as a philosophy lecturer in Kent (The Wire, 2017; Simon & Schuster, Flatline Constructs ). A decisive break came in 2003. The Wire records that, despondent at the pressures of further education and impatient with academic structures, he began the blog k punk . Fisher explained the shift in a 2010 interview quoted by The Wire : blogging was a more informal space and "a way of tricking myself back into doing serious writing", because a blog post did not carry the weight of an academic paper. The blog's live archive runs from September 2003 to July 2015, with posts on philosophy, music, film and politics. In 2004 he co founded the discussion forum Dissensus with the blogger Woebot (Matthew Ingram), again according to The Wire . He joined The Wire as a contributor in 2007 and became Acting Deputy Editor in 2008 (The Wire, 2017; k punk archive). Fisher's later institutional base was Goldsmiths, University of London, in the Visual Cultures department; Repeater Books and Reynolds confirm this, with Repeater describing him as a Visiting Fellow. He also worked as a commissioning editor for Zero Books, the imprint with which he had forged a close alliance after leaving The Wire . Reynolds identifies Tariq Goddard as the founder of Zero Books and says Fisher worked alongside him; Repeater's own au

title: Paul Sweezy: Monopoly Capital and the Transformation Problem
description: A research profile of the Marxist economist and Monthly Review editor, his theory of monopoly capital and the debates around value and prices.
text: Paul Sweezy was a Marxist economist and, for more than half a century, the editor of Monthly Review . Two books carry his reputation. The Theory of Capitalist Development (1942) introduced English speaking readers to the technical core of Marx's economics, including the argument about how values become prices. Monopoly Capital (1966), written with Paul A. Baran, moved the question to monopoly capital: an economy in which a few large corporations dominate their markets and administer prices instead of competing them down.
