Its central claim was that such a system generates a growing surplus, meaning the income left above wages and other costs of production, which ends up as profit and other returns to property, while at the same time becoming prone to stagnation. Sweezy defended that argument in print and in occasional teaching for decades afterwards. This profile sets out what he argued, what the opened records show, and where critics from several directions objected. Biography Paul Marlor Sweezy was born in New York on 10 April 1910 and died at his home in Larchmont, New York, on 27 February 2004, aged 93; the Monthly Review memorial gives congestive heart failure as the cause (Monthly Review memorial, 2004). Some newspaper obituaries imply 28 February, and the discrepancy was not resolved here. His father, Everett B. Sweezy, was a vice president of the First National Bank of New York; the family wealth later gave him the freedom to leave academia (Foster, 2004; Monthly Review , The Editors ). He attended Phillips Exeter Academy and Harvard. The Monthly Review record of Christopher Phelps's 1999 interview says he graduated in 1931; Foster says his father's death in 1931 interrupted his senior year and that he graduated magna cum laude in 1932. The two accounts agree that he began graduate work at Harvard and spent 1932–33 at the London School of Economics, where the Depression, the rise of fascism and radical students pushed him towards Marxism (Phelps interview record; Foster, 2004). He later described the Marxism he brought back to Harvard as that of a "convinced but very ignorant" person, in words quoted by Monthly Review ( The Editors ). His doctorate came in 1937, and the dissertation appeared in 1938 as Monopoly and Competition in the English Coal Trade, 1550–1850 , published by Harvard University Press as Harvard Economic Studies volume 63 (Niigata University catalogue). The Phelps interview abstract gives the title as "1550–1800", which conflicts with every catalogue record examined and appears to be an error in that abstract. Sweezy taught economics at Harvard from 1938, took over a course on the economics of socialism, and wrote The Theory of Capitalist Development out of those lectures. In 1942 he went on leave to the Office of Strategic Services, where he edited the classified European Political Report . After the war he resigned from Harvard, expecting to be denied tenure, and declined an academic career ( The Editors ; Phelps interview record). Heilbroner's contemporary review says he was "released from Harvard in 1942", a different framing that was not reconciled (Heilbroner, 1966). He worked in Henry Wallace's 1948 Progressive Party campaign and headed it in New Hampshire. In 1949 he and Leo Huberman launched Monthly Review: An Independent Socialist Magazine , its first issue carrying Albert Einstein's "Why Socialism?". Foster records about 2,500 subscribers after the first year and a peak circulation near 12,000 in 1977; these are figures reported in a secondary essay, not measurements checked against a dataset here (Foster, 2004). During the McCarthy period Sweezy refused to surrender his lecture notes or name political associates to a New Hampshire attorney general, was jailed for contempt, and won in the United States Supreme Court, Sweezy v. New Hampshire , on 17 June 1957; the Monthly Review editors' page describes the decision as 5–4 (Foster, 2004; The Editors ). He later taught occasionally as a visitin

title: Mike Davis: Famine, Slums and Urban Capitalism
description: A research profile of the historian's account of colonial famine, capitalist urban development and the politics of the city, with criticism of his figures.
text: Mike Davis wrote about two subjects that are usually kept apart: the famines of the late Victorian empire and the cities of the United States and the global south. His argument joined them. A drought, in his account, became a famine because of the policies of ruling elites; urban growth produced wealth alongside a vast population outside formal work and housing. He wrote as a Marxist and a polemicist, and his estimates have been disputed by scholars who broadly accepted the direction of his argument. This profile sets out what he claimed, what the opened sources support and where the objections remain unresolved. Biography Verso, Davis's main publisher, records his dates as 1946–2022 and describes him as a writer, political activist, urban theorist and historian, best known for City of Quartz , Late Victorian Holocausts and Planet of Slums (Verso author page). Its obituary, written by Tariq Ali and published on 26 October 2022, calls him an American working class intellectual who was radicalised in the 1960s by the US Communist Party, and says he never ceased to acknowledge the people in the Party who educated him (Tariq Ali, Verso, 26 October 2022). The obituary says he taught classes at UC Irvine, worked with Michael Sprinker on a US list at Verso and on the American Socialist Yearbook published between 1985 and 1988, and stayed intellectually active to the end, commenting on articles submitted to New Left Review . A Verso podcast account adds that he came to writing late, after periods as a truck driver and a meat cutter, and that the civil rights movement was part of his radicalisation (Verso Podcast, 30 May 2024). The archive record of a 2014 radio interview says he had been an SDS organiser in Austin in the late 1960s and was then a Distinguished Professor in the Department of Creative Writing at the University of California, Riverside (Rag Radio archive record, 31 October 2014). Verso records that he held a MacArthur Fellowship and a Lannan Literary Award; the radio record dates the MacArthur fellowship to 1998, and an archived Verso page from 2009 already noted the award (Verso author page, Rag Radio archive record, archived Verso title page, 2009). In a statement quoted by Verso in 2022, he rejected consoling endings: "I'm writing because I'm hoping the people who read it don't need dollops of hope or good endings but are reading so that they'll know what to fight, and fight even when the fight seems hopeless" (Ali, 2022). The obituary says he had been ill for many years, was survived by his partner, the artist Alessandra Moctezuma, and four children, and that shortly before his death rumours about his condition produced what he described as surprisingly warm public tributes. No precise birth date, birthplace or date of death was confirmed in an institutional or publisher record opened for this profile. Verso gives only the years 1946–2022 and dates the obituary 26 October 2022. More precise dates were not used. Intellectual tradition Davis wrote from within the Marxist and New Left tradition, but his work is not easily reduced to a single school. Verso's obituary emphasises his education in the American Communist Party and his lifelong location on the Left, while noting that his writing targeted the economic, political and military apparatus of the US state and the brutality of empires generally (Ali, 2022). His long association with New Left Review is documented by the journal's own author record, which lists more than twenty articles between 1980 and 2020 on labour, cities, US politics, climate science and Marx ( New Left Review author record). "Who Killed Los Angeles? A Political Autopsy" (1993) and "Marx's Lost Theory" (2015) show the range, the latter being a re reading of Marx's political writings on class, nation and the world market. Verso describes Old Gods, New Enigmas as his first book on Marxism itself and as an attempt to clarify "proletarian agency" for the present (Verso, Old Gods, New Enigmas ). He di

title: Jason Hickel: Global Inequality, Extraction and Degrowth
description: A research profile of the economic anthropologist's account of imperialist appropriation, global inequality and the case for degrowth, with critics.
text: Jason Hickel argues that global poverty is made rather than found: poor countries are poor because they are integrated into the world economy on unequal terms. His central term is appropriation, meaning the taking of land, materials and labour without equivalent payment in return. In his account the wealthy North appropriates from the global South through ecologically unequal exchange — trade in which the South exports far more embodied resources and labour than it imports, because its wages and prices are held down while the North monopolises technology and capital goods. His proposed remedy is degrowth: reducing excess resource and energy throughput while improving human well being, rather than simply shrinking output. This profile reports those arguments as his claims, sets out the evidence he and his co authors offer, and records the objections raised against them. The site's source policy governs what can count as evidence here. No book was opened as a full text, no physical archive was available, and all verification was of online pages or registry metadata. Biography Hickel describes himself as a political economist, an author and a Fellow of the Royal Society of Arts. He holds an ICREA professorship at the Institute for Environmental Science and Technology (ICTA) and the Department of Political Science and Public Law at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. He also serves on the Climate and Macroeconomics Roundtable of the US National Academy of Sciences, the advisory board of the Green New Deal for Europe, the Rodney Commission on Reparations and Redistributive Justice and the Lancet Commission on Sustainable Health (author's About page). Penguin's author record adds detail that his own page omits: it calls him an economic anthropologist, says he is originally from Eswatini (Swaziland), says he spent a number of years with migrant workers in South Africa writing about exploitation and political resistance after apartheid, and says he lives in London and Barcelona (Penguin author record). The ICREA memoir for 2025 confirms the Barcelona chair, a visiting professorship at the London School of Economics and a Chair Professorship of Global Justice and the Environment at the University of Oslo, and records an ERC Synergy Grant titled REAL: A Post Growth Deal (ICREA memoir). Some biographical details could not be confirmed. A search result for his ICREA curriculum vitae listed an MA and a PhD in anthropology at the University of Virginia, a Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship at the LSE, an associate professorship at Goldsmiths and a move to Barcelona in 2021. The URL returned a PDF that was not parsed in this research, so those dates are not verified and are not used here. No birth date or birth year appeared in any author, employer or publisher record opened for this profile. His first book grew out of earlier ethnographic work on colonialism, anti colonial struggle and the labour movement in South Africa. His own About page dates that work to Democracy as Death (University of California Press, 2015) and lists two co edited ethnographic volumes, Ekhaya (2014) and Hierarchy and Value (2018). Hickel describes the shift from southern African anthropology to global inequality and ecological economics as a change of research focus. In the new afterword to The Divide he says that degrowth was an idea he engaged only in the final weeks of writing that book and developed properly afterwards (New Afterword). Intellectual tradition Hickel works in the tradition of anti colonial political economy and dependency theory, updated with ecological economics and degrowth. He does not present himself as a doctrinal Marxist, and he has criticised parts of the socialist left for defending growth. In a 2021 interview he summed up his position in a formula that has become a signature phrase: "ecosocialism is the horizon, degrowth is the way" ( The Trouble interview, 11 February 2021). In the same interview he argued that most degrowth advocat

title: John Bellamy Foster: The Metabolic Rift and Ecological Marxism
description: A research profile of the Marxist sociologist's account of the rift between society and nature, monopoly-finance capital and his critics.
text: John Bellamy Foster is a Marxist sociologist and the editor of Monthly Review . His central claim is that Karl Marx identified a break in the material exchange between human society and the natural world, and that capitalism deepens it. Foster calls this the metabolic rift : in plain terms, industrial farming and city life draw fertility out of the soil, concentrate human and animal waste in cities, and fail to return what was taken, so that the "metabolism" between people and the earth is disrupted. In his own words, Marx "employed the concept of metabolic rift to capture the material estrangement of human beings in capitalist society from the natural conditions of their existence" (Foster, 1999). The same framework led Foster and Robert W. McChesney to the condition they analyse as monopoly finance capital : an economy in which a few large firms dominate their industries and accumulate more capital than they can profitably invest, leaving growth dependent on financial activity that cannot last. This profile sets out what Foster argued, what can be checked in his published texts and first party records, and where critics, including other ecological Marxists, objected. Biography Foster was born in 1953 in Seattle, Washington. Monthly Review's editors page names his father, William Foster, a schoolteacher who had attended school under the G.I. Bill, and his mother, Patrica Bellamy Foster, an administrative secretary. Both parents were socialists, and Foster describes an informal socialist education at home through his parents and his father's library. The same page says he was concerned with environmental issues from his earliest years, but that in the late 1960s the urgent question for him was United States imperialism: he gave talks and took part in protests against the Vietnam War and the nuclear arms race while still in high school (Monthly Review, The Editors ). His degrees are recorded in his curriculum vitae and confirmed in part by the University of Oregon: a BA in Liberal Arts from The Evergreen State College in 1975, an MA in Political Science from York University in 1977, and a PhD in Political Science from York University in 1984, with a major area in political theory and a minor in international relations theory. His dissertation, supervised by Robert Albritton, was The Theory of Monopoly Capitalism: An Elaboration of Baran and Sweezy's Approach to Political Economy . The Oregon directory independently confirms the York PhD and lists him as Professor Emeritus in Sociology (Foster CV; University of Oregon directory). Monthly Review adds that he began studies at Evergreen in 1971, met Robert W. McChesney there and was introduced by him to Monthly Review . The two studied neoclassical and Marxian economics together and helped organise the Northwest Symposium on Chile after the United States backed coup against Salvador Allende. Foster entered graduate study at York in 1976, studied with Neal Wood and Ellen Meiksins Wood, worked with the historian Gabriel Kolko, and shifted from a "fundamentalist" Marxian political economy towards a more historical and empirical approach that included Michał Kalecki and Joseph Steindl alongside Baran and Sweezy (Monthly Review, The Editors ). After a short period teaching political economy at Evergreen, Foster became a professor of sociology at the University of Oregon, in a post advertised around "Marxism, political economy, class analysis, and imperialism"; according to Monthly Review he taught Marx's Capital every year for the next forty years. He retired, teaching his last course in 2026, and is now professor emeritus. The two first party records differ on the editorship. Monthly Review's public page labels him "Editor (2000–present)" and says he joined the editorial committee in 1988–89 and became a director of the Monthly Review Foundation at that time. His own CV is more specific: member of the Monthly Review editorial advisory committee 1989–99, board member of the Monthly Revi

title: Rosa Luxemburg: Accumulation, Mass Strikes and Socialist Democracy
description: A research profile of the Marxist theorist's critique of imperialism, reformism and party centralism, with her economic arguments and their critics.
text: Rosa Luxemburg's arguments were about two limits: the limits of capitalism and the limits of revolutionary parties. She held that capitalism drew on markets and peoples outside its own class relations, that reforms could not replace the abolition of capitalism, and that a socialist movement which denied its own members a voice would reproduce the rule it wanted to end. Most of her writing was produced inside arguments among socialists. This profile follows those arguments in her own texts, records what the opened sources say about her life, and reports the objections made by contemporaries and later writers. Biography Rosa Luxemburg was born on 5 March 1871 in Zamość, then in the Russian controlled part of Poland, and was killed in Berlin on 15 January 1919. Both dates and places appear in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry and in the Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung's biographical page. The SEP calls her the youngest of five children in an assimilated Jewish family of timber merchants; the Stiftung says her father was a wood merchant and that the family moved to Warsaw when she was two. The SEP adds that a hip illness contracted at about the age of three left her with a limp for life, and that she taught herself to read and write during a year in bed. These are secondary biographical claims, reported as the two sources give them, not facts drawn from a primary document opened for this profile. Both sources agree that she was drawn to illegal revolutionary groups while at school in Warsaw, left Poland in 1889 under threat of arrest, and enrolled at the University of Zurich. The Stiftung says she first studied natural sciences and then political science and economics, and that she obtained her doctorate in 1897. The SEP says she switched from philosophy to law, wrote a dissertation called "The Industrial Development of Poland", and places her move to Germany in 1898. Paul Mattick, writing in 1978, dates the dissertation to 1898. The discrepancy over 1897 and 1898 has not been resolved in the sources opened here. In Zurich she worked with Leo Jogiches and helped found the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland (SDKP), which later became the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland and Lithuania (SDKPiL). Her opposition to Polish independence within the existing capitalist order was already argued in the dissertation and remained a constant of her politics. She moved to Germany in 1898 through a marriage of convenience that secured German citizenship, and became known in the SPD through her intervention in the debate over revisionism, the view associated with Eduard Bernstein that the final goal of socialism could be set aside in favour of reforms inside capitalism. The Stiftung records her first major international appearance at the Zurich congress of 1893, where she sought a mandate for the SDKP and was refused, though her ally Julian Marchlewski was admitted and read a speech she had written. The Stiftung's archive FAQ adds that in 1893 she declared at Zurich that "our current goal is not to fight for an independent Polish state, but for political freedom". That wording comes from a later biography quoted by the FAQ, so it is a quotation at second hand. From 1907 to 1914 she taught economics at the SPD party school in Berlin. The SEP says she taught "Introduction to Economics" and "Marx's Capital" to rank and file members. She was repeatedly imprisoned: for anti war speeches in 1914 and, according to the Stiftung, from July 1916 to November 1918 in Berlin, Wronki and Wrocław. The Junius Pamphlet and the manuscript on the Russian Revolution were written in prison. The Stiftung says she was released on 9 November 1918, edited Die Rote Fahne with Karl Liebknecht, helped found the Communist Party of Germany at the turn of 1918–19, and was murdered with Liebknecht on 15 January 1919 by officers and soldiers of Reichswehr units. The SEP gives a fuller account of the final days: a mass demonstration in Berlin in early January,

title: José Carlos Mariátegui: Indigenous Socialism and Peruvian Reality
description: A research profile of the Peruvian Marxist's account of the Indian question, the land question and the socialist tradition he founded in Latin America.
text: José Carlos Mariátegui argued that the oppression of Peru's Indigenous majority was not a racial problem or a shortage of education but a question of land and power. He founded a socialist party, edited two journals and wrote essays that made Peru central to Latin American Marxism. He also insisted that socialism in the Americas had to be made out of local reality rather than copied from Europe, a phrase later read both as a declaration of independence and as a move inside a specific polemic with Peruvian nationalists. This profile reports what he argued, what the research dossier records for it, and where historians and other socialists objected. Quotations from Spanish texts are given in the Spanish recorded in the dossier; where an English rendering appears, it is the dossier author's translation, not a quotation from a published English edition. Biography The institutional chronology gives José Carlos Mariátegui La Chira's birth as 14 June 1894 in Moquegua, the son of María Amalia La Chira Ballejos and Francisco Javier Mariátegui Requejo, with two siblings, Guillermina and Julio César (Casa Museo chronology). This date is not settled by the opened sources. His own autobiographical letter of 10 January 1927 says "Nací el 95" ("I was born in '95"), and the dossier records both dates rather than resolving the difference (Mariátegui, "Apuntes autobiográficos"). A school accident in 1902 led to a long convalescence in Lima and a permanently weak leg. In the 1927 letter he says only that in 1924 he "lost a leg" and was left in delicate health, without naming which leg; the chronology alone says the May 1924 amputation was of the right leg, after the 1902 accident had left the left one weak. No medical record was opened, so the two accounts are recorded side by side rather than reconciled (chronology; "Apuntes autobiográficos"). He entered the newspaper trade as a copy boy at La Prensa in 1909 and moved through reporting and proof reading posts at La Prensa , El Tiempo and La Razón , where he supported the university reform movement. In 1918 he helped found Nuestra Época , a socialist oriented review, and was attacked by military officers after an article criticising the army; in 1919 La Razón was closed under pressure from Augusto Leguía's government (chronology). In October 1919 the Leguía government sent him to Italy, in the chronology's words "as a propaganda agent for Peru abroad, as a way of covering his deportation". He spent more than two years there, married Anna Chiappe in 1921, attended the Livorno congress of the Italian Socialist Party as a correspondent, and travelled in France, Germany, Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Belgium. His own account compresses the period: "De fines de 1919 a mediados de 1923 viajé por Europa. Residí más de dos años en Italia, donde desposé una mujer y algunas ideas" — "From the end of 1919 to the middle of 1923 I travelled through Europe. I lived more than two years in Italy, where I married a woman and some ideas", in the dossier's translation ("Apuntes autobiográficos"). He returned to Peru in March 1923 and began lectures at the Universidad Popular, interviews, and what he called "the investigation of national reality according to the Marxist method" (Ibid.). The chronology records the public career that followed. He contributed to Mundial in 1924; in October 1925 he founded Editorial Minerva and published his first book, La escena contemporánea ; Amauta appeared in September 1926. A police and press campaign in 1927 led to his detention in the San Bartolomé military hospital and to the closure of Amauta and Minerva, with Amauta reappearing in December (chronology; Archivo, Amauta series record). In April 1928 he broke with Haya de la Torre, in September published "Aniversario y balance", and on 8 October the Peruvian Socialist Party was formally constituted with him as general secretary. 7 ensayos and the fortnightly Labor appeared in November 1928. title: Peter Kropotkin: Mutual Aid and Anarchist Communism
description: A research profile of the geographer and anarchist's account of cooperation, decentralised federation and the critique of the state.
text: Peter Kropotkin made two connected arguments: that cooperation is a force in evolution, and that socialism cannot be built through the state. By mutual aid he meant practical support between members of the same species in the struggle against harsh physical conditions, which he set against the competition for scarce resources that many Darwinists treated as the main fact of evolution. "Sociability is as much a law of nature as mutual struggle", he wrote, and "those animals which acquire habits of mutual aid are undoubtedly the fittest" (Gould 1988 [Scholarly Secondary, quoting Mutual Aid ]). By anarchist communism he meant what he called "the no government system of socialism": a society of free groups and communes joined by agreement rather than law, with land and capital held in common and goods enjoyed according to need (MIA, "Anarchist Communism: Its Basis and Principles" [Primary Theoretical]). This profile sets out those arguments in his own words, records the objections made by Marxists, scientists and other anarchists, and marks where the evidence is thin. Biography An Internet Archive catalogue record gives the subject heading "Kropotkin, Petr Alekseevich, kniaz, 1842 1921" (Internet Archive, The anarchist prince [Primary Official, catalogue metadata]). The Marxists Internet Archive index gives the fuller dates 9 December 1842 and 8 February 1921, but its biographical paragraph is attributed to "a tertiary encyclopedia", so the exact days are not verified here and are not used as evidence under the book's editorial source policy (MIA, Kropotkin archive index [directory, not evidence]). The scholarly biography identified through the catalogue is George Woodcock and Ivan Avakumovic, The Anarchist Prince: A Biographical Study of Peter Kropotkin , New York: Schocken Books, 1971, with a bibliography at pages 455–459. The scan is access restricted and its argument was not read. His own memoir is the best first person source for the early years. The MIA edition is arranged in six parts: childhood, the Corps of Pages, Siberia, St Petersburg and a first journey to Western Europe, the fortress and the escape, and Western Europe (MIA, Memoirs of a Revolutionist , table of contents [Primary Theoretical]). The transcription carries inconsistent publication metadata: it labels the work "Written: 1899" but names In Russian and French Prisons , Ward and Downey, 1887, as its source. Catalogue records place Memoirs of a Revolutionist in London with Smith, Elder and in Boston and New York with Houghton, Mifflin in 1899, with later Swan Sonnenschein editions in 1906 and 1908 and a Dover edition in 1971 (Internet Archive catalogue search [Primary Official, catalogue metadata]). One catalogue entry dated 1916 is titled Memoirs of a revolutionary ; the modern title has some bibliographic support, but the standard English text used here is the 1899 Memoirs of a Revolutionist . Kropotkin described his scientific formation himself. In the introduction to Mutual Aid he recalled two impressions from his youth in Eastern Siberia and Northern Manchuria: the severity of the struggle against an inclement climate, and his failure to find "that bitter struggle for the means of existence, among animals belonging to the same species, which was considered by most Darwinists (though not always by Darwin himself) as the dominant characteristic of struggle for life, and the main factor of evolution" (MIA, Mutual Aid , Introduction [Primary Theoretical]). Gould, using Daniel Todes's study of Russian evolutionary thought, places those years at 1862–1866 and says Kropotkin went as a military officer but used the commission to study geology, geography and zoology (Gould 1988 [Scholarly Secondary]). Kropotkin dated the origin of his theory more precisely: a lecture "On the Law of Mutual Aid" given by the zoologist Kessler at a Russian Congress of Naturalists in January 1880 gave him the idea, and he began collecting material after encountering it in 1883; Kessle

title: Mikhail Bakunin: Collectivist Anarchism and the State
description: A research profile of the anarchist's critique of state socialism, his role in the First International and the scholarly disputes around his politics.
text: Mikhail Bakunin argued that the state, not capital alone, was the central obstacle to working class emancipation. His writings on authority, federation and the "People's State" gave anarchism a theory of domination and a warning about revolutionary governments that later movements returned to repeatedly. This profile explains those arguments from his own texts, records the organizational disputes they produced, and reports the criticisms made of them without smoothing them over. Biography The published chapter on the First International already covers the Association's founding, its address and rules, the weekly work of the General Council, the Alliance crisis and the Hague expulsion of 1872; this profile adds the arguments Bakunin himself made, the texts in which he made them and the scholarly disputes about his politics rather than retelling the organisation's history. Mikhail Aleksandrovich Bakunin was born on 18 May 1814 by the old Russian calendar, or 30 May by the Western calendar, at the family estate of Priamukhino in Tver province, north west of Moscow, and died in Berne on 1 July 1876. These dates and places come from Marshall Shatz's introduction and chronology to the Cambridge edition of Statism and Anarchy , not from a primary document opened for this profile (Shatz, Scholarly Secondary). Shatz describes a well off gentry family owning about 500 male serfs, with the children educated at home on Rousseauist principles. Bakunin was sent to St Petersburg in 1828 to prepare for the Artillery School, received his officer's commission, but was dismissed for disciplinary reasons in 1834 and sent to a provincial garrison. He then immersed himself in philosophy in Moscow, first in Fichte and then in Hegel, and met Herzen and Ogarev. Paris was the decisive place in the 1840s. Shatz records that Bakunin met Marx in 1844 and became fast friends with Proudhon, whose combination of the critique of capitalism with hostility to the state he later adapted while rejecting much of Proudhon's programme. The Russian government ordered him home, stripped him of noble status and sentenced him in absentia to hard labour in Siberia after he refused. In 1847 he spoke at a Paris banquet marking the Polish uprising of 1830–31, and in 1848 he returned to Paris, went to Germany, took part in the Prague Slav Congress and its insurrection, and published the Appeal to the Slavs . In May 1849 he joined the Dresden insurrection, was arrested, was sentenced to death by Saxon and then Austrian courts, and was extradited to Russia in 1851. Shatz's chronology gives May 1851 for incarceration in the Peter Paul Fortress, July–August 1851 for the "Confession" to Nicholas I, March 1854 for transfer to Schlüsselburg Fortress, March 1857 for release and exile to Siberia, October 1858 for his marriage to Antonia Kwiatkowska in Tomsk, July 1861 for his escape via Japan and San Francisco, and December 1861 for his arrival in London. The later chronology is tied to the organizational history: a failed attempt to reach the Polish insurrection of 1863, arrival in Italy in 1864, the International Brotherhood of 1866, joining the International in 1864 and the Geneva Central Section in 1868, the International Alliance of Socialist Democracy in September 1868, its formal dissolution and admission as the Geneva Section in March 1869, the Russian Brotherhood and Slavic Section of Zurich in 1872, expulsion at The Hague in September 1872, publication of Statism and Anarchy in 1873, the abortive Bologna insurrection of 1874, and death in Berne in 1876 (Shatz). The MIA archive index prints 1817 in its heading while its own text gives 1814 and attributes the paragraph to a tertiary source; neither the heading nor that paragraph is used here as evidence (MIA index, directory only). Intellectual tradition Bakunin called himself an anarchist and accepted the name. In Statism and Anarchy he wrote that "we are the enemies of every government and every state power, and of governme

title: Emma Goldman: Anarchism, Freedom and the Critique of the State
description: A research profile of the anarchist writer's politics of individual freedom, her critique of marriage and the state, and her break with the Bolsheviks.
text: Emma Goldman argued that individual freedom and a critique of property belonged to one politics. Anarchism, as she defined it, was "the philosophy of a new social order based on liberty unrestricted by man made law; the theory that all forms of government rest on violence, and are therefore wrong and harmful, as well as unnecessary." She also took up the phrase "free love", meaning that love and sexual choice should be free of legal, marital and economic compulsion, and answered those who used the phrase against her with the question, "Free love? As if love is anything but free!" Her life ran from Russian Jewish immigration and factory work to lecture tours, imprisonment, deportation and a public break with the Bolsheviks after 1921. This profile reports her arguments in her own words, marks where the evidence is uncertain, and sets out the objections made by Marxists and by other anarchists. Biography The outline of Goldman's early life comes from her own writings, which are retrospective and select what serves the argument of the book in which they appear. Hippolyte Havel's biographical sketch prefacing Anarchism and Other Essays states that she "was born of Jewish parentage on the 27th day of June, 1869, in the Russian province of Kovno" (Havel, in Anarchism and Other Essays ). Havel describes a childhood divided between Kurland, Königsberg and St Petersburg, and says the struggle over the 1881 assassination of Alexander II drew her into revolutionary student circles. He records that she became a factory worker at seventeen and emigrated with her sister Helena, and that life in the United States quickly destroyed her expectation of a free republic: "Instead of one Tsar, she found scores of them; the Cossack was replaced by the policeman with the heavy club." Her autobiography opens with a precise date: "It was the 15th of August 1889, the day of my arrival in New York City. I was twenty years old" ( Living My Life ). She describes the Haymarket executions of November 1887 as the event that turned her towards anarchism. After hearing Johanna Greie speak in Rochester, she wrote, "A great ideal, a burning faith, a determination to dedicate myself to the memory of our martyred comrades, to make their cause my own." In New York she met Alexander Berkman on her first day, heard Johann Most speak and began lecturing in German and Yiddish. Berkman's 1892 attempt on Henry Clay Frick's life at Homestead drew her into a defence of "propaganda by the deed" that she later abandoned. Havel records her trial in October 1893, a year's imprisonment on Blackwell's Island, a 1895 European trip that included midwifery training in Vienna, and her first major American lecture tour in 1897. The later chronology can be checked against her own works. She was arrested in the birth control case in 1916 and wrote in an essay for Mother Earth in April of that year that she was "to be tried at Special Sessions April 5th" ( Mother Earth , April 1916). A Mother Earth advertisement for June 1916 described her as "Just out of the New York Workhouse where she spent 15 days for advocating BIRTH CONTROL"; that text was seen in search output and not opened directly (periodical text). In 1917, the year of the October Revolution, she and Berkman were arrested for opposing conscription and served two years. In her Russia book she writes that when the New York courts "upheld the fraudulent methods by which I was disfranchised and my American citizenship of thirty two years denied me, I waived my right of appeal in order that I might return to Russia" ( My Disillusionment in Russia ). She records the deportation precisely: "On the night of December 21, 1919, together with two hundred and forty eight other political prisoners, I was deported from America." She left Soviet Russia in December 1921. Her autobiography was written in Saint Tropez and dated by her "January 1931"; she says Berkman suggested the title. She acted as English language spokesperson for the Spani

title: Murray Bookchin: Social Ecology and Libertarian Municipalism
description: A research profile of the social ecologist's account of hierarchy, cities and face-to-face democracy, and his break with anarchism.
text: Murray Bookchin (1921–2006) argued that the domination of nature has its roots in the domination of human by human. He called this argument social ecology : the claim that the idea of dominating nature arises from hierarchy, by which he meant institutionalised, coercive ranks of command and obedience that exist apart from the particular people who occupy them. His politics of libertarian municipalism — direct, face to face democracy in citizen assemblies, coordinated through confederated councils of elected, recallable delegates — was offered as a way to replace state power with popular self rule. He spent much of his career inside left wing movements and ended it arguing that neither Marxism nor anarchism was adequate to the task. This profile sets out what he claimed, what can be checked in the texts opened for the dossier, and where readers and scholars objected. Biography The Institute for Social Ecology gives Bookchin's dates as 1921–2006, describes him as a cofounder of the Institute and professor emeritus at Ramapo College of New Jersey, and records in its chronology that he died in 2006 (ISE author page; ISE History). In the 2001 Harbinger interview he gave a first person account of his early political life. He said he was born in January 1921 in the Bronx, that Russian was the first language he knew, and that his family were Russian revolutionaries. He entered the American Communist movement as a child, joined the Young Pioneers in the early 1930s and the Young Communist League in 1934, broke with the Communists over the Popular Front line at fourteen or fifteen, rejoined during the Spanish Civil War, then left for good. After high school he did not go to college but worked in a foundry near New York; he became a Trotskyist during the Second World War and was disillusioned with orthodox Marxism when the war ended without a revolution. He then worked in the automobile industry and studied electronic engineering at the RCA Institute, where he came to the view that machines could replace much human toil. These are his own recollections, recorded decades later, and are reported as such (Harbinger interview). In the same interview he traced the development of his thought: a critique of hierarchy from 1952, dialectical naturalism based on Hegel but without what he called Hegel's teleological approach, work on urbanisation and appropriate technology, and later "face to face democracy, under the name libertarian municipalism or communalism". He described the early 1960s counterculture, said anarchism then seemed nearly defunct, and explained that he first advanced his views "under the rubric of anarchism" and that they later "were called 'eco anarchism'". The ISE chronology places the first Conference on Social Ecology at Goddard College in 1973, a summer programme in 1974, incorporation of the ISE in 1981, and Bookchin's keynote at the first US National Greens Gathering in 1987 (ISE History; Harbinger interview). In his 1998 reply to anarchist critics he wrote that he had ended his professional connections with both Goddard College and Ramapo College in 1981 and was living on a pension and Social Security, a self report made in the course of a polemic and not independently checked here (Whither Anarchism?). The dossier records several biographical gaps. The ISE confirms only that he died in 2006; the commonly given date of 30 July 2006 and the cause of death were not verified from an opened institutional or family record. His birth name, parents' names and family migration history were not verified from the primary sources opened; the 2001 interview confirms a January 1921 Bronx birth and a revolutionary Russian family, but no more than that. Intellectual tradition Bookchin wrote from a current that he eventually named communalism and located beyond both Marxism and anarchism. In the 2001 interview he said that "we have to go beyond the economism of Marx and beyond the individualism that is sometimes latent, sometimes explic

title: José María Sison: National Democracy and the Philippine Revolution
description: A research profile of the Filipino Marxist's theory of national democracy, the CPP's 1968 refounding and the disputes over his account of Philippine society.
text: Biography The existing chapter on communist movements in the Philippines and Japan (Two Archipelagos) covers the Hukbalahap, the 1950 State Department paper on the Huks, the Army counterinsurgency chronology, the re establishment of the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) on 26 December 1968, the founding of the New People's Army (NPA) in March 1969, the break with the older pro Moscow party and Sison's account of torture after his arrest on 10 November 1977; this profile sets out his argument as an argument, gives his own definitions, examines his economic writings, checks his book titles against catalogues and publisher records, and engages the criticism made against him. The dates 8 February 1939 and 16 December 2022 are given by the INPS memorial archive's "About" page, but that page could not be fetched directly, so they are recorded here as first party claims seen in a search excerpt rather than independently verified institutional facts. The NDFP's own notices confirm that Sison died in a hospital in Utrecht on 16 December 2022, aged 83 (NDFP notice, Primary Official ; NDFP National Council, Primary Official ). The IIRE library author record gives the fuller form Jose Maria Canlas Sison, the variant "Amado Guerrero" and the birth year 1939 (IIRE, Primary Official ). Abinales, writing as a scholar, describes him as born into a prominent Spanish speaking family of Chinese descent in Cabugao, Ilocos Sur; the OCR of the accessible page garbles the place as "Cayuga, Locos Sure" (Abinales, Scholarly Secondary ). Sison's own account supplies the intellectual chronology. He says his study of Philippine history and of the old Communist Party of the Philippine Islands began in the latter half of the 1950s, and that in 1966 he and his comrades separated from the Lava leadership of that party (kites interview, Primary Theoretical ). The political line he was working out in those years was what he called national democracy: a stage of revolution in which a working class led alliance of workers, peasants, the petty bourgeoisie and the national bourgeoisie sought national independence and democratic reforms before a separate socialist stage. The term named a political line, not simply a commitment to elections or civil liberties ( Struggle for National Democracy , Primary Theoretical ). In the preface to the third edition of that book he records that it gathers speeches and essays from 1964–68, written while he was founding chairman of Kabataang Makabayan from 30 November 1964, vice chairman or general secretary of the Socialist Party of the Philippines, and general secretary of the Movement for the Advancement of Nationalism, and that he went underground in 1968 ( Struggle for National Democracy , Primary Theoretical ). He was an English major at the University of the Philippines, published poems in the Philippine Collegian and brought out a first book of poems in 1961, at twenty two; he had attended Ateneo and Letran in high school (kites interview, Primary Theoretical ). The CPP was re established on 26 December 1968 and the NPA founded on 29 March 1969, dates given in his interview and in the party documents he drafted (kites interview, Primary Theoretical ; Foundation for Resuming the Philippine Revolution , Primary Theoretical ). His preface to Detention and Defiance against Dictatorship fixes the prison chronology: "Detention and Defiance against Dictatorship covers the period from my capture on November 10, 1977 to the fall of the Marcos fascist dictatorship on February 25, 1986." He says he was presented to Marcos on the day of capture, that the worst torture was solitary confinement lasting more than five years, interrupted by partial isolation with his wife Julie in 1980–81 when their fourth child was born, and that the confinement ended in 1985 after a Supreme Court ruling ( Detention and Defiance , Primary Theoretical ). This confirms the arrest date already used in the existing chapter. The editorial introductions t

title: Jane Kelsey: The New Zealand Experiment and Its Critics
description: A research profile of the legal scholar's analysis of neoliberal restructuring in Aotearoa New Zealand, its social consequences and the debate around her account.
text: Jane Kelsey is a New Zealand legal academic whose work treats the remaking of Aotearoa New Zealand after 1984 as a case study in how market reforms are introduced, defended and made hard to reverse. Neoliberal restructuring, in her usage, means the deliberate rebuilding of an economy and state around market rules: privatising public assets, limiting the scope of government, keeping inflation down with tight monetary policy, deregulating labour and restraining public spending. Structural adjustment means the package of such policies that the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank required of poorer countries in exchange for loans. Kelsey's central claim is that New Zealand adopted the same package voluntarily, and that its apparent success was then promoted as a model for other countries. This profile sets out her arguments, the evidence she offers for them and the objections made against them. It does not treat her claims as established findings. Biography The institutional record establishes the outline of Kelsey's career but not every date. The University of Auckland lists her as Emeritus Professor in Law, with an ORCID identifier 0000 0003 1437 0080; that staff profile page did not render during the research for this profile and was seen only as a search result excerpt. The university's news service says she taught at Auckland for four decades from 1979, describes her as a "self described legal subversive", and records that a $2,500 annual award, the Te Whainga i te Tika Award for Social Justice, was established on her retirement. Her Conversation profile gives the same starting year and says she retired at the end of 2021. A University of Auckland news item of September 2022 instead speaks of a "recent retirement", and her valedictory lecture was delivered on 28 July 2022. No single authoritative retirement date was verified, so the discrepancy is left open here. No birth date or birth year was found in any institutional, publisher or author record opened for this profile (University of Auckland news; The Conversation). Her own account supplies personal detail that publisher copy omits. In the 2022 valedictory lecture she says her father was from Hokianga and left school at fourteen at the start of the Depression to work as a barrow boy, later becoming Director of the Tourist Department; her mother's forebears were settlers in Taranaki. She describes growing up in Mt Wellington, taking a law degree at Victoria University where women were a small minority, a BCL at Oxford funded by her parents, and an M Phil in Criminology at Cambridge that she calls "the intellectual game changer". At Cambridge she was taught by Colin Sumner and Alison Young and read Stuart Hall's Policing the Crisis , Carol Smart on women, crime and criminology, Alan Hunt on Marxism and law, and Foucault's Discipline and Punish . A sabbatical in 1984 placed her in Britain during the miners' strike and the Greenham Common peace camp at the same time as the Rogernomics revolution began in New Zealand (valedictory lecture). She was recruited to Auckland Law School in mid 1979 to teach criminology. She describes replacing Alan Nixon, a prison abolitionist whose teaching she later came to regard as compromised by eugenic ideas, and helping to transform the first year legal system course with David Williams and later Ani Mikaere so that students met contemporary issues from contrasting theoretical perspectives, grounded in history and Te Tiriti o Waitangi. The same lecture records that she joined the Auckland Committee on Racism and Discrimination after a challenge from Ripeka Evans, worked with Māori liberation theologians on Tiriti based analysis, and provided legal support to people facing prosecution over the Springbok tour and Bastion Point. Moana Maniapoto, who introduced the lecture, recalls Kelsey on the frontline of the 1981 anti apartheid protests and filming the 2005 anti WTO protests in Hong Kong (same source). Intellectual tradition Kelsey

title: Epeli Hauʻofa: Oceania, Development and the Sea of Islands
description: A research profile of the Tongan-Fijian writer's critique of development discourse and his account of Pacific identity and resistance.
text: Epeli Hauʻofa (1939–2009) wrote against two habits of thought that he saw as connected. The first was the habit of describing the islands of the Pacific as small, remote and dependent. The second was what this profile calls development discourse : the language and assumptions through which aid workers, planners, academics and governments described those islands and prescribed what should be done to them. Hauʻofa used the word Oceania for the region as he understood it, a connected world of ocean, kinship and movement rather than a collection of isolated pieces of land. In 1998 he wrote that "anyone who has lived in our region and is committed to Oceania is an Oceanian", and he called the official categories "Pacific Islands Region" and "Pacific Islanders" as redundant as "South Seas" and "South Sea Islanders" (Hauʻofa 1998). His best known essay argued that "There is a world of difference between viewing the Pacific as 'islands in a far sea' and as 'a sea of islands'" (Hauʻofa, 1994 text). This profile sets out that argument, the institutions he built, and the objections other Pacific scholars made against it. Biography Epeli Toʻimuli Hauʻofa was born in 1939 at Somona in the Louisiades, in Milne Bay province of what was then the Territory of Papua. Thomas Malm, who knew him and quotes his own writing, records that he was the second of five children of the Wesleyan missionary Reverend ʻIsikeli (1908–1995) and Mele (1909–1974), and that he grew up among Dobu and Mekeo people far from his parents' Tongan homeland (Malm 2026). The University of Hawaiʻi Press gives the years 1939–2009 and says he was born in Papua New Guinea and educated in Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Fiji, Australia and Canada (UH Press). Colleagues at the University of the South Pacific later described him as "Tongan by name, Papuan by birth, Tongan, Fijian, Canadian and Australian by upbringing and education, and Fijian by citizenship" (USP memorial). The more precise birthday of 7 December 1939 could not be verified from a primary or institutional record opened for this profile. Hauʻofa gave his own account of this beginning to Nicholas Thomas in 2006. His parents went to Papua New Guinea in 1937 or 1938, and he did not know he was Tongan until he was seven or eight: "I grew up as a Papuan." The family left in September 1947, travelled through Madang, Townsville, Magnetic Island, Sydney and New Caledonia, and reached Tonga in January 1949. "While we were traveling, we all spoke Dobuan. We were still Papuans." He spent seven years in Tonga, then four years at Lelean Memorial School in Fiji, then studied history at the University of New England in Armidale from 1960. A scholarship took him to McGill University in Montreal, where sociology and anthropology were in one department; he took a master's degree in 1968 after fieldwork in Trinidad. He worked as a senior tutor at the University of Papua New Guinea, then took a PhD scholarship at the Australian National University and did fieldwork among the Mekeo. When his parents retired to Tonga he followed them, intending to stay two years; he stayed seven, revised his thesis for publication and began writing fiction. Afterwards he moved to Suva (Thomas's 2006 interview). At the University of the South Pacific he became professor of sociology and head of the School of Social and Economic Development, a position from which he commissioned responses from colleagues to his 1993 essay. Ratu Joni Madraiwiwi recalled that Hauʻofa spent a few years in the late 1970s as deputy to Tonga's King Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV, and that he lived at Wainadoi outside Suva (Wesley Smith, editor, 2010). He married Barbara Brown, an Australian, in 1966 (Malm 2026). In 1997 the university appointed him first director of the new Oceania Centre for Arts and Culture. USP's own history says the Centre was set up that year as a special project of the University Council and that Hauʻofa was appointed first Director "supported by a Programme Assistant and

title: Oskar Lange: Market Socialism and the Calculation Debate
description: A research profile of the Polish economist's model of a socialist pricing board, its debate with Mises and Hayek, and later criticism of the model.
text: Oskar Lange was the Polish economist whose essays of 1936 and 1937 became the standard answer to the claim that a socialist economy could not work out how to use its resources without markets. His market socialism — the view that a socialist economy could keep prices and markets while the state owned the main means of production — rested on trial and error pricing: setting a price, watching whether buyers wanted more than sellers offered, and changing it until supply and demand matched. He wrote in several registers at once, as a Marxian economist, a user of neoclassical price theory and a participant in Polish public life. This profile sets out what he argued, what can be checked in the texts, and where later writers objected. Biography The existing chapter on economic calculation covers the Soviet textbook claim that planning was an economic law, Stalin's 1952 distinction between commodity production and the law of value, Soviet economic accounting, cybernetics and the Chilean network, and the incentive problem, and states that Mises, Hayek, Lange and Lerner are absent from its source base, while this profile supplies Lange's own texts, the primary statements of Mises and Hayek, and the scholarly criticism that grew around them. Oskar Ryszard Lange was born on 27 July 1904 in Tomaszów Mazowiecki, Poland, and died in London on 2 October 1965. These dates and the place of birth come from the University of Chicago's finding aid to his papers, which calls him "Oskar Richard Lange" and names his parents Arthur and Sophie (Rosner) Lange, and which also gives the date and place of death (University of Chicago finding aid, Primary Official). A Polish biographical essay read only as a search index preview gives the birthplace as Tomaszów Lubelski and says he died in Westminster Hospital after surgery following a recurrence of childhood bone tuberculosis. The discrepancy over the birthplace was not resolved, and this profile uses the Chicago record (Winczewski, 2023, Scholarly Secondary, preview only). The title page of the 1938 volume identifies him as "Lecturer in Economics, University of California; Lecturer (on leave) at the University of Cracow and at the Polish Free University in Warsaw" (1938 volume, contents page, Primary Theoretical). The Chicago finding aid records that he attended the University of Kraków, taking a B.A. in 1926 and a Master of Law in 1928, worked at the Ministry of Labor in Warsaw from 1926 to 1927, and held a research assistantship at Kraków from 1927 to 1931. He was an honorary lecturer in statistics at Kraków in 1931, lecturer in economics at Michigan in 1936, honorary lecturer at Kraków again in 1936, honorary lecturer at the Polish Free University in Warsaw in 1937, and lecturer at California and Stanford in 1937–38. He had visited the United States from 1934 to 1937 under a Rockefeller grant, studying at Harvard and Minnesota before returning to Poland. On 1 July 1938 he began as associate professor of economics at Chicago, a post held until 1945. He and his wife Irene Alice Oderfeld became United States citizens in 1943; their son Christopher Stephen was born in 1940. In 1945 he renounced American citizenship, became a Polish citizen again and was the first Polish ambassador to the United States. The finding aid notes the controversy over his 1944 interview with Stalin, reports that by the mid 1950s he was spoken of as a possible premier of Poland, records his return to Chicago in 1962 to give a talk called "Planning Under Socialism", and says that by 1962 he was vice chairman of the Polish State Council (finding aid, Primary Official). The archive is small: a quarter linear foot, one box, containing an untitled manuscript, reprints of the two Review of Economic Studies articles, press releases and one incomplete letter from Maynard Krueger dated 30 January 1941. title: Alec Nove: Feasible Socialism and the Limits of Planning
description: A research profile of the economic historian's account of how actually existing socialist economies worked and what a feasible alternative would require.
text: Alec Nove (1915–1994) spent his career asking what a socialism that could actually work would look like. His term for it was "feasible socialism": in his words, "a state of affairs which could exist in some major part of the developed world within the lifetime of a child already conceived, without our having to make or accept implausible or far fetched assumptions about society, human beings and the economy", which also required "the dominance of social ownership in the economy, together with political and economic democracy" (Nove, 1991). By central planning he meant the direction of output and investment from a centre rather than by enterprises deciding what to make and buy for themselves. He defined it from the Soviet system he had studied, where the planning body Gosplan depended on information held by ministries. This profile sets out what he argued, what his texts support, and where economists and socialists objected. Biography The existing chapter on planning, incentives and shortage covers how plans were made, how workers and managers answered them, and why goods remained scarce; this profile adds Nove's economic explanation of why that pattern recurred and the alternative he sketched in response. Alexander Novakovsky was born into a Russian Jewish family in Petrograd on 24 November 1915 and died in hospital in Voss, Norway, on 15 May 1994, after a heart attack while on holiday (University of Glasgow, World Changing ; Brown and Cairncross, 1997; Wallace, The Independent , 20 May 1994). His father, Jacob, had been a Menshevik, was imprisoned under the tsars and again by the Bolsheviks, and left Russia in 1922; his mother, a doctor, brought Alec to Britain to join him the following year. The family adopted the name Nove, already used by relatives in Manchester. He went to school at King Alfred School in London, graduated from the London School of Economics in 1936 with an upper second in the B.Sc. (Econ.), joined the Territorials in 1939 and served in the Royal Signals and then intelligence until 1946, finishing as a major. He joined the Civil Service in 1947, working on price control and export targets at the Board of Trade. An attachment from 1952 to 1954 to Glasgow's Department of Soviet Studies turned him towards full time scholarship; he returned to Whitehall, moved to the Treasury's Economic Section in 1956, and in 1958 became Reader in Russian Social and Economic Studies at the LSE. In 1963 he took the James Bonar Chair of Economics at Glasgow and the directorship of the Institute of Soviet and East European Studies. He retired from those duties in 1982 but remained an honorary senior research fellow until his death. He was elected FBA in 1978, FRSE and an honorary fellow of the LSE in 1982, and received honorary doctorates, including one at Stockholm days before he died; a chair in Russian and East European Studies was named for him at Glasgow in 1996 (Glasgow biography; Brown and Cairncross). Biography matters here because Nove drew method from these institutions. He said that his Board of Trade years taught him what governments could and could not do, and the British Academy memoir links his later scepticism about central control directly to that experience (Brown and Cairncross; Nove, 1991). His family history gave him Russian without making him a communist. In his own preface he wrote: "Brought up in a social democratic environment, son of a Menshevik who was arrested by the Bolsheviks, I inherited a somewhat critical view of Soviet reality: if this really was socialism, I would prefer to be elsewhere. (Luckily, I was elsewhere!)" (Nove, 1991). Intellectual tradition Nove worked in the political economy tradition of Adam Smith and the British civil service economics of the postwar years, not in Marxism. title: János Kornai: Shortage, Soft Budgets and the Socialist Firm
description: A research profile of the Hungarian economist's account of chronic scarcity and incentive structures in state socialist economies, and its critics.
text: János Kornai was a Hungarian economist who was born and schooled under capitalism, lived through four decades of socialism and then observed its collapse. He built his reputation by asking which constraint actually stopped a firm from expanding, and by arguing that in state socialist economies the answer usually lay in physical bottlenecks and in managers' expectation that the state would cover their losses. He later turned the same comparative method on capitalism. This profile sets out what he argued, which passages and dates can be checked in the opened sources, and where other economists objected. Biography The existing chapter on planning, incentives and shortage assembles contemporary documents on raised quotas, worker letters, empty shelves and contested explanations of why goods remained scarce; this profile adds the incentive mechanisms and the comparison of whole economic systems that Kornai built from such evidence. Kornai was born in Budapest on 21 January 1928. The date is stated in his own memoir, where he writes that his father was forty seven on that day, and it is corroborated by the title of a 2019 Acta Oeconomica editor's preface, "János Kornai Turns 90 on January 21", recorded in the reference list of the in memoriam by Péter Mihályi. He grew up in a Jewish professional family: his father was Dr. Pál Kornhauser, a lawyer, and he changed the family surname from Kornhauser to Kornai in 1945. He attended a German language school in Budapest and lived through the anti Jewish laws, forced labour and the siege of Budapest; the memoir describes his father's refusal to join any political party and his own adolescence under racial persecution. Mihályi, a long time disciple and the editor of Acta Oeconomica , says Kornai completed his schooling in Budapest, became a convinced communist after the fall of the fascist regime in 1945 and became disillusioned with Marxist Leninist thought between 1953 and 1956 (Kornai, By Force of Thought , 2006; Mihályi, in memoriam, 2021). He joined the staff of the Communist newspaper Szabad Nép in June 1947 and left eight years later, in 1955; his memoir treats that period as a first hand education in how the party state actually worked. In August 1953 he was admitted to prepare for a "candidacy" degree, the Soviet style qualification treated as equivalent to a PhD; the dissertation became the research published as Overcentralization in Economic Administration . He began work at the Institute of Economics of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in June 1955, just before the Hungarian Revolution of October 1956. He did not take a conventional university degree in economics. The memoir is explicit that he taught himself modern Western economics from books in 1957, starting with Samuelson in German translation and then reading Arrow, Hicks, Hayek, Kalecki, Pigou and others. Mihályi records that he was elected to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in 1976, took an occasional professorial appointment at Harvard in 1986, the Allie S. Freed Professorship there in 1991 and retired as emeritus in 2002, while spending half the academic year in Budapest and half in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He was a founding fellow of Collegium Budapest and Honorary Professor Emeritus at Corvinus University of Budapest. After a long illness he died at home, surrounded by his family, on 18 October 2021, aged ninety three; the same date appears in the abstract and opening paragraph of Mihályi's article, and Kornai's homepage now carries a mourning notice. The in memoriam contains an apparent typographical error, giving the Collegium Budapest fellowship as running "from 1912 to 2011"; that is not repeated here as a fact. Intellectual tradition Kornai wrote from the tradition of comparative economic systems rather than from Marxism, and he described his method in his own terms. title: Elinor Ostrom: Governing the Commons Beyond State and Market
description: A research profile of the political economist's evidence for self-governed common-pool resources and its relevance to socialist economic alternatives.
text: Elinor Ostrom showed that people who share a resource can often govern it well without either privatising it or handing it to a central state. Trained as a political scientist, she spent much of her career at Indiana University studying fisheries, forests, irrigation systems and groundwater basins in which users made and enforced their own rules. She set out the conditions under which such arrangements lasted, and she rejected the idea that markets and governments are the only two possible forms of economic organisation. In 2009 she received half of the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, the first woman to do so. This profile states what her evidence showed and where critics thought it too narrow. It also states plainly what it did not show: no source opened for this profile has Ostrom calling herself a socialist or setting out a socialist blueprint. Her relevance here lies in collective governance and economic alternatives, not in a socialist programme. Biography Elinor Ostrom was born Elinor Clair Awan in Los Angeles on 7 August 1933 and died in Bloomington, Indiana, on 12 June 2012. The Nobel Foundation's facts page records that she grew up in a family of simple means, studied political science at the University of California, Los Angeles, took her doctorate there in 1965, worked at Indiana University in Bloomington and was also affiliated with Arizona State University and Virginia Tech. It records her marriage to the political scientist Vincent Ostrom in 1963. The Royal Swedish Academy awarded her half of the 2009 prize "for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons"; Oliver Williamson received the other half. The Ostrom Workshop and the Nobel interview transcript identify her as the first woman to receive the economics prize (Nobel facts; Workshop Nobel page). Her autobiographical essay, written for the award, gives the detail behind that record. She grew up during the Depression, attended Beverly Hills High School because her mother arranged it, and joined the debate team; debate taught her that public questions have at least two sides and that a good argument must be made for each. No one in her immediate family had been to university. She worked in a library, a dime store and a bookshop, and finished her undergraduate degree in three years. When she looked for a job, employers asked about typing and shorthand, so she took a correspondence course in shorthand, later finding it useful for note taking in interviews rather than for dictation. She worked for a year as an export clerk and then became an assistant personnel manager at a firm that had not previously employed a woman outside secretarial work (Nobel biographical essay). The economics department at UCLA discouraged her from doctoral study in economics because she had not taken mathematics beyond algebra and geometry, and political science was also reluctant to admit women. She says she was one of four women in a class of forty and was told that the faculty had criticised the admissions committee for admitting women and offering them assistantships. These are her retrospective recollections, published in 2009–10, not independently checked records. In graduate work she joined a team studying the Southern California water industry, framed by Vincent Ostrom, Charles Tiebout and Robert Warren, and was assigned the West Basin groundwater basin. She says she did not know at the time that she was studying a common pool resource problem: a shared stock, such as a groundwater basin, fishery, pasture, lake or forest, from which many people withdraw units, so that what one person takes reduces what remains for the others. Hardin's "Tragedy of the Commons" and Olson's The Logic of Collective Action appeared only after she defended her dissertation in 1965 (Nobel biographical essay). title: Yanis Varoufakis: Financial Capitalism and Technofeudalism
description: A research profile of the economist's account of the euro crisis, technocratic power and the claim that capitalism has been displaced by cloud rent.
text: Yanis Varoufakis is a Greek economist, former finance minister and political organiser whose work moved from the mathematics of industrial disputes to a claim about what capitalism has become. He became known during the euro crisis for The Global Minotaur and for the Modest Proposal, a set of policy measures written with Stuart Holland and James K. Galbraith. The argument that has drawn the formal scholarly response recorded below is that capitalism has been displaced by technofeudalism : his name for a social formation in which a handful of firms own the digital platforms that have replaced markets, and rent has taken the place of profit as the force running the economy. At the centre of that claim is cloud rent , which he defines as the payment the owners of those platforms extract from producers who need access to them in order to sell anything. This profile sets out what he argues, the sources he uses, and the objections made against him. Biography Varoufakis was born in Athens on 24 March 1961 according to his own CV as hosted by the University of Athens and reproduced in an Institute for New Economic Thinking listing seen in search results; the direct CV address returned a 404, and his own site gives only "born in Athens, 1961". The exact date should therefore be read as reported rather than confirmed from an opened document. In his first person account he says he was six in April 1967 when a military coup installed the dictatorship of the Colonels, and that the experience left him with a strong sense of what it means to be unfree and, at the same time, convinced that progress was possible (Beginnings). His 2025 memoir Raise Your Soul gives a fuller family story: an uncle, Panayis, imprisoned and tortured under the junta, hid a message to fellow prisoners inside a model aeroplane made of matchsticks and cigarette paper, and his mother Eleni broke the plane open after a prison visit in September 1969 (author's site, 15 October 2025). He calls the book "fictionalised history" and says he put words into people's mouths only where he had been told they were spoken or where he judged them plausible from conversations he witnessed. That is his own method statement, not a guarantee of documentary accuracy. He left Greece in 1978 to study in Britain. He first wanted to study physics, then chose economics because it was, in his words, the "lingua franca of political discourse"; after a few weeks he moved from the economics school to the mathematics school at the University of Essex because he found the economics teaching simplistic and its mathematics poor. He took a BA (Hons) in Mathematical Economics at Essex in 1981, an MSc in Mathematical Statistics at Birmingham in 1982 and a PhD in Economics at Essex in 1987, with a dissertation titled Optimisation and Strikes on models of industrial disputes, supervised by Monojit Chatterji. He says he returned to economics only because an econometric study of strikes angered him by its methodological sloppiness, and that a career in economics departments followed as "an atheist theologian ensconced in a Middle Ages monastery" (Beginnings). His academic posts, recorded in his own CV and in the Istanbul Policy Center profile (institutional profile), were at Essex, the University of East Anglia, Trinity College Cambridge and the University of Glasgow, followed by a long period at the University of Sydney from 1990 to 2002. He returned to Greece in 2000, became Associate Professor of Economic Theory at the University of Athens that year and Professor of Economic Theory from September 2006. He was a visiting professor at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas from 2013 to 2015 and worked as Chief Economist at Valve Software in Seattle in 2012. He was Minister of Finance of Greece from January to July 2015 and a member of the Hellenic Parliament for Athens B from January to September 2015. He launched DiEM25 in February 2016 and later led MeRA25 in Greece. Pen

title: David Graeber: Debt, Bureaucracy and Direct Action
description: A research profile of the anthropologist and anarchist's account of debt, meaningless work and collective action, with scholarly criticism.
text: David Graeber wrote about debt, bureaucracy and collective action with an anthropologist's eye for small details and an anarchist's distrust of rules imposed from above. He argued that money began in debt rather than barter, that modern economies conceal violence behind the language of freedom, and that much paid work is pointless. His term "bullshit job" means paid work so pointless, unnecessary or harmful that the worker cannot justify it, yet feels obliged to pretend it is worthwhile. By "direct action" he meant acting as if one were already free when faced with unjust authority, rather than petitioning the state or waiting for permission. Both phrases entered political debate far beyond anthropology. This profile sets out what Graeber argued, what the opened sources support, and where the evidence is thin or disputed. Biography Graeber's own website identifies him as "David Rolfe Graeber (1961–2020)". His exact date of birth is not established by the opened sources: a 12 February 1961 date appeared only in an obituary search result excerpt that was not opened, so it is not used here. Penguin gives the date of death as 2 September 2020, and the London School of Economics posted its departmental condolence on 3 September 2020 (LSE condolence). In his autobiography he says he was born and raised in New York, the son of Kenneth Graeber, a plate stripper in offset photolithography originally from Kansas who had fought with the International Brigades in the Spanish Civil War, and Ruth Rubinstein Graeber, born in Poland, a garment worker and homemaker who had been the female lead in the 1930s Labor Stage musical Pins & Needles (autobiography). He grew up in the Penn South Coops in Chelsea, attended local public schools, and says he was "discovered by some Maya archaeologists because of an odd hobby I had developed of translating Maya hieroglyphics". A scholarship took him to Phillips Academy at Andover for three years; he returned to state school at SUNY Purchase and graduated with a BA in anthropology in 1984. He then went to the University of Chicago, living there for over a decade apart from two years of fieldwork in highland Madagascar between 1989 and 1991, and received his PhD in 1996. The thesis title is not verified here: his autobiography calls Lost People his first book and says it was effectively written in 1997, while an unopened obituary excerpt described it as his PhD thesis. He describes a series of academic jobs: graduate teaching at Chicago, a year at Haverford, a year of unemployment, and a junior faculty post at Yale. The break with Yale is in his own words. "In 2004, the Yale department voted not to continue my contract, before I could begin the process of coming up for tenure." He calls the procedure "very unusual" and says "new rules had to be invented for my case (i.e., no student or outside reviews were allowed)". Yale gave "no reason for its decision other than dissatisfaction with my scholarship but some felt it might not have been entirely irrelevant that I was by this time quite active in the Global Justice Movement and other anarchist inspired projects". His site's press archive lists student petitions and letters of support from faculty at Chicago, Sussex and Glasgow and from Maurice Bloch at LSE, but those individual letters were not opened, so the campaign is verified only through his own summary and the archive listings. No statement from Yale was retrieved, and the university's formal reason remains unverified (autobiography). He moved to Goldsmiths, University of London, from 2007 to 2013 and then to the London School of Economics, where his autobiography calls him "a full professor". Laura Bear, head of the anthropology department, called him "a hugely influential anthropologist, political activist and public intellectual" whose work ranged from Madagascan funerary practices to bureaucracy, financialisation, kings, puppets and pirates (LSE condolence).
